0.title: Romans
0.overview:
The message. Romans sets out the gospel of God from beginning to end. All people, Jew and Gentile alike, stand guilty before a holy God, and no one can put himself right with him. But in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and was raised, God gives his own righteousness as a free gift to everyone who believes. Those he justifies he also unites to Christ, fills with his Spirit, adopts as his children and keeps to the end, so that nothing “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (8:39). The theme stands in 1:16–17: the gospel “is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.” Luther counted Romans the chief part of the New Testament; Calvin said that whoever understands it has a road opened into the whole of Scripture.

Background: the writer. Almost no one doubts that Paul wrote Romans, dictating it to a scribe, Tertius, who adds his own greeting (16:22). He wrote at a turning point. From Jerusalem round to Illyricum, on the Adriatic, he had “fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ” (15:19), and he now looked west to Spain (15:24). First he had to take the gift of the Gentile churches to the poor believers in Jerusalem (15:25–28), a journey he knew was dangerous (15:30–31). He was probably at Corinth, in the three months he spent in Greece (Acts 20:2–3), about AD 57. Phoebe, who probably carried the letter, served the church at Cenchreae, Corinth’s eastern port (16:1), and his host Gaius is very likely the Gaius he baptised there (16:23; 1 Corinthians 1:14).

Rome and its church. Rome was the capital of the empire, a crowded city of perhaps a million, many of them slaves or freed slaves, with a large Jewish community. Nero was emperor, still in the steadier early years of his reign; 13:1–7, on submitting to the governing authorities, was written under him, a few years before he turned on the Christians of Rome after the fire of AD 64. No apostle founded the church, and Paul had never visited it (1:13). Luke lists “visitors from Rome” at Pentecost (Acts 2:10), and the gospel probably reached the capital through Jewish believers like them. About AD 49 Claudius “had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome” (Acts 18:2), probably after disputes in the synagogues about Christ, and for a time the congregations were largely Gentile. When Jewish believers such as Prisca and Aquila came back (16:3), they returned to churches whose leaders and habits had changed. The strain between Jewish and Gentile believers lies behind much of the letter, especially chapters 9–11 and 14–15.

Why Paul wrote. He wanted to introduce himself and his gospel to a church he hoped would help him on to Spain; to answer the charges that dogged his preaching, that free grace encourages sin (3:8; 6:1) and that he had abandoned Israel (9:1–5); and to teach Jewish and Gentile believers to “welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God” (15:7). So he set out the gospel itself, more fully and in better order than anywhere else, because only the gospel could make such a church one.

A question about Paul. Since the 1970s scholars of the New Perspective, such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright, have argued that first-century Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation, that “works of the law” means chiefly the marks that set Jews apart, such as circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath, and that justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people. They are right that the unity of Jew and Gentile is a real concern of Romans (3:29–30; 15:7), and that Judaism has sometimes been described unfairly. But Paul’s deeper question is how a sinner can be right with God. His charge in 1:18–3:20 is that all have broken God’s law, “so that every mouth may be stopped” (3:19). Justification answers that guilt: it is God’s verdict of acquittal, given to the one who “believes in him who justifies the ungodly” (4:5), on the ground of Christ’s blood (5:9). Belonging to God’s people follows from it. This commentary takes that Reformation reading.

How the letter makes its case. After the greeting and theme (1:1–17), Paul shows the need: God’s wrath is revealed against the pagan world (1:18–32), the moralist who judges others (2:1–16) and the Jew who trusted in the law (2:17–3:8), until “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (3:23). Then comes “But now” (3:21): God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (3:25), so that he is “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (3:26). Abraham, justified by faith before he was circumcised, shows this is the old way, not a new one (chapter 4). Chapters 5–8 show the life of the justified: peace with God, and Christ undoing what Adam did (chapter 5); union with Christ in his death and resurrection (chapter 6); the law holy and good yet powerless to make anyone holy, and the believer’s honest struggle with remaining sin (chapter 7); and life in the Spirit, adoption, creation’s groaning and the unbreakable chain from foreknowledge to glory (chapter 8). Chapters 9–11 ask whether God’s word to Israel has failed, and answer from his free choice of mercy, Israel’s unbelief, the remnant saved by grace and the olive tree into which Gentiles are grafted, to the promise that “all Israel will be saved” (11:26), which this commentary holds most naturally looks for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ. The argument ends in praise (11:33–36). Chapters 12–16 show the gospel lived “by the mercies of God” (12:1): in the body of Christ, under the state, between the weak and the strong (14:1–15:13), and in Paul’s plans and greetings (15:14–16:27).

Where it leads: to Christ. The gospel is “concerning his Son” (1:3), descended from David and declared Son of God in power by his resurrection (1:3–4). He is the propitiation who bears God’s just wrath (3:25), the second Adam through whose obedience “the many will be made righteous” (5:19), the one in whom there is “no condemnation” (8:1), and “the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (10:4). He became “a servant to the circumcised” to confirm the promises to the patriarchs, so that the Gentiles too might glorify God for his mercy (15:8–9). The righteousness Paul preaches was promised “through his prophets in the holy Scriptures” (1:2); it is not his invention but the Old Testament fulfilled in Christ.

For us. Romans has changed lives as few books have. Augustine was converted on reading 13:13–14; Luther found the gate of paradise in 1:17; John Wesley felt his heart warmed hearing Luther’s preface to Romans read aloud; Martyn Lloyd-Jones preached on it for thirteen years and never reached the end. This commentary draws on such interpreters, with Calvin, John Stott, Timothy Keller, Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner. The letter tells you the worst about yourself and then the best about God. Your standing with him rests on Christ’s righteousness, not your record, so you may have peace (5:1) without fear of condemnation (8:1). And it calls you to offer your whole life as “a living sacrifice” (12:1), to welcome believers unlike yourself, and to carry the gospel to those who have not heard it. Come expecting to be undone and remade.

1.title: The Gospel and the Wrath of God
1.overview:
Where we are. Paul introduces himself and his gospel to a church he has never visited, states the theme of the whole letter (vv. 16–17), and begins the case, running to 3:20, that every human being needs that gospel.

The message. God’s good news about his Son, risen in power, is his own power to rescue everyone who believes, because in it God gives sinners a righteousness they could never produce. It is needed, because God’s wrath is already revealed against a humanity that knows him and will not honour or thank him, that trades the Creator for created things, and that God has handed over to what it chose. The good news is only as good as the bad news is real.

Why it was said. A church of Jewish and Gentile believers, strained since Claudius’s expulsion of the Jews, needed to see the one gospel that made them one people, and Paul needed their help for his mission to Spain (see the introduction). In a city that despised crucifixion, they also needed to hear that this message was nothing to be ashamed of.

How the chapter makes its case. The greeting already holds the gospel: promised in Scripture, centred on the Son, aimed at the obedience of faith among the nations, and given to readers who are loved by God and called to be saints (vv. 1–7). Paul prays for them and longs to come, in debt to everyone (vv. 8–15); then comes the theme: God’s power, revealing a righteousness received by faith (vv. 16–17). Then “for” opens the indictment. The truth about God is plain and suppressed (vv. 18–20); he is refused honour and thanks and exchanged for images (vv. 21–23); and three times God gives people up (vv. 24–28), until they not only do evil but applaud it (vv. 29–32).

Where it leads. The wrath revealed from heaven (v. 18) and the righteousness revealed in the gospel (v. 17) meet at the cross, where the wrath fell on the one man who never suppressed the truth. And “God gave them up” returns later of God’s own Son: he “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (8:32).

For us. Verses 18–32 describe not other people but every culture, and every heart, that suppresses the knowledge of the God it cannot stop knowing; Paul springs the trap on the reader who enjoys the list (2:1). So hear the opening again, spoken to people just like that: loved by God, called to be saints, grace to you and peace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Paul, the Gospel, and the Grace of Apostleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel is God’s good news about his Son, and it makes ordinary people his own. Rome used the word gospel for public good news, such as a new emperor’s accession; Paul uses it for better news. In one long sentence he introduces himself as Christ’s slave, called and set apart for that gospel (v. 1); shows that it was promised in Scripture and centres on the Son, born of David’s line and declared Son of God in power by his resurrection (vv. 2–4); and names its goal, the obedience of faith among all nations, Rome included (vv. 5–6). Only then does he greet them, and before he asks anything he tells them who they are: loved by God and called to be saints (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Promised Beforehand

Paul insists that his gospel was “promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures” (on why that mattered in Rome, see the note on vv. 2–3): Jesus is David’s promised son (2 Samuel 7) and the Son of Psalm 2. Calvin saw in this the unity of the two testaments: the Old Testament is the gospel in promise; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul called himself a doulos, a slave, of Christ Jesus in a world where slavery meant degradation, and counted it his highest dignity. Now: In an age that prizes autonomy, the claim that the best life is one of belonging wholly to Christ still offends, and it still frees those who find that his yoke is easy and his burden light (Matthew 11:30).

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul introduces himself by whom he belongs to and what he is for: owned by Christ, sent by Christ, reserved for God’s good news. Before his name is fully out of his mouth, Paul has pointed away from himself three times.

A servant of Christ Jesus. Most English Bibles soften doulos to “servant”, a man with a job. The word meant a slave: in Roman law a possession, not a person, with no right to his own time, body or plans. Perhaps a quarter to a third of Rome was enslaved, so when this letter was read aloud in a house church there were slaves in the room, and probably people who owned them. Into that room the apostle introduces himself by the legal status of the lowest people present.

The highest title in Israel. A Jewish reader would have heard something else in the same instant, and Paul intends both. “Servant of the LORD” is one of the great titles of the Old Testament, given to Moses, to David, and supremely to the Servant of Isaiah. So in one word Paul makes the lowest rung on the Roman ladder and the highest title in Israel’s Scriptures the same rung: to be owned by Christ is the highest honour there is. That is the pattern of the gospel he is about to explain.

Called to be an apostle. Not self-appointed (Galatians 1:1). An apostle is one sent with authority, an eyewitness of the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 9:1). The word “called” (klētos) comes twice more before the sentence ends: called to belong to Jesus Christ (v. 6), called to be saints (v. 7). Paul keeps no special word for his own calling and a lesser one for everybody else’s. Neither Paul on the Damascus road nor you volunteered, and neither of you was consulted.

Set apart for the gospel of God. “Set apart” (aphōrismenos) echoes in Greek what the name Pharisee probably meant in Hebrew: the separated ones, whose whole discipline was keeping apart from whatever might defile. Many interpreters think Paul intends the echo. God keeps the separated man separated, but changes what the separation is for: no longer apart from people, but for a message that sends him straight to the Gentiles he had spent his life avoiding. Nothing in him was wasted; God took it over for his own use (Galatians 1:15). And it is “the gospel of God”: his good news before it is anyone’s message.

The title his Lord wore first. Paul uses this same word of the Son of God coming to us: Christ “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). The Lord of all knelt to wash his disciples’ feet (John 13:5) and was valued at the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32; Matthew 26:15). Paul is the slave of the one who became a slave: the Son who owned everything took the form of the one who owns nothing, so that people who belonged to sin could come to belong to him. And belonging to him is concrete: your time, body, money and plans are his to direct, for you are not your own (1 Corinthians 6:19), and whether you live or die, you are the Lord’s (14:8).

In everyday life. A slave does not own his own time, and the quickest way to find out what you believe about ownership is to listen to yourself when a day is interrupted: for the word that arrives (my morning, my weekend), and for the resentment when someone spends it for you. That reaction is not a small sin to be scolded over; it shows who you really think owns your life.

What it does not mean. Paul is describing ownership, not exhaustion. This Master told his workers to come away and rest a while (Mark 6:31), and a church that quotes this verse at a tired person to extract more work has understood neither the slave nor the Master. Nor must every Christian have a dramatic calling like Paul’s. His assignment is not yours, but if you belong to Christ you were called, in exactly the sense he was.

Isn’t belonging to anyone the end of freedom? That is the modern instinct, and history gives it reason. But nobody actually lives the life no one directs. The novelist David Foster Wallace, not a Christian, told graduating students in 2005, “There is no such thing as not worshipping. Everybody worships,” and warned that whatever they chose, money, beauty, power or being thought clever, would eat them alive, because it would never tell them they had enough. So the choice is between masters. Most masters take, and keep taking; this one gave himself first. The Book of Common Prayer calls God the one “whose service is perfect freedom”. Paul is not boasting of his chains; he has met the one owner who gives you yourself back.

Does the church still have apostles? Not in Paul’s sense. An apostle of Christ had seen the risen Lord and been sent by him personally (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8), and Paul calls himself the last to see him. The apostles laid the church’s foundation once for all (Ephesians 2:20), and their teaching is now in the New Testament: when we want to hear an apostle, we open this letter. Some churches call pioneering leaders apostles; the word can bear the sense of a sent missionary, but no such leader adds to the foundation or speaks with Paul’s authority.
verseByVerse.note: “Servant” translates the ordinary word for a slave, one wholly owned by his master. Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably around AD 57, before taking the collection to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel is not a new idea but God’s oldest promise kept, and it is about a person: God’s Son, born a true man in David’s line.

Promised beforehand. Rome respected age and distrusted new religions, and here was a sect barely twenty-five years old, gathered round an executed provincial. Paul answers that the gospel is as old as God’s first promise (Genesis 3:15; 12:3; Isaiah 53), and a promise is tested by the wait. In a garden God promised that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head, and then let millennia pass. He swore to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, and the family went down to Egypt and ended in slavery. He told David that a son of his would have a throne for ever, and the line dwindled to a carpenter in a village nobody respected. God’s delays run to centuries, and he has never yet failed to arrive.

Through his prophets in the holy Scriptures. Paul preached the gospel out of a book his hearers already owned; he had no New Testament. So the three-quarters of your Bible you may find hardest are not the run-up to the gospel but the gospel in promise, as Jesus showed on the Emmaus road: “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27).

Concerning his Son. The gospel is about a person, not first a system, a method or a moral code, and everything Paul argues for fifteen chapters unfolds this phrase. It is news, not advice: not what you should do, but what he has done. He lived, died for our sins and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Advice depends on you to carry it out. News is true whether or not you feel it, and you receive it by believing it.

Descended from David according to the flesh. That is, in his human nature: a true man of David’s line, fulfilling the promise of a son of David who would reign for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16). God’s Son entered a family with a documented history, and you know what is in it: David, who arranged a man’s death to conceal an adultery; Manasseh, who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood; a prostitute in Jericho. The Son of God consented to join that family, and not at a safe distance. He took their flesh.

A report, not a principle. So Christianity is not timeless principles a thoughtful person could have discovered in any century, but a report of something that happened, to a particular man, in a family Scripture records. That is why it could be false, and why, if it is true, it is not merely inspiring but binding.

How do I find Christ in the Old Testament without forcing it? Read each passage first for its plain meaning in its own setting. Then ask where it is heading: which promise it carries forward (a seed, a king, a new covenant), which pattern it sets up that Christ fulfils (the Passover lamb, the priest, the temple), and which longing it leaves open that only he answers. Jesus and the apostles read it this way. You are not hunting for hidden codes; you are following a road to where it arrives.

parallels.desc: the promised son of David

verseByVerse.quote: and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The resurrection is God’s public verdict that Jesus is his Son, now reigning in power. It did not make him the Son; it declared before the world who he had been all along.

Declared, not made. “Declared” (horisthentos) means appointed, installed in the open. It does not mean made, as those argue who say God adopted the man Jesus as his Son at the resurrection. The sentence itself answers them: the gospel is “concerning his Son, who was descended from David” (v. 3). He was the Son before he had a family tree to enter, and no one can be promoted into a position he already holds.

In power. What changed at the resurrection was not the Son but the public record: from weakness to power, from humiliation to exaltation (Philippians 2:6–11). A verdict does not create the fact it announces. The world published its verdict on Jesus in the notice nailed above his cross, in three languages. Then God overturned it in public: the Father standing up in the courtroom of the world, after the sentence was carried out and the body sealed in rock, to announce that the accused was his Son the whole time. Peter sets the verdicts side by side: “God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36).

According to the Spirit of holiness. The two phrases describe one person in two states. “According to the flesh” (v. 3) is Jesus in his earthly life, able to tire, weep and die; “according to the Spirit” is Jesus since Easter, risen, enthroned and pouring out the Spirit on his people (Acts 2:33). And the Spirit who raised him lives in you: “he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (8:11).

By his resurrection from the dead. The resurrection is the proof (Acts 13:33; 17:31), and it matters for the whole letter, because Christ was “raised for our justification” (4:25). If the world’s verdict on the Son was overturned, the guilty verdict on everyone joined to him has been overturned with it. The empty tomb is God’s receipt: the debt was accepted as paid.

Jesus Christ our Lord. Kyrios rendered the divine name in the Greek Old Testament and was also a title the empire gave to Caesar; Paul claims both for Jesus at once. To be declared so, the Son who had the Father’s glory before there was a world to be glorious in consented to be reduced to a corpse in a borrowed grave, so that the announcement could be made from the one place where no one could argue with it. And after such titles comes one small word, “our”: the one who holds the name above every name is spoken of, by a slave writing to a house church in the capital, as though he belongs to them.

In everyday life. Suppose someone told you tomorrow that they had found the body. Not whether you could refute it, but whether it would matter. If your faith is mainly a set of values, a way of being decent and hopeful, the news would be sad but survivable. Paul’s faith would not survive it for an hour, and he says so: if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:14–19). He staked everything on an event a corpse could disprove.

Uncertain wording. “The Spirit of holiness” occurs only here in the New Testament. It is a Hebrew way of speaking (in Psalm 51:11 “your Holy Spirit” is literally the spirit of your holiness). Most interpreters take it as the Holy Spirit, by whose power Christ was raised and through whom he now gives life (8:11); some take it as Christ’s own holy, divine nature, set beside his human nature. Since the contrast with verse 3 is most naturally between two stages of his work, earthly weakness and risen power, the Holy Spirit is the likely meaning. Either way, one person is meant, truly human and truly the Son of God.

parallels.desc: you are my Son

verseByVerse.quote: ...through whom we have received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations, including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ... — Romans 1:5-6
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through the risen Lord, Paul received the grace of being sent, to bring people of every nation to trust and obey Christ for the honour of his name; and the believers in Rome are part of that harvest.

Grace and apostleship. Almost certainly not two gifts but the grace that consisted in being made an apostle. The man commissioned to preach had been arresting preachers, and he never got over it: “I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). The commission was not a reward that followed the pardon; it was the pardon made visible. God handed the persecutor the message and sent him to the people he had been hunting.

To bring about the obedience of faith. The phrase brackets the letter, returning at the very end (16:26), so that everything between is its explanation (on its exact sense, see “Uncertain wording” below). The letter that insists most fiercely on justification by faith apart from works opens and closes by calling for obedience. Faith does not replace obedience, and obedience does not earn what faith receives. It costs nothing to admire Jesus; this asks you to stop relying on yourself and trust your whole life to Christ, which is why the New Testament can call unbelief disobedience.

For the sake of his name among all the nations. Not first for the nations or the church’s growth, but for the name: the name above every name, given to the Son who humbled himself to death on a cross, so that every knee should bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:8–11). “All the nations” echoes God’s oath that in Abraham’s offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 22:18). Paul’s travel plans are a promise sworn on Mount Moriah being kept on actual roads, by a man with a tentmaker’s hands.

The nations as the Son’s inheritance. The Son declared in power by his resurrection (v. 4) is the King of Psalm 2 (Acts 13:33), and to that King the Father says, “Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage” (Psalm 2:8). Paul’s mission is that promise being paid out: every Gentile brought to the obedience of faith is part of the inheritance the Father promised his Son.

Including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ. The Christians in Rome are not the audience of this mission but the thing itself: “all the nations” become a room with people in it. And they are called not to achieve, or to understand, or to be useful, but to belong. If you trust Christ, the name for whose sake the whole world is being reached has been written over you.

So am I saved by obeying? No. Paul spends chapters 3 and 4 proving that no one is declared right with God by works (3:20, 28). Obedience is never the ground of our acceptance; Christ’s obedience is (5:19). But real faith never stays alone. The faith that rests on Christ begins to follow him, and that obedience is the fruit of being accepted, not the price of it.

Uncertain wording. “The obedience of faith” is compressed, and the grammar allows several readings: the obedience that consists in faith, so that believing the gospel is itself the first act of obedience to God; the obedience that springs from faith, the life that follows believing; or obedience to “the faith”, the body of Christian teaching. (The closing doxology where the phrase returns, 16:25–27, stands elsewhere in the letter in some ancient manuscripts, but nearly all include it.) This commentary’s view: faith is the first thing God commands, and the root from which every other obedience grows: not faith versus obedience, but faith working through love (Galatians 5:6).

parallels.desc: the obedience of faith

verseByVerse.quote: To all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. — Romans 1:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Paul asks anything of a divided church, he tells all of them who they are: loved by God, called, set apart as his, and given grace and peace from the Father and the Son. The gospel is gift before it is demand.

To all those in Rome. The greeting is warmer than the situation was. After Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome, which is how Priscilla and Aquila came to be in Corinth (Acts 18:2), the congregations were for some years largely Gentile, and the Jewish believers came home to churches with other leaders and customs (see the introduction). Much of the letter, from Jew and Gentile equally justified to the strong and the weak of chapter 14, speaks into that. Paul writes into a congregation with a seam running through it, and gives everyone on both sides one description: loved by God, called, saints.

Loved by God. Before they are anything else, they are loved: not because they loved their way into God’s favour, and still after they have failed at a good deal. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (5:8). His love was at full strength at the worst possible moment; it cannot become greater than it already is.

Called to be saints. Not aspiring to be saints, but saints already, by the call that placed them in Christ. The word does not mean exceptional Christians in stained glass. In the Old Testament “holy” is used constantly of things, the vessels of the tabernacle. A bowl in the tabernacle was not a better bowl; it was a bowl set aside for God and no longer available for anything else. So when Paul calls a mixed room of tradesmen, slaves and immigrants the holy ones, he describes not their record but what has happened to them (Acts 9:13).

Grace to you and peace. The greeting joins Greek and Hebrew: grace (charis) plays on the standard Greek hello, chairein, and peace is the Jewish shalom. To a church with Greeks and Jews eyeing each other across a room, even the greeting brings the two together. Grace is God’s undeserved favour; peace is what it produces, reconciliation with God and wholeness of life. The order never reverses in Paul’s greetings, and he pronounces both before he has written a sentence of argument.

From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Jesus is set beside the Father as the single source of grace and peace, and only God gives grace: a quiet but clear statement of Christ’s deity. This is also the letter’s first “God our Father”; by chapter 8 a room of former slaves and shopkeepers will be crying “Abba! Father!” (8:15). The God who is about to spend a chapter and a half describing his wrath is introduced to these people, by name, as their Father.

Peace across the seam. This peace is not a mood. Christ himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14), and he made it by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). It runs two ways: reconciled to the same God by the same blood, the sinner is reconciled to the brother across the room. The greeting does not ask them to get on. It tells them the ground on which they already stand together.

Be what you are. If holiness began as your achievement you would have to keep proving it. If it is God’s setting you apart, failure contradicts what you are without disproving it, for your standing rests on Christ’s obedience (5:19). So Paul opens a letter about lawsuits, drunkenness at the Lord’s table and a man sleeping with his stepmother by calling the Corinthians saints (1 Corinthians 1:2). He does not withdraw the word in order to rebuke them; he rebukes them on the strength of it. To be called a saint is a comfort, and a summons to treat your body and life as his, never again as common property, by the Holy Spirit who now lives in you (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

How do I know I am called? Paul’s word means God’s effective summons, the call that actually brings a person to Christ (8:30). You do not need to remember a dramatic moment. If you trust Christ, rest your hope on him and want to follow him, that faith is the evidence that God called you, for no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44).
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people, that is, all believers. The church at Rome was not founded by Paul; he had never been there.

parallels.desc: visitors from Rome at Pentecost

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Paul's Longing and His Debt to All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Whoever has received the gospel owes it to everyone, and longs to give it. Paul thanks God for the Romans’ famous faith and assures them he prays for them without ceasing (vv. 8–9). He has asked for years to come and been prevented (vv. 10, 13). He wants to strengthen them, and corrects himself to say that he expects to be strengthened by them too (vv. 11–12). And he counts himself a debtor to every kind of person, so he is eager to preach the gospel in Rome as well (vv. 14–15). His longing is personal, not only strategic, and it leads straight into the theme of the letter.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pastoral and Missionary Logic of Paul

Romans 1:8–15 shows that Paul’s mission cannot be separated from his affection for the church. The Roman Christians are not an audience for his theology or a resource for his travels, but brothers and sisters he longs to see. Mission comes from the church and builds the church, and Paul, for all his travelling, is an apostle within the body of Christ, not a lone evangelist.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s debt to Greeks and barbarians, the wise and the foolish, cut across every cultural and social rank: the gospel belonged to no class. Now: Churches are always tempted to shape the gospel for people already like themselves. Paul’s debtor language corrects that: the gospel is owed to everyone within our reach, whether or not they seem likely converts.

verseByVerse.quote: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I mention you
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God for the Roman believers’ faith and assures them, with God as his witness, that he has prayed for them without fail. A church that had never met him needed to know that his interest in them was love, not strategy.

First, I thank my God. Paul’s settled habit, even with the Corinthians; only Galatians has no thanksgiving, a sign that something was seriously wrong there.

Through Jesus Christ. Not a formula. Paul cannot even say thank you to God on his own account; gratitude goes up through the Mediator, because the problem the letter is about to describe is not only that we sin but that we have no right of our own to come before God. So every thank you before a meal is carried by the same blood that carried the thief into paradise.

Your faith is proclaimed in all the world. He thanks God not for their numbers or strategic position but for their faith, which is itself God’s gift, so the Giver receives the thanks. What travelled out along the roads from Rome was the news that these people believed God.

For God is my witness. Why swear to something as unremarkable as praying for people? Because they could not check, and had reason to wonder. He hoped to use their city as a base for a mission further west (15:24), and someone might conclude that the famous apostle’s sudden interest was strategic. So he calls God to witness what nobody else can verify: for years, unseen, they have been on his list.

Whom I serve with my spirit. “Serve” (latreuō) is temple language, the word for priestly service in the holy place. Paul applies it to talking about Jesus in rented rooms, workshops and prisons (15:16): not something like worship, but worship itself. His praying and his preaching were one act of worship.

That without ceasing I mention you. Paul was not praying every waking second; he made tents, argued in synagogues, sailed, ate and slept. The phrase was ordinary Greek for something regular and unremitting: these people never dropped off his list. Read as a demand for continuous spoken prayer, it would soon convince you that you cannot pray at all, the very result it was not written to produce.

He always lives to make intercession. Somewhere an old woman, a friend from a church you left, or a parent mentions your name to God with a regularity you know nothing about. And above them all is the Son himself, who always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and has never once let your name drop off his list.

In everyday life. Look at what fills your praying. For most of us it is situations: the diagnosis, the interview, the money; when the situation resolves, the subject disappears. Paul’s prayers were populated by people, most of them absent, some not yet met; in his last chapter he greets about two dozen by name in a city he had never visited.

How do I pray for people like this? Make it small enough to keep. Write down the names God has put on your heart and pray for a few each day, so that every name comes round each week. Pray Paul’s own prayers for them (Ephesians 1:17–19; Philippians 1:9–11; Colossians 1:9–12), so that you ask for what matters most, not only for problems to go away. And when someone comes to mind during the day, turn the thought into a sentence to God on the spot.

verseByVerse.quote: always in my prayers, asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul keeps asking God, plainly and for years, to let him reach Rome, and leaves the how and the when with God.

Now at last. The words of a man who has waited a long time: “I have longed for many years to come to you” (15:23). A plan formed for the best reasons had been blocked again and again, and he was still asking.

Somehow by God’s will. Paul did not know how. This is not the verbal tic “if it be your will” often becomes, a disclaimer attached in advance so that nothing has really been asked. He asks for the specific thing, plainly and repeatedly, and leaves the outcome with God (James 4:15), neither giving up nor forcing the door. Most of us manage desire without submission, which is impatience, or submission without desire, which is resignation wearing a pious face. Paul keeps both.

The delays are not neglect. Most delays feel like a door closing for no reason: the job that went to somebody else, the years of waiting for a child. Paul was not always told what a prevention was for (Acts 16:7), so the honest claim is not that you will be shown every reason, but that delays are neither random nor neglect. Here the proof is in your hands. Had Paul reached Rome when he first wanted to, we might not have this letter: the fullest account of the gospel in the New Testament exists because a man could not get to the city he wanted to visit, and had to write instead.

Answered in his way. When the prayer was answered, it was in a form he had not asked for. He reached Rome as a prisoner, after two years in custody and a shipwreck, at the empire’s expense, chained to a soldier (Acts 27–28). He got the city, not the itinerary. And Acts leaves him there, proclaiming the kingdom of God with all boldness and without hindrance: exactly what this prayer had asked for.

The Lord who kept the timetable. Paul had learned from his Master to want things within the Father’s timing. Jesus lived by an hour not his to choose: “My time has not yet come,” he told his brothers (John 7:6), until the night he lifted his eyes to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come” (John 17:1). And it was the risen Christ who answered this prayer for Rome. When Paul’s arrest in Jerusalem seemed to have closed the road for good, the Lord stood by him at night and said: “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome” (Acts 23:11). The road to Rome ran under a promise from Christ’s own mouth.

How do I know whether a closed door is God’s no, or something to push through? Doors close for many reasons, so do not read God’s will from circumstances alone. Ask first what Scripture says: God’s commands settle what is right, and no open door can make a wrong thing right. Within what is right, use wisdom, take counsel from mature believers, keep praying, and keep trying where it is wise, as Paul did for years. Then accept the outcome God gives. His providence (his ruling of all events) is understood looking back; it is not a signal to steer by in advance. Paul did not know why Bithynia was closed until Macedonia opened.

verseByVerse.quote: For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you — that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith, both yours and mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul longs to come and strengthen the Roman believers, and expects them to strengthen him too: in Christ’s body, encouragement runs both ways. He corrects himself mid-sentence so that no one hears condescension in his longing.

Some spiritual gift to strengthen you. Paul begins with the gift running one way, from apostle to church. “Spiritual gift” (charisma pneumatikon) is not a technique for handing over one of the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 like a parcel. He is deliberately vague, “some gift”, because he does not yet know what these people will need when he arrives, and he trusts the Giver to supply it then. “To strengthen” (stērichthēnai) is to make firm, as a building is made stable.

That is. Then he hears himself: a man stopping mid-flow, catching a note of condescension in his own sentence, and reaching for one in which the encouragement runs both ways. Even the apostle expected to receive from those he served (Acts 28:15). Ordinary believers in Rome could teach the man who wrote Scripture nothing about justification, but he expects to be encouraged by their faith, and faith is not expertise. A frightened woman still trusting God after a bad year has something the most learned man in the room cannot produce for himself by knowing more.

Strengthened by Christ preached. The same verb returns in the letter’s last sentence, which says how such strengthening is done: “Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ” (16:25). The strength is not Paul’s personality or learning but Jesus Christ set before them. So the mutual encouragement he longs for is not two groups admiring each other’s faith, but two groups looking at the same Christ from different places, each seeing him more clearly for the other’s eyes.

The body has no passengers. If you usually teach, lead, host or fix, notice that Paul’s strong Christian is not a man with no needs, but one who admits them to people less impressive than himself. And if you are newer or quieter, convinced you are in the room only to receive, the apostle to the Gentiles was looking forward to being helped by people exactly like you. Christ has so made his body that its greatest member cannot do without its least, and the faith he gives the weakest believer is a gift to the strongest. That is why sitting with a believer who is suffering well can leave you steadier than a conference will.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented), in order that I may reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has not stayed away from Rome by choice: he has often planned to come and been prevented, and he still hopes for a harvest among them.

I do not want you to be unaware, brothers. Paul’s signal that he is about to correct something his readers might get wrong (11:25). Someone in Rome had almost certainly noticed that the apostle to the Gentiles had worked the eastern Mediterranean for years and never once come to the capital of the Gentile world, and drawn an unflattering conclusion. (As the ESV notes, “brothers” includes sisters in the church.)

But thus far have been prevented. Not too busy, though that would have been true: prevented, as if someone were behind the obstacle. Part of it was the work elsewhere (15:22), and the Spirit who forbade him Bithynia (Acts 16:6–7) had other work for him first. The account you give of a year changes how it feels to live inside it. “I never got round to it” leaves you the manager of a life that is not going well; “I was prevented” leaves you a servant whose Master has other arrangements.

Some harvest among you. Harvest (karpos, fruit) means conversions and growth. It is slow, and it is not manufactured: a farmer can plough, sow and water, but cannot make one seed germinate: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). It is seasonal, which is why Paul can be prevented for years without the work being lost: a field left unvisited is not abandoned, only not yet ripe. Nor is a field ever finished: their faith is famous (v. 8), yet Paul still expects a harvest. A building is completed; a field is either being worked or going back to weeds.

The grain that made the harvest. Jesus gave the reason Gentile fruit exists on the day some Greeks came asking to see him: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Every Gentile believer comes from that single grain, which went into the ground outside Jerusalem and came up on the third day. Paul ploughs, sows and waters, but he gathers a crop Christ’s death has already guaranteed.

In everyday life. Think of the situation you have privately written off: the relative who will never believe, the colleague too far gone, the part of your own character you have decided is simply how you are. Ask not when you stopped trying, but when you stopped expecting anything there. And if you have sown for years and seen nothing: often one sows and another reaps (John 4:37–38). The growing is not your department, and the absence of fruit in June says nothing about what is happening underground.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “brothers” can include sisters in the church.

verseByVerse.quote: I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome. — Romans 1:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul owes the gospel to every kind of person, because it was entrusted to him for them, so he is eager to preach it in Rome too. The debt has become a desire.

I am under obligation. Not willing, or burdened, or available: Paul is a debtor (opheiletēs), a man who owes and has not yet paid. Suppose someone hands you money to deliver to another man: you are then in debt to a stranger, for money that was never yours, until he has it in his hand. On the Damascus road Paul was given something that was not for him: a message with a name on it, addressed to the nations. To withhold it would be theft.

Both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. The first-century way of saying everyone: the cultured and the crude, the clever and the slow. A preacher instinctively avoids both groups for opposite reasons: the sophisticated frighten us, and the unsophisticated seem unpromising. Paul is in debt to both. The church does not get to choose its creditors.

So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also. To believers: Christians need the gospel preached to them too. And Paul feels not guilt but eagerness.

In the flow. Verses 8–15, taken up again at 15:14–33, bridge into the theme: eager to preach, for not ashamed, for the gospel is God’s power, for in it God’s righteousness is revealed (vv. 16–17), each step giving the reason for the one before. Until he comes, Romans is the gospel he would have preached.

Where barbarian stands beside Greek. Paul’s word returns in a list of divisions Christ has ended: “Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all” (Colossians 3:11). That is why the debt runs to both ends of the human scale. The message is not a philosophy that suits the clever or a comfort that suits the simple, but a person. The Athenian and the Scythian are owed the same gospel because they need the same Christ, and in him they will sit at the same table.

What it does not mean. A debt can be preached in a way that crushes. If you owe everybody, and the payment is their eternal life, every conversation you did not have becomes an unpaid debt, and a sensitive Christian can be flattened by that arithmetic. But Paul is one man with one life who cannot reach Spain and Rome in the same year, and does not pretend otherwise. Your debt is to the people God has put within your reach: those whose names you know, whose kitchens you sit in, who work at the next desk. He never asked you to be the apostle to the Gentiles; that post is filled.

How do I pay the debt without being pushy? Begin with the people you already know, and with honesty about yourself. Live in a way that raises questions, and answer them with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Pray for opportunities and notice them: a friend’s grief, a question about why you go to church, a conversation about what makes life worth living. Say simply what Christ has done, and leave the result to God. You are responsible to deliver the message, not to produce the response.
verseByVerse.note: Greeks thought of all non-Greek speakers as “barbarians.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — The Theme: The Righteousness of God by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: These two verses are the thesis of the letter: the gospel is God’s power to save everyone who believes, because in it God gives sinners his own righteousness, received by faith alone. “Not ashamed” is an understatement that says more than a boast: Paul is eager to bring a crucified Lord to the capital of the empire that crucified him. The gospel is power, not advice, and it reaches the Jew first and also the Greek through one door, faith (v. 16). Verse 17 says why: it reveals a righteousness from God, from faith for faith, as Habakkuk promised. Luther’s discovery of this verse (see the note) lit the Reformation, and nearly everything later in Romans unfolds a phrase from here.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Righteousness of God: Attribute or Gift?

Reformed interpreters have read “the righteousness of God” in Romans 1:17 as a righteousness that comes from God and is given to the believing sinner. This is imputation (explained in the note on v. 17). Calvin called this the “wonderful exchange”: Christ takes our sin, and we receive his righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luther’s discovery of Romans 1:17 freed him, and many after him, from trying to earn salvation by merit and religious performance. Now: Every generation rebuilds the system of merit. These verses are its lasting answer: the gospel is not something you do but something done for you, received by faith from the merciful God who justifies the ungodly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. — Romans 1:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will not be ashamed of a message about a crucified man, because that message is God’s own power to rescue everyone who believes, Jew and Gentile alike. His confidence rests not on his nerve but on what the gospel is.

For I am not ashamed of the gospel. He would not say it unless the pull towards shame were real. We have had two thousand years to get used to the cross; his readers had not. Crucifixion was a deliberately degrading death, reserved in practice for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals, and Roman citizens were normally exempt from it by law. Cicero, arguing a case a century earlier, said the very word ought to be kept away not only from a Roman citizen’s body but from his thoughts, his eyes and his ears. And at the centre of Paul’s message was a Jewish provincial put to death that way: a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Alexamenos worships his god. Scratched into plaster on the Palatine in Rome, probably a century and a half after this letter arrived, is a cartoon: a figure on a cross with a donkey’s head, a man beside it with his hand raised in worship, and underneath, in scrawled Greek: Alexamenos worships his god. To confess this gospel in Rome was to be found faintly ridiculous, and Paul had felt the pull himself. Beaten out of Philippi and mocked in Athens, he came to Corinth “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3).

For it is the power of God for salvation. Not merely true, or reasonable, though it is both: the gospel is the power of God, not a description of something powerful happening elsewhere, but the instrument by which God does the thing. That is why ordinary Christians saying ordinary sentences about Christ keep producing results out of all proportion to the people involved. (The word, dynamis, means effective might, not “dynamite”.) “Salvation” is rescue from sin, wrath and death into eternal life.

What it means to be saved. “Saved” can sound like jargon: saved from what? But Timothy Keller often pointed out, in The Reason for God and elsewhere, that nobody lives without a saviour. Everyone looks to something to make them feel they count and are safe: a career, a marriage, a child’s success, a reputation for being decent. Those saviours are hard masters; they must be earned every day, and when you fail them they cannot forgive you. To be saved is to be rescued, done for you by someone else when you could not get yourself out. That is why the gospel is God’s power, not a programme of self-improvement.

To the Jew first and also to the Greek. “First” (prōton) does not mean that Jews are saved more easily, more fully or another way: there is no distinction, for all have sinned and all are justified by faith (3:22–23; 10:12). It means first in time and in the privilege of history. God made his promises to Israel; the Messiah came from Israel as its king; the gospel was preached first in Jerusalem, and in city after city Paul went first to the synagogue (Acts 13:46; 17:1–2). “Greek” means the whole Gentile world. For a divided congregation that settles what mattered most: one power, one condition (faith), two peoples, one door.

In the flow. The rest of Romans unfolds these verses: righteousness by faith (3:21–4:25), God’s saving power (chapters 5–8), the Jew first and also the Greek (chapters 9–11; 14–15).

Christ, the power in the message. Paul says the same of Christ himself: to those who are called, he is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). The power in the gospel is the crucified and risen Lord at work through it. “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15): he came down to where we were, took the danger on himself at the cross, and now lives to bring the rescued all the way home. And the Lord who “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2) is not ashamed to call such people his brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

In everyday life. Shame usually shows itself quietly, long before anyone questions you: the sentence begun and not finished, the small disclaimer (“I’m not really religious, but”) attached so that nobody takes you for a keen believer. Watch for those small edits this week. The answer is not to work up more nerve, for the verse ends not with a demand for courage but with an argument: for it is the power of God. And when you catch yourself working to prove you are worth something, at the desk or the dinner table, remember: the rescue has already happened, and it was never yours to do.

Then why doesn’t everyone believe when it is preached? The same message that saves some is folly to others (1 Corinthians 1:18). The gospel is the power of a living God who works through it as he wills; the Spirit must open blind eyes (2 Corinthians 4:4–6; Acts 16:14). That is why we preach and pray together. We are never the power. We carry it, and ask God to use it.

Does “to the Jew first” set a priority in mission today? Some Christians read it as a standing rule that the church must take the gospel to Jewish people before others. More likely it describes the order of salvation history, which Paul’s own practice followed, and does not put one people ahead of another in the queue. But it forbids the opposite error. Paul’s heart’s desire and prayer to God for Israel is that they may be saved (10:1), and a church that left Jewish people out of its witness would have forgotten whose promises it is preaching.

verseByVerse.quote: For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith.' — Romans 1:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel reveals a righteousness that comes from God as a gift, received by faith from first to last, just as Scripture promised. It answers the question every sinner must face: how can I stand before a holy God?

The righteousness of God. Everything turns on this phrase. Is it an attribute (God’s own perfect rightness), an activity (God putting things right), or a gift (a righteous standing God gives to people who have none)? If the gospel only revealed God’s standard, it would not be good news but the problem restated more clearly. And here the verse becomes a biography.

The monk and the open gates. Martin Luther was a monk who took sin seriously enough to be destroyed by it. He fasted, kept vigils, confessed for hours at a stretch and found no peace, and he later wrote that he had hated this phrase. Then the meaning broke open: the righteousness revealed in the gospel is not the standard God demands but the standing God gives; not the righteousness by which he condemns, but the righteousness with which he clothes (3:21–22; Philippians 3:9). He felt, he wrote, that he had entered paradise itself through open gates. The gospel does not tell you how to produce a righteousness for God; it announces one from God, the spotless obedience of his own Son, put to the account of every sinner who trusts him.

An alien righteousness. The Reformers called it iustitia aliena: alien not as strange but as belonging to someone else, not produced in you but credited to you. Justification is a verdict, not a renovation: God declares a person righteous, as a judge pronounces sentence rather than reforms a character (Deuteronomy 25:1). Christ’s obedience is reckoned as yours; your sin was reckoned as his and dealt with at the cross, the exchange Luther called joyful. Only so can God be “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (3:26): the debt paid, not waived, the guilty acquitted, not excused. This righteousness is imputed (counted to your account), not imparted (worked into you). Justification is complete the moment you believe; sanctification, God’s lifelong work of making you holy in fact, follows (6:22).

Is revealed. Present tense, still happening. Whenever this gospel is preached, what Luther saw is shown to somebody else.

From faith for faith. The righteousness God gives is received by faith, and by faith alone, from beginning to end (on the phrase, see “Uncertain wording” below): not faith at the entry point and works for maintenance, and not faith plus works. The Christian life does not begin in grace and continue in effort.

As it is written, “The righteous shall live by faith.” The words are from Habakkuk 2:4, and the prophet was not enjoying a settled faith. He had cried out to God about injustice and chaos, and God answered that the proud Babylonians would come, and fall, on a timetable Habakkuk would not choose; but the righteous would live by his faith, trusting God through the disaster. The Hebrew word can mean faithfulness as well as faith, but the faithfulness meant is the steady trust of one who relies on God’s word and waits for it, the trust Abraham showed (Genesis 15:6); Paul is not changing its meaning but showing its heart. The faith that receives a righteousness you did not earn is the faith you go on living by in the dark.

What living by faith looks like. Faith is how the Christian life is lived on ordinary days, not only how it starts. You begin the day remembering not your record but Christ’s: his obedience counted to you, his blood enough for yesterday. You decide by what God has said rather than by what you can see or control, and leave the outcome with him. When you sin, you go straight back to the cross instead of waiting until you feel fit to pray. When you are afraid, you hold a particular promise up to God, as Habakkuk did when the fig tree did not blossom and the fields yielded no food (Habakkuk 3:17–18). Paul put his own life into one sentence: “the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). Faith lives on a Person, not a feeling, and the Person does not change.

In everyday life. If you were asked tonight why God should accept you, notice what rises first. If the answer includes “I try”, or “at least I never”, your account is being kept in your own name. The gospel’s answer contains no information about you at all, only about Christ, and the righteousness it gives does not fluctuate after a bad day, because you never generated it and cannot damage it.

If my righteousness is credited, does it matter how I live? Paul saw the question coming and gives chapter 6 to it: shall we go on sinning that grace may abound? By no means (6:1–2). The faith that receives Christ’s righteousness unites us to Christ himself, and no one can be joined to Christ and stay as he was. You are not made right with God by how you live, but you will not stay comfortable living as if you were not.

Where Christians differ: what is the righteousness of God? Roman Catholic teaching sees it mainly as a righteousness God works into us over time, making us just. Some recent scholars (the New Perspective, a school that reads Paul’s debates as chiefly about how Jews and Gentiles belong together in God’s people) see it as God’s covenant faithfulness. This commentary’s view: it includes God’s faithfulness and his righteous character, but at its heart in Romans it is the gift of a righteous standing before God, credited to the believer on the basis of Christ’s work (3:21–26; 4:5–6; 5:17). We are justified by Christ’s righteousness imputed to us, not by our own righteousness imparted. This is the heart of the Reformation, and of the gospel.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases here can be read more than one way. “From faith for faith” (ek pisteōs eis pistin) has been taken as (1) from God’s faithfulness to our faith; (2) from the preacher’s faith to the hearer’s; (3) from Old Testament faith to New Testament faith; (4) faith growing from one degree to another; or (5) faith from first to last, which the ESV note renders “beginning and ending in faith”. This commentary’s view: the fifth is most likely. The phrase is emphatic, like “from death to death” (2 Corinthians 2:16), meaning nothing but death, and Paul proves it at once with a text about faith. The quotation, too, can be read “the righteous shall live by faith” or, as the ESV note gives it, “the one who by faith is righteous shall live”. Both are true, and the letter explains both: chapters 1–4 show how a person is righteous by faith, and chapters 5–8 how the righteous person lives.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “from faith for faith” can also be rendered “beginning and ending in faith,” and the quotation “The one who by faith is righteous shall live.”

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–32 — The Wrath of God and the Ruin of Idolatry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everyone needs the gospel, because everyone knows God and holds that knowledge down, and God’s wrath is already at work against it. The problem is not ignorance but suppression: God has made himself plain in creation, so no one is without excuse (vv. 18–20). People refused to honour or thank him and exchanged his glory for images (vv. 21–23). Three times God gives them up, to impurity (vv. 24–25), to dishonourable passions (vv. 26–27) and to a debased mind (v. 28), until the heart overflows with every kind of wrong and applauds it (vv. 29–32). This is not a portrait of the worst of humanity but of ordinary human life without God’s restraining grace; Rome would have recognised itself, and so will any honest heart.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Wrath of God

Reformed theology has held that the wrath of God is real, personal and active. It is not merely the impersonal working out of a moral law (as C.H. Dodd argued), but the holy, settled opposition of the living God to everything that contradicts his character. Leon Morris showed at length that in both Testaments God’s wrath is personal and purposeful. Why the gospel is good news only because this wrath is real is shown at v. 18.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rome’s temples were full of gods in human form and deified emperors: creatures honoured in the Creator’s place, as verses 22–23 describe. Now: The idols have changed shape but not substance: the successful career, the perfect family, the autonomous self. Any created thing made to bear the weight only God can carry produces futile thinking and darkened hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good news is needed because God’s holy anger is already being revealed against all human godlessness and wrongdoing, in people who know the truth about him and hold it down. Before Paul explains the cure he shows the disease, and the disease is not ignorance but suppression.

For the wrath of God. The small word “For” is the key to the next three chapters: a righteousness from God is revealed (v. 17) because the wrath of God is revealed against everyone (v. 18). The case runs until every mouth is stopped (3:19–20) and Paul can say “But now” (3:21). And the word needs rescuing, because most people hear temper, like the capricious, easily offended gods of Rome. God’s wrath is not a mood. It is his settled, personal, holy opposition to everything that ruins what he has made: not the opposite of his love, but the form his love takes when it faces what is destroying those he loves. A parent who feels nothing on hearing what was done to their child has not achieved serenity. They have stopped loving the child.

Is revealed from heaven. The same verb as verse 17, in the present tense. The wrath is being uncovered now, as God gives people over to their sins (vv. 24, 26, 28), and will be revealed fully at the judgment (2:5). “From heaven” is the language of a throne. Some propose that wrath in Paul is only an impersonal process by which bad actions produce bad results. But consequences simply happen; this comes from God, and the argument leads to a cross that would be needless if the only problem were bad consequences. If nobody is angry, nobody needed to die.

Against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. Ungodliness is sin against God; unrighteousness is sin against people, and the rest of the chapter argues that the second grows out of the first: the morality problem is the symptom of a God problem. No subgroup is named: the case is against everyone, and the moment the list ends Paul turns on the reader who has been enjoying it (2:1).

Who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth. “Suppress” (katechontōn) means to hold down by force, and it describes an action, not a condition. Think of holding a football under the surface of a swimming pool: the ball pushes up the whole time, and the moment your attention wanders it is on the surface again. That is Paul’s picture of unbelief: not innocent ignorance, but a continuous effort to keep down something that keeps rising.

The wrath has already arrived somewhere. Put verses 17 and 18 side by side: the righteousness of God revealed, and the wrath of God revealed. There is one place in history where both were revealed together. At the cross the wrath of God fell, more terribly than in any judgment ever recorded, on the only man who had never once held the truth down. God put him forward as the propitiation (3:25), the sacrifice on which God’s wrath falls so that it does not fall on us, and so those who are his are saved by him from the wrath of God (5:9). For everyone who trusts him, the place the wrath arrived was not you. It was him.

In everyday life. Think of the moments when the pressure slips: a graveside, three in the morning after bad news. Something surfaces, the sense that there is Someone and that you are known, and it is usually pushed back under within the hour. Paul’s claim is that nobody is short of evidence; we are all working very hard to hold it down.

Isn’t unbelief simply following the evidence? From the inside it often feels so, and many unbelievers are honest people. But Paul says the problem goes deeper, and one candid philosopher agrees more than he might like. Thomas Nagel, an atheist, admitted in The Last Word (1997), “I want atheism to be true”, and, “I don’t want the universe to be like that.” He called it the cosmic authority problem: if there is a God, he has a claim on me. None of us, believers included, comes to the question as a neutral judge, because the answer will cost somebody their independence. Paul’s gospel goes straight to that fear: the God we hold under the water is about to be revealed in this letter as the one who justifies the ungodly (4:5). What rises to the surface is not a tyrant but a Father.

Is God angry with me when I sin as a Christian? Not with the wrath of this verse. For those in Christ, that wrath was spent on the cross, and there is now no condemnation (8:1). God still grieves over our sin and disciplines us, but as a Father who corrects the children he loves, for our good (Hebrews 12:5–11). Discipline is not wrath in smaller doses. It is love making sure we share his holiness.

Where Christians differ: is God’s wrath real? Some say a loving God cannot be wrathful, or that wrath is only the natural consequence of sin. This commentary’s view: God’s wrath is personal and real, the reaction of his holiness to evil. Love and wrath are not opposites; a God who did not oppose evil would not be good. And the gospel is God’s answer: Christ bore that wrath (3:25; 5:9).

verseByVerse.quote: For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone knows enough about God to be answerable to him, because God has made his power and his Godhood plain in everything he has made. Creation leaves no one able to plead ignorance, though it cannot tell anyone how to be forgiven.

Plain to them, because God has shown it to them. This is general revelation: God shows himself to everyone through creation (Psalm 19:1–4; Acts 14:17). Calvin called the world a theatre of God’s glory. Creation is not a set of clues left lying about for the curious, but his own voice, at conversational volume, everywhere, all the time.

His invisible attributes. The unseeable is clearly seen, the way you can see someone is exhausted: you are seeing a face, and reading it. Paul is precise about how much it says: God’s eternal power (he must be powerful to make all this) and his divine nature (he is God, of an altogether different order from what he has made). It does not say that God is merciful or that there is forgiveness. It is enough light to know you are answerable, not enough to be saved.

So they are without excuse. Having no defence to offer (anapologētos), a courtroom word. Paul does not claim that nobody is ever honestly confused, or that everyone secretly believes and is lying, but that when the case is heard no one will stand up and say the evidence was insufficient.

The Maker who came to be seen. The creation Paul describes has a Maker with a name. All things were made through the Son, and without him was not any thing made that was made (John 1:3); he is the image of the invisible God, and by him all things were created (Colossians 1:15–16). What creation could never say, he said in person: “No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). The God whose power is written across the sky did not leave us with the sky alone. He sent his Son, so that the God who could be known only as Maker could be known as Saviour.

In everyday life. Take the last thing that genuinely stopped you: a night sky with no streetlights, a piece of music that went through you before you had decided anything about it, the face of someone you love asleep, the plain fact that there is something rather than nothing. Your first response was not an argument. It was awe, and awe is a response to a someone. That reflex, not the argument afterwards, is the knowledge of God arriving. Then watch what you do with it thirty seconds later.

What it does not mean. This is not a licence for contempt. If this passage has ever made you treat the sceptic at your table as a liar, you have taken a truth about the human race and used it as a weapon against one member of it. The suppression Paul describes is yours too: it is the reason you can know God is real and still live for stretches of a week as though he were not.

What about those who never heard? Paul answers part of this and leaves the rest with God. People are not judged for rejecting a Christ they never heard of; they are judged for suppressing the light they did have, in creation and in conscience (2:12–16). God is perfectly just, and no one will be condemned unfairly (Genesis 18:25). If you grieve over a particular person, this verse does not settle their case; it settles that God is not unjust in having one. But that light cannot save, because no one responds to it rightly (3:10–12). On whether anyone is saved without hearing of Christ, see “Where Christians differ” at the end of this note.

What about infants, and people who cannot understand? Paul is speaking of those able to perceive and suppress what God shows them. Infants who die, and people never able to understand, are in a different position. Scripture gives real hope here (2 Samuel 12:23), and the Reformed confessions say that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (the Westminster Confession 10.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3): not by innocence, but by the same Saviour as everyone else. If you have buried a little one, you may entrust that child to the Saviour who took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

Where Christians differ: can people be saved without hearing of Christ? Inclusivists hold that some who never hear the gospel may be saved by Christ’s work if they respond in faith to the light of creation, appealing to God’s justice and to believers outside Israel such as Melchizedek and Job. This commentary’s view: Scripture gives no warrant for that hope. General revelation leaves people without excuse (v. 20), not with a way of salvation; there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12); and Paul’s own logic assumes that people cannot call on one they have not heard of (10:14–15). God is free to work as he wills, and he can bring the gospel to anyone; but the church’s task is clear: go and tell. Those who hope more widely usually do so out of compassion, and the motive is a good one even where the reading does not persuade.

parallels.desc: the heavens declare the glory of God

verseByVerse.quote: For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Humanity’s ruin began with worship: knowing God, people refused to honour him or thank him, and their thinking went empty and dark while they called it wisdom.

They did not honor him as God. Humanity had the knowledge, the evidence and the obligation, and refused two things. To honour God is to give him his proper weight in the actual running of a life. You can believe in him and arrange your week, your money and your ambitions exactly as you would if he were not there. That is not atheism but knowing God and giving him no weight, and every sin begins here.

Or give thanks to him. The passage ends in murder and ruthlessness, and the first item on the charge sheet is failing to say thank you. That looks out of proportion until you see what gratitude is: an admission that you have received what you did not produce, and nothing about you was produced by you, not even the intelligence you use to argue about God. Thanklessness is not rudeness but a claim about ownership, the quiet insistence that what I have, I hold by right. There is even a religious way to fail here. The Pharisee in the temple thanked God that he was not like other men (Luke 18:11). True thanks says I received it; his said I deserved it.

They became futile in their thinking. Made empty, vain (emataiōthēsan). In the Greek Old Testament this word group is often used of idols themselves: the vanities, the empty things. So Jeremiah can make the pun that carries the whole indictment: your fathers went after worthlessness, and became worthless (Jeremiah 2:5). You catch the emptiness of what you serve. The Psalms give the mechanism: idols have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, and those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Psalm 115:5–8). What you choose instead of God has no mouth to speak your name and nothing to give back, while the God set aside is the only one who was ever able to love you in return.

Their foolish hearts were darkened. The heart, the centre of the person, darkened, and the verb is passive: in view of what follows, the lights were most likely turned down by God, in judgment. It is the first hint of the phrase that will sound three times over the rest of the chapter: God gave them up. And a dark room is the one place where you cannot tell how dark it has become.

Claiming to be wise, they became fools. The claim is not incidental to the foolishness; it is the evidence of it (1 Corinthians 1:20–21; Psalm 14:1). Paul is not describing primitives, or scorning learning; he is writing to the capital of a civilisation with law courts, aqueducts, libraries and centuries of philosophy behind it, in which serious men carried food to statues.

The one man who gave thanks. Against this refusal stands one human life that never withheld either. Jesus gave God his full weight in every decision, down to the hour of his death. On the night he was betrayed he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, this is my body, which is for you (1 Corinthians 11:23–24). Where humanity began its ruin with ingratitude, the Saviour began its rescue with a thanksgiving.

In everyday life. You cannot usually see your own idol, but since we become like what we worship, look at what you are becoming and read backwards. More anxious and grasping? You may be worshipping something that can be taken from you. Exhausted and unable to rest?
