Something that never says “Enough, well done.” The same law runs the other way, and that is the hope: beholding the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The cure for what you have become is not to stare at yourself but to look at Christ, and keep looking.

parallels.desc: they went after worthlessness

verseByVerse.quote: and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People traded the glory of the living God for images of creatures, and every such trade is a step down.

Exchanged. The word the chapter turns on (vv. 23, 25, 26) is commercial. An exchange is entered into deliberately, because at the moment of the trade you preferred what you were getting: not drift, but a swap somebody wanted to make.

The glory of the immortal God for images. On one side, the glory (doxa) of the immortal God: the weight and blazing splendour of the One who cannot die. On the other, not even the creatures but likenesses of them: the living God traded for a picture of a lizard. Jeremiah put it as bewilderment: has a nation changed its gods, even though they are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit. Be appalled, O heavens, at this (Jeremiah 2:11–12).

Mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things. A staircase that only goes down: man, birds, beasts, reptiles. Idolatry never levels out. Whatever a person puts in God’s place begins as something reasonably impressive, a career, a cause, a version of yourself, and the thing you serve keeps asking for slightly more and offering slightly less. Nobody sets out to worship a creeping thing. They set out to worship something a good deal higher up, and the staircase does the rest.

The golden calf. Paul writes with Israel’s own story in his ear. The nation had heard the voice of God out of the fire at Sinai, and within weeks had made a calf. The psalm describes it in almost these words: “They exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass” (Psalm 106:20). The people with the true revelation did this too, faster and with less excuse, which prepares for chapter 2, where Paul turns to the religious.

Glory in the likeness of man. Paul’s phrase is exact: the glory of the immortal God traded for the likeness of an image of mortal man. In chapter 8 the same word comes back, turned round: God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (8:3). The human race wanted a god shaped like a man; God gave not a likeness but a true man, his own Son, and in him the glory they had traded away walked among them: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father (John 1:14). The Son of the immortal God took mortal flesh and died in it. The exchange was reversed from God’s side.

Today’s idols. Ours are not carved in marble, but the definition has not changed: an idol is any created thing given the job that belongs to God. A career cannot forgive you. A marriage cannot make you unashamed. A child handed the job of being a parent’s meaning will feel its weight long before either can name what has gone wrong. And religion itself can be the image. A moral record, a correct theology or a respected place in the church can be given the one job that belongs to God, the job of making you acceptable, and then the religious person has made the same trade as the pagan, only with better furniture.

parallels.desc: they exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s present judgment on idolatry is to hand people over to the desires they have chosen, so that those who would not honour him end by dishonouring themselves. The reason is the deeper exchange: they traded the truth about God for the lie, and served the creature instead of the Creator.

Therefore God gave them up. Three times this phrase falls like a gavel (vv. 24, 26, 28). Paredōken is what a magistrate does when he consigns a prisoner to the jailer: not God losing interest, but a judicial act. This is the present revelation of God’s wrath (v. 18): not fire from heaven, but God letting people have what they want. The worst judgment is to be left to yourself.

In the lusts of their hearts. God manufactures no appetite in this passage. He lifts the restraint that held an existing appetite in check, and lets the person have what he wants. That is more frightening than fire, because from inside it feels like nothing, or even pleasant: the internal argument that once took an hour now takes a minute and then stops happening, and it registers as freedom.

To the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves. The sentence fits the crime. They refused to honour God (v. 21), and are given up to dishonouring their own bodies: refuse God his honour and you do not gain honour for yourself; you lose your own. The sentence is the sin allowed to run its course. And “among themselves”: it is what they do to one another once nothing is holding them back.

They exchanged the truth about God for a lie. The Greek says “the lie”: not any falsehood but a particular one, first told in a garden by a creature who suggested that if they took matters into their own hands they would be like God (Genesis 3:5). The lie is that something other than God is God, and every idolatry since has been a variation on it. It is usually felt not as a theology but as the reasonable conviction that you are the best judge of what your life is for.

Worshiped and served. Two verbs, which is why idolatry is so hard to spot in a culture where nobody kneels. Worship in the Bible is never only what you revere but what you serve: what you organise your hours around, what gets the first call on your energy and the last word in your decisions. Check the diary and the bank statement, which are less polite than the conscience and better informed.

Who is blessed forever! Amen. In the middle of one of the darkest paragraphs he ever wrote, Paul cannot get through the words “rather than the Creator” without stopping to bless him. God’s blessedness is untouched: idolatry does not injure God; it destroys the idolater. And the man writing the vice list is a worshipper, not a prosecutor. Whoever recites Romans 1 with relish has missed the spirit of the man who wrote it.

The same verb twice more. Paul uses paredōken at two great moments later in this letter. Jesus “was delivered up for our trespasses” (4:25), and God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (8:32). God handed sinners over to what they had chosen; then God handed his Son over to what they deserved. The second handing over is the answer to the first, and that is why the sentence in this chapter, terrible as it is, has never been the last word about anyone willing to have it lifted.

Shouldn’t I just follow my heart? It is the creed of many films and songs, which sociologists call expressive individualism: find what you truly desire and have the courage to live it out. Paul’s verse turns it upside down, for the judgment of God here is precisely to be handed over to the desires of our hearts. Desires are not a reliable compass: they contradict one another, change with age and mood, and bend towards things that cannot carry their weight. Augustine, in The City of God, defined virtue as love rightly ordered. Our problem is not that we love too much but that we love in the wrong order, putting good things in God’s place. Christ does not cure that by killing desire. He becomes what the heart was made to love most, and every other love finds its place beneath him: “Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Psalm 37:4).

Does God cause sin when he gives people up? No. God never makes anyone sin or tempts anyone to evil (James 1:13). Giving up means that God withdraws the restraints of his common grace (the kindness by which he holds back human evil in everyone) and lets people go where their own hearts already want to go. It is a judicial sentence, and also a warning: the greatest mercy is that God does not give us all up, but holds us back and calls us home.

Could God have given me up? If you are troubled by the thought, that trouble is itself the sign that he has not. The people of this verse are not distressed by their sin; they enjoy it and defend it. A conscience that still aches, a heart that still wants to come back, is the work of God’s Spirit calling you home. Come back, and you will find that no one who comes to Christ is ever cast out (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: “Gave them up” means God handed them over to what they chose: his judgment working through their own desires.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature; and the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another, men committing shameless acts with men and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the second giving up, idolatry’s disorder reaches the body: having exchanged God for idols, people exchanged the Creator’s design for sex, and the disorder became its own penalty. Paul is tracing what happens to a humanity that lets go of God, not ranking sins or singling out one group of sinners.

For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. The second giving up moves from inward corruption to outward expression. Many readers reach this passage already wounded, so the true things need saying in the right order. Paul’s analysis is not that sexual disorder causes idolatry but that idolatry causes disorder: when the fundamental relationship, creature to Creator, is disordered, every other relationship is disordered downstream. He takes one illustration because in it the exchange is visible in the created order itself. He is not ranking sins: the list he is building ends with envy, gossip, boasting and disobedience to parents, under the same verdict.

Contrary to nature. “Exchanged” again: the exchange of God for idols is mirrored in this one. “Contrary to nature” (para physin) means against the created order of male and female (Genesis 1:27; 2:24). Most interpreters, ancient and modern, take verse 26 as the only place in Scripture that speaks of women in same-sex relations, and the word “likewise” in the next sentence points that way.

The men likewise. Paul grounds his judgment of these acts not in the customs of his culture but in the created order, which is why his word is nature and why the passage reaches back past Moses to Genesis. The church has understood him so for two thousand years, and honesty requires saying it plainly rather than softening the text.

The due penalty for their error. “Due penalty” (antimisthia) is a fitting return, a recompense; “error” (planē) is wandering, going astray, and refers back to the exchange of God for idols (vv. 23, 25). The penalty for exchanging God for idols is to be given over to the disordered desires themselves: it is in the sin, not only after it.

“And such were some of you.” Paul writes to Corinth, lists the sexually immoral, adulterers, men who practise homosexuality, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, revilers and swindlers, and then says: “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). The past tense was the whole of their hope, as it is of ours. The blood of Christ has never met a sinner it could not wash.

What it does not mean. Paul is describing the human race, not diagnosing an individual; the sentence is corporate throughout. It does not say that a fifteen-year-old who discovers he is attracted to other boys arrived there by personally trading God for an idol, and anyone who tells him so has gone beyond what Paul wrote. Nobody chooses what they find themselves wanting; everyone is answerable for what they do with it, and that is true of every desire in this chapter. And temptation is not sin. Our Lord was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), so an unwanted desire, however persistent, is not itself guilt. A Christian who is same-sex attracted and has spent years refusing to act on it is not failing at holiness. He is doing holiness by the Spirit’s strength (8:13), and a harder version of it than most of his congregation is asked to do.

The burden and the family. What makes this painful is usually not the ethics but loneliness. The church often asks such a brother or sister for lifelong celibacy without the supports that ever made it bearable: deep friendship, a household to belong to, a place at somebody’s table on ordinary Tuesdays, people who notice when they are ill. If this passage is going to be preached, the church that preaches it, made one household in Christ (Ephesians 2:19), must be the family it is asking people to do without. And to the parent who was told something by a son or daughter recently and has not slept properly since: you may hold what you believe, and you may keep your child. Nothing in this passage tells you to withdraw your affection, and the Gospels tell you whose houses your Lord sat in.

The trap Paul sets. Paul knows the small, warm sense of not being one of those that comes over a religious reader here, and a few sentences later he springs the trap on the one who judges (2:1). God’s design for sexuality is good, and his grace is for every sinner, including you.

Where Christians differ: same-sex relationships. Some today argue that Paul had in mind only the forms common in his world, such as men using boys, sex with slaves, temple prostitution, or excessive lust, and that committed, loving partnerships were not in view. This commentary’s view: the text does not bear this out. Paul says the men were consumed with passion for one another, which describes mutual desire, not one party exploiting another, and he says nothing about age, payment or force. He includes women, which the pederasty reading cannot cover. He grounds his teaching in creation (“nature”, “the Creator”), the ground Jesus himself gives for marriage (Matthew 19:4–6), and the rest of Scripture speaks with one voice (Leviticus 18:22; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11; 1 Timothy 1:10). This is the historic Christian view, and it must be held with compassion. Many who argue otherwise do so out of love for friends and family, and that love should be honoured even where the argument is not accepted.

verseByVerse.quote: And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because people judged God not worth keeping in mind, God gave them over to a mind that fails every test, and so to doing what should never be done.

Since they did not see fit to acknowledge God. The play on words is itself the verdict. They did not dokimazein, did not think God worth approving and keeping on the books, so God handed them over to a mind that is adokimos, the same word with the negative on the front. They tested God as a metalworker tests a coin, marked him rejected, and were marked the same. They refused not the knowledge of God (vv. 19–20) but keeping him in view. This is practical atheism: God is not denied, he is simply not consulted, and the mind quietly reorganises itself around his absence.

A debased mind. Adokimos belonged to the metal trade: a coin tested and failed, whatever it looked like. A debased mind is not a stupid one. It still reasons, argues, builds bridges, writes laws and wins prizes. What has gone is its ability to reach the right conclusion about anything that matters, which is why the most sophisticated societies in history have been perfectly capable of organising atrocities with excellent paperwork. Intellect will work just as hard for a lie.

To do what ought not to be done. The words were the standard vocabulary of the Stoic moralists for what is not fitting for a rational creature. These people never had the law of Moses; they fail the standard their own philosophers set. And everyone still keeps such a list, including people who say morality is a social construct: watch what happens when the promise is broken or the credit taken. Nobody is a relativist about being wronged.

The stone the builders rejected. The human race put God to its test and marked him not worth keeping. When God came in the flesh, the verdict was passed again: the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes (Mark 8:31), the stone that the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22; Mark 12:10). The one mind that had always kept God in view, that could say I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29), was tested by sinners and thrown on the waste heap. And God reversed the verdict. The rejected stone has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes (Mark 12:10–11).

A new mind. This is not a diagnosis without a cure. Paul reaches for the same root eleven chapters later: be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect (12:2). The remedy for the mind that would not keep God in view is a new mind, and in this letter that is one more thing God gives.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay: because they did not “see fit” (edokimasan) to acknowledge God, he gave them up to a “debased” (adokimon, literally “unfit”) mind.

verseByVerse.quote: They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. They are gossips,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Left without God, the human heart fills with every kind of wrong, from murder to the envy and gossip of an ordinary week. This is not unusual criminality but the ordinary heart left to itself.

They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness. Some twenty-one sins, moving from inward dispositions outward, under the word “filled”: a vessel with no room left in it. Sin is not a stain that sits where it lands but a liquid that finds every space. The list is long so that grace can be seen to be longer.

Envy, murder. Envy and murder side by side, two words that sound almost alike in Greek (phthonos, phonos), much as Jesus set anger beside murder, the inward sin as the seed of the outward crime (Matthew 5:21–22). Anyone can read murder and feel excluded; then come envy, strife and deceit, an ordinary week in an ordinary office: wanting what a colleague has and being unable to be glad for him; the argument continued for the pleasure of winning it; the small deceit that improves on the facts; the ill will you would never act on but enjoy holding. These are the sins of people who are quite pleasant to have lunch with.

Covetousness. The settled hunger for more, especially for what belongs to someone else. Coveting is the one sin in the Ten Commandments that happens wholly inside a person, invisible from outside, which is why it flourishes in respectable people, and why Paul calls it idolatry (Colossians 3:5).

They are gossips. Whisperers (psithyristas), listed in the same breath as murder. Gossip takes a person who is not in the room and makes them smaller, at no cost to the speaker. It is often accurate, which is its best disguise, and almost always done in a tone of concern, which is the disguise underneath that one.

Every item, done to him. Read the list again at Golgotha. It was out of envy that the chief priests delivered Jesus up, and Pilate knew it (Mark 15:10). Deceit came with a kiss in a garden; malice went looking for false witnesses, whose testimony did not even agree (Matthew 26:59; Mark 14:56); strife shouted for crucifixion; and murder finished the work outside the city wall. The ordinary sins of verse 29 were the very instruments by which the human race put the Son of God to death.

Textual note. The KJV list is a little longer, adding fornication (v. 29) and implacable (v. 31) from later manuscripts; the earliest lack them, so most modern Bibles omit them.

verseByVerse.quote: slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list ends where the trouble began, in hatred of God, and shows its fruit in pride, cruelty, broken families and hearts gone cold.

Slanderers, haters of God. “Haters of God” is the root of it all, and almost nobody would own the phrase. From inside it shows up as a sense that God is a rival: that his claims and your happiness pull in opposite directions, so that every command reads as something taken away from you rather than something kept safe for you.

Insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil. Pride in its many forms, and then the strangest item in the list. The power to invent is part of God’s image in us, and here it is put to work for evil: sin is creative. No child has ever needed lessons in finding the exact sentence that will wound a sibling most efficiently. Cruelty is inventive on its own. It is kindness that has to be taught.

Disobedient to parents. Listed among the serious sins, not because it equals murder, but because the breakdown of the family is the breakdown of the social order that reflects God’s order. A family coming apart is a sign of a society turned from God (2 Timothy 3:2).

Foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless. Four Greek words beginning with the negative a-: without understanding, without faithfulness, without natural affection, without mercy. Paul finishes not on murder but on coldness. The word behind “heartless” is family affection with the negative on the front, the one form of love nobody has to be talked into. “Faithless” is a person whose signature means nothing. The passage that began with the heavens (v. 20) ends in a house, with family love gone: the kitchen is where the damage is finally measured.

Enemies, and reconciled. The root of the whole list, hatred of God, is exactly where the gospel goes looking. While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (5:10). The haters of God in verse 30 are the people for whom the Son of God died, and he died praying for those who were killing him: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34). (Some early manuscripts lack that prayer; most modern Bibles keep it.) The love this list has driven out of the human race came back in the person of the one they hated, and it came back praying.

Into a world of the heartless. The Son was subject to his parents at Nazareth (Luke 2:51) and, dying, gave his mother into the keeping of the disciple he loved (John 19:26–27). He brought the faithfulness and affection the world had lost, and now God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (5:5), so that the love this list describes as gone can begin again where the damage was measured: in the kitchen.

What it does not mean. Somebody will reach the word heartless and go cold, because they have felt nothing for months: a mother who cannot find the love for her baby that everyone said would come, a man numb at his father’s funeral, someone so exhausted or depressed that the affection they know is there will not switch on. That is not what Paul means. He means a hardness that is chosen, defended and eventually preferred. Numbness that grieves you is not hardness of heart but a symptom, and your distress is the proof; the people in this verse are not distressed. If it has lasted for weeks, tell a pastor or biblical counsellor, and see your doctor too: illnesses such as depression after childbirth are real, and treating them is no failure of faith. The enemy of souls is very willing to quote Romans 1 to a tired woman at three in the morning. Do not let him.

verseByVerse.quote: Though they know God's righteous decree that those who practice such things deserve to die, they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the bottom of the descent people still know God’s verdict that such things deserve death, yet they not only do them but applaud others who do.

Though they know God’s righteous decree. Knowledge has now appeared four times in this chapter (vv. 19, 21, 28, 32), and not once as a charge of ignorance. The human problem is not a shortage of light but what is done with it, and even at the bottom of the descent, with the mind handed over and the list complete, the knowledge is still there. The conscience knows (2:14–15).

Those who practice such things deserve to die. This strikes a modern reader as out of all proportion. But Paul states what such things deserve before God, and explains why in his plainest sentence: the wages of sin is death (6:23). Wages, not a penalty imposed from outside. If God is the source of life, a settled turning from him has one possible end, and calling it a sentence is God telling the truth about where the road goes.

But give approval to those who practice them. The climax: not merely doing evil but applauding it, calling evil good (Isaiah 5:20). Why would applause be worse than the act? A man who does wrong and knows it is wrong is at war with himself, and that war is the last thing standing between him and ruin; approval ends the war and dismantles what could have called him back. Approval costs nothing, and it recruits. Doing wrong damages you; applauding it manufactures more of it in other people, the difference between having an illness and being a carrier. Every society has contained plenty of sin. A society is destroyed when it begins to praise it.

The one who did not deserve it. The chapter ends on what people deserve, and the Gospels end on the same question. Beside Jesus on the hill a dying thief said it aloud: “we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong” (Luke 23:41). Pilate said it three times (John 18:38). The only man who did not deserve to die is the one who died, and that is not an accident in the story of God’s righteous decree but the decree being satisfied: the death the guilty had earned was borne by the innocent in their place (3:25–26; 5:6).

Small approvals. Approval is mostly small and silent. It is the laugh you gave because not laughing would have been awkward, the anecdote passed on because it was entertaining. Most of all it is consuming as recreation behaviour that would appal us in our own street: a small vote, cast repeatedly, for more of it.

What it does not mean. Not every silence is approval. Sometimes speaking would be self-righteous, or a thing is not your business, or the standing to speak has to be earned first. The line falls where your silence is doing work you would be embarrassed to admit to: where you said nothing not out of wisdom but because you wanted to be liked.

Does “deserve to die” mean the death penalty? No. Paul is not telling the state to execute people for gossip or envy, which are in the same list. Death here is the sentence God has decreed on sin, death in its full biblical sense, physical death and the second death (5:12; 6:23). The second death is Scripture’s name for God’s final judgment: conscious, eternal punishment, shut out from his presence and favour (Revelation 20:14–15; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). Everyone in the list deserves it, which includes every reader. That is the point Paul is driving toward in 3:23, and the reason the gospel of 3:21–26 is needed.

In the flow. The chapter ends at its lowest point, and the lowest point is a bridge. The very next sentence turns to the person who disapproves: “Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges” (2:1). “Without excuse” is the word of verse 20 again: the one who applauds sin and the one who condemns it from a height stand in the same dock. Paul will not finish with the human race until every mouth is silent before God (3:19), because only the silenced are ready to hear the “But now” of 3:21.
