keyVerse.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.
keyVerse.note: This verse states the theme of the whole letter, and the chapter turns on it. Before it Paul has set out the gospel and its Son (vv. 1–15); after it he shows why the gospel is needed, God’s wrath revealed against all ungodliness (vv. 18–32). He is not ashamed because the gospel is not his argument but God’s own power, and it saves the very people the rest of the chapter describes.

1.reflection:
Paul introduces himself first as a “servant”, literally a slave, of Christ Jesus (v. 1). What would it mean in practice for your time, body, money and plans to belong to Christ? Why does Paul find that to be freedom rather than loss?

Where are you most tempted to be ashamed of the gospel (v. 16)? How does Paul’s reason, “for it is the power of God for salvation”, change what you need in those moments?

Paul traces human ruin to a refusal to honour God and give him thanks (v. 21), and to exchanging him for created things (vv. 23, 25). Which good things most easily take God’s place in your life or in our culture, and how would you know?

Verses 18–32 can be read with a quiet sense of being better than “those people”, yet 2:1 springs the trap on that reader. How should this passage shape the way we speak to and about people whose sins differ from ours, and what hope does the cross, where God “gave him up for us all” (8:32), hold out to all of them?

2.title: God's Impartial Judgment
2.overview:
Where we are. Paul is proving that everyone needs the righteousness God gives (1:17), before showing how he gives it (3:21). Chapter 1 indicted the pagan world; chapter 2 turns on the reader who has been agreeing: the moral, religious person, above all the Jew who has God’s law.

The message. Knowing right from wrong, condemning others, holding God’s law and bearing his covenant sign: none of it shields anyone from God’s judgment. God judges every person impartially, by what he has truly done, down to the secrets of the heart. Privilege increases the reckoning: the one who condemns others while doing the same is more to blame than the pagan, because he knows better. What God looks for is a heart he has himself changed by his Spirit.

Why it was said. A Jewish reader would have heard chapter 1’s catalogue of Gentile vice with some satisfaction, trusting that belonging to God’s covenant people would keep him safe. In a Roman church of Jewish and Gentile believers, both needed to see that the same verdict falls on all (3:9; see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The judge condemns himself, and God’s patience is meant to lead him to repentance (vv. 1–5). God renders to each according to his works, without partiality (vv. 6–11), each judged by the light he had, the law of Moses or the law written on the heart (vv. 12–16). The Jew who teaches the law breaks it, and God’s name is blasphemed because of him (vv. 17–24). The sign without obedience is worthless; the true Jew is circumcised in heart by the Spirit (vv. 25–29).

Where it leads. Paul disqualifies every human judge and names the one who is left: Christ Jesus, the only judge with no log in his eye, who came down from the bench into the dock beside the accused. The chapter shuts every mouth so that “But now” can be spoken (3:21): one man has done the law in full, by whose obedience “the many will be made righteous” (5:19), and his Spirit performs the circumcision of the heart that Moses promised.

For us. This is the chapter for church people. Ask where you judge others by their actions and yourself by your intentions, where you read God’s patience as approval, and what you trust in place of a changed heart. Then go, not to a better record, but to Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — God's Righteous and Impartial Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one escapes God’s judgment by sitting on the judge’s side of the bench. The moralist who condemns others condemns himself, because he does the same things (vv. 1–2), and God’s patience with him is meant to lead him to repentance, not to make him comfortable (vv. 3–5). God judges by truth, by works and without partiality, the Jew first and also the Greek (vv. 6–11). Each person is measured by the light he had, the law of Moses or the law written on the heart, to which conscience bears witness, so no one is left without excuse (vv. 12–15). And on the last day God will judge even the secrets of the heart, by Christ Jesus (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment According to Works

Romans 2:6–11 can look like salvation by works, since God will give eternal life to those who persist in doing good. Reformed interpreters have read it as the principle of judgment (God judges the whole life) rather than the means of salvation (which is faith alone). How this fits with justification by faith is set out at vv. 5–6 and in the boxes at the end of the notes on vv. 7–8 and 12–13.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Many in Paul’s day trusted covenant privilege (circumcision, the law, the temple) to shield them: Gentiles might face judgment, but the covenant people were secure by their membership. Paul shows that it cannot. Now: The equivalent is the nominal Christian who trusts in baptism, church membership or moral respectability instead of faith and repentance. God looks for a heart he has changed.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things. We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The person who condemns others has no excuse before God, because by his own verdict he condemns himself. He does the same things, and God’s judgment, unlike his, rests on the truth.

Therefore you have no excuse. This is the sentence chapter 1 was built to deliver. Paul spent fifteen verses on idolatry, sexual chaos, envy, gossip and the collapse of the family, knowing what a religious reader does with them: he agrees, warmly. That agreement is the trap, for a man nodding for fifteen verses has persuaded himself he stands above it all. Then “therefore” arrives, and the paragraph he has been applauding turns out to be a mirror. “No excuse” (anapologētos) is the word of 1:20: the pagan had no defence, and neither has the moralist.

O man. Chapter 1 was plural: they, them, humanity in the dock, comfortable enough to read. Here it is singular. Paul rounds on an imaginary objector, a device from the lecture halls, so that nobody can pass this verse along to somebody else. It is addressed to one person, and that person is holding the letter.

The very same things. The instinctive reply is: I have never done what that man did. Paul means not an identical list of acts but the same root disorder, living for self instead of for God, and the list of 1:29–31 includes respectable sins: envy, deceit, gossip, pride. By judging, you show that you know right from wrong, and so you condemn yourself. We judge other people by their actions and ourselves by our intentions. Another man is short with his child, and he is impatient; I am short with mine, and I had a difficult day. The filing is done before any conscious dishonesty, which is why it is so hard to catch.

Rightly. Literally “according to truth” (kata alētheian): God judges reality, not appearances, and allows none of the exemptions we grant ourselves.

The log in the eye. Our Lord gave this its permanent image: why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye and not notice the log in your own (Matthew 7:3–5)? Because the log is in the eye. It is not on the table where it could be pointed out; it is lodged in the very organ you are using to look at him.

The only Judge without a log. Paul’s argument disqualifies every human judge, and he names the one who is left: “God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus” (v. 16). The Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), the one judge in history with no log in his eye, and what he did with that sight is the gospel: “God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17). The one person qualified to pass this sentence came down from the bench and took his place in the dock beside the accused.

What it does not mean. Paul is not forbidding moral judgment: he has just made judgments of unusual severity, and later he will tell churches to deal with sin in their members. Nor does Jesus end with the log: the speck is still to come out (Matthew 7:5). What changes is the order, and with it the whole character of the man doing the work. Someone who has just had a log taken out of his own eye handles other people very differently.

So how do I correct someone without being the man in this verse? Start with yourself, honestly and first: what in me is like this? Then go to the person privately, not to others about him (Matthew 18:15), and gently, as one who could fall the same way (Galatians 6:1). Name the specific thing rather than his character, and listen before you conclude. Ask whether you hope to win him or to be proved right. And if you find you enjoy it, wait: the pleasure is a sign the log is still there.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you suppose, O man — you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself — that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not mistake God’s patience for indifference: his kindness in holding back judgment is meant to lead you to repentance. The man who condemns others and does the same has no argument for escaping, only a settled sense that his case is different.

Do you suppose, O man, that you will escape? Paul asks rather than asserts. Nobody has ever said that sentence out loud; it is an assumption underneath the beliefs, and Paul drags it into daylight so that the man hears it in his own voice.

Do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience? “Presume” (kataphroneis) means to despise, take for granted. Three words for God’s goodness are stacked up. Kindness (chrēstotēs) is his active goodness, not mere tolerance. Forbearance is holding back what could justly be done. Patience (makrothumia) is long-temper, the opposite of a short fuse: being provoked for a very long time and not acting. So this is not a God who does not notice. He notices, is entitled to act, and does not, yet. His kindness waited out the golden calf, the judges, the kings, the prophets who were stoned and four hundred years of silence, and went on waiting while the men it was aimed at were sharpening the charges against his Son.

How presumption sounds. Almost never like defiance, but reasonable: it cannot be that serious, or something would have happened by now; God knows what I am like and has made his peace with it. Each treats a delayed sentence as an acquittal. The prisoner whose appeal is pending is not free because the corridor is quiet.

God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance. The verse turns here. The verb is the ordinary word for leading someone somewhere: God’s goodness is not a backdrop to your life but is working on you, with a destination, giving you time to repent (2 Peter 3:9). The mercies you enjoy are not evidence that the subject is closed but the means by which it is being reopened. They should melt you, not make you comfortable; the same sun softens wax and hardens clay.

Forbearance with a cross at the end of it. Paul uses the word once more in this letter, at the centre of the gospel: God put Christ forward as a propitiation (a sacrifice that turns away his wrath) by his blood, to show his righteousness, “because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins” (3:25). So the patience of verse 4 was never indifference. For centuries God held back what sins deserved, waiting for the cross, where every sin he had passed over would be dealt with in full. The kindness that leads to repentance has a face: “when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us” (Titus 3:4–5).

“God will forgive me; that’s his job.” The poet Heinrich Heine is reported to have said something very like this on his deathbed, and it catches a modern instinct: if there is a God, forgiving is simply what he does, as a tap gives water. In fact it is the presumption Paul describes, made polite. Forgiveness treated as automatic becomes an entitlement, and nobody has ever been moved to tears by an entitlement; the friend who says, “You’ll forgive me, you always do,” has not really said sorry. Paul’s answer is not that God is less kind than we assume, but far kinder, and that his kindness is not cheap. It is not his job; it cost him his Son (3:25). Kindness like that does not leave a person comfortable. It breaks him open, and then it leads him home.

What it does not mean. Somebody will read this and conclude that they have used up their allowance, that for them alone the offer has expired. Read the sentence again. It is not a warning that the kindness is running out but a complaint that it is being wasted, and you cannot waste what has stopped being given. That this frightens you is proof that the kindness is still at work. Presumption is a comfortable condition. It does not lie awake.

What does repentance actually involve? Turning from sin to God. It begins by seeing your sin as God sees it, not only as harmful to you but as offensive to him, and grieving over it. It takes hold of God’s mercy in Christ, because repentance without hope only drives a person away. And it turns: you forsake the sin and set yourself to walk with God in new obedience (the Westminster Confession 15.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 15.3). In practice: name the specific sin to God, not a vague apology; put right what can be put right; remove what feeds it; and start again the next time you fall, without waiting to feel worthy. It is not a single event at conversion but the shape of the whole Christian life.

parallels.desc: slow to anger

verseByVerse.quote: But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God's righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works:
verseByVerse.commentary:
A heart that will not repent is adding to its own judgment, and on the last day God will repay every person according to what he has done. Kindness refused does not cancel the reckoning; it adds to it.

Hard and impenitent heart. Hardness (sklērotēs, from which we get sclerosis) is not a mood but a condition, like a callus: it forms slowly under repeated friction, and its whole function is to stop you feeling anything at that spot. So it is nearly impossible to diagnose from inside, and here it is the settled state of a religious man who has heard sermons for decades.

Remorse or repentance? Impenitent means refusing to repent, and two things that feel alike must be told apart. Scripture gives us two men in the same week: Judas was sorry enough to die of it, Peter wept bitterly, and only one of them came back. The difference is not the amount of feeling. Remorse is mostly about me: what I have lost, how I look, what this will cost. Repentance is about God: I agree with him about the thing, and I turn to him. Remorse can be intense and leave a person exactly where it found him (2 Corinthians 7:10).

Storing up wrath. The verb is the one behind our word treasury, the one Jesus used: “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matthew 6:20). Verse 4 spoke of the riches of God’s kindness; verse 5 says you are banking wrath, not drifting toward a bad end but making deposits.

The day of wrath. The day of judgment, at Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). God’s wrath is not spite but his fixed and holy resistance to evil, as steady as his love (Psalm 7:11; Habakkuk 1:13). This is the third thing said to be “revealed” in barely twenty verses: the righteousness of God (1:17), the wrath of God (1:18), and now his righteous judgment.

According to his works. Paul is quoting his Bible (Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12), and the psalm says it in the same breath as something else: “to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love. For you will render to a man according to his work.” And “each one”: no one will be graded on a curve against the people around him or lost in a crowd, which is unnerving, and is also the only arrangement that could be just (Matthew 16:27; Revelation 20:12).

The Judge who comes back for his own. The balance can be changed: not by a man improving his deposits, the one remedy that cannot work, but by his being credited with an account that was never his, Christ’s righteousness. For those who trust him, the wrath they had stored up was poured out at the cross, on the Son. And the Judge is the same Jesus who rescues his people: believers “wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come” (1 Thessalonians 1:10). The impenitent are storing up wrath against that day; those joined to Christ are waiting for it, because the Judge who comes is their Saviour coming back for them.

In everyday life. Take something you know is wrong in your life and ask what has actually happened about it in six months: real change, or only a cycle of failure, discomfort and private promises? A heart that repents moves; a heart that merely regrets goes in circles. If you find yourself in that circle, do not conclude you are lost (see the note on vv. 7–8).

What it does not mean. If you are afraid this describes you, take the fear as good news (see the note on vv. 3–4): a callus does not worry about itself. Grief, depression and dry seasons are not hardness either.

Does judgment by works contradict justification by faith? No; they answer different questions. Works are produced in court as evidence, not paid at the counter. Nobody is saved by evidence, and there will be evidence: the tree is not made alive by its fruit, but at harvest the inspection is of fruit. And the only people found with good evidence will be those already justified freely by faith, whose lives the Spirit has begun to change.

Will Christians be judged too? Yes, but not to decide whether we belong to God: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). What that day means for a believer is set out at v. 16.

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

verseByVerse.quote: to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life; but for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives eternal life to those whose lives patiently seek his glory, and wrath to those who live for themselves and obey unrighteousness. How anyone comes to walk the first road is the gospel Paul is about to explain.

Patience in well-doing. Taken alone, this sounds like salvation by works, from the apostle who says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (3:28; see the box below). But “patience” (hypomonē) is steady endurance under weight, and “seek” means a life aimed at God’s glory and the immortality only he can give, still after it rather than arrived. Paul describes not a spotless record but the direction a life faces over time.

Glory, honour and immortality. Paul does not contrast the successful with the failing but those who seek these things with those who are self-seeking. Both are seeking; the last day asks what the life was after. Wanting glory, honour and immortality is not condemned as ambition. It is the right ambition. Our desires are not too strong but too weak: the self-seeking (selfish ambition; on the word, see below) wanted glory for themselves, and settled for a cheap version of it. And “obey unrighteousness” shows sin not as mere weakness but as loyalty to another master, willingly served.

The one who kept these terms. If you have read verse 7 and concluded that you fall short, you have read it correctly; the man who thinks he qualifies has misread it. Christ endured with patience, did good without a break, sought his Father’s glory and not his own, and never once obeyed unrighteousness. He met verse 7 in full, and the eternal life he merited is given to people who plainly did not merit it. Your patient well-doing is not the payment for it but the evidence that it has already been given to you.

I keep falling into the same sin. Does that mean I am not persevering? No. Perseverance is not sinlessness; Paul assumes interruption, which is why his word is patience. The question is the direction of travel and what you do when you fall. A believer falls and gets up again, hates the sin, confesses it and fights it, sometimes for years (7:15–25; 1 John 1:8–9). What Scripture warns against is the settled life that has made peace with sin and stopped fighting. If you are grieved by your sin and still running to Christ with it, that grief and that running are themselves the Spirit’s work in you.

Where Christians differ: who receives eternal life in vv. 7, 10 and 13? Those who hold firmly to justification by faith alone read them in two main ways. The first (Douglas Moo, for example) sees these verses as God’s standard in principle: if anyone did persist in doing good, he would receive eternal life; but Paul will show in 3:9–20 that no one does, so the verses shut every mouth and drive us to Christ. The terms are honest, like a scholarship advertised for candidates with a flawless record: the money is real, though nobody collects. The second (C. E. B. Cranfield and Thomas Schreiner, for example) sees them as describing real people: believers whose lives, changed by the Spirit, show persevering good works, and whom God will vindicate on the last day. In support, the law-keeping Gentile later in this chapter has a heart circumcised by the Spirit (vv. 26–29), and those who sow to the Spirit reap eternal life (Galatians 6:8). This commentary’s view: the second reading is most likely, and the first contains an important truth. God’s judgment will follow the evidence of a person’s life (v. 6), and the only people found persevering in good will be those whom God has justified freely by faith and renewed by his Spirit (Ephesians 2:8–10; Philippians 1:6). Their good works are not the ground of their acceptance, which is Christ’s righteousness alone (3:21–26), but its fruit and evidence. And no one can reach this standard by the law in his own strength, which is exactly what Paul goes on to prove.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s word for “self-seeking” (eritheia) is rare before the New Testament; Aristotle uses it of men canvassing selfishly for public office. Older translations linked it with the word for strife and rendered it “contentious” (the King James Version). The likely meaning is selfish ambition, the opposite of seeking God’s glory.

verseByVerse.quote: There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek, but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Evil leads to distress and good to glory and peace, for every human being alike, and the Jew, first in privilege, is first in responsibility. Paul sets the two destinies out a second time, now in reverse order: evil first, then good.

Tribulation and distress. The words are concrete. Tribulation is pressure, the crushing of something under weight. Distress pictures a narrow space: hemmed in, with no room to turn. Paul pictures the outcome of a life apart from God not as a distant fire but as a closing in.

The shape of sin. Every temptation presents itself as an enlargement: more freedom, more experience. Then watch what it delivers over twenty years. The man ruled by drink ends with a world the size of one room. The bitter woman ends with a life organised around a single grievance she can no longer put down. The pornography habit that promised variety produces a man who cannot look at his own wife properly. Whatever is finally meant by tribulation and distress, it is this, continued, with the restraints gone.

Glory and honour and peace. Verse 7 promised immortality; here the third word is peace, shalom: not merely the absence of conflict but everything in its proper place, working. The contrast is expansion against contraction: a life given room to become what it was made for, or a life closing in until nothing is left but the thing it chose.

The Jew first and also the Greek. The phrase of 1:16, now cutting the other way. There the Jew was first to be offered salvation; here he is first to face judgment. First in privilege, first in responsibility. Amos put it bluntly: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos 3:2). To whom much was given, of him much will be required (Luke 12:48).

The light that walked their streets. Israel’s highest privilege was not the law or the temple but the Messiah himself, born of their race and sent first to them: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). And Jesus taught this verse before Paul wrote it: woe to Chorazin and Bethsaida, for if the mighty works done in them had been done in Tyre and Sidon, those cities would have repented long ago (Matthew 11:21–22). Every reader who has heard the gospel of that same Christ sits in the seat of Chorazin and Bethsaida, and the seat is also a mercy: the light that increases the reckoning is the very gospel that has come to you.

Who is first today? The person raised in a Christian home who cannot remember not knowing the gospel. The one who has sat under good preaching for thirty years, owns four Bibles, could answer any doctrinal question, and has friends who pray for him by name. Each is a mercy, and this verse quietly turns each into something to answer for. The most dangerous seat in any church is not the back row. It is the one occupied by somebody who has heard everything and been changed by very little.

verseByVerse.quote: For God shows no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God judges without favouritism: nothing a person brings can raise him in God’s eyes, and nothing he lacks can lower him. This is the reason behind verses 6–10, and verses 12–16 show how it works for those with the law and those without it.

No partiality. The Greek word is literally “face-receiving”: a judge who lifts the bowed head of the man before him and favours him because he is somebody, which Israel’s law forbade (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 10:17). Paul applies the oldest principle in Israel’s law to Israel: God will not lift your face because of anything you bring to court.

Peter learned it the hard way. It took a vision and a two-day journey. Standing in a Gentile’s house, Peter began: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality” (Acts 10:34). He was watching a wall come down that he had believed held up the roof.

The lifter of my head. Yet the psalmist could say, “you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head” (Psalm 3:3). By the end of this letter it is clear how a guilty man has his head lifted in that courtroom: not because the Judge was impressed by him, but because the Judge’s own Son stood in his place. He is “Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him” (10:12; Acts 10:36). Even his enemies said it of Jesus, meaning it as flattery: “you do not care about anyone’s opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances” (Matthew 22:16). He ate with tax collectors and touched lepers. Every face that comes to him meets the same welcome, because the only thing he looks for is the one thing he gives: faith in himself. The impartiality that closes every door in chapter 2 opens one door for everyone in chapter 3 (3:22–23).

No face raised, no face lowered. Nothing you bring can raise your chin: not your family, not having been in church since you were four, not your giving, competence or reputation. But run it the other way, the half that goes unpreached: if no advantage lifts a face, no disadvantage lowers one. God is not more ready to hear the articulate, the theologically trained or those whose lives look tidy. The woman who cannot pray aloud, the man who came to Christ at sixty with a wrecked history, the believer with a criminal record: none is further down the list, because there is no list. Impartiality is terrifying to anyone trading on advantage, and the best news in the world to anyone who has none.

In everyday life. James makes it a rule about Sunday morning: if a man in fine clothes is given the good seat and the poor man told to stand, have you not become judges with evil thoughts (James 2:1–4)? The modern version is who gets followed up after missing three weeks, and which visitor is introduced to someone and which gets a handshake at the door. Take the last two conversations you had at church and ask what those people could do for you. Then, since Christ welcomed you when you could do nothing for him (15:7), seek out the person who can do nothing for you at all, and whose company is slightly hard work.

Does impartiality mean God loves everyone the same? It means no status can move his judgment, and his love cannot be bought. It does not mean he has no particular love for particular people; chapter 8 insists on the opposite in some of the warmest words Paul ever wrote. God has no favourites in judgment, and yet he has a people he loves with a special and extravagant love.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified. — Romans 2:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone will be judged by the light he actually had, and what counts before God is not hearing his law but doing it. Those without Moses’ law perish for sins against what they knew; those who have it are judged by it.

Without the law. Paul builds a symmetry: sinned without the law, perish without the law; sinned under the law, judged by the law. There is real mercy in that: the tribesman who never heard of Sinai will not be tried by Sinai. But the mercy does not end where we would like. He is judged by less, and he still perishes, for sins against what he knew (1:20; 2:15). Fewer rules did not mean he kept them.

Not the hearers. “Hearers” (akroatai) would have stung a Jewish reader. Israel’s central confession begins “Hear, O Israel”, and every Sabbath in every synagogue in Rome the law was read aloud to people who had come specifically to hear it. Paul says that what was done faithfully every Sabbath for a lifetime will not make one person righteous. Our generation, with preaching on every device, faces the same danger, because hearing feels like doing: a person can feel recognition, warmth and resolve every week for a lifetime and be unaltered, deceiving himself (James 1:22).

The doers of the law who will be justified. “Will be justified” (dikaiōthēsontai) is future, at the final judgment, and it is the letter’s first use of the verb. It belongs in a law court, and means not to make someone good but to declare him in the right: Moses tells judges to acquit the innocent and condemn the guilty (Deuteronomy 25:1), and the Greek Old Testament uses this very verb for acquit. In principle a perfect law-keeper would be justified; but no one is one (3:10, 20, 23), so this shuts the mouth of anyone relying on having the law. Yet it also points forward: those justified by faith in Christ and given the Spirit begin truly to do what the law requires (8:4), and on the last day God will acknowledge them as righteous.

The one doer of the law. If only doers are justified and no one does, the door is closed, unless a doer could be found who stands for others. Paul names him: “as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (5:19). Jesus is the doer of the law in the full sense: not a hearer who agreed with it but a man who did all of it, every day, from the manger to the cross: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). The doers of the last day are those clothed in his doing and changed by his Spirit, and their own doing, never perfect, is accepted for his sake.

Two kinds of hearing. Here hearers are not justified; eight chapters later “faith comes from hearing” (10:17). Both are true, because there are two kinds of hearing. One receives information and files it, which changes nothing and can go on for a lifetime. The other is the hearing a drowning man does when someone on the bank tells him where the rope is. That kind is not the opposite of doing. It is the first thing a man does, and the only kind that has ever justified anybody.

In everyday life. Listen for the sentence “yes, that is a good point” in your own mouth this week, after a sermon, a book, or a friend who told you the truth about yourself. It sounds like agreement and works as a full stop. After the next sermon, ask the Spirit to work that word into you, and before you leave the building name one specific thing you will do differently, and tell someone.

Where Christians differ: does Paul teach salvation by works here? Roman Catholic teaching, and some recent scholars, read vv. 6–13 as teaching that final justification depends in part on the good works a person does with God’s help. This commentary’s view: no. Paul establishes that God judges according to deeds, and that hearing or possessing the law saves no one. He then shows that no one meets the law’s standard (3:9–20), so justification must be by faith apart from works (3:21–28; 4:4–5). The good works of believers are the evidence of a true and living faith, not its ground: we are justified by faith alone, and judged according to works that show whether that faith was real (James 2:14–26). Romans 2 and Romans 3 do not contradict each other: the first shows the standard and the evidence; the second, the only ground of acceptance.

verseByVerse.quote: For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even people without God’s written law know his moral law, because it is written into human nature, and their conscience testifies to it. So no one will stand before God without having known better.

By nature do what the law requires. Gentiles without Moses’ law still often honour parents, refuse murder and keep promises. This is common grace: the goodness God shows to all people, believers or not, by which he restrains evil and leaves a sense of right and wrong in every heart (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). Paul is not teaching that they can be saved by following conscience, but that they are accountable.

They are a law to themselves. Not that they make up their own rules, but that their own nature carries God’s law within it, as part of the image of God.

Their conscience also bears witness. Conscience (syneidēsis) means co-knowing: the strange fact that a human being can stand at a slight distance from himself and pass judgment on what he finds. A dog can fear consequences; it cannot lie awake at four in the morning because of what it said to somebody in 1998. Paul describes a courtroom, with a witness and thoughts that accuse and excuse; even the excusing is revealing: nobody mounts a defence in a court he does not believe exists.

The defence the conscience cannot make. The word for “excuse” is the word for a defence in court. The conscience can argue a man’s case, but it cannot win it. The gospel does not tell the accused that his conscience is lying; it brings in a defence no conscience could mount, a Saviour who does not plead that the charges are false but pleads his own death: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died, more than that, who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us” (8:33–34).

Conscience is a witness, not the judge. A witness can be mistaken: it can testify from a distorted upbringing, a frightening father, or a church that taught a rule God never made. It fails in two opposite ways. One conscience will not stop accusing, and believers confess the same forgiven sin nightly for years. To them Scripture says, “whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (1 John 3:20), including what his Son has done. The other is the conscience seared like scar tissue (1 Timothy 4:2), which is quiet, and whose quietness is its danger.

In everyday life. Do not ask whether you feel guilty; that measures how loud your conscience is, not whether it is right. Ask of the last thing it convicted you about: can I name the command of God this broke? If so, that is real conviction, and the answer is repentance, not reassurance; if nothing is behind it but a vague feeling of not being good enough, it may be a witness giving evidence it does not have. And does this drive me toward God or away from him? The Spirit’s conviction is specific and takes you to the cross. The accuser is vague, and always advises you to keep your distance for a while.

Should I always follow my conscience? Never act against it, but always be willing to have it corrected. To do what you believe is wrong is sin, even if the thing is allowed, because it is not done in faith (14:23). But a conscience can be too strict or too loose, and must be trained by Scripture. When it troubles you about something God’s word does not forbid, do not simply override it: study Scripture, ask mature believers, and let the truth reshape it over time. When it is silent about something God’s word condemns, believe the word over the silence.

If the law is written on every heart, why do cultures disagree so much about right and wrong? Less than it seems, and mostly about how to apply what they know. No culture admired the man who betrays his friends or abandons his children; every people has some form of honesty, justice, care for the weak and keeping of promises, even where it draws the circle of who counts far too small. Paul has already explained the disagreement that remains: human beings suppress the truth they know (1:18), and a conscience resisted long enough grows callous (Ephesians 4:19). The remarkable thing is not that the writing has been smudged but that it has never been rubbed out. Even the man who says all morality is relative protests the moment someone wrongs him.

Where Christians differ: who are these Gentiles? Some, from Augustine to Cranfield, take them to be Gentile Christians, in whom the new covenant writes the law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Others say Paul means unbelieving Gentiles who show moral awareness. This commentary’s view: the context points to unbelieving Gentiles. Paul is still proving that everyone is accountable (1:18–3:20); he speaks of what Gentiles do “by nature”, of a conscience that accuses (v. 15), and of people who “perish without the law” (v. 12). Jeremiah promised the law itself written on the heart; Paul speaks here of the work of the law, its demands. This is not saving obedience, but evidence of accountability.
verseByVerse.note: Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong that God has given to every person.

parallels.desc: I will write it on their hearts

verseByVerse.quote: on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the last day God will judge everything, even hidden thoughts and motives, and he will do it through Jesus Christ; Paul counts this as part of his good news. Nothing is hidden from him (1 Corinthians 4:5; Hebrews 4:13).

In the flow. The chapter began with a man judging others (v. 1); this movement ends with the true Judge, preparing for 3:21–26: no better-looking record can save, only a righteousness God himself provides.

According to my gospel. Judgment is not the awkward small print at the end of the good news; Paul files it under the good news: not that there is no judgment, but that there is a way to be safe in it, and that the universe is just. Ask whom it is good news for: the woman whose abuser was never charged and kept his job and his pew; a family whose village was burned by men who were promoted afterwards. The world has told each of them the file is closed. This verse says the file is open, the evidence is kept, and a date has been set. A universe with no judgment is not gentler. It is one in which the powerful got away with it permanently.

The hidden good. Jesus said: give in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:4). That day does not uncover only hidden wrong. The eleven years of caring for a parent with dementia that nobody watched; the money given quietly by a man everyone thought was tight-fisted: none of it was recorded by anyone else, and none of it was lost. For a great many obscure people, that day will be the first time anyone has seen what they actually did with their lives.

By Christ Jesus. Jesus is the judge (Acts 17:31; John 5:22). The Father has given him authority to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man (John 5:27): because he is human. He was poor, exhausted, misrepresented, betrayed by a friend, and tried in a rigged court himself. Nobody will be able to say the Judge did not understand the circumstances. And he will learn nothing new that day: he went to the cross already holding the complete file. You were found out long ago, and he came anyway.

Should I be afraid of that day as a Christian? Not of condemnation, because your standing was settled in another court, at the cross: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). What is assessed for a believer is his work, not his welcome, and Scripture is honest that some work will not survive the fire, while he himself will be saved (1 Corinthians 3:15). Loss is possible; losing Christ is not. So the right response is not dread but honesty now: bring your secrets into the light with God, confess them, and where it is right, to a trusted believer (James 5:16). What is confessed now is covered.

Uncertain wording. How verse 15 joins verse 16 is not clear. Read straight on, conscience accuses or excuses “on that day”, yet it plainly works now. Some translations (the King James Version among them) bracket the verses before, so that “on that day” completes vv. 12–13. Others take Paul to mean that conscience’s present verdicts will be laid open on that day. Either way the likely sense is the same: conscience bears witness now, and on that day its testimony, with every secret, will be brought into the open.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–29 — The Failure of Israel: Circumcision of the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having God’s law and the sign of his covenant does not make anyone his; only a heart he has changed does. Paul lists the Jew’s real privileges and his confidence in them (vv. 17–20), then asks whether the teacher keeps what he teaches (vv. 21–22). Breaking the law, he dishonours God, whose name is blasphemed among the nations because of his people (vv. 23–24). Circumcision is worthless without obedience, and the uncircumcised man who keeps the law will condemn the one who has the sign (vv. 25–27). The true Jew is one inwardly, circumcised in heart by the Spirit, as Moses and the prophets promised, and his praise comes from God (vv. 28–29).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Purpose and Limits of the Law

Romans 2:17–29 is the letter’s first extended treatment of what the law can and cannot do. Of the law’s three uses Calvin named (to reveal sin, to restrain wickedness, to guide the redeemed life), Paul is drawing on the first. The Jew who has the law has a clearer mirror than the Gentile, and so a clearer sight of his own failure. The law cannot save; it exposes the need for a Saviour, which is why chapters 3–4 follow: the righteousness the law demands but cannot provide is given freely in the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Circumcision was the defining covenant mark in Paul’s day, and to question its saving value was to question the whole shape of Jewish identity. Paul shows that the sign without the inward reality condemns rather than protects. Now: The same holds for any outward mark Christians trust instead of the heart changed by the Spirit (see the note on vv. 25–26).

verseByVerse.quote: But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God and know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jew’s privileges were real, God’s law, a relationship with God and a trained moral sense, but he had come to rest his confidence on having them.

But if you call yourself a Jew. Now Paul names his hearer: the Jew who has every privilege. He is setting out, for a mixed church, the argument he had pressed in synagogue after synagogue, so that Jewish believers could see why their privileges never saved them, and Gentile believers that the same verdict falls on everyone (3:9). Verses 17 to 20 are one long unfinished sentence, piling up claim after claim, until the questions of verse 21 bring it all down. And the name carries a pun that many readers hear Paul spring at the end of the chapter: Jew comes from Judah, named by his mother with the words “This time I will praise the LORD” (Genesis 29:35). Hold that until verse 29.

Rely on the law. “Rely” (epanapauē) means to rest on, to lean back, to settle one’s weight. The law was given as a path to walk, and he has made furniture of it. A path only helps while you are moving along it; a chair helps most when you have stopped.

Boast in God. Boasting in God can be good: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31; compare 5:11). The fault is not that this man is proud of God, but that he is proud of having God. From inside the two are hard to tell apart; from outside the difference is plain. Boasting in God makes a person smaller and warmer. Boasting in having God makes him larger and colder.

Approve what is excellent. Literally to test and distinguish the things that differ: the verb used of the mind that refused to acknowledge God (1:28) and of the renewed mind that discerns his will (12:2). Paul credits him with a real privilege (9:4–5), and so removes his last excuse: his problem is plainly not that he cannot see.

Where the weight can rest. The trouble is not that this man leans; everyone leans on something. It is that the law was never built to take the weight of a sinner. It tells him what God requires, and then has nothing to give him when he fails. Paul will name what it was pointing to: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (10:4). And the one the law points to offers exactly what this man was looking for in the wrong place: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Paul’s word for rely and Jesus’ word for rest share the same root. The rest he wanted was a person all along.

In everyday life. When someone asks what you believe, listen to what comes out: a position, what your church teaches and where you stand relative to people who have it wrong, or a Person? Both may be orthodox. Only one sounds like someone who has met him.

verseByVerse.quote: and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s calling to teach the nations was real, but this man has turned the calling into a title, and a teacher can stand beside the truth without standing under it.

A guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness. Israel had been called to be a light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6), so these titles describe a real calling. But he recites them as honours, forgetting that a calling makes demands, and all four are teaching roles: not worshipper, servant or forgiven sinner, but a position above people who know less. Jesus called the Pharisees blind guides (Matthew 15:14; 23:16).

A teacher of children. Here is the occupational hazard of every teacher, parent, preacher and elder, and of the person in the small group who always knows the answer: not error, but a relationship to the truth that has become professional. He reads a passage and thinks it would make a good sermon; he hears a sermon and assesses it. None of it is dishonest, and all of it puts him beside the word rather than under it. The Bible stops being a word addressed to him and becomes material.

The embodiment of knowledge and truth. The law really did embody truth. The word (morphōsis) is the outline or shape of a thing, and here it is positive: the law is the outline of what God is like. But Paul uses the same word of “the appearance of godliness” without its power (2 Timothy 3:5). Everything depends on whether there is anything inside the shape. Having it is not obeying it.

The true Guide. One Teacher never stood beside the word, because he is the Word. The one true Guide to the blind did not stand in the dark giving instructions. He spat on the ground, made mud, anointed a blind man’s eyes and sent him to wash, and the man came back seeing (John 9:6–7). Then he said: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). The teachers who were sure they could see stayed blind, and the beggar who knew he was blind went home with eyes: he does not hand the blind a lecture; he gives them sight.

Should I stop teaching if I fall short of what I teach? No. Paul does not tell this man to put the law down; he asks, do you not teach yourself? The remedy for standing beside the word is not silence but getting back underneath it. Keep teaching, and let every passage you prepare speak to you first. A teacher who admits he needs it too teaches grace better than one who seems to have no struggles. If there is a sin you are living in, deal with it before God, and if it is serious, step back while it is put right. But the answer to hypocrisy is repentance, not resignation.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been called to be a light to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The teacher of the law breaks the law he teaches, so the law he points at others condemns him too. Paul does not accuse; he asks, and leaves the man alone with the answer.

You then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? The question brings the long boast of vv. 17–20 down. Tell a man what he is and he starts building a case; a question leaves him alone in the room with the answer. It is the method God used on the first man who hid from him: Adam was not handed a list of charges but asked, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). God knew the answer. The question was so that the man would have to say it himself.

While you preach against stealing, do you steal? Paul is not saying that Jewish people were characteristically thieves and adulterers; he puts to an imagined objector charges any moralist would recognise. He is a Jew himself, and will say he could wish himself cut off from Christ for their sake (9:3). The point is that the law you teach condemns you too, and Jesus showed that it reaches the heart: lust is adultery in the heart, and anger is murder in the heart (Matthew 5:21–28).

You who abhor idols, do you rob temples? The most searching of the three. Israel was forbidden not only to worship idols but to profit from them: “You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves” (Deuteronomy 7:25). Pagan temples were full of precious metal, money for anyone prepared to melt it down and ask no questions, and the charge was live: the town clerk of Ephesus defends Paul’s companions as “neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess” (Acts 19:37), using the word for temple-robbers. So the accusation is exact: you denounce idolatry at the front and take the silver off it at the back (on the wording, see below).

The den of robbers. Paul’s three charges, stealing, adultery, idols, were not first his. Jeremiah stood at the temple gate and asked: will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, make offerings to Baal, and then come and stand before me in this house and say, we are delivered? Has this house become a den of robbers in your eyes (Jeremiah 7:9–11)? Six centuries later Jesus overturned the tables in the same courts and turned that sentence on the men profiting from the worship of God: “you have made it a den of robbers” (Mark 11:17). He did not take a share at the back; he cleared it. And John records that at a cleansing of the temple he spoke of the temple of his own body, which they would destroy and he would raise in three days (John 2:19–21).

The shape of our inconsistency. That third question is the shape most of our hypocrisy takes: we rarely do the thing we condemn; we benefit from it. You do not spread the gossip; you listen to all of it. You disapprove of how a colleague got the result, and you were glad of the result. You have views about where money comes from, and there are questions about your own you have decided not to ask. You genuinely do abhor the idol. You simply also take the gold.

The law as a mirror. The Reformers said that the law’s first use is to show a person what he really is: a mirror, superbly designed to show you the dirt on your face, which has never once removed any of it. The error of the man in these verses is not that he owns a mirror. It is that he has framed it, hung it on the wall, and started showing it to visitors as evidence of how he looks. The mirror is meant to send us to the only place we can be washed.

Uncertain wording. “Rob temples” (hierosuleō) can mean robbing pagan shrines, as above; robbing God himself by withholding what is owed him (Malachi 3:8), as the Pharisees condemned idols while loving money (Luke 16:14); or sacrilege more widely. The likely meaning is the literal one, which makes the charge exact.

verseByVerse.quote: You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who boasts in the law dishonours God by breaking it. To claim God loudly and live as though he were not there is to misrepresent him.

Boast in the law, dishonour God. The section opened with a man who boasts in God (v. 17) and closes with one who boasts in the law, valued as a possession rather than a demand. The verdict is one heavy word: he dishonours God, as humanity did in chapter 1 (1:21, 24). The pagan dishonours God by worshipping something else; the religious man, by claiming him loudly and living as though he were not there.

Why it is worse. A man who makes no profession and does wrong damages himself; a man who has told everyone he belongs to God, and does the same, attaches God’s name to it. He has made a statement about what God is like, and others will believe it, because a life persuades more than a doctrine. Taking the Lord’s name in vain is not chiefly about swearing; it is carrying his name as though it weighed nothing. And it needs no scandal. It is the Christian known at work for being sharp about money; the father whose family go quiet when he comes in; the believer whose neighbours have concluded, without discussing theology, that whatever he has does not seem to make him kinder.

I honour my Father. Accused in the temple of having a demon, Jesus answered that he honoured his Father, and they dishonoured him (John 8:49). They carried the law and boasted in it, and dishonoured the Son; he carried the Father’s name through every hour of an ordinary life and never once took it in vain. At last the third commandment had someone who kept it.

Does my failure really damage God’s honour? Not God himself: he is no more diminished by being misrepresented than the sun is dimmed by a bad photograph of it. What is at stake is what the people around you are being shown. So do not hide failure, which adds a lie to the sin, but own it: when you have dishonoured Christ in front of others, say so plainly to them, apologise without excuses, and put right what you can. Nothing honours God in front of unbelievers more than a Christian who admits he was wrong and shows where he goes for forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: For, as it is written, "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world forms its opinion of God from the people who carry his name, so the sins of his people bring his name into contempt. Christians who live badly bring reproach on the name of Christ (1 Timothy 6:1; Titus 2:5).

As it is written. The words come from Isaiah 52:5, with an echo of Ezekiel 36:20. In the prophets the nations mocked God’s name because Israel had been defeated and exiled; Paul applies the sentence to what is done by God’s people rather than to them.

Ezekiel’s answer. Ezekiel 36 does not stop at verse 20. In the same chapter God announces the remedy: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26), exactly where Paul is going in five verses (v. 29). His people had dragged his reputation through the nations, and God did not demand that they repair it; he undertook to repair it himself, by changing them from the inside. The name blasphemed because of us will finally be honoured because of what he does in us.

Isaiah’s answer. Isaiah 52 does not stop at verse 5 either. At the end of the chapter the Servant appears: high and lifted up, his appearance marred beyond human semblance, sprinkling many nations (52:13–15; Paul quotes that last verse in 15:21), the passage that runs straight into Isaiah 53. The name blasphemed among the nations because of Israel’s failure is vindicated among the nations by Israel’s Messiah, despised and rejected, who bore the sin of many. Ezekiel promises the new heart; Isaiah shows the Servant whose suffering pays for it.

Hypocrisy is not persecution. When a church covers up the abuse of children to protect its reputation, when a ministry’s finances turn out to be a private fortune, when a celebrated preacher was a different man off the platform, the contempt that follows is not persecution. It is an accurate response to the evidence, and Christians should be the last to confuse the two. Peter draws the line: let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer, but if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed (1 Peter 4:15–16). Being despised for the cross is an honour; being despised for hypocrisy is a debt we have earned. When such things are exposed, the right response is truth, justice for the wronged and repentance, never protecting the institution.

Because of you. But do not let the headline scandals take this verse off your own shoulders. Paul writes “because of you”, to the same single man he has been questioning. Nobody in your street has met a famous pastor; they have met you. Their working theory of what God does to a person is assembled from two or three Christians they happen to know, in unguarded moments, and that sample includes you.

parallels.desc: my name is continually despised

verseByVerse.quote: For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant sign has value only with the obedience it signifies; without it the sign is empty, and God can count an outsider whose heart he has changed as one of his own.

Circumcision indeed is of value. Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham (Genesis 17), the mark of belonging to God’s people, permanent on the body, the one credential a Jewish man could not lose; some Jewish teachers, in sayings preserved in later rabbinic writings, held that it guaranteed a place in the age to come. Paul grants that God gave it and that it meant something. What he denies is that it works on its own, regardless of the life attached to it.

Your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. The sign without the reality is worthless, and Paul is not spiritualising Moses but following him. The command to circumcise the heart is in the law itself (Deuteronomy 10:16), and Jeremiah said it six hundred years earlier: the days are coming when God will punish all who are circumcised merely in the flesh, for all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:25–26). A sign does not work automatically. A wedding ring has never kept anyone faithful; on the hand of a man conducting an affair it does not become neutral. It becomes a lie in metal.

If a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law. Who is this man? Some take him as hypothetical, like the doers of the law in v. 13. Others take him as a real person, a Gentile believer whose heart the Spirit has changed, so that the law’s requirement is beginning to be fulfilled in him (8:4). The second is more likely, because Paul is moving toward the circumcision by the Spirit of v. 29. Such a man’s obedience is not perfect and is not the ground of his acceptance, but the evidence of a heart God has circumcised. And “regarded” is an accountant’s word, to credit to an account. It will dominate chapter 4, where Abraham believes God and it is counted to him as righteousness. Here, the first time the letter uses it of crediting, God is counting an outsider in.

The one on whom the sign was true. At the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus (Luke 2:21). Born of woman, born under the law, he kept the covenant from the inside, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). On every other body the sign stood beside a broken law; on his it never lied. Because of him Paul can say: “in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). The outsider is counted in because he is in Christ.

A lesson for baptism and the Lord’s Supper. So with the signs Christ has given his church: valuable and commanded, they do not save without faith. This commentary holds believer’s baptism, because in the New Testament baptism follows repentance and faith and declares them (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:12); many faithful Christians baptise the infants of believers as a sign of God’s covenant promise, and they too insist that the sign never replaces faith. Few today trust in circumcision; many trust in an event: a decision at fourteen at a summer camp, a card signed, a baptism, a week when everything seemed clear. The event may have been entirely genuine. Paul’s question is whether the thing it signified is present now.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s signs are unimportant; Paul says the opposite in his first words. Nor does a conversion you can barely remember mean no real faith: assurance was never meant to rest on your memory of the beginning. Nobody proves he is alive by producing a birth certificate. A person who cannot date his conversion and loves Christ today is in an incomparably better position than one with a certificate and no pulse.

How can I know my faith is real? Look for present evidence. Do you trust Christ alone for forgiveness, not your record? Do you hate your sin and fight it, even when you lose? Do you love other believers and want to be with them (1 John 3:14)? Do you want to obey God, and grieve when you do not? Is Christ precious to you? None needs to be strong, only real. And the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (8:16). If you find these marks, however weak, take comfort. If you find none, do not despair: go to Christ now, because he receives everyone who comes.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the last day the obedient outsider will stand as evidence against the insider who had the law and the sign but did not keep them.

Will condemn you. The man who has spent the chapter as a judge now faces the last witness he expected: the uncircumcised outsider he had been instructing, who condemns him not by argument but by an obedient life. Jesus used the same device: the men of Nineveh and the queen of the South will rise up at the judgment and condemn this generation, because they responded to less, and something greater is here (Matthew 12:41–42). They did with a candle what others would not do with the sun.

The written code. “Written code” (gramma) is the letter: the outward, written law, without the Spirit. The code and the mark had become part of his problem, giving him a reason not to look at himself. A man with no credentials at least knows he has nothing to plead. Give him a credential and you have handed him somewhere to hide.

The faith Jesus marvelled at. Jesus acted out this verse himself. When a Roman centurion, uncircumcised and without the law, trusted his word to heal a servant at a distance, Jesus marvelled: “with no one in Israel have I found such faith. I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness” (Matthew 8:10–12). The outsider condemns the insider not by being cleverer but by trusting the Christ the insider would not receive. The verdict of the last day turns on Christ.

In everyday life. Think of a believer you find slightly irritating: the recent convert with no advantages, whose zeal seems naive and whose theology is thin, and whose obedience is not. Sometimes the irritation is real discernment. Very often it is the discomfort of watching someone do easily what you have stopped doing, and the quickest way to manage that feeling is to find something in him to correct. Instead, thank God for him, and ask him what has been helping him.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. His praise is not from man but from God. — Romans 2:28–29
verseByVerse.commentary:
Belonging to God’s people is not a matter of outward birth or ritual but of a heart God himself has changed by his Spirit, and such a person’s praise comes from God. Paul defines Jewish identity from the inside out, completing the logic of the Old Testament itself.

Circumcision is a matter of the heart. The Old Testament already said it (Jeremiah 4:4), and Moses says it twice: first as a command, “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart” (Deuteronomy 10:16), and later, when it was plain no one had, as a promise: “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart” (Deuteronomy 30:6). The prophets never promised that Israel would try harder; they promised that God would operate. And circumcision was done to a man, not by him: an eight-day-old boy contributes nothing, and someone else holds the knife, which is why it produces no boast. Moses says in the same verse what it is for: “so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.” The hard covering is cut away, and a person who once found God dull or threatening now loves him and wants to obey him.

By the Spirit, not by the letter. The Spirit does what the written law cannot: he changes the heart (2 Corinthians 3:6; Ezekiel 36:26–27). The contrast is not between spirit and law as such, but between the outward written requirement and the inward power of the Spirit, who creates the obedience the law commands but cannot produce.

His praise is not from man but from God. Remember what Jew means: Judah, named with the words “This time I will praise the LORD.” So the closing line is a definition delivered as a pun: the true Praise is the one whose praise comes from God. Jesus asked the religious leaders of his day: “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?” (John 5:44). The contrast is not between external and sincere (chapters 12–16 will demand very visible obedience) but between what people can see and award, and what God sees and awards. Only God can see the circumcision Paul describes, so only God can praise it.

In the flow. So ends Paul’s case against the religious man. It raises two objections he takes up at once (3:1, 3), and the Spirit named here in a single phrase will fill chapter 8.

The circumcision of Christ. The New Testament names where the operation is done: “In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ” (Colossians 2:11). It happens in union with Christ, and the Spirit he pours out (Acts 2:33) performs it. His death and resurrection, and his Spirit given to all joined to him, are the cutting away of the old life and the beginning of the new. The circumcision of verse 29 is not a better human effort. It is Christ’s work, applied.

The first entirely accurate sentence about your life. Paul has spent a whole chapter taking away every commendation human beings can give, so that God can give one they cannot take back. The Christian nobody notices will not be asked for the platform, the record or the esteem of respectable people. It will come from the one who saw all of it, what was done badly and what was done at cost and never noticed, and it will be spoken because of his Son: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21). Nothing in it will be exaggerated, because he has no need to flatter, and nothing will be left out. It will be the first entirely accurate sentence ever spoken about your life.

Then do Jewish people today need Christ to be saved? Yes, and Paul says so with tears. The heart-circumcision Moses promised comes only through the Spirit whom Christ gives, and there is no other name by which anyone is saved (Acts 4:12). That is why Paul’s heart’s desire and prayer for Israel was that they might be saved (10:1), and why he went to the synagogue first in city after city. Love for Jewish people, and gratitude for the Messiah who came from them, mean sharing him with them, humbly and gladly, never with contempt.

How do I live for his praise rather than people’s? Notice whose reaction you check after you speak, post something or serve. In Christ the decisive word has already been spoken. Over him the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and those who belong to him are blessed “in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6). You do not have to win from people what you already have from God. Do some good in secret on purpose: give, pray and help where no one will ever find out, because your Father sees in secret (Matthew 6:3–4, 6). Let praise pass through you to him. When criticism comes, ask whether it is true and change if it is, but do not let it reach the place where your worth is kept. That place is in Christ, and only his Father’s voice is heard there.

Where Christians differ: has the church replaced Israel? Some read this verse as saying that Gentile believers are now the true Jews, linking it with Philippians 3:3, “we are the circumcision”. This commentary’s view: that is not quite what this verse says. Paul is still speaking to the Jew of v. 17, and he is saying who is a Jew in the full sense: not everyone with the outward mark, but the one whose heart God has changed, as Moses and the prophets had said all along (compare 9:6). He does not erase Israel. In the next breath he asks what advantage the Jew has and answers, much in every way (3:1–2), and chapters 9–11 still speak of Israel as a people with a future in God’s purposes. Gentile believers belong to Abraham’s family by faith (4:11–12; Galatians 3:29), but this verse makes a narrower point: within Israel the outward mark never made anyone God’s.

keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this short sentence. Neither the moralist’s verdicts on others (vv. 1–5) nor the law, the teaching and the covenant sign (vv. 17–29) can move the Judge, who looks at the truth of a life down to its secrets. The same impartiality that shuts every mouth here opens one door for everyone in 3:22: the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe.

2.reflection:
Paul catches the reader who has been agreeing with chapter 1 (v. 1). Why is it so easy to judge others by their actions and ourselves by our intentions? Where do you most often do it?

Verse 4 says God’s kindness and patience are meant to lead us to repentance. How can a long experience of God’s goodness make a person comfortable rather than repentant, and how does the cross (3:25) show that his patience is not indifference?

Paul names real privileges: the law, sound teaching, the covenant sign (vv. 17–20, 25). What are their equivalents in church life today, and how can we tell whether we are resting on them or on Christ?

Verse 29 says the true member of God’s people has a heart changed by the Spirit, and receives praise from God, not from people. Whose verdict do you find yourself waiting for, and how does Christ’s welcome free you from needing it?

3.title: No One Righteous — But Now, Righteousness
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 is the hinge of Romans. Paul closes the case he opened at 1:18 until “every mouth” is stopped; then, with “But now” (v. 21), he announces the righteousness from God that the whole letter exists to explain.

The message. Every human being stands guilty before God with nothing to say in his defence, and no one will be put right with him by keeping the law. But God has provided what we could never bring: his own righteousness, given freely to all who believe in Jesus, through Christ’s death as the sacrifice that turns away his wrath. So God stays perfectly just while he justifies the guilty.

Why it was said. Paul’s preaching of free grace was charged with making Israel’s history pointless and with encouraging sin (v. 8; see the introduction). Jewish believers in Rome needed to hear that their privileges were real but could not save, and Gentile believers that they stood on equal terms.

How the chapter makes its case. Objections answered (vv. 1–8): Israel’s advantage was real, God stays faithful, and his bringing good out of sin does not excuse it. The verdict (vv. 9–20): a chain of Psalms and Isaiah walks down the human body, mind, mouth, feet and eyes, and finds no one righteous; the law stops every mouth and gives knowledge of sin, not justification. The remedy (vv. 21–26): God’s righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, so that he is “just and the justifier”. The consequences (vv. 27–31): boasting is shut out, Jew and Gentile are justified alike by faith, and the law is upheld.

Where it leads. The Judge himself supplies the righteousness the prisoners could never bring. At the cross the mercy seat, the holiest thing in Israel, was carried outside and shown to the world: God did not set his justice aside to forgive us, but satisfied it in his own Son. The righteousness of God that condemned us becomes the gift that clothes us, and every stopped mouth is opened to praise him.

For us. Stop defending yourself before God; your mouth is stopped so that it can be opened to call on Christ. Rest your standing on what he has done, not on your record. Leave no room for boasting or for looking down on anyone, and let the law stand at its full height, because you no longer need it to be easy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — God's Faithfulness and Human Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Human unfaithfulness cannot cancel God’s faithfulness, and his bringing good out of sin never excuses it. Israel’s advantage was real, above all that they were entrusted with God’s own words (vv. 1–2). If some proved faithless, God remains true, as David confessed after his own sin (vv. 3–4). Two objections then try to turn this into licence: if my sin shows off God’s righteousness, why punish it (vv. 5–6), and why not do evil that good may come (vv. 7–8)? Paul answers that God could then not judge the world, and condemns the slander behind the second; the full answer waits for chapter 6, and the question of Israel for chapters 9 to 11.
verseByVerse.theology:
God’s faithfulness and human failure

Can human sin defeat God’s purposes? Romans 3:3–4 answers that it cannot. Calvin wrote that God's truth stands firm even against the unfaithfulness of the whole world. So a Christian’s standing does not rest on his faithfulness but on God’s. He who called us is faithful; he will do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish readers would have welcomed Paul’s affirmation of Israel’s privileges and been troubled by his insistence that they gave no exemption from judgment. Now: Christians face the same tension. Scripture, preaching, baptism, the Lord’s Supper and prayer are real and great gifts, and none of them is a substitute for personal faith and repentance. Privilege and accountability travel together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being a Jew was a great privilege, above all because God entrusted Israel with his own words. Chapter 2 did not make the privilege worthless; it showed that privilege cannot save.

Then what advantage has the Jew? Paul has just argued that circumcision without obedience is worthless, and he knows what his hearer is thinking: then two thousand years of covenant history were wasted. A lesser writer would have let the misunderstanding stand. Paul stops his own case to answer a question against it, which is the difference between winning a debate and telling the truth.

Much in every way. Paul does not retreat an inch from chapter 2, and he will not let the privileges be belittled. In chapter 9 he lists them with an ache in his voice: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, the Christ (9:4–5). A gift can be magnificent and still not save the man holding it.

They were entrusted. Not the language of possession but of deposit: something handed to you that belongs to somebody else, and about which you will be asked. A trustee does not own the fund; he answers for it. A trust is the one kind of advantage that increases your liability instead of reducing it.
