The oracles of God. The things God actually said: the Scriptures, entrusted to Israel to keep and to pass on. Paul could have named the temple, the land or the throne; he names one thing. Other nations had priests who claimed to read the gods’ wishes from entrails, from stars, from the mutterings of a woman at Delphi. Israel had words the living God had spoken, in a known language, that could be copied, memorised, argued about and read aloud to a child, and he guarded them through exile, conquest and the slow centuries of copying. Every Gentile believer who opens the Psalms is in debt to the scribes of Israel who copied them letter by letter. The God who could have stayed silent chose to talk to his creatures, and the book on your table is the evidence that he has never stopped.

The trustee who kept the deposit. The trust was real, and so was the failure, for some were unfaithful (v. 3). But one son of Israel received the oracles exactly as they were meant to be received. He answered the tempter from Deuteronomy (Matthew 4:4) and went to his arrest saying that the Scriptures must be fulfilled (Mark 14:49). Then, risen, he opened the whole deposit to two disciples on a road: beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). Israel was entrusted with the words. Christ is what the words were saying.

The advantage we hold. A Christian holds this advantage more fully than Israel did: more of God’s speech than Isaiah ever saw, in a language you can read, probably in several copies. But a deposit does not benefit a man who never opens it. Scripture has no category called owning the word of God, only hearing it and doing it, or hearing it and not.

Do Jewish people still have an advantage today? Paul’s full answer belongs to chapters 9 to 11, and Christians who love those chapters read the details differently. But this much he says plainly: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (11:29), the privileges of 9:4–5 were never a mistake, and God has not rejected his people (11:1). What no privilege can do is justify. A Jewish heritage of Scripture, like a Christian upbringing, is a great mercy and a heavy responsibility, and it saves no one apart from faith in Christ. The fitting response of a Gentile believer is gratitude, not arrogance (11:18), and a longing that the people who gave us the Bible should receive its Messiah.

Is the Old Testament still God’s word for me? Yes, every page of it. Paul calls it the oracles of God and never treats it as out of date. Jesus said the Scriptures bear witness about him (John 5:39), and whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope (15:4). Not every command applies to you in the same way: the sacrifices are fulfilled in Christ, and Israel’s civil laws governed a nation. But all of it is God speaking, all of it points to his Son, and all of it is for you.
verseByVerse.note: “The oracles of God” are the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, "That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Human unfaithfulness cannot cancel God’s faithfulness: he stays true even if every person proves false. When he judges sin, as David confessed after his own, God is shown to be in the right.

What if some were unfaithful? The sentence turns on a play on words English cannot keep. Their faithlessness (apistia) and God’s faithfulness (pistis) are the same word in Greek, with a “not” in front of the first: does their un-faith cancel the faith of God? One is something real in God; the other is only something missing in us, and something missing cannot cancel something real. The dark in a room has never once put out a lamp.

By no means! The strongest negative Paul has (mē genoito), used ten times in this letter for a conclusion not merely wrong but intolerable. The older “God forbid” catches the tone: a man recoiling from a proposition, not weighing it.

Let God be true. God’s faithfulness does not depend on ours (2 Timothy 2:13). You have broken more vows to God than you can count; he is true, and will be when every liar has fallen silent. Sooner or later what God has said and what you can see will fail to agree. He says he works all things for good, and you are standing in a hospital corridor. He says he is near to the brokenhearted, and you have felt nothing for eight months. One of the two has to give, and Paul says which. Your eyes and your heart at four in the morning are admitted as evidence, and they lose, not because your experience is unreal, but because a witness who has been wrong before may not overrule one who never has.

Justified in your words. Psalm 51 is David after Bathsheba, after arranging for her husband, a loyal soldier, to be abandoned in the front line. That is the man who says, “Against you, you only, have I sinned”, and adds, “so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment” (Psalm 51:4). He agrees with the verdict in advance: when God judges him, God will be in the right. So God’s truthfulness is not damaged by human failure but displayed by it. God had said that men are sinners, and David turned out to be exactly that.

The truthfulness of God in person. Paul later names where this rule was proved: Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God’s truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs (15:8). He sent David’s Son, the one son of David who never needed a Psalm 51 of his own, and at the cross God was shown true in his warnings and his promises alike: justified in his words, because sin was judged exactly as he had said; faithful to his promise, because the judgment fell on that Son so that sinners like David could be forgiven.

What it does not mean. Not a call to pretend. Half the Psalter is people telling God exactly what they see, without editing. You may say that it looks as though he has forgotten you; you may not conclude it. Say the whole of what you see, then let his word have the last say.

In everyday life. Take the last time you were rebuked, by Scripture, a sermon, or someone who loved you enough to say it. Did you come out agreeing with God, or explaining yourself: the context, the tiredness, the other party’s share? David lets God be right about him. You can afford to: the verdict you are agreeing with has already fallen on David’s Son, and what comes back to you is forgiveness. So say the one specific thing to God in one plain sentence, with no clause beginning with but.

Did God’s faithfulness mean every Israelite was saved anyway? No. God is faithful to what he promised, and he never promised to save people who refused him: not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel (9:6). He kept his word by preserving a believing remnant, chosen by grace (11:5), and by sending the Messiah through Israel as he had said; he kept it too when he judged unbelief, because his covenant always carried warnings as well as promises. His faithfulness is not a guarantee that no one will be lost, but that nothing he has said will fail.

If I am faithless, will God still keep me? If you belong to Christ, yes: he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:13). But the line before it says, if we deny him, he also will deny us (2 Timothy 2:12). Paul distinguishes the believer who wavers, doubts and fails, as Peter did on the night of the trial, from the person who finally and deliberately turns his back on Christ. The first is held, because what holds him is God’s faithfulness, not his own grip; the second shows he never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). If you are worried about your faithlessness and still turning to Christ, that worry is a sign of life, not of abandonment.

parallels.desc: so that you may be justified in your words
all mankind are liars

verseByVerse.quote: But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.) By no means! For then how could God judge the world?
verseByVerse.commentary:
That God brings good out of our sin never makes the sin excusable, or he could not judge the world. An argument that would abolish the final judgment refutes itself.

If our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God. A twisted objection: if my sin makes God look good, why punish me? In modern dress: God gets glory from forgiving sinners; no sinners, no forgiveness, no glory; so my sin is, in a roundabout way, a service. Nobody says this aloud, but many run some version of it quietly, the oldest trick in the human repertoire: finding a way in which the thing you were going to do anyway turns out to be useful.

I speak in a human way. Paul flags his own sentence. He has voiced an argument close to blasphemy and will not leave it in the air with his name attached. Then he refutes it, not with philosophy, but with a question.

For then how could God judge the world? That is not evasion; it is the argument. Jew and Greek agreed that God will judge the world. Abraham had said it long ago: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). The objection, followed to its end, abolishes that fixed point: if evil that serves God’s glory cannot be punished, and all evil somehow serves his glory, nothing can be punished at all. The objector has not found a loophole; he has sawn off the branch he is sitting on. A God who did not punish evil would be a worse God, not a kinder one, and a Judge who could be argued out of a verdict by a clever man would protect nobody. You cannot talk him out of a just verdict, and neither can the person who wronged you; the widow, the orphan and the murdered have their hope in exactly that.

Good out of evil. God can and does bring good out of evil; that does not make him guilty of the evil, or the evil good. Joseph told his brothers so and softened neither half: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20).

The supreme instance. At the cross the worst act in human history accomplished the salvation of the world, and Peter puts both truths in one sentence: delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed him (Acts 2:23). Nobody at Pentecost heard that as an acquittal. And the unbending Judge of verse 6 is the one who, a few verses on, himself provides the sacrifice that turns his own wrath away (v. 25).

In everyday life. Watch when you reach for the sovereignty of God, because what matters is the tense. Looking back on something you regret, saying that God has brought good out of the wreckage is faith, and it is what Genesis 50:20 is for. Beforehand, while a decision is still open, “God can bring good out of this” is a permission slip, the objection of verse 5 in your own voice. It is worship in the past tense and self-permission in the future one.

Does God cause sin, then, if he uses it? No. Scripture holds two truths together without apology: God rules over all things, including the evil acts of men, and God is never the author of sin, and the men who do it are fully responsible (Westminster Confession 3.1; 5.4; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1; 5.4). Joseph’s brothers chose freely and wickedly; God overruled their choice for good. We cannot fully explain how both are true, any more than how one Person is both God and man, but we can see both in the same story and refuse to give up either. God’s sovereignty is a comfort when you are sinned against, and never an excuse when you are the one sinning.

parallels.desc: shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?

verseByVerse.quote: But if through my lie God's truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? And why not do evil that good may come? — as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Their condemnation is just.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Using God’s glory as a reason to sin is not a conclusion from the gospel but a slander on it, and those who argue that way are justly condemned. Paul blocks the road here and answers the question fully in chapter 6.

If through my lie God’s truth abounds to his glory. The same objection, made personal and pushed to its extreme: why not do evil that good may come, and maximise the glory by maximising the sin? Every attempt to turn God’s purposes into an excuse for sin ends here if it is followed honestly.

As some people slanderously charge us. The remarkable detail is the aside: people claimed this was Paul’s actual teaching. He had preached free grace so unreservedly, God justifying the ungodly, nothing to bring and nothing to pay, that respectable religious people concluded he must be telling converts sin no longer mattered (compare 6:1).

A test of preaching. Nobody seems to have accused the Pharisees of encouraging immorality, and a sermon about trying harder is seldom misheard as permission to sin. The charge of licence is only levelled at grace so free that it sounds dangerous. A gospel nobody could possibly abuse is usually a gospel with a condition quietly attached.

Their condemnation is just. Paul answers with a verdict, not an argument, and rightly. Some propositions are to be refused, not debated, because arguing them on their merits concedes they might have some. A man who asks whether it might be good to do evil has not made an error you can correct with information. He has revealed what he wants and dressed it up as logic.

Why the full answer waits. Paul returns to this exact question in chapter 6, “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?” (6:1), and the answer there is not a rule but a fact: you died to sin, so how can you still live in it? That answer needs union with Christ, not yet laid out, so here he simply blocks the road; three chapters later he shows you the country on the other side of it.

The friend of sinners. The slander was laid against Paul’s Master first. When Jesus ate with tax collectors, the respectable muttered, “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2), and called him “a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19). Jesus answered with the lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son, and then went to a cross where sin was taken more seriously than any Pharisee had ever taken it. The grace slandered as licence is the grace that cost him his life.

This is forgivable. The everyday form is subtler. What a man thinks, at eleven at night, is: this is forgivable. And it is; that is the whole trouble. Forgiveness is being used, in the moment before the act, to make the sin seem cheaper: the abuse not of a bad doctrine but of the best one there is. For a man who has understood the gospel, knowing what forgiveness cost makes the sin more expensive, not less. He is restrained not by fear of punishment, which was settled, but by something stronger: the difficulty of casually doing the thing that killed his friend.

I have used grace as an excuse before. Is there hope for me? Yes, and that it troubles you is part of the hope. The men of verse 8 were not troubled; they had turned grace into an argument. If you are grieved that you have treated forgiveness as a discount, grace is doing what it does: it trains us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12). Bring that very sin, the sin of presuming on him, to Christ, and he will forgive it as freely as any other (1 John 1:9). Then let the cost of the forgiveness, not the fear of losing it, make the next temptation heavier. Scripture warns not against a Christian who has fallen this way, but against a settled life that has made peace with it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — No One Is Righteous: The Verdict of Scripture
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every human being stands guilty before God with nothing to say in his defence. Jews are no better off than Gentiles: all are under sin’s power and guilt (v. 9). Paul proves it from Israel’s own Scriptures, a chain from the Psalms and Isaiah that finds no one righteous and walks down the whole person: mind and will (vv. 10–12), throat, tongue, lips and mouth (vv. 13–14), feet (vv. 15–17) and eyes (v. 18). Because the law speaks to those who have it, every mouth is stopped (v. 19). The law was never meant to supply righteousness but to show its absence (v. 20), so that the remedy, like the verdict, can be for all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total depravity

Romans 3:9–20 is the classic text for the doctrine of total depravity (defined in the box “Where Christians differ: how bad is human nature?” at vv. 11–12): sin has corrupted every part of human nature: the mind (“no one understands”), the will (“no one seeks for God”), the affections, the speech and the conduct. That is why Paul can say in v. 24 that justification is given freely: there is nothing in us that could earn it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The psalms Paul quotes were sung in the temple and prayed in the synagogue, and Israel heard them turned on her own guilt. Now: Many prefer to speak of human potential and say little about the fall. Romans 3:9–20 corrects that. The doctrine of depravity is not pessimism but realism, and realism about the disease is what makes us grateful for the cure.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin, as it is written: "None is righteous, no, not one;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jews stand before God no better than Gentiles: all alike are under the power and guilt of sin, and Scripture says that no one is righteous. Privilege is real, but it does not change the verdict.

Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. Privileges, yes; a better verdict, no. This does not contradict verse 2: the advantage was real, but in the courtroom having the law only means being judged by it, so Jew and Gentile stand together.

For we have already charged. The word belongs to a prosecutor bringing a formal accusation. Chapters 1 and 2 were the evidence, and the reader has been in a courtroom since 1:18.

Under sin. Paul does not say that all have committed sins, but that all are under sin: under its power and its guilt, as a soldier is under orders or a slave under a master (7:14; Galatians 3:22). The plural sins are the symptom; the singular Sin is the disease. If the problem were only sins, a man would need a pardon for his record; because it is Sin, a power he is under, he needs to be rescued. This letter says God did both, spending chapters 3 to 5 on the first and 6 to 8 on the second.

As it is written. Paul strings together quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah (Psalm 14:1–3; 53:1–3; 5:9; 140:3; 10:7; Isaiah 59:7–8; Psalm 36:1), as the rabbis argued. Israel found it easy to sing Psalm 14 about other people: the evildoers who eat up my people (Psalm 14:4), the wicked outside. Paul turns it on the very people who sang it, like a congregation indicted by its own hymnbook: everyone knows the tune, and this morning the words are about you.

No, not one. Paul closes the last exit, because the human mind, presented with a universal negative, hunts for the exception, usually itself.

Shut up to one door. Paul gives the purpose of this verdict elsewhere: the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe (Galatians 3:22). Every other exit is walled up so that one door is left, and it opens onto a Person. Christ came under the very things we are under: born under the law to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5), made sin for us though he knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). The verdict that shuts the whole human race in together sends the whole human race to the same Saviour.

But I know decent people. Of course. Paul has just conceded that Gentiles sometimes do by nature what the law requires (2:14). His claim is more serious: a man may be honest, generous, faithful to his wife and admired by all, and still live his entire life without reference to the God who made him. That is being under sin in a respectable neighbourhood. The chains are not always the kind that chafe.

Are people not basically good? Many hold that evil comes from outside us: from poverty, ignorance, a bad upbringing or unjust systems. Circumstances do shape people, and Christians should work to change cruel ones. But the twentieth century strained the idea. The novelist William Golding, who served in the Royal Navy in the Second World War, wrote that anyone who lived through those years without seeing that man produces evil as a bee produces honey must have been blind. In Lord of the Flies the darkness comes to the island with the well-brought-up schoolboys. Paul agrees, and goes further. If the problem were only outside us, better systems could save us. Because it is inside every one of us, someone has to come from outside. That is strangely hopeful: nobody is in a worse category than you, and nobody is beyond the reach of the same grace.

What about babies, who have done nothing? We are sinners from birth, not only from our first wrong act: in sin did my mother conceive me (Psalm 51:5), and in Adam all were made sinners (5:12, 19). So no one stands before God on the ground of innocence, which is exactly why the hope for little ones who die is grace. This commentary’s view, with the Reformed confessions, is that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (Westminster Confession 10.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3). Grieving parents may rest their child in the hands of the God who is rich in mercy and took little children in his arms (Mark 10:16).

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “Are we Jews any better off?” (proechometha) is rare, and its form can be read more than one way: are we better off?, are we at a disadvantage?, or even are we making excuses? Most translations take it as the ESV does, which best suits the question of verse 1, and the answer is the same whichever is meant: Jews and Greeks alike are under sin.
verseByVerse.note: Paul strings together quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah to show that all are under sin.

parallels.desc: not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins

verseByVerse.quote: no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Left to ourselves, no one understands God, no one seeks him and no one does what is truly good; every one of us has turned aside. Sin has reached the mind, the will and the whole direction of life.

No one understands. Paul begins with the mind. Not a comment on intelligence, but on a faculty that fails where God is concerned, which is why brilliant people can come away unmoved while a person of no education grasps the gospel. The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them (1 Corinthians 2:14): not merely unwilling, but unable.

No one seeks for God. The world is full of seekers, so how can Paul say nobody is looking? Because of what is sought. People look tirelessly for what God gives: meaning, peace, forgiveness, the assurance that they are loved. What nobody seeks, left to himself, is God on his own terms: a God with authority over him, who names his sin, will not be edited, and cannot be left when he becomes inconvenient. We look for the benefits, not the Person, and religion is often the most sophisticated way of having the first without the second.

Behind a tree. After the fall, God comes walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man is not looking for him; he is hiding among the trees (Genesis 3:8). The Bible is the record not of humanity’s search for God but of God’s search for humanity.

All have turned aside. Turned off the road, the shepherd’s picture Isaiah chose for the same condition: all we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned, every one, to his own way (Isaiah 53:6). Nobody follows a common script: depravity does not produce uniformity. It produces a world of highly individual people going, with great originality, in the same general direction.

Together they have become worthless. Useless, good for nothing (ēchreiōthēsan). Behind it is the Hebrew of Psalm 14:3: gone bad, like milk that has turned. The creature made to bear God’s image and fill the earth with his glory has become, in the matter for which he was made, good for nothing.

No one does good, not even one. Not that no one does anything kind, but that no one does what is truly good before God: from a heart that loves him, in obedience to his word, for his glory.

The search began with God. If nobody is searching, somebody has to come, and our Lord defined his mission in exactly those terms: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). If you find that you do want God, that his existence is a comfort rather than a threat, then something has happened to you which this verse says does not happen naturally: no one can come to him unless the Father who sent him draws him (John 6:44). The seeking you are conscious of is the far end of a search that began with God, who came at last in his Son to find you behind your tree.

In everyday life. Think of what you most want God to do for you. Suppose he offered it in full, the healing, the restored relationship, the job, on condition that you would have nothing further to do with him. Would you take it? That is the difference between seeking God’s hand and seeking his face, and Asaph settled it in Psalm 73: with God in heaven as his portion, he wanted nothing else on earth (Psalm 73:25). If your honest answer troubles you, the trouble is a good sign: a heart that minds about wanting God more than his gifts is already being drawn to him.

Then are the good deeds of unbelievers worthless? Not in every sense. When an unbeliever nurses the sick or gives to the poor, the deed may be right and a real blessing, and God in his common kindness preserves much good in the world. What such deeds cannot do is please God as acceptable worship or earn his favour, because they do not come from a heart made right with him by faith, nor aim at his glory (Hebrews 11:6; Westminster Confession 16.7; 1689 London Baptist Confession 16.7). So we can honestly admire a good neighbour and still say he needs Christ. Admiration and evangelism are not in tension.

Is there any point in an unbeliever reading the Bible or coming to church? Every point. God uses means to seek those who do not seek him: faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (10:17). Many have begun reading out of curiosity, or come to church to please a friend, and found that God was the one doing the seeking. The invitation of the gospel is sincere and goes to everyone. Keep inviting, keep praying, and keep the Bible open in front of the people you love.

Where Christians differ: how bad is human nature? Some believe people are basically good, or that fallen humans keep the ability to seek God on their own. This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches total depravity: not that people are as bad as they could be, but that every part of human nature, mind, will and affections, is affected by sin, and no one can, by his own power, seek God or do spiritual good (8:7–8; Ephesians 2:1–3). This is why salvation must be entirely by grace. Many Christians who differ from this commentary elsewhere, such as Arminians (who hold that God’s grace enables every person to accept or refuse him), agree that without grace no one would seek God at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive." "The venom of asps is under their lips." "Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin shows itself first in our words: what comes out of the mouth reveals the death inside. Deceit, smooth poison and open cursing all flow from the same heart.

Their throat is an open grave. Paul walks down a body: throat, tongue, lips, mouth, then feet (v. 15) and eyes (v. 18). Four of the six are organs of speech. Our Lord gave the reason: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:34). You can hide your character in most departments for years, but you cannot talk for long without giving yourself away; so people will give account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36), the words we did not stop to edit.

An open grave. The image, from Psalm 5:9, carried two things for a Jewish reader. An open tomb gives off the smell of what is inside; if what comes up out of a man smells of death, it tells you what is down inside him. And under the law, a man who so much as touched a grave was unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16): an open grave contaminated people who had done nothing but come near. Human speech does not stay with the speaker.

They use their tongues to deceive. The organs form a sequence: the throat is the source, the tongue the method, and the verb describes a habit: they keep on deceiving.

The venom of asps is under their lips. From Psalm 140:3, and the sharpest of the four: speech lethal precisely because it is smooth. Not the shouted insult, which at least announces itself, but the compliment with a hook in it; the concerned question that plants a doubt about somebody and leaves no fingerprints; the remark in front of others that is perfectly accurate and perfectly timed to humiliate. None of it would stand out on a recording. All of it is under the lip.

Curses and bitterness. From Psalm 10:7: the overflow, the point at which a man stops bothering to hide it. James calls the tongue a restless evil, full of deadly poison (James 3:8), and puts this verse in a church rather than a gutter: with the same mouth we bless our Lord and Father and curse people who are made in the likeness of God (James 3:9). The mouth that sang in the service dismantles somebody in the car afterwards, and does not even change gear.

Every mouth turned on him. Once this whole anatomy was aimed at one man, by false witnesses, passers-by, rulers, soldiers and robbers: the one in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Peter 2:22). From him came the opposite of every word in this chain. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23), and from the cross he prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34; a few early manuscripts lack this prayer, but most modern Bibles keep it). The bitterness of the human mouth was poured out on him, and he answered it with intercession for the people pouring it. This is the reversal the letter is heading for: the organ chapter 3 calls an open grave is, in chapter 10, the mouth that confesses Jesus as Lord and is saved (10:9–10). The Word made flesh went down into a real open grave, so that graves like ours might be made into mouths of praise.

The open grave with a distribution network. Our generation has industrialised this: a sentence composed in ninety seconds of irritation can reach thousands and still be sitting there in five years.

In everyday life. Do not ask whether you swear. Think of one sentence this week that was entirely polite, that nobody would have called unkind, and that you knew, as you formed it, would land somewhere tender. That sentence is not on your lips. It is under them, and it is the one this verse is about. The blood of the one who answered every mocking mouth with intercession has covered that sentence too; go back, forgiven, and mend it.

How do I actually change the way I speak? Start where Jesus starts, with the heart, because the mouth only reports what is there. Ask God to deal with the bitterness or contempt underneath, and pray before the day begins: set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips (Psalm 141:3). Then build small habits. Be quick to hear, slow to speak (James 1:19). Before you speak or post about someone, ask whether it is true, whether it is needed, and whether it builds them up (Ephesians 4:29). When you have wounded someone, go back and name it plainly instead of waiting for it to fade. And fill the mouth with better things: thanks, Scripture, encouragement, prayer.

parallels.desc: their throat is an open grave
the venom of asps
his mouth is filled with cursing

verseByVerse.quote: "Their feet are swift to shed blood;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin moves from words to deeds, and feet that hurry to harm show what the heart wants. The eagerness, more than the violence, is the evidence.

Their feet are swift to shed blood. From Isaiah 59:7. The mouth speaks; the feet go and do. The disturbing word is swift: speed measures desire, and the eagerness tells you what is in the runner.

Evil as belonging. The words echo the father in Proverbs 1 warning his son about men who will invite him along: come with us, let us lie in wait for blood, we shall find all precious goods, throw in your lot among us. Then the father’s comment: their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood (Proverbs 1:11–16). Evil rarely presents itself as evil; it offers company, adventure and a share of the proceeds. It presents itself as belonging.

The sixth commandment at its root. We want to file this verse under people unlike ourselves. Our Lord traced the sixth commandment to its root: everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment, and whoever says “You fool!” will be liable to the hell of fire (Matthew 5:21–22). John says it flatly: everyone who hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15). A harsh word does not equal a killing in its consequences, but the same root lies under both: the desire to see someone diminished, silenced, humiliated, ended. It is available to respectable people at their own kitchen tables. Most of us never reach the deed for lack of opportunity, nerve or anonymity, which is a mercy but not innocence.

Clean bloodshed. Bloodshed has always had tidy forms, in which nobody’s feet appear to move. David never touched Uriah; he sent a letter and let the Ammonites do it. Ahab did not stone Naboth; a court was convened and witnesses were found. Pilate washed his hands in public and gave the order anyway. Distance between the decision and the death is the oldest device in the world for keeping one’s feet unmarked, and it works on the conscience without deceiving the Judge for a moment.

The swiftest feet of all. Every strand of this verse met on one Friday, when Jesus was led to Pilate at dawn (Mark 15:1) and crucified before the day was done. Yet he had long before set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), walking toward that blood of his own will. Soon afterwards Peter told the same city that they had asked for a murderer and killed the Author of life (Acts 3:14–15), and in the same sermon offered them the blotting out of their sins (Acts 3:19). Scripture uses the same image in the opposite direction. Isaiah pictured a runner coming over the mountains whose feet were beautiful because of what he carried: good news, peace, salvation; and Paul quotes it later in this letter of those who bring the gospel (Isaiah 52:7; Romans 10:15). Feet that ran to shed blood are not, in the end, cut off. They are sent somewhere else, in a hurry, carrying something worth the speed.

In everyday life. Watch what you move toward quickly: passing on news of trouble for someone you resent, believing a story that confirms what you already thought of someone. What our feet hurry toward is evidence in this trial. Choose one of those and be slow, leaning on the Spirit of the Christ who set his face toward Jerusalem for you.

Is all anger sinful, then? No. Scripture says be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26), and Jesus himself was angry at hardness of heart (Mark 3:5). Righteous anger is aimed at real evil, grieved on God’s behalf rather than offended on mine, and wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored. The anger Jesus calls murder in seed form is about me, nurses itself, and wants the other person smaller. The test is what it wants. If your anger is pushing you to pray, to protect the vulnerable or to speak the truth in love, it may be right. If it is pushing you to rehearse speeches and enjoy imagining someone’s downfall, it has already crossed the line.

parallels.desc: their feet run to evil

verseByVerse.quote: "in their paths are ruin and misery, and the way of peace they have not known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin leaves ruin and misery behind it in other people’s lives, and on its own the human race never finds the way to peace. The wreckage lies in the path already walked.

In their paths are ruin and misery. From Isaiah 59:7–8. The ruin is not ahead of them as a destination but in their paths, behind them, where they have already been. Ruin is breakage; misery is what it costs the people living in it. Sin is never only an offence registered in heaven: it lands somewhere on earth, and usually on a person.

The wreckage we cannot see. We experience our lives from the inside, as a sequence of understandable decisions, so the wreckage is out of sight. It is in other people: the child who learned to read a father’s mood before coming into a room; the friend who stopped calling and was never asked why; the colleague made to look foolish in a meeting years ago who still thinks about it; the marriage that did not end but went quiet. None of it appears in the sinner’s account of his life. All of it is in the path.

The way of peace they have not known. Peace here is not the absence of trouble but shalom: everything in its proper place, working, whole. And the wording is exact: not that they refuse the way of peace, but that they have not known it. So every generation produces its confident method, better education, systems, technology or politics, and each a fresh crop of ruin along the way.

The arm that brought salvation. Paul’s quotation stops at the darkest line, but Isaiah 59 does not. The LORD saw that there was no one to intercede, and then his own arm brought him salvation (Isaiah 59:16), and the chapter ends with the Redeemer who will come to Zion (Isaiah 59:20; Romans 11:26). The human race cannot find the way of peace, so God himself would come and make it. John tells us whose arm that was: when Israel would not believe the report about the arm of the LORD, Isaiah was speaking of Jesus (Isaiah 53:1; John 12:38–41). The way of peace was not known, so somebody had to come and be it: he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). The road nobody could find is a Person, the Prince of Peace, who came looking for the people leaving ruin in their paths, and this letter will shortly say that he died for them while they were still doing it (5:8).

But many unbelievers seem to live peaceful lives? Many do, in the ordinary sense, by God’s kindness. But the peace in view is deeper: peace with God, which no one has apart from Christ (5:1), and the wholeness that flows from it. A life can be calm on the surface and at war with its Maker, and at death the surface calm ends. Equally, a believer may live through great turmoil and still have the peace of God guarding his heart (Philippians 4:7). The question is not how quiet your life is but whether you have been reconciled.

Do I need to go back and put things right with people? Where you can, yes. Repentance in Scripture often involves other people and not only God. Zacchaeus did not merely confess; he worked out fourfold and promised to repay it (Luke 19:8). Our Lord told a man to leave his gift at the altar and first be reconciled to his brother (Matthew 5:23–24). But not every path can be walked back down. Some people are dead, some unreachable, and some would be harmed by your return; there the road back is closed, and God’s forgiveness is not thereby withheld. Where it is open, walk it, humbly and without demanding a particular response. It is usually the last thing we want to do, and often the most freeing.

parallels.desc: the way of peace they do not know

verseByVerse.quote: "There is no fear of God before their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the root of every sin lies this: God does not weigh with us, and we live as though he were not there. Sin is a failure of worship before it is a failure of morality.

There is no fear of God. From Psalm 36:1. With the eyes the body is complete, and the earlier charges turn out to be symptoms of this cause. Before a man does wrong things he has already stopped treating God as God, which is how Paul began his charge: they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him (1:21).

What the fear of God is. Not terror. “That boy has no fear of his father,” we say, not meaning the father ought to be frightening, but that his reality does not weigh with the boy, who behaves in his father’s presence exactly as in his absence. That is the charge: God makes no practical difference to them, and they have no sense that they must answer to him.

Before their eyes. What a man keeps in view while he is deciding. Everyone knows a speed limit exists, yet a patrol car in the mirror alters behaviour instantly. The belief has not changed, only what is in the frame. The Christian’s problem is rarely that he stops believing; it is that at the moment of choosing God is simply not in the picture, and the picture governs conduct.

The beginning of wisdom. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7) and of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10); its absence is the beginning of folly. Verse 11 said no one understands; verse 18 says why. A man reasoning about his life with God left out of the frame will reason with great sophistication to conclusions that are reliably wrong.

His delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. Of one man the opposite of this verse was wholly true. Isaiah says the Spirit of the LORD would rest on the shoot from Jesse, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD, and that his delight would be in the fear of the LORD (Isaiah 11:2–3). Jesus lived every hour with his Father before his eyes: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). The fear of God missing from the whole human race was present, complete and joyful, in the Son, and he died for people with no fear of God before their eyes.

“In your light do we see light.” Paul’s last quotation carries its own cure. Psalm 36 opens with the wicked man who has no fear of God before his eyes, and then turns: your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds; for with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light (Psalm 36:5, 9). The psalm that diagnoses the eye supplies the light, and Paul knew where it shines: in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), the one sight that puts the fear of God before the eyes for ever.

Is a Christian supposed to fear God? Yes, though not with the fear of punishment. Perfect love casts out fear, John says, and he specifies which fear: fear has to do with punishment (1 John 4:18). The dread of condemnation is gone (8:1). What remains, and grows, is the other thing. A child of a good father is entirely at ease on his knee, and would go white to hear someone speak of his father with contempt: both at once, neither weakening the other. That is the fear this verse says is missing, and it is a covenant gift: I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me (Jeremiah 32:40). It is not the opposite of assurance but part of the means by which God holds on to his people.

How do I grow in the fear of God? Not by working up reverence, which does not last past Tuesday, but by looking at God as he has shown himself. Read the passages where his holiness is on display, Isaiah 6, Exodus 19 and 20, Revelation 4 and 5, and let them be large. Above all look at the cross, for Scripture says something surprising: with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared (Psalm 130:4). Nothing makes God weightier to a forgiven sinner than knowing what his forgiveness cost. Then practise remembering him in the ordinary hours: a sentence of prayer before a hard conversation, a pause before you open something you should not. And ask him for it; he has promised to give it.

parallels.desc: there is no fear of God before his eyes

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin. — Romans 3:19-20
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law leaves every mouth without a defence, because no one will be declared righteous before God by keeping it. What the law gives is knowledge of sin, not the cure for it.

Whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law. The first clause closes the last door. A Jewish reader could grant every quotation and apply it to the nations. Paul blocks it: those texts were addressed to the people who possess them, and you may not pass the word along without receiving it yourself.

So that every mouth may be stopped. A courtroom where the defendant, having heard the indictment, has nothing to say: no excuses, no protests, no plea of mitigating circumstances, no claim of comparative righteousness. He was guilty already; but until the defence ends, nothing can be given. A man still presenting his case is asking for a verdict on his record, and grace has nothing to say to a man who believes he might win. That is why religion can be the hardest place for grace to land: a moral person’s whole life can become one long speech for the defence, while the irreligious man often has fewer arguments to drop.

The whole world. Chapter 1 caught the pagan, chapter 2 the moralist and the man with the law; here the doors are shut and the room is full.

No human being will be justified. The conclusion of 1:18–3:20, echoing Psalm 143:2: enter not into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you. At 2:13 Paul stated the rule, not the hearers of the law but the doers will be justified, and left one question open: who has done it? Here is the verdict: no one. Chapter 2 was the statute; chapter 3 is the judgment.

The road is impassable. The law is not bad, nor the standard lowered; by this road no one arrives, and the report comes from the surveyor who laid it out. One man did walk it to the end. Jesus kept every commandment from the heart, and it is by his obedience, not ours, that the many will be made righteous (5:19). The road no one could travel was travelled once, by a substitute, for people who had failed on it.

Through the law comes knowledge of sin. The law’s purpose is not to save but to show sin (7:7): a mirror, not a washbasin. The word (epignōsis) is full recognition: the law turns a vague unease into particular sins, and so drives us to Christ. You cannot want a Saviour while your problem is only a feeling that something is wrong.

In everyday life. When Scripture shows you something true about yourself, where do you go next? Some go to despair, which is the law doing half its work and stopping. Some go to resolve, which is the law doing none of it: the man has heard that he cannot climb and responds by training harder. The law has done its full work only when a man stops climbing and starts looking for a rescue. Stop defending yourself before God. Let your mouth be stopped, and then open it to call on Christ.

What about those who have never heard of Christ? The whole world is accountable, and Paul has already said on what basis: those without the written law are judged by the light they had, creation and conscience, and they have not lived up to it (1:20; 2:12–15). No one will be condemned for failing to believe a gospel he never heard; he will be judged for real sin against real light. But no one is saved apart from Christ, and people cannot call on one of whom they have never heard (10:14). The answer of this letter is not speculation but mission, the reason Paul was going to Spain. The question should send us to our knees and to our neighbours.

Where Christians differ: what are works of the law? Some scholars (the New Perspective on Paul) take them to mean mainly the Jewish identity markers. This commentary’s view: those markers are included, but the verse ends, through the law comes knowledge of sin: Paul means any obedience offered as a basis for acceptance, and no one keeps the law.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — But Now: The Righteousness of God Through Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Into the silence of the courtroom God has spoken: he gives his own righteousness, freely, to everyone who believes in Jesus. Apart from the law, yet witnessed by it, this righteousness comes through faith to all without distinction (vv. 21–22), because all have sinned and are justified by grace through the redemption in Christ (vv. 23–24). God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood, so that he is both just and the justifier (vv. 25–26). So boasting is shut out (vv. 27–28), the one God justifies Jew and Gentile by the same faith (vv. 29–30), and faith upholds the law (v. 31), as chapter 4 will show from Abraham.
verseByVerse.theology:
Propitiation

In Romans 3:25 Paul calls Christ a hilastērion, a propitiation: an offering that turns away God’s wrath by satisfying it. Leon Morris argued at length that this is the right reading, against C.H. Dodd's proposal to read it as expiation, which only removes sin, without reference to wrath (the debate is set out in the box at the end of the note on vv. 25–26). If Christ did not bear the whole of that wrath, some of it is still left for us, and the forgiveness is not truly free.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Verses 24–25 echo the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), when blood was sprinkled on the mercy seat for the sins of the people. What that day pointed to, Christ has accomplished once for all. Now: People still deal with guilt by ritual, moral effort, distraction or denial; Romans 3:21–31 says that the only remedy is the one God provided, the death of his own Son in our place, received by faith.

verseByVerse.quote: But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it—the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction:
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has now revealed a righteousness that comes from him, not from keeping the law, and gives it through faith in Jesus Christ to everyone who believes. The Old Testament pointed to it all along, and it is open to all without distinction.

But now. Two small words, and the whole letter turns on them. Everything from 1:18 has been a closing down, until every mouth is stopped, and into that silence God has acted (Ephesians 2:13). Paul does not write “therefore”, because nothing in 1:18–3:20 leads on to grace. The gospel interrupts the argument, an announcement from outside the courtroom: news, not advice: a righteousness from God, apart from law, held out to the very people the law had that moment finished condemning, and priced at the life of the only innocent man who ever lived. Blessed be the God who did not wait for us to climb up to him, but came down, in his Son, with a righteousness already finished in his hands.

Has been manifested. Not invented but brought into the open; the tense describes something done once that still stands. It has happened, in public, and the announcement is catching up with it.

His character, or his gift? Paul holds both together. A righteousness that comes through faith for all who believe is a status God gives (1:17): his verdict that a sinner is in the right with him (compare Philippians 3:9). Yet in vv. 25–26 the same cross shows God’s own righteousness, so that he is just and the justifier. Luther found the gospel when he saw that God’s righteousness in this letter is not only the standard that condemns us but the gift that clothes us: the right standing that belongs to Christ, given to the guilty as a robe to someone with nothing fit to wear (Isaiah 61:10).

The Law and the Prophets bear witness to it. The law never produced this righteousness, but it pointed to it from the beginning (Genesis 15:6; Habakkuk 2:4), as chapter 4 will prove. Every sacrifice, every high priest going in on the Day of Atonement, every prophet who spoke of a servant wounded for our transgressions, was a signpost. Paul is not founding a new religion; he is announcing that the old one has arrived at what it was for.

For all who believe. Paul adds nothing after “believe”: no probation, no minimum improvement, no requirement that you first become the sort of person to whom such an offer could decently be made. He has spent three chapters showing that no such person exists. It is open to all and received by faith alone, and faith is not an achievement God rewards but the empty hand that receives.

For there is no distinction. Jew and Gentile alike, the moralist and the pagan, the man with four Bibles and the man who has never opened one. The ground was levelled in vv. 9–20 so that one door could serve everyone.

Justification. To be justified is to be declared righteous by God as judge, on the basis of Christ’s work: a legal verdict, not a process of being made righteous. Its opposite is to condemn (8:33–34), and no one thinks that condemning a man makes him wicked. Being made holy, which Scripture calls sanctification, really does begin at the same moment and always follows, but it is a different gift, and justification never rests on it.

In everyday life. Think of your worst week this year, the failure you have told nobody about. If you suspect your standing with God dropped that week and has since partly recovered, you are still living under chapter 2, whatever you believe about chapter 3. A righteousness manifested apart from the law is not affected by your performance under the law, because it never rested on it at any point.

Is that not a legal fiction, calling me righteous when I am not? No, because the verdict rests on something real. God does not pretend you have kept the law. He declares you righteous because you are joined to Christ by faith, and Christ really has kept it, and really has borne the penalty for your breaking it. His obedience is reckoned to your account as truly as your sin was reckoned to his (2 Corinthians 5:21). A fiction would say the debt never existed; the gospel says it has been paid. And the person God justifies he also begins to change.

What exactly is faith? More than believing facts, though it includes them. Faith knows who Christ is and what he has done; it agrees that this is true, and true for me; and it trusts him, leaning the whole weight of your hope on him. The Westminster Confession calls it accepting, receiving and resting upon Christ alone for justification (Westminster 14.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 14.2). Knowing a chair is there, agreeing it would hold you, then sitting down: faith is the sitting down. Not a feeling, nor the strength of your confidence, but where you are resting.

Where Christians differ: our faith in Jesus Christ, or his own faithfulness? The Greek (pisteōs Iēsou Christou) can mean faith in Jesus Christ or the faithfulness of Jesus Christ, and some scholars prefer the second, emphasising Christ’s obedience unto death. This commentary’s view: Christ’s faithful obedience is indeed the ground of our justification (5:19), but here the phrase most naturally means faith in Christ, since Paul immediately adds for all who believe. We are justified by faith in Christ, whose faithful obedience is credited to us. Both truths stand, and nobody who holds both has lost anything.
verseByVerse.note: To be “justified” is to be declared righteous by God as judge.

verseByVerse.quote: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone has sinned, and everyone who believes is declared righteous freely, as a gift of God’s grace, because Christ paid the price to set us free. The diagnosis and the remedy arrive in a single breath.

One sentence. We are used to hearing verse 23 on its own, but in Paul it has no full stop: the next verse hangs on it. All have sinned, and are justified by his grace as a gift.

For all have sinned. Three chapters have built a list long enough to catch everybody, so this lands as a description, not an insult.

And fall short of the glory of God. Not a moral score. The glory of God is what we were made to reflect as his image (Genesis 1:27), and what we were meant to share. We miss it, like an archer whose arrow drops short of the target. That explains the ache of being human: the sense of falling short of yourself, of being meant to be more truly what a human being should be. The intuition is accurate, and this verse explains it. Have sinned is a completed fact; fall short is present and continuous, describing this morning, for the Christian too. And “are justified” is in the same present tense: the believer who falls short today stands justified today.

By his grace as a gift. Grace is undeserved favour, and the word for gift (dōrean) means freely, for nothing, at no cost to the one who receives it. The same word turns up in a sentence our Lord applied to himself: “They hated me without a cause” (John 15:25). There was nothing in him to justify the hatred, and there is nothing in you to justify the gift.

Through the redemption. Redemption (apolytrōsis) belongs to the marketplace: the price paid to buy a slave’s freedom or release a prisoner of war. Christ paid the price to free us from sin (Mark 10:45; 1 Peter 1:18–19). It tells you what your position was: not a man with a poor record, but a man owned by somebody else.

That is in Christ Jesus. Grace was free to you, but not to the one who gave it. A gift that cost the giver nothing is a formality; a gift that cost him everything, given to someone who could not contribute a penny, is what this verse means by grace. The Lord of glory, whom we fell short of reflecting, came down to where we had fallen, and bought back his own image out of the slave market with his own blood.

In everyday life. Say this verse in the first person: I have sinned, and I fall short of the glory of God; and I am justified freely by his grace. Notice which half is harder to say without qualifying it. If it is the second, the reason is instructive: a diagnosis that puts us with everybody else is easier to accept than a gift that puts us in debt to somebody. Say both today, and add nothing to the second.

Who received the price of our redemption? Some early Christian writers said the devil, who held humanity captive. Scripture never says so. The debt was owed to God’s justice, which is why Paul goes straight on to propitiation (v. 25); the ransom picture is not meant to be pressed further.

Does “all have sinned … and are justified” mean that everyone is saved? No. The all who are justified are the all who believe: the sentence runs straight on from “for all who believe. For there is no distinction” (v. 22). Every human being has sinned; every believer, without exception, is justified. The gift is offered to all without distinction, and received only by faith (5:17). The good news is not that everyone is already forgiven, but that anyone, however far gone, who comes to Christ is.
verseByVerse.note: “Redemption” was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: ...whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. — Romans 3:25-26
verseByVerse.commentary:
God set Christ forward as the sacrifice that bore his wrath against sin, so that he could forgive sinners and remain perfectly just. The cross settles the account of every sin God had passed over before it, and every sin since.

Whom God put forward. The initiative is entirely God’s: not a reluctant God persuaded by a loving Son, but the loving God satisfying his own justice, showing his love by giving his Son (5:8) and his justice by punishing sin in his Son. In Israel the mercy seat stood in the innermost room, where once a year, in the dark, the high priest sprinkled blood over the covering of a box that held the law they had broken. God put Christ forward in the open, in daylight, on a hill outside a city wall. The holiest thing in Israel had been hidden behind a curtain for centuries; at the cross it was carried outside and shown to the crowd.

As a propitiation by his blood. A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. The word (hilastērion) is used in the Greek Old Testament for the mercy seat, the lid of the ark of the covenant, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15; Hebrews 9:5). Christ is the true mercy seat, where God’s wrath against sin is satisfied and his mercy given. Wrath is real and being revealed (1:18; 2:5), and at the cross it was absorbed, not deflected. God did not simply decide to stop being angry with sin; his anger fell, in full, on Christ, so that nothing of it is left to fall on those who trust him (5:9; 8:1).

He had passed over former sins. Why did the cross have to happen? Paul’s answer is not first that we needed rescuing, but that God had a problem with his own record: for centuries he had been forgiving people. Abraham lied twice about his wife and remained the friend of God. David committed adultery and murder and was told that the LORD had put away his sin (2 Samuel 12:13). The whole sacrificial system ran on the blood of animals, which, as Hebrews says flatly, can never take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). On what grounds had all this been let through? The word is not the ordinary word for forgiveness but to let go by, leave unpunished for the present: a judge suspending sentences for two thousand years without explaining himself.

This was to show God’s righteousness. The cross is evidence produced in court: God clearing his own name. The Old Testament saints were forgiven on credit, and at the cross the account was settled.

Just and the justifier. The heart of the gospel. A judge who acquits the guilty is not merciful but corrupt. Proverbs says so plainly: “He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD” (Proverbs 17:15). God’s own law forbade the very thing his gospel appears to do. So the question of Romans is not how a loving God can forgive, but how a just God can, and remain just. He punished sin in his Son. Nothing was waived: the sentence was carried out in full, on somebody else, with the Judge providing the substitute out of his own household.

Righteousness and peace kiss. “Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other” (Psalm 85:10). The psalmist sang it as a hope; Calvary made it history. God did not compromise between love and justice but satisfied both, at his own expense, so that he might be at the same moment the Judge who does not bend and the Father who runs to the guilty.

In everyday life. Ask yourself why God accepts you, and listen for whether the answer leans on his kindness, his willingness to overlook, his understanding of your circumstances. If it does, your assurance will not hold on the worst night, because a God who overlooks things could change his mind about overlooking them. The answer this passage gives is harder and infinitely steadier: he accepts you because the debt was paid, and it would be unjust of him to collect it twice. Justice, the thing you feared, has become the ground you stand on.

Is it not unjust to punish an innocent person instead of the guilty? It would be, if God took an unwilling third party. The one who bore the penalty is God himself in the person of the Son, who came willingly: no one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). The Judge bore the cost himself. Nor is the substitute a stranger to us: he took our nature and stands as head of his people, so that what he did, he did as us and for us (5:12–19). Father, Son and Spirit together planned it, accomplished it and apply it, with one love and one justice.

Where Christians differ: propitiation or expiation? Some translate hilastērion as expiation, the removing of sin, and deny that God’s wrath needed to be satisfied; others prefer simply mercy seat. The mercy seat picture is real, since the same word is used in Hebrews 9:5. This commentary’s view: the context is God’s wrath (1:18; 2:5) and his justice (vv. 25–26), and in 5:9 Paul says that since we are justified by Christ’s blood, we shall be saved by him from the wrath of God. Christ’s death removes sin, yes, but by bearing the wrath it deserved. This is penal substitution: Christ suffered the penalty of our sins in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13). It is the centre of the gospel. Christians who stress the cross as victory over evil or as the supreme example of love are right that it is all of that; this commentary holds that it is never less than this.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “put forward” (protithēmi) can mean to set out publicly or to plan beforehand; Paul uses it for intending in 1:13. Most translations and commentators take it as public display here, which suits the repeated “to show” of vv. 25–26. Either way the initiative is God’s.
verseByVerse.note: A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. The same word is used in the Greek Old Testament for the “mercy seat,” the lid of the ark where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement.

parallels.desc: blood on the mercy seat

verseByVerse.quote: Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because we are justified by faith and not by works, no one has anything left to boast about before God. Boasting is not merely discouraged; the way God saves leaves it nothing to stand on.

Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. Boasting is claiming credit before God, and the word is stronger than “excluded” suggests: shut out, the door locked behind it, not moderated or permitted in small quantities among mature believers. If salvation is God’s gift, received by faith, no one can boast (Ephesians 2:8–9; 1 Corinthians 1:29–31). The proud Jew of 2:17, boasting in the law, and the proud moralist alike are silenced.

By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. Law here means principle. A system of works would allow boasting; the principle of faith excludes it. What excludes it is not humility or a rule, but the way salvation itself works. A man told to stop boasting will learn to boast more quietly, and self-congratulation driven underground is harder to detect and no less pleasant. Paul describes not a prohibition but a demolition: there is nothing left to boast about. You cannot be proud of a gift you did not choose, earn, deserve or contribute to. The impulse is not forbidden. It is unemployed.

Why has God arranged salvation this way? If any element of your standing rested on you, you would have grounds for comparison, the seedbed of everything Paul has denounced since chapter 2. God has closed off boasting not because he cannot bear rivals, but because boasting is a poison whose only cure is a salvation in which no one has anything to show. And the deepest reason is his glory: he saves so that the whole praise goes to the one who did the saving (1 Corinthians 1:31).

One is justified by faith apart from works of the law. The thesis of the Reformation. “We hold” (logizometha) means we count it settled, a finding entered in the record. It does not clash with the judgment according to works in 2:6–8: the works weighed on that day are the fruit and evidence of the faith by which a person has already been justified, never the ground of the verdict.

Luther’s word. Luther translated the verse as “by faith alone” (allein), and was attacked for life for adding a word. It is not in the Greek, but it is exactly what the sentence means: if works are excluded, faith is the only thing left standing.

The tax collector went home justified. Jesus told it first, of two men praying in the temple. The Pharisee listed his record: not like other men, fasting twice a week, tithing everything. The tax collector would not lift his eyes, but beat his breast and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” And Jesus gave the verdict: “this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other” (Luke 18:9–14). That is verses 27 and 28 told as a story. The verb in his plea, “be merciful”, comes from the same word family as “propitiation” in verse 25, and the mercy he asked for is the mercy God put forward at the cross.

The locked door. It is a kindness. Keeping score makes you anxious when losing and insufferable when winning, and Paul has removed the scoreboard. One thing is left to say: “far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14). You have nothing to boast of before God except Christ, and in him you have everything, so that the mouth stopped in verse 19 is opened at last, not to plead its record, but to praise its Redeemer.

What it does not mean. Here people often grow anxious about their faith instead of their works: the same disease at a new address. If you ask whether your faith is strong, sincere or doubt-free enough to count, you are treating faith as a work, something you produce and God rewards. It is not. A weak hand and a strong hand take hold of the same rope, and the rope does the holding. What saves is not the excellence of your grip but the strength of what you are gripping.

In everyday life. Listen to what you mention when you want somebody to think well of you spiritually: how long you have been a Christian, what you have read or given up, how much you serve. Whatever the currency in your congregation, it is a boast, and this verse says the door it is trying to come in by is locked. When you catch yourself, turn the sentence round and say something true about Christ instead.

But does James not say the opposite? No: the apostles answer different questions. Paul asks how a guilty sinner is put right with God; James asks what kind of faith is real, and shows that a faith without works is dead. We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

What about baptism? Is it not needed to be saved? Baptism matters greatly: Christ commanded it, and it signs a believer’s union with him in his death and resurrection (6:3–4). This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that it is for those who profess faith, because in the New Testament baptism follows repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:12), and many paedobaptist brothers, with the Westminster Confession, baptise the children of believers too. But both agree on this verse: baptism is not the instrument of justification, and grace and salvation are not so tied to it that no one can be saved without it (Westminster 28.5). The thief on the cross was promised paradise unbaptised. Be baptised because Christ commands it, not in order to be justified.

Where Christians differ: faith alone? The Council of Trent (1547), the Roman Catholic council that answered the Reformation, condemned the teaching that we are justified by faith alone. This commentary’s view: apart from works of the law leaves faith alone as the instrument. Not faith plus baptism, faith plus penance, or faith plus good works. Good works are the necessary fruit of justifying faith (Ephesians 2:10; James 2), but they are not part of its ground. This is sola fide, the article on which the church stands or falls.

verseByVerse.quote: Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one—who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because there is only one God, he saves Jews and Gentiles in exactly the same way: by faith. A God who belongs to everybody has one way of salvation open to everybody.

Or is God the God of Jews only? If salvation were by the law, only Jews could have it. Nobody in the synagogue would have said aloud that God was the God of Jews only; the Scriptures they read every week said the opposite in a hundred places, from the promise that in Abraham all nations would be blessed to Isaiah’s house of prayer for all peoples (Isaiah 56:7). Paul shows them that their practice had quietly contradicted a creed they could recite in their sleep.

Since God is one. The phrase echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Devout Jews said it morning and evening, and its obvious force had been separation: the nations have many gods; we have the one true God. Paul boldly turns the same words outward. If there is only one God, he is not our God as opposed to theirs. He is theirs too, whether they know it or not, and a God who belongs to everybody cannot have arranged a way of salvation that only one group can use.

By faith and through faith. Paul uses two different prepositions, most likely simply for variety. Both groups are justified by the same faith: two doors, the same width, and neither of them a back entrance.

The fight that nearly tore the church apart. In Paul’s day this was far from settled. Whether Gentiles had first to become Jews, taking on circumcision, the food laws and the calendar, filled a council at Jerusalem (Acts 15), produced the letter to the Galatians, and put Paul in open conflict with Peter at a common table in Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14). Paul saw, with a clarity that cost him dearly, that a gospel with a cultural entrance fee is not the gospel at all.

One God, one Lord, one new man. Paul sets Christ inside the very confession he echoes here: for us there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6). The one God justifies Jew and Gentile through that one Lord, who in his flesh broke down the dividing wall between them, to create in himself one new man in place of the two and reconcile both to God in one body through the cross (Ephesians 2:14–16). The Shema had been the creed that set Israel apart; in Christ it becomes the creed that gathers the nations in. One day a multitude no one can number, from every nation, tribe, people and language, will stand before the throne crying out that salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb (Revelation 7:9–10), and the Shema will be sung in every tongue.

The modern form. It is rarely doctrinal, which makes it hard to see. It simply turns out, over time, that the people who thrive in a congregation already share the accent, the education, the politics, the family shape, the taste in music, the ease with a particular vocabulary. Nobody voted for it, and the tell is not what a church believes about who may come, but who is comfortable once they have. Of the last person who came for a few weeks and did not return, did anyone find out why?

Does one God for all mean every religion leads to him? It means the opposite. Because God is one, there is one way to him for everyone, and that way is faith in Jesus Christ (v. 22). There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). No one comes to the Father except through Christ (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). Other religions are not different roads up the same mountain; they are human attempts, sometimes earnest, to reach a God who has come down to us by one road. That is not narrowness. It is the widest door in the world: open to every nation, every culture and every record, through the one Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: “God is one” echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession.

parallels.desc: the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Justification by faith does not set the law aside; it is the only thing that lets the law stand at its full height. In Christ its demands are met in full, his Spirit writes it on believers’ hearts, and the law itself bore witness to faith.

Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? If salvation is by faith, is the law pointless? This is not a stray thought but the slander of 3:8, that Paul taught people to do evil so that good might come. Now that the doctrine is fully stated, he faces it.

We uphold the law. The verb is a word for making something stand, setting it firmly on its feet. The claim is not that the law survives the gospel, but that it was never standing properly until now.

How the law is lowered. A man trying to be justified by the law must, if he is to have any peace, lower it. He cannot live with “You shall not covet” meaning what it says, so he quietly translates the commandments into things that can be achieved: no adultery becomes no affair, no murder becomes no violence, honour your father becomes a phone call at Christmas. He has kept it by redefining it down to his own size: the most thorough disrespect the law ever suffers, always done by its admirers.

How faith establishes it. The gospel does the reverse and lets every commandment stand at full height: “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (7:12). Christ fulfilled the law’s demands and bore its penalty (8:3–4): nothing is discounted, and the sinner is justified without a single letter of the standard adjusted in his favour. And those justified by faith are given the Spirit, who enables them to fulfil the law’s righteous requirement (8:4; 13:8–10). Only the man who has stopped needing the law to be manageable is free to see how magnificent it is.

The law itself testified. Faith upholds the law in a second sense: the law itself, the books of Moses, teaches it. In chapter 4 Paul brings out Abraham from Genesis, counted righteous by believing God before he was circumcised and centuries before the law was given. Justification by faith is not a novelty smuggled in past Moses. It is the oldest thing in the book.

In everyday life. Read the Sermon on the Mount slowly this week and watch your reaction. If your instinct is to soften it (“he cannot mean that literally”), something in you is still trying to pass, because only a candidate needs the exam to be easier. If you can let it stand at full height, agree with every word, and not be frightened, you are upholding the law. The man who is not being examined can afford to admire the standard.

So is a Christian still bound by the Ten Commandments? Yes, as a rule of life, though not as a way of earning life. The Reformed confessions distinguish the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments and in love for God and neighbour, which binds everyone always, from the ceremonial laws, fulfilled in Christ, and Israel’s civil laws, which expired with that state (Westminster Confession 19.3–5; 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.3–5).
