Christ does not cancel the moral law for believers; he frees us from its curse and writes it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Christians differ honourably on how the fourth commandment applies now that Christ has risen on the first day of the week; this commentary sets out those views where the Sabbath is discussed, taking the view that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ and that the Lord’s Day is a gift Christians gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, not a law by which anyone may bind another’s conscience (Romans 14:5–6; Colossians 2:16–17). But every Christian agrees that the law shows us how to love.

keyVerse.quote: It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.
keyVerse.note: The chapter shuts every mouth and then asks how a holy God can forgive anyone at all; this verse is the answer. God did not lower his justice in order to forgive, nor withhold forgiveness in order to stay just: at the cross he punished sin in full in his Son, so that he can acquit everyone who trusts in Jesus and remain perfectly just. The justice we had every reason to fear has become the ground we stand on.

3.reflection:
Paul says the law speaks “so that every mouth may be stopped” (v. 19). What does it look like for a religious or moral person to keep making a case for the defence before God? Why must that stop before grace can be received?

Verses 10–18 walk down the human body: mind, will, mouth, feet and eyes. Which of these charges do you find easiest to apply to other people, and which is hardest to accept about yourself?

God is “just and the justifier” (v. 26). Why does it matter that God forgives us by satisfying his justice rather than by overlooking our sin? How does that change the way you face a bad week, or the memory of a past failure?

If boasting is excluded and there is “no distinction” (vv. 22, 27, 29–30), what forms of quiet boasting or unspoken entrance fees might be at work in us or in our church, and how does the gospel answer them?

4.title: Abraham: The Father of All Who Believe
4.overview:
Where we are. Paul has just announced that God’s righteousness is given “through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe” (3:22), that boasting is excluded, and that this upholds the law (3:21–31). Chapter 4 proves it from the Old Testament; chapter 5 will show what the verdict brings.

The message. God has always put people right with himself in one way: he credits righteousness to those who believe his promise, not to those who earn it. Abraham, the strongest case anyone could name, was counted righteous because he believed God, not because of his works or his circumcision. So he is the father of every believer, Jew and Gentile, and what was counted to him is counted to us when we trust the God who raised Jesus.

Why it was said. If justification is by faith, a Jewish reader would at once ask about Abraham, held up by the teachers of the day as the great example of a righteous man, faithful under testing. And the mixed church in Rome needed to know whether Gentile believers were full members of Abraham’s family or guests at its edge (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First Scripture: Genesis 15:6 says Abraham’s faith was counted as righteousness, a gift and not a wage, and David calls blessed the man whose sins are forgiven (vv. 1–8). Then the calendar: Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, years before his circumcision in Genesis 17, so the sign sealed a righteousness he already had (vv. 9–12). Then the promise: it was given centuries before the law, which brings wrath, so that it rests on grace and is guaranteed to all his offspring (vv. 13–16). Then the faith itself: Abraham looked hard at a body as good as dead and trusted the God who gives life to the dead (vv. 17–22). Finally, the words were written for us (vv. 23–25).

Where it leads. The chapter opens with an old man under the stars and ends at an empty tomb. The God who brought life from bodies as good as dead raised Jesus our Lord, “delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (v. 25). The offspring promised to Abraham is Christ, and the righteousness counted to every believer is his. The gospel does not overturn God’s covenant with Abraham; it fulfils it.

For us. No one comes to God with a record that counts, not even Abraham. Come as he did, with empty hands and a promise, and you stand where he stood: counted righteous, a child of his family, and an heir with him of the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Abraham Justified by Faith, Not Works or Circumcision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has always counted people righteous by faith, not by their works or by belonging to the right people, and Abraham proves it. Genesis 15:6 says righteousness was credited to Abraham because he believed: a gift, not a wage, given to one who brought nothing, for God “justifies the ungodly” (vv. 1–5). David adds a second witness, calling blessed the man whose sins are forgiven and will never be counted against him (vv. 6–8). Then the calendar settles who may share it: Abraham was counted righteous years before he was circumcised, so the sign sealed a righteousness he already had, and he is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not (vv. 9–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Imputation

The verb logizomai (count, reckon, credit) appears eleven times in Romans 4. Imputation means that God credits Christ's righteousness to the believing sinner's account, and it is the hinge of justification (on credited rather than infused, see the note on vv. 3–4). Luther called it an "alien righteousness" (iustitia aliena): foreign to us by nature, ours by grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Abraham was the strongest witness a Jewish opponent could call. If even he was justified by faith, the case for earning God’s favour has lost its founding father. Now: Every form of religious merit (I’m basically a good person, I go to church, I’ve never done anything really terrible) falls before Romans 4. Abraham stood before God with nothing but faith in the promise, and so must we.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Abraham, the greatest man Israel could name, had nothing to boast about before God. If anyone could have been put right with God by what he did, it was Abraham; Paul calls him as a witness and shows that he was not.

Why Abraham. Having claimed that faith upholds the law (3:31), Paul calls the one witness no opponent could dismiss: if the father of the nation was justified by faith, there is nobody further back to appeal to. And justification is a courtroom word, God the Judge declaring a person righteous, not making him good inside (Deuteronomy 25:1).

What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? Jewish teachers held Abraham up as the great example of a righteous man, who kept the law before it was given and was tested and found faithful. One well-known book of the period, 1 Maccabees, quotes the very verse Paul is about to use and attaches it to the binding of Isaac: Abraham was found faithful when tested, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (1 Maccabees 2:52). On that reading Genesis 15:6 is a verdict on Abraham’s proven obedience, very nearly the opposite of Paul’s point. So Paul is taking the text back, and his instrument will be the calendar: what Genesis 15 says, and when it happened.

Something to boast about. Paul does not say Abraham had nothing to show. He left a settled city, a family and an inheritance on the strength of a word from a God he had not known before. He pleaded with God for a wicked city, from fifty all the way down to ten (Genesis 18:22–33). And at the end he was willing to give up the son he had waited a lifetime for. Any tribunal on earth would have decorated him, and Scripture three times calls him the friend of God (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23).

But not before God. Paul grants all of it, then adds four words that take away its weight: the record belongs to a different courtroom. Before men Abraham towers; before God he is a man counted righteous because he believed a promise, exactly the position of everyone else who has ever been counted righteous. Paul leaves him as tall as he is and observes, quietly, that height was never the measurement being taken (3:27). Before the Holy One the friend of God stands where the thief on the cross stands: with empty hands and a promise.

The one son of Abraham with a record. One descendant of Abraham could have stood before God on his record. In an argument about Abraham, Jesus asked which of them could convict him of sin, and then told them, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:46, 58). He is the only man who ever had something to boast about before God, and he did not boast. He spent his record instead, offering his obedience and his death for people whose record was empty. That is how even Abraham could be counted righteous: what was credited to him by faith was the righteousness of the offspring God had promised him.

In everyday life. Write down the three things you would most want said about you at your funeral. Then ask what weight any of them would carry in a court where the charge is that you have not loved God with all your heart and your neighbour as yourself. The list may be genuinely creditable, but it is testimony in a different case. The greatest believers had nothing to boast of before God, and neither do you, which is freedom.

Does God then not care about my good works? He delights in them. “God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name” (Hebrews 6:10), and he promises to reward labour in the Lord (1 Corinthians 15:58). But he receives your works as a Father receives his children’s gifts, not as an employer pays a wage: the fruit of your acceptance, never its price. So you can offer them gladly and without anxiety; they are not being weighed to decide whether you belong.

Uncertain wording. The Greek of v. 1 is compressed: word for word, What then shall we say Abraham our forefather according to the flesh to have found? The ESV takes “found” as “gained” and joins “according to the flesh” to “forefather”: Abraham, ancestor of the Jews by physical descent. Some join it to “found” instead: what did Abraham gain by human effort? A few scholars read a different question: have we found Abraham to be our forefather only according to the flesh? The flow is hardly affected: Paul asks what Abraham had to show before God, and v. 2 answers that he had nothing of his own.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers held up Abraham as the great example of a righteous man.

verseByVerse.quote: For what does the Scripture say? "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham was right with God because God credited righteousness to him when he believed, not because he earned it. A wage is owed; a gift is credited; and Scripture says Abraham’s righteousness was the second kind.

For what does the Scripture say? Paul settles it not by what the teachers have said about Abraham but by what God has said, in Genesis 15:6, the key verse of the chapter, quoted also in Galatians 3:6 and James 2:23. Counted (logizomai) is a bookkeeping word: credited to his account. Paul uses it eleven times in these twenty-five verses, because his question is how righteousness gets onto a person’s account. God puts it there.

An old man under the stars. God has just taken old, childless Abraham outside at night, told him to number the stars if he can, and said, “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5). There is no child and no evidence: an old man in the dark, looking up, with nothing in his hands but a sentence God has spoken. And the next line is: “he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). Faith in the Bible is not a mood or a temperament. It is taking God at his word when the word is all you have.

Wages. Either a sum is earned, and entering it is bookkeeping, not generosity; or it is credited from outside, and the recipient contributed nothing but an account number. Righteousness is credited as a gift. And if you ever feel that God owes you something, after a hard season of faithfulness or a sacrifice nobody noticed, you have quietly moved yourself into the wages column, and the wages column has no grace in it anywhere.

What was not counted. Not Abraham’s obedience or his character, but that he believed God. So faith can never be reclassified as a small work that earns the rest. The hand that takes a parcel has not contributed to its contents: faith justifies not because it is a fine quality but because of what it lays hold of.

Credited, not infused. God does not merely decline to count Abraham’s sins (vv. 6–8); he puts something positive on the account, a righteousness the man did not have. This is what the Reformers meant by imputation. The righteousness is not infused into you like a medicine that gradually improves your condition, but credited like a sum entered in a book. If it were infused, your standing would rise and fall with your progress. Because it is credited, it is complete the day it is entered: a Christian ten minutes old and one of fifty years stand in exactly the same righteousness.

The account was empty. The account was empty when God made that entry. He has written the same entry against the name of every believer, and what he enters is the spotless righteousness of his own Son, the very offspring promised under those stars. “He determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names” (Psalm 147:4), and he has never lost count of a single sinner he has counted righteous.

But does James not say the opposite? James says Abraham was “justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar”, and that “a person is justified by works and not by faith alone” (James 2:21, 24). Three things fit Paul and James together. They speak of different moments: Paul quotes Genesis 15, when Abraham first believed; James points to Genesis 22, perhaps thirty years later, when that faith was tested and proved real. They answer different errors: Paul opposes those who think they can earn acceptance by works; James, those who think a faith that produces no works can save. And they use “justified” differently: Paul means declared righteous before God; James means shown to be righteous, proved genuine (“show me your faith”, James 2:18). James himself quotes Genesis 15:6 and says Abraham’s obedience fulfilled it (James 2:23). The faith that rests on Christ alone goes on working through love (Galatians 5:6).

Was Abraham saved by believing in Christ, or only in a promise about children? By believing the promise, and the promise was Christ: “And to your offspring,” who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Jesus said that Abraham “rejoiced that he would see my day” (John 8:56). Abraham did not know the name Jesus or the details of the cross, but he trusted the God who promised to bless the world through his offspring, and that offspring came. Old Testament believers were saved exactly as we are, by grace through faith in God’s promised Redeemer: they looked forward to him, and we look back.
verseByVerse.note: “Counted” is a bookkeeping word: credited to his account.

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God declares right with himself the person who brings nothing but faith, even the ungodly. It is the most startling sentence in the chapter: the Judge of all the earth acquits the guilty, and does it justly.

And to the one who does not work. Not that believers do no good works, but that they do not work in order to be justified. The qualification is having nothing to offer, which makes this one of the hardest verses for respectable people: most would rather be forgiven a great deal than be told their good record buys nothing.

Him who justifies the ungodly. Behind the phrase lie God’s own instructions to Israel’s judges: “He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD” (Proverbs 17:15); “I will not acquit the wicked” (Exodus 23:7). Paul takes the phrase straight out of Israel’s standard of justice and makes it a description of God, as if defining the Almighty by the one thing his own law calls an abomination. A holy God pronouncing right the people who are plainly wrong, without telling a lie: the words ought not to be able to stand together. They stand because a cross holds them up.

The ungodly. Paul does not soften it to the weak, the struggling, or the sincere but inconsistent. The word (asebēs) shares its root with the “ungodliness” of 1:18, against which God’s wrath is revealed. The very people charged there are acquitted here: good news for the worst sinner.

How God can do it. Justly, because Christ bore their punishment (3:25–26). The guilt was not overlooked but transferred and dealt with. Justification is not God deciding the ungodly are not so bad after all; it is a verdict already paid for. The gospel is not the announcement that God is lenient: a judge who can be talked round can be talked round by your accuser as well. Calvin and the Reformers loved to call it the wonderful exchange: Christ takes our ungodliness, and we receive his righteousness.

Two readers. This verse is written for two opposite readers. If you have been quietly afraid that you are too far gone, that God might save people like you in general but not you in particular, read the category again: he justifies the ungodly, not the improved ungodly. If God justified only good people, your fear would be rational. And if you have been decent all your life, attended faithfully and raised your children well, and none of this feels urgent, the word ungodly is yours too; the letter has spent three chapters establishing it, and you come on exactly the same terms as the man who has wrecked everything he touched. There is one door, and it is marked with a description you would not have chosen for yourself.

If I still feel ungodly after years as a Christian, was I ever justified? Feeling ungodly is not evidence against your justification; it is the condition God justifies. The verdict never rested on how godly you felt, and it does not move when your feelings do. What you feel is the war of a justified sinner against remaining sin, which Paul describes with anguish (7:15–25). God declares you righteous in an instant, then spends your life making you holy. If you hate your sin and keep running to Christ with it, that is exactly what a justified person looks like from the inside. Keep looking at him, not at the feeling.

Is it fair that the decent and the wicked come in on the same terms? It would be unfair if God marked on a curve, but he does not. Against a holy God the decent man and the wicked man are both bankrupt, one owing more than the other, neither able to pay (3:23). The objection usually comes from the heart of the older brother in Jesus’ parable, angry that his father threw a feast for the son who had wasted everything (Luke 15:28–30); his complaint showed that he too had been serving for wages, not loving his father. Grace offends us only while we think we are owed something. Once you see that you are the ungodly too, the same terms are the best news you have ever heard.

parallels.desc: I will not acquit the wicked

verseByVerse.quote: just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: "Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David agrees with Abraham: the blessed man is not the one with a clean record but the one whose sins God has forgiven. A second witness, a man who had done great evil, shows that God credits righteousness apart from works.

David also speaks. A second witness, as the law required: “Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15). Abraham, the nation’s founder, comes from the age before the law; David, its greatest king, from the age under it: two men on opposite sides of Sinai, both counted righteous by God, not by their record. And David answers a harder question. Abraham shows that God can count righteous a man who has done nothing to earn it; David, that he can count righteous a man who has done great evil.

Lawless deeds forgiven. From Psalm 32:1, traditionally read as written after David’s adultery and murder. Every religious instinct says the blessed man has a clean record. David says the blessed man is the one whose lawless deeds are forgiven, so by definition a man with lawless deeds. His blessing lies at the point of his worst failure, because that is where the forgiveness is; the psalm pronounces no blessing on anything David got right.

Covered. The two verbs answer two fears. Forgiven is a word for lifting and carrying away, the load taken off a man’s back. Covered means hidden from God’s judgment (Psalm 85:2). If your trouble is that you cannot carry it, the first word is for you; if it is that you cannot bear to have it seen, the second is. Paul has just named Christ as the true mercy seat (3:25), and what covers David’s sin, and yours, is his blood.

In everyday life. Take the thing you would least want read aloud, and ask which you have: is it unmentioned, or covered? Unmentioned means nobody knows and you are managing it, and the arrangement holds as long as nothing surfaces. Covered means it has been named to God without qualification and dealt with at the cost of blood; a covered sin is safe precisely because it has already been fully seen. The difference is the difference between Psalm 32:3–4 and Psalm 32:1–2. If it is only unmentioned, say it to God today.

What it does not mean. Covered does not mean that God looks the other way, or the file has been mislaid, or enough time has passed. The psalm rules out that fiction: while David kept silent, his bones wasted away and God’s hand was heavy on him day and night (Psalm 32:3–4). Its relief is not that of a man who has stopped thinking about it, but of one who said it out loud and found it had been dealt with.

Do I have to confess every single sin to be forgiven, even the ones I forget? Your justification does not hang on the completeness of your list. When you came to Christ, all your sins were forgiven, including those you have forgotten and those you never noticed (Psalm 19:12). Confession is not a fresh payment each time but the honesty of a child with his Father, which keeps the relationship open and warm: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). So confess what you know, specifically and without excuses, ask him to cleanse you from what you do not know, and rest. The blood covers more than your memory does.

parallels.desc: blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven

verseByVerse.quote: "blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The forgiven person is blessed because God will never count his sin against him. The promise is absolute, and it faces forward.

Will not count. Psalm 32:2, the other side of God’s counting. The construction (ou mē logisētai) is the double negative Greek keeps for absolute denial: will never, under any circumstances, the form of Jesus’ promises that “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37) and that his sheep “will never perish” (John 10:28). This is not a statement about God’s present mood. It is a door welded shut.

Not counted, and counted. Sin is not counted against us, because it was counted against Christ (2 Corinthians 5:19–21); righteousness is counted to us (v. 6), because his righteousness is ours. A man whose debts are cancelled has nothing; a man whose debts are cancelled and whose account is then filled from another’s fortune is rich. Justification is not a return to zero. It gives a standing you did not have even before you sinned.

Counted to his Son and Lord. David wrote this from the bottom of his life, confronted by a prophet and with nothing to say, and he wrote “blessed”, the word the Psalter uses of the righteous man in Psalm 1. The sin David could never pay for was counted in full to his Son and Lord, and the Lord who counted it there will never count it anywhere else.

In everyday life. When you have failed badly and confessed it, do you then keep your distance for a few days, praying less, not quite able to sing on Sunday, until you feel you have re-established something? That interval is the tell: it belongs to someone who believes his sins are not counted but suspects his standing must be earned back. Verses 6 and 8 together are the cure. The righteousness on your account was never your own doing, so there is nothing to re-establish. If you are in Christ, God will never count your sin against you, today included, with no waiting period.

What it does not mean. A verdict this absolute can be turned into permission, and Paul gives chapter 6 to the objection. He answers not by weakening the promise but by pointing to what has happened to the believer, who has died to sin with Christ (6:2). You do not answer such mercy by testing its limits, any more than a man pardoned at the scaffold spends the afternoon looking for another capital offence.

What about the sins I have not committed yet? It is natural to assume that the past was dealt with at the cross and the future runs on some kind of account. But look at the tense: not “has not counted” but “will not count”. The verb faces forward. When Christ died, every sin you would ever commit was still future, and last week’s were no more unknown to him than those of your childhood.

Then why do I still pray, “forgive us our debts”? Because you are now a child, not a defendant. Justification settles once for all that you will never be condemned. But a justified believer can still grieve his Father, fall under his fatherly displeasure, and need to come back humbly, confess and ask for the joy of fellowship to be restored (Westminster Confession 11.5; 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.5). David prayed, “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Psalm 51:12), not restore my salvation. So you pray the Lord’s Prayer not to be readmitted to the family but because you are in it, and children who love their Father do not let wrongs sit unspoken between them.

parallels.desc: blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity

verseByVerse.quote: Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessing of forgiveness is for Gentiles as well as Jews, because Abraham himself was counted righteous before he was circumcised. Paul settles the question not by an appeal to God’s generosity but by a date.

Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? Blessings are the sort of thing people quietly assume belong to their own kind. Does the forgiveness of Psalm 32 belong to the household only, available to insiders through the proper channels?

Was it before or after he had been circumcised? This is the calendar argument promised at the start of the chapter, and it is quietly devastating. Paul disputes no word of the text his opponents value. He does not say circumcision was unimportant, or Genesis misread, or the covenant provisional. He simply asks when, and there is only one answer: Genesis 15 comes before Genesis 17, and no amount of theology can move it.

Not after, but before. Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15 and circumcised in Genesis 17, at least fourteen years later. Between them lie the birth of Ishmael and thirteen more years: the boy is thirteen when the command comes (Genesis 16:16; 17:24–25). For a decade and a half the man the whole nation traced itself to was justified before God and outwardly indistinguishable from any pagan in Canaan. So circumcision was not necessary for justification, and Gentiles can be justified without it.

Justified as a Gentile. Abraham was justified while he was, in every visible respect, a Gentile: a man from Mesopotamia, from a family that served other gods (Joshua 24:2), with no law, temple, priesthood, sign or religious community. The God of Abraham has never been the God of insiders only. He went looking for a pagan in Ur, made him his friend under the open sky, and built a nation around him so that in the fullness of time its door could be thrown open to the whole world through Abraham’s Son.

The gospel preached beforehand. “The Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, ‘In you shall all the nations be blessed’” (Galatians 3:8). The uncircumcised man under the stars was a preview of the nations coming in, and the blessing reaches them as it reached him, through his offspring: “in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham” comes to the Gentiles, “so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith” (Galatians 3:14).

The arrangement. The instinct Paul dismantles is not only Jewish but human: the assumption that the promises of Scripture are addressed, in practice, to people properly inside the right arrangement: baptised, confirmed, on the roll, in the right church. It is rarely stated. It shows in the quiet confidence of those who have the arrangement, and in the hesitancy of those who do not.

What it does not mean. Not that the sign is worthless, as the next verse shows; the argument is about which came first, not about value. The sign could not produce what its owner already had, and a man who has the sign and nothing else has the receipt without the purchase.

Does it matter which church I belong to, then? Yes, but not for this. Belonging to a faithful church matters greatly: for sound teaching, for baptism and the Lord’s Supper rightly given, for care, discipline and love (Hebrews 10:24–25). Christ loves his church, and you should too. But no membership, however orthodox, justifies anyone, and no believer is shut out of God’s promises because he came to faith in an unremarkable congregation, or late, or alone. The church is the family the justified belong to, not the door by which they become justified. That door is Christ, received by faith.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15 and circumcised in Genesis 17, some years later.

verseByVerse.quote: He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well, and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Circumcision did not make Abraham righteous; it confirmed the righteousness he already had by faith, so that he could be the father of every believer, circumcised or not. What makes someone Abraham’s child is walking in his faith, not bearing his sign.

A sign and a seal. A sign points to something; a seal confirms it. A seal pressed into wax did not create an agreement; it authenticated one already made and showed whose the thing was. A seal on an empty page certifies nothing.

The father of all who believe. Here is what the chronology was for. Because Abraham was justified before he was circumcised, he is not merely an example Gentiles may study from a distance; he is their father, by faith and not by blood (Galatians 3:7). A believing Gentile is not like one of Abraham’s children. He is one.

The footsteps of the faith. He is father of believing Jews too, and the qualifier “not merely circumcised” does real work: the sign alone does not put anyone in the family. The picture is a child walking behind his father across a field, placing his feet where the bigger prints already are. Sonship is shown by direction of travel, not by paperwork.

Children through the one Offspring. God’s promises were spoken to Abraham and his offspring, and Paul insists the word is singular: it means Christ (Galatians 3:16). So no one becomes Abraham’s child by being added to a family tree, but by being joined to the one Son in whom the family is gathered: “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). The footsteps of faith all lead to him. And the God who once pressed a seal into Abraham’s flesh now seals his children with a seal no knife could make, the promised Holy Spirit, “the guarantee of our inheritance” (Ephesians 1:13–14), bought by the blood of Abraham’s Son. God promised Abraham a family like the stars, and he is keeping that promise one name at a time, in every language under heaven.

A lineage. If you are the first Christian anybody in your family can remember, this verse hands you a lineage. You are not a recent addition tolerated at the edge of somebody else’s story; your family history runs back four thousand years to a man under the stars in Canaan, and Paul argues it not as sentiment but as fact.

In everyday life. Abraham left security on the strength of a promise, waited twenty-five years, and believed what was physically impossible. Take one of those footprints and ask where in your life you are actually depending on something God has said, in a way that would look foolish if he did not exist. If nothing comes to mind, bring that to the God who gave Abraham the faith that walked; he gives it still.

My faith feels far too small to walk in his footsteps. Paul describes a pattern, not a standard of performance. He will shortly admit that Abraham considered his own body as good as dead, and Genesis records his lapses with complete honesty. The footsteps are evidence not of a great faith but of a faith pointed at the same object. A child does not have to fill his father’s footprint. He only has to be going the same way.

And our sign? Baptism stands in a similar relation to faith: commanded by God, truly meaningful, and never the thing itself. Paul’s argument cuts against the man who trusts his baptism as much as against the man who trusts his circumcision. Yet the sign is not nothing: it is given on Christ’s authority and declares what he has done. What it cannot do is manufacture what it declares.

I was baptised as a baby, so should I be baptised now? If you hold, as this commentary does with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism is for those who profess faith, then being baptised now is not a second baptism but obedience to Christ’s command for the first time as a believer, and many take that step gladly. Others, persuaded of the paedobaptist view, believe their infant baptism was valid and that they need to own it by faith, which they do. Whatever you conclude, do it from Scripture and with a clear conscience, after talking with your pastor, and never treat brothers and sisters who differ as anything less than fellow children of Abraham. The faith the sign points to matters more than either view of the sign.

Where Christians differ: circumcision, baptism and infants. Paedobaptists argue that baptism replaces circumcision as the sign and seal of the covenant (Colossians 2:11–12), and since circumcision was given to infants, baptism should be too; they also point to the households baptised in Acts (16:15, 33). These are serious arguments, held by many godly Christians. This commentary’s view: Paul says circumcision sealed the righteousness Abraham had by faith; in his case it followed faith. Circumcision was given to every male of Abraham’s household and line, Ishmael as well as Isaac, believing or not. In the new covenant all its members know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11), and the sign is given to those who believe (Acts 2:41; 8:12), as Colossians itself says: buried with him in baptism, raised with him through faith (Colossians 2:12). Credobaptists hold that baptism belongs to believers, while honouring paedobaptist brothers and sisters as fellow heirs of Abraham.

Uncertain wording. The Greek of v. 12 is awkward. Read word for word, it seems to speak of two groups, the circumcised and those who walk in Abraham’s faith, because Paul repeats the article before the second phrase. But the argument requires one group, circumcised people who also believe, as the ESV renders it (“not merely circumcised but who also walk”). The meaning is not in real doubt.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and confirmed that something was genuine.

parallels.desc: the sign of the covenant

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Promise Through Faith: Abraham's Hope Against Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The promise rests on grace and is received by faith, and the faith that receives it trusts the God who raises the dead. The inheritance never depended on the law, which brings wrath, but on faith, so that it is guaranteed to all Abraham’s children, Jew and Gentile (vv. 13–16). Abraham believed the God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence what does not exist, and he faced his own body, as good as dead, without letting go of the promise (vv. 17–22). Those words were written for us: the same righteousness is counted to all who trust the God who raised Jesus, handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification (vv. 23–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith and the resurrection

Romans 4:24–25 ties justification to the resurrection. Christ was raised for our justification: his resurrection is not only proof of who he is but the Father’s public declaration that his atoning work was accepted. Easter is not the happy ending of a sad story; it is the announcement that sin, death and wrath have been answered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul reads the promise to Abraham in its full scope (v. 13): a redeemed humanity in a renewed creation, fulfilled in Christ and received by faith. Now: Abraham’s hope against hope (v. 18) is the model for faith wherever circumstances say it is impossible. The God who gave life to Abraham’s and Sarah’s bodies raises the dead still: spiritually in every conversion, and bodily at the last day.

verseByVerse.quote: For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s promise that Abraham and his offspring would inherit the world never depended on keeping the law; it came through the righteousness received by faith. If the inheritance had to be earned by law-keeping, no one would receive it, and the promise would be worthless.

Heir of the world. Genesis never uses the phrase. God promised Abraham a land (Genesis 12:7; 15:18), countless offspring, and that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Paul reads the promise in its full scope: a blessing for every family on earth was never going to be exhausted by a strip of land (on the land itself, see the box at the end of this note). The heir is Abraham’s offspring, Christ, to whom God gives “the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession” (Psalm 2:8).

Not through the law. The law came 430 years later (Galatians 3:17). The promise was made, ratified and believed long before Sinai, so it cannot have depended on the law.

Null and void. If the inheritance depended on keeping the law, no one would inherit, since no one keeps it. Null means emptied; void, put permanently out of use. Faith and promise would not be weakened but cancelled: if the estate goes to those who perform, performance secures it, and faith is left as an ornament that holds nothing up. A contract binds two parties and is only as secure as the weaker signatory; a promise binds one party and names another as recipient, whose conduct is not what keeps it in force.

The God who walked alone. Genesis 15 itself shows it. When Abraham asked how he could know he would inherit, God told him to cut animals in half and lay the pieces opposite each other (Genesis 15:9–10). In a covenant ceremony the parties walked between the halves, calling the same fate on themselves if they broke the agreement (compare Jeremiah 34:18). Then a deep sleep fell on Abraham, and after sunset a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch, the presence of God, passed between the pieces alone (Genesis 15:12, 17). Abraham slept through the ratification. God bound himself, took the whole liability, and left the other party lying on the ground.

Heir. Nobody earns an inheritance; an heir need only be named. And an inheritance takes effect by a death (Hebrews 9:16–17). The promise made over the divided animals was finally carried out when the God who walked between them alone came in his Son and bore in his own body the death that ceremony threatened.

In everyday life. Try to describe what you are going to inherit. If it comes out vague and largely elsewhere, a good place after death, notice that Paul says heir of the world, and means it: this creation healed, a body that works, work worth doing, the earth under a good King. The promise ends with “the dwelling place of God” with man on a new earth (Revelation 21:1–3), so treat the world now as an estate you will inherit, not a waiting room you will leave.

Where Christians differ: does the land promise still belong to the Jewish people? Dispensational Christians (who see Israel and the church as distinct peoples in God’s plan) hold that it does: God promised Canaan to Abraham’s descendants “for an everlasting possession” (Genesis 17:8), and his promise cannot be cancelled. This commentary’s view: with many others, it reads the promise as not cancelled but enlarged. Paul says Abraham would be heir of the world; Hebrews says he “was looking forward to the city that has foundations” (Hebrews 11:10); Jesus says the meek “shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). Canaan was the down payment, and the renewed creation is the inheritance, belonging to all who are Christ’s, Jew and Gentile (Galatians 3:29). What God will yet do for ethnic Israel Paul takes up in chapter 11.

verseByVerse.quote: For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression. That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring — not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law cannot deliver the promise, because to sinners it brings wrath; so God made the promise depend on faith, to rest on grace and be certain for every believer. Only a promise resting on grace can be guaranteed, and only one received by faith can belong to Jew and Gentile alike.

For the law brings wrath. The law is good (7:12), but given to sinners it cannot give life; it exposes and condemns. It turns sin into transgression, and transgression brings God’s judgment (orgē, wrath). It brings not the inheritance but the charge sheet, like installing a speed camera on a road everyone was already speeding down: nothing is made worse, but everything is made explicit, and the fines start arriving.

Where there is no law there is no transgression. Transgression (parabasis) means stepping over a line. People without the law still sin and perish (2:12; 5:13–14), but transgression is the deliberate breaking of a known, stated command. You can be lost without a map, but you cannot trespass until somebody has put up a fence. Once God gave the law, sin became wilful rebellion against his spoken word (5:20; 7:13), so a promise hanging on the law would bring wrath, not blessing.

That the promise may rest on grace. Grace is God’s kindness to people who deserve the opposite, a gift with no wage in it (11:6), and faith receives what grace gives. A promise that cannot fail has to rest on grace, for any arrangement involving human performance is only as reliable as the human, and we have three chapters of evidence about that.

Guaranteed. A word from business and law (bebaian): a title that holds up, a deed that stands when challenged. Paul offers not a warm hope but a valid title, the difference between wanting something to be true and being able to produce the paperwork. Every human guarantor dies. This guarantee was given by the God who cannot lie, ratified in his Son’s blood and sealed by his Spirit, and it stands as firm on your worst day as on your best.

Wrath borne, promise guaranteed. If the law brings wrath, a guaranteed promise needs someone to stand between the wrath and the heirs. Paul has named him: God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (3:25), the sacrifice that turns wrath away. The law’s wrath was not cancelled; it was spent, on the Son. So the guarantee has a face. Hebrews calls Jesus “the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22), a priest who “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24). The title is as secure as his life, and his life can never end.

The father of us all. Jew and Gentile believers alike, not one nation with an annexe for outsiders: the argument lands on a family, which a promise, unlike a contract, can produce. God built salvation not on the sand of our performance but on the rock of his grace, so that every child of Abraham, weakest to strongest, stands on the same ground.

In everyday life. Compare how you approach God after a week in which you did well, prayed, resisted something, were generous, with how you approach him after a week in which you did none of it. If those feel very different, something has been fluctuating, and it is not the promise. That does not make you a hypocrite, but it shows where the work lies, and the work is not more effort: it is learning to believe that the title is secure in both weeks.

Can I really be sure I am saved? Yes, and this verse is one of the reasons. Assurance comes not from how well you are doing but from three things God gives together: his promises, which cannot fail because they rest on grace; the fruit of his grace in you, however small, such as love for Christ and hatred of sin; and the witness of his Spirit with your spirit that you are a child of God (8:16; Westminster Confession 18.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.2). A true believer may lose the feeling of assurance for a time and have to wait for it, but the title does not change. Doubting your assurance is not losing your salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is written, "I have made you the father of many nations" — in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, "So shall your offspring be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham believed the God who raises the dead and creates out of nothing, and so he went on hoping when there was nothing left to hope in. His faith rested not on any likelihood of a child but on who God is and what he had said.

I have made you the father of many nations. From Genesis 17:5, when God renamed Abram, “exalted father”, as Abraham, “father of a multitude”. God does not say “I will make you” but “I have made you”, to a childless old man: he does not describe reality, he establishes it. So everyone Abraham met called him father of a multitude while the promised son was unborn, and every conversation was a small act of faith or a small humiliation, depending on whether the One who named him could be relied on.

In the presence of the God in whom he believed. Abraham is not reasoning about a distant deity but standing before someone. Faith in the Bible is never a calculation of probabilities but a posture before a Person, which is why it can survive evidence a calculation could not.

Who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. These are the only two situations in which a human being has nothing whatever to contribute: when there is nothing there yet, and when what was there has died. A corpse cannot cooperate with its own raising, and nothing cannot assist in its own creation. Both applied to Abraham literally: the offspring did not yet exist, and the bodies through which they would come, his and Sarah’s, were as good as dead (v. 19). Later he would receive Isaac back from the altar as if from the dead (Hebrews 11:19).

In hope he believed against hope. With nothing in the situation to hope for, he hoped in God. This is not positive thinking or a refusal to admit facts; the next verse says outright that he faced them. Hope in Scripture is not a mood about the future but a settled expectation resting on something said. So the question is never how much hope you can generate, but whether the One who spoke can do it.

So shall your offspring be. From Genesis 15:5. Paul’s readers must believe something at least as unlikely: that a man executed in a province they have never visited is alive, and that his death has settled their account with God. So he gives them a father who stood in the same place.

He works with nothing and with the dead. God is not described here as the God who improves things; nothing and death are his usual raw material. He spoke, and a universe stood up out of nothing. He spoke, and a dead womb bore a son. He spoke, and on the third day a dead man walked out of a tomb. And that risen Son will speak once more, and “all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28–29).

In everyday life. Take the thing you are praying for and cannot see a way through: the marriage, the son, the diagnosis, the part of your own character that has not moved in twenty years. Ask which description in v. 17 it falls under: something that does not exist and would have to be created, or something that was alive and is now dead. Those are the specialities of the God you pray to. There is no third department for cases that are merely difficult, which suggests that difficulty was never the relevant measurement.

What it does not mean. This verse has been used to promise outcomes God never promised. Believing hard that a particular result will come is not the faith described here; faith fastens on what God has said (see “What he had promised” at v. 21). Where he has spoken plainly, that he will forgive, keep you, raise the dead, and work all things for the good of those who love him, you may believe against every appearance and will not be put to shame. Where he has not spoken about your particular case, ask, leave the answer with him, and keep believing what he has said while you wait.

Will God really raise my believing loved ones who have died? Yes. This is exactly the God described here, who gives life to the dead. “He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (8:11), and “through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:14). Their souls are already with the Lord, and their bodies will be raised, recognisable and glorious, when Christ returns. You may grieve, but not “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The grave is not a category God finds difficult.

verseByVerse.quote: He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb. No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham looked squarely at the facts that made the promise impossible and still did not let go of it; his faith grew stronger as he gave glory to God. Faith is not ignoring reality but trusting God in the face of it.

When he considered his own body. “Considered” is the verb for taking careful stock. Abraham was about a hundred, and Sarah ninety and barren. He did the arithmetic, got the right answer, and believed God anyway. Some teaching implies that doubt comes from looking too hard at reality; Paul says the reverse. The deadness was not the obstacle to the promise but the material it would work with, the very category God had just named (see the note on vv. 17–18), and Abraham could see both facts at once.

No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God. Many Christians have used this sentence against themselves: it sounds like unbroken confidence, and mine wavers weekly. But Genesis records that in these years Abraham lied about his wife to save himself (Genesis 20), took Hagar because waiting had become unbearable (Genesis 16), and, when God repeated the promise, fell on his face and laughed and said to himself, “Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?” (Genesis 17:17). Sarah laughed too, behind the tent door. His faith was not perfect, but in the end it did not turn from the promise itself. Paul is not rewriting the history but describing the direction of a life rather than auditing every hour of it. This is God’s summary of a long life (Hebrews 11:8–12): a man who staggers, not a man who defects. The striking thing is not that God failed to notice the failures but that this is how he chooses to remember a believer.

He grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God. Faith grows by looking at God, not at ourselves; trying to have more faith is like trying to fall asleep by concentrating: the harder you work at it, the more awake you are. Giving glory to God means saying back to him what he is like: that he keeps his word, that nothing is too hard for him, that he has never yet failed anyone. Faith honours God simply by trusting him to keep his word, as unbelief “has made him a liar” (1 John 5:10).

The faith that never staggered. Abraham looked at a body as good as dead and trusted the God who gives life to the dead. One descendant of his looked at his own death, not as good as dead but certain, and trusted the same God to the end. Peter says David’s words, “you will not abandon my soul to Hades”, were spoken of Jesus (Acts 2:27–31, quoting Psalm 16:10), and Jesus’ last breath was an act of faith: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). Abraham’s faith staggered and held. Christ’s held without staggering, and a staggering faith is safe because it is joined to his.

A gentler pen. Twenty-five years of nothing happening, two episodes of frank cowardice, a laugh, and one line in the New Testament that says he did not waver. Abraham looked at his dead body, and then he looked at God, and the second look was the longer one. The God who wrote that line over his life has a gentler pen than any of us, because every failure he leaves out of the record was written instead into the account of his Son, and paid.

Is faith believing what you know isn’t so? Mark Twain gave the line to a schoolboy: “Faith is believing what you know ain’t so.” Abraham’s faith was the opposite: he looked hard at the facts, and then at Someone else as well. Faith in the Bible is not a leap in the dark but trust in a person’s word, the kind we place every day in a surgeon, a pilot or a husband, and it is only as reasonable as the person is reliable. So the real question is not how much faith I can summon but whether this God is worth trusting, and Paul answers with an event, not a feeling: the God who raised Jesus from the dead (vv. 24–25).

What should I do with my doubts? Bring them to God rather than hiding them. The father in the Gospel cried, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24), and Jesus healed his son. Doubt is not unbelief: unbelief refuses God, while doubt is faith struggling and asking. Talk to a mature Christian; doubts grow in the dark. Go back to the evidence God has given, above all the resurrection of Jesus and the promises of Scripture. And do what Abraham did: give glory to God for what you know is true.

Does faith mean I should ignore medical facts or refuse help? No. Abraham considered the facts honestly; faith never requires pretending. Trusting God and using the means he provides go together: the God who heals gave us doctors, medicine and wisdom (1 Timothy 5:23; Colossians 4:14), and using them is no failure of faith. Refusing treatment to prove your faith is not faith but presumption, putting the Lord your God to the test (Matthew 4:7). Pray for healing, take the treatment, and leave the outcome with God. Faith says God is able, and God is good, whatever he decides; it does not say that facts are lies.

Textual note. The KJV and NKJV read that he did not consider his own body, following later manuscripts that add “not”; the earliest lack it. Either way, his faith did not give way before the facts.

verseByVerse.quote: fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham was fully persuaded of one thing: that God was able to do what he had promised. Faith rests on God’s promise and God’s power, not on our feelings or our ability.

Fully convinced. Brought to complete conviction (plērophorētheis): not a decision made once but a settled state. And the object is narrow, which is the mercy of the verse. Abraham was not convinced that he understood what God was doing, only that God could do what he had promised: far smaller and far harder than general spiritual confidence, and the whole of what is required.

That God was able. Our difficulty is often not God’s ability at all. Could he heal the illness, restore the marriage, save the son, break the habit? Of course. The doubt sits elsewhere and is rarely said aloud: whether he will bother, whether he has noticed, whether in this case he is inclined to. The letter answers that too: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (8:32).

What he had promised. Faith in Scripture always has a word behind it and can go only as far as that word goes. Abraham held on to a specific sentence God had spoken, and his confidence was exactly as wide as the promise. So when your faith is thin, do not try to generate more conviction; go and find the promise. This verse does not ask you to be strong, but to be convinced about somebody else’s strength. Abraham’s whole greatness was that he thought better of God than his circumstances did, and the God he trusted “is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think” (Ephesians 3:20).

Must I be fully convinced before God will count anything to me? No. Faith justifies not because it reaches a certain intensity but because of what it is attached to. Paul describes the character Abraham’s faith had settled into over twenty-five years, not its state on the first morning. Full assurance of this kind is the fruit of a long walk with God, not the fee for beginning one.

How do I know which promises are really mine? Ask to whom they were made. Some were given to particular people for particular events: Abraham’s son, Gideon’s victory, Paul’s safe arrival in Rome. Those show you God’s character, but they are not addressed to you. Others are made to all who belong to Christ, and those are yours in full, for “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). That he will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5), that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6), that nothing can separate you from his love (8:38–39): these are written to you. Learn them by heart, and lean on them by name.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why his faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. — Romans 4:22–24a
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s faith was counted as righteousness, and those words were written for us as well as for him. The way God dealt with Abraham is the way he deals with everyone who believes.

Not for his sake alone, but for ours also. Paul repeats Genesis 15:6, the sentence the chapter has unfolded, and says not merely that Abraham’s example is inspiring but that the very words “it was counted to him” had a second audience in view from the beginning; whatever was written in former days “was written for our instruction” (15:4). When God did something for a childless man in Canaan, he was also making a record that would hold your weight. You are not reading somebody else’s mail and hoping some of it fits. The letter has your name on it, addressed before you existed by the God who had you in mind when he took an old man outside to count the stars.

Moses wrote of me. The words were written for us because they were written, finally, about him. Jesus said that Moses “wrote of me” (John 5:46), and after his resurrection told his disciples that “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). The offspring promised under the stars is Christ, and the righteousness counted to Abraham is the righteousness Christ would bring. The record holds our weight because he stands inside it.

Not first a gallery of examples. This settles how to read Old Testament stories. Many of us were taught them as moral examples: be brave like David, faithful like Daniel, patient like Job. That reading exhausts you, asking for qualities you do not have, and it is not what the stories are first for. Paul does not say, “Be like Abraham.” He says the way God dealt with Abraham is the way God deals with you. The point of the story is not the patriarch’s faith but the Lord’s reckoning.

So should I never read Old Testament stories as examples? You should, but second, not first. Paul says these things “happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10:11), and Hebrews 11 sets the saints’ faith before us to imitate. The difference is order. First ask what the story shows of God, his grace, promises, judgment and patience, and how it points to Christ. Then ask what response that God deserves, and the example falls into place: not a standard to reach in your own strength, but the shape of a life that trusts the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. — Romans 4:24b–25
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteousness is counted to all who trust the God who raised Jesus, who was handed over to death for our sins and raised for our justification. Abraham’s faith and ours rest on the same God, doing the same kind of thing.

Him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord. This name for God closes the loop. Abraham believed the God who gives life to the dead (v. 17) and looked at a body as good as dead (v. 19). We believe the God who gave life to the dead and look at a body that was truly dead, laid in a tomb until the third day. The first was pointing to the second.

Delivered up for our trespasses. Handed over (paredothē): the word of Isaiah 53:12 in the Greek Old Testament, and of Judas’s betrayal. It is also the verb that fell three times like a gavel when God “gave them up” to the desires of their hearts, to dishonourable passions, to a debased mind (1:24, 26, 28). There God handed sinners over to what they had chosen; here he hands his own Son over to what they deserved. The letter’s most terrible verb and its most merciful one are the same word, and one handing over is the answer to the other.

Raised for our justification. Our trespasses were the reason he went to the cross, and our justification, accomplished there, the reason he came out of the grave (on the small word “for”, see the box at the end of this note). He was raised because the work was done, and the living Christ applies his righteousness to us (5:10; 8:34).

The receipt. Without the empty tomb, a man dies claiming to bear the sins of the world and stays dead, and no one can know whether the payment was accepted. Death releasing him is the public statement that there was nothing left to hold him for. The resurrection is God’s own signature on the transaction, given before witnesses who would not stop saying so even under threat of death. A payment can be doubted at three in the morning: was it enough, for me? The Father does not raise men whose work is unfinished.

Handed over and handed back. An old man in Canaan and a grave in Jerusalem are joined by one sentence: it was counted to him; it will be counted to us. Between them lies a Son handed over by his Father and handed back, and on that one weekend the standing of everyone who would ever believe hung on the Father’s verdict concerning him. The verdict was life.

In everyday life. When you have sinned badly and the accusation arrives, “You cannot possibly be forgiven for that”, listen to your reply. If it is your repentance, or how sorry you are, or a resolution about the future, the accusation will win, because none of those is strong enough and you know it. This verse puts in your hand a historical event you had nothing to do with: he was raised. Nothing you have done this week can un-empty that tomb. Say it back to the accuser, and to yourself: he was delivered up for my trespasses, and raised for my justification.

Who handed Jesus over: Judas, the rulers, Pilate or God? All of them, in different ways and with opposite purposes. Judas handed him over for money, the rulers out of envy, Pilate out of cowardice, and each was guilty. Yet he was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23), and Herod, Pilate and the peoples did “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:27–28). Above them all, the Father “gave him up for us all” (8:32), and the Son gave himself: “the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). Men meant it for evil; God meant it for the salvation of the world.

Why does the resurrection matter for my justification, and not only the cross? Because the cross is where the debt was paid, and the resurrection is where God declared it paid. Without it, “your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). The risen Christ also lives to apply what he won, interceding for us at God’s right hand (8:34), and faith is joined to a living Saviour, not a dead martyr. So the gospel is not only that Christ died for our sins, but that he was buried and raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Both halves belong in your confidence.

In the flow. This verse closes the case Paul opened at 3:21; chapter 5 begins to show what the verdict brings, starting with peace with God (5:1).

Uncertain wording. Paul uses the same small Greek word (dia) in both halves of v. 25, and with this construction it normally means “because of”. In the first half the sense is clear. In the second it may mean that he was raised because our justification had been accomplished and accepted, or raised in order to bring it to us. The ESV’s “for” leaves both open. The matching halves favour the first, and this commentary reads it so, but both are true in Paul, for the risen Christ lives to apply what he won (5:10; 8:34).

4.text: <sup>1</sup>What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh?<sup>2</sup>For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.<sup>3</sup>For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”<sup>4</sup>Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.<sup>5</sup>And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,<sup>6</sup>just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works:<sup>7</sup>“Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;<sup>8</sup>blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin.”<sup>9</sup>Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness.<sup>10</sup>How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.<sup>11</sup>He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well,<sup>12</sup>and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.<sup>13</sup>For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith.<sup>14</sup>For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.<sup>15</sup>For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression.<sup>16</sup>That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring—not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,<sup>17</sup>as it is written, “I have made you the father of many nations”—in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.<sup>18</sup>In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, “So shall your offspring be.”<sup>19</sup>He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah’s womb.<sup>20</sup>No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,<sup>21</sup>fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.<sup>22</sup>That is why his faith was “counted to him as righteousness.”<sup>23</sup>But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone,<sup>24</sup>but for ours also. It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord,<sup>25</sup>who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification.

keyVerse.quote: For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”
keyVerse.note: Every argument in the chapter unfolds this one sentence from Genesis 15:6: what it means that righteousness was counted (vv. 4–8), when it was counted (vv. 9–12), on what footing (vv. 13–22), and to whom (vv. 23–25). It shows that righteousness before God is a gift credited to faith, not a wage earned, and Paul says it was written for us as well as for Abraham.

4.reflection:
Paul takes the greatest man Israel could name and shows that he had nothing to boast about before God (vv. 1–2). What are you most tempted to lean on for your standing with God, and why is letting it go a relief rather than a loss?

Verse 5 says God “justifies the ungodly.” Why is that hard to accept both for someone who feels too far gone and for someone who has always been respectable? Which of the two are you more like?

Abraham was counted righteous years before he received the sign of circumcision (vv. 9–12). In what ways are we tempted to rest on belonging to the right church or having received the right sign, and how does this chapter answer that?

Abraham looked honestly at a body “as good as dead” and still trusted God’s promise (vv. 19–21). Where are you facing something that looks impossible, and what has God actually promised that you can hold on to while you wait?

5.title: Peace, Joy, and the Two Adams
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 1 to 4 have shown that all stand guilty and that God justifies the ungodly by faith in Christ, as he justified Abraham. Chapter 5 turns the corner: its first word, “Therefore”, opens four chapters on life inside that verdict.

The message. Those whom God has declared righteous are at peace with him, and nothing can undo it. They stand in his favour and will share his glory, and even their sufferings serve that hope, because God, who gave his Son for them while they were his enemies, will certainly bring his friends home. Behind it all stand two men. Adam’s one trespass brought condemnation and death to all who belong to him; Christ’s obedience brings righteousness and life to all who belong to him; and grace is far stronger than sin.

Why it was said. The believers in Rome were a small, suspected minority, some lately expelled from the city, with harder days ahead (see the introduction), and suffering could make them wonder whether God was really for them. And a church of Jews and Gentiles needed to see that the whole race stands under one of two heads, not under Israel’s law: all lost in the same way, and saved in the same way.

How the chapter makes its case. First, what justification brings: peace, access and the hope of glory (vv. 1–2), a hope that suffering strengthens, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts by the Spirit (vv. 3–5). Then the proof: Christ died for the ungodly, his enemies, so “much more” will God save those he has reconciled, and we rejoice in God himself (vv. 6–11). Then the larger story: sin and death entered through one man and reigned over all (vv. 12–14), but the gift outweighs the trespass at every point (vv. 15–17): condemnation for all in Adam, justification and life for all in Christ (vv. 18–19). The law made sin increase, but grace abounded all the more and now reigns (vv. 20–21).

Where it leads. The chapter begins with a man at peace with God and ends with grace on a throne, and both are the work of one Man. The second Adam obeyed where the first disobeyed, and walked into the death Adam let loose, and out again. Both halves of the chapter end on his name (vv. 11, 21).

For us. You do not have to re-earn your standing with God each morning; the war is over, and the peace rests on Christ, not on your week. When life is hard, read it by the cross, never the cross by your life. And the question for everyone is not whether we will be represented before God, but by whom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Peace, Access, Hope, and the Love of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those God has justified are at peace with him, and the love that made the peace will finish the work. Peace, access and a standing in grace are already ours, with the sure hope of sharing God’s glory (vv. 1–2). Even suffering serves that hope, producing endurance, character and hope, and the hope is safe because God’s love has been poured into our hearts by the Spirit (vv. 3–5). Paul proves that love from the cross: Christ died for the weak, the ungodly and sinners (vv. 6–8), and if God reconciled enemies by his Son’s death, much more will he save his friends by his Son’s life (vv. 9–10). The section ends not with the benefits but with the Giver: we rejoice in God himself (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Peace with God and assurance

Romans 5:1 is a foundation of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The believer’s peace with God is not the peace he feels on good days but the settled peace established by Christ’s finished work and received by faith. The Reformers taught this against the Roman Catholic view that a believer cannot ordinarily be certain of his justification: when God has spoken the verdict, to doubt it is to question his word. As Calvin taught, faith without assurance is not the faith of the New Testament.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ancient world met suffering by gritting its teeth, as the Stoics taught, or by avoiding pain, as the Epicureans taught; neither set it within the love of a personal God. Paul’s rejoicing in suffering (vv. 3–5) was new: suffering has a direction, and it ends in a hope the Spirit guarantees. Now: Many today treat suffering simply as the enemy of a good life, to be avoided at all costs. Romans 5:3–5 does not call suffering good, but it shows that God uses it to make his children steady and hopeful. A Christian who suffers and keeps holding on is not an oddity but a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand... — Romans 5:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has declared us righteous, the war between us and him is over, and we stand in his favour with a sure hope of glory. Paul is no longer arguing that a sinner can be justified; he is telling the justified what is now true of them.

Therefore. Everything from 1:18 has been a court case. Chapters 1 to 4 establish the verdict; chapters 5 to 8 describe life inside it.

Justified by faith. A completed fact: the verdict has been pronounced and the court has risen. God the Judge has declared you righteous: not guilty, and more, accepted, because Christ’s righteousness has been credited to you (4:5–6). Everything in this chapter rests on this, and on nothing else.

Peace with God. Not first a feeling of calm but a fact: the hostility between the holy God and the sinful creature has ended, because Christ made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). The hostility ran in both directions, though not in the same way. On our side it was real enmity: we were “alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds” (Colossians 1:21). On God’s side it was not bad temper but a just Judge’s settled opposition to evil, his wrath revealed from heaven (1:18). Our hostility could be overcome by God winning our hearts; his holy wrath could not be talked away but had to be satisfied, and Christ bore it. So the word is peace, not ceasefire. A ceasefire can be revoked on an afternoon’s notice; this treaty was signed in blood by the offended party. We did not negotiate it and we do not maintain it. He made it, and it stands as long as he stands.

Access. Access by introduction (prosagōgē); a related word named the official who brought visitors into a king’s presence. Nobody simply walked in to see a king; you were brought in by someone with the standing to bring you. And the tense describes a finished act whose result lasts: the introduction has already been made. You are not applying each morning to see whether today you may approach.

This grace in which we stand. Grace here is a place: something under you, bearing your weight. The tense is the same: we took our stand and are still standing. You do not have to re-establish your position with God every morning, any more than you must re-lay the floorboards before crossing the room.

Hope of the glory of God. To rejoice here is to boast, to exult (kauchōmetha), the word for the boasting excluded in 3:27.
