Boasting in our own record is shut out; a right boasting takes its place, in God’s glory, which we will share (8:18, 30). The charge sheet against the human race was summed up in these very words: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (3:23). Paul has made the phrase that stated our ruin the description of our future: not merely forgiveness for falling short of the glory, but the glory itself. We were made to reflect it as a mirror reflects the sun, and sin turned the mirror away. In Christ we are already being changed into his likeness, and when he appears we shall be like him (2 Corinthians 3:18; 1 John 3:2).

Hope is not wishful thinking. In the New Testament hope is confident expectation of what God has promised and not yet delivered. The uncertainty is only about the date, never about the thing.

How to use the access. An open door is wasted if you stand outside it. Hebrews draws the same conclusion: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). So come straight away after you have failed, not after a decent interval, because the access was never based on your week. Come in his name, which is why Christians pray through Jesus Christ: he is the one who brings you in. Come with small things as well as large; a king’s child needs no appointment to mention a scraped knee. Come briefly and often, in the car and at the sink, as well as at set times. And come with others, for the access belongs to the whole family: “through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18).

In everyday life. Which of these two sentences describes your normal week: I am trying to get right with God, or I am right with God? If the background hum of your spiritual life is effortful and anxious, a project not yet completed, hear Paul’s first word: therefore. The case is closed. Pray today not as one applying for an audience but as one who has been brought in and is still standing there.

If I have peace with God, why do I still feel anxious or guilty? Because feelings report on many things, and God’s verdict is not one they report well. Your peace is a fact about his judgment of you, settled in Christ, and a bad night does not reopen it. Guilt you still feel may point to something real; then confess it and believe 1 John 1:9. Or it may be the leftover echo of sins already forgiven (see the note on vv. 15–16). Anxiety may be temperament, tiredness or illness, none of which alters your standing. Do not try to feel your way into peace. Look at the verdict, and let the feelings follow when they can.

Textual note. The ESV footnote records that some manuscripts read “let us have peace”. The difference is a single Greek letter, a long o for a short one, pronounced alike in Paul’s day, so a scribe taking dictation could easily write one for the other. The “let us have” reading has strong early support, but most modern translations read “we have”, and rightly: the context lists what we have, and Paul is drawing a conclusion, not urging us to do something. Even on the other reading the peace would still be a fact: it would mean “let us enjoy the peace we have”, never “let us try to obtain it”.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “let us have peace.”

parallels.desc: the effect of righteousness will be peace

verseByVerse.quote: Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers can rejoice even in their sufferings, because God uses them to produce endurance, proven character and a firmer hope. The joy is not in the pain itself but in what God is doing through it.

In our sufferings. “Not only that”: the verb is the same as in verse 2. That joy looked at the future; this one is found in the present at its worst (James 1:2–4; 1 Peter 1:6–7), not merely in spite of sufferings but in them. For the first readers this was not theory. Some had been expelled from Rome under Claudius (Acts 18:2), all lived as a small, suspected minority, and within a few years Nero would blame them for the great fire of AD 64 (see the introduction).

Endurance. “Suffering” (thlipsis) is pressure, the crushing of something under weight. “Endurance” (hypomonē) is not passive resignation but “remaining under”: staying put beneath a load instead of crawling out from under it. Hardly anyone has become patient in a comfortable year; some of the qualities we most want are made only in conditions we would never choose.

Character. A word from the testing of metals (dokimē): metal that has been through the refiner’s test and come out proved genuine. It shares its root with the failed test of 1:28, where those who would not acknowledge God were given up to a mind that, like bad metal, did not pass. Here the metal passes. A proving does not create the quality; it shows it, to the man himself, and most of us do not know what we believe until something has tried to take it away. Trouble also shows what we were leaning on: when health, money or reputation is taken, we find out whether it was a gift we enjoyed or a god we trusted.

Hope. We would expect hope to make endurance possible; Paul says hope is the result. A tested believer hopes because he has evidence: he was where he was certain he could not go on, and he went on, and looking back he can see that he was carried. This hope is not optimism about the future but a conclusion drawn from the past.

The road the Son walked first. Paul’s chain is the road Christ walked. The risen Lord asked two disciples on the way to Emmaus, “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26), and the order of those words is the order of these verses: affliction first, glory after. The Father vindicated him by raising him, and so Paul can say that we suffer with him “in order that we may also be glorified with him” (8:17). A believer’s affliction is not a detour from Christ’s road but a share in it, and it ends where his ended.

What it does not mean. Not that suffering is good or to be sought; the Lord himself wept at a grave he was about to empty. Paul says rejoice not because of sufferings but in them: joy inside a situation that remains bad, because of something else that is true. Nor is this a formula that promises outcomes. Anyone who has watched a man come out of a hard decade smaller and harder knows that suffering by itself produces bitterness at least as often as endurance. The difference is not the quantity of pain but what the sufferer holds on to, which is why the paragraph ends at the love of God poured into the heart (v. 5).

In everyday life. Write down the three hardest things you have been through as a Christian. Beside each, write what you feared would happen: that you would lose your faith, or not cope, or never be happy again. Then write what actually happened. If you cannot reconstruct how you got through, you were carried. That list is the raw material of hope, made as Paul says hope is made. Keep it for the start of the next hard thing.

If I cannot feel any joy in this. If you can find no joy in your suffering at all, you have not failed this passage. Paul describes a direction of travel over years, not a mood to produce on demand. Endurance mostly looks like simply not leaving. If you are still, in some ragged fashion, holding on, the first link of this chain is being forged in you now, and it will not feel like anything while it happens.

Does this include suffering I brought on myself? Yes, though differently. Peter distinguishes suffering for doing good from suffering for doing wrong (1 Peter 2:20), and the second calls first for repentance. But God does not waste even the consequences of our folly. Once the sin is confessed and forgiven, the pressure that remains is still pressure, and God still works endurance, character and hope through it. Grace is not too proud to work with the wreckage.

Does God send suffering, then? Scripture holds two things together without embarrassment. Suffering is an intruder in God’s world, the fruit of the fall that this very chapter goes on to describe, and God takes no pleasure in it for its own sake (Lamentations 3:33). Yet nothing reaches a believer that has not passed through his hands, and he works all of it for good (8:28). Joseph could tell his brothers that they meant it for evil and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20), in one sentence, about one event. You do not have to call the thing good. You may call God good in it.

verseByVerse.quote: and hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our hope will never let us down, because God has already poured his love into our hearts by the Spirit he has given us. Its safety rests not on the strength of our character but on what God has done inside us.

Hope does not put us to shame. Not chiefly embarrassment. In the Old Testament, to be put to shame is what happens when confidence proves misplaced: the ally does not come, the god does not answer, and you are seen to have backed the wrong thing (Psalm 25:3). This hope will not do that, not because we hope sincerely, but because of what is holding the other end.

Because God’s love has been poured into our hearts. Tested character produces hope (vv. 3–4), but Paul does not rest hope’s safety on our character; he rests it on something given. And this is not first our love for God but his love for us, poured in and made real to the heart, so that we do not only work out that he loves us but know it. “Poured” (ekkechytai) is an extravagant word, used of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:17) and of the blood of the covenant poured out for many (Matthew 26:28): something emptied out without measuring. The tense describes a finished act whose results remain. The reservoir was filled before today, and a bad week does not empty it.

The Spirit who has been given to us. Every believer has the Spirit (see the question below), and it is the Spirit who assures us of God’s love, so that we cry “Abba! Father!” (8:15–16). He is the firstfruits of the coming glory (8:23), God’s own pledge that the hope will be honoured.

The stone that will not shame. Paul has a prophet’s promise in mind, and later in this letter he tells us whom it is about. Isaiah 28:16 spoke of a tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion, and Paul applies it directly to Christ: whoever believes in him will not be put to shame (9:33; 10:11). And the love poured into us does not come by a different route from the cross. It was the exalted Christ who received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and poured him out on his people (Acts 2:33). The hope that will not disappoint rests on a stone laid in Zion and a gift sent from a throne, and both are Christ.

What if I have never felt anything of the kind? Many faithful Christians read this verse and conclude that it has not happened to them. Three things, carefully. First, Paul is not describing one kind of experience, a single moment or something that could be arranged at a meeting. It is in the man who finds, to his surprise, that he wants to pray; in the sudden conviction, halfway through an ordinary Tuesday, that you are not facing your life alone; in tears at a line of a hymn sung a hundred times; in the fact that you mind about your sin at all. None of those announces itself as the love of God being poured out, and all of them are.

Temperament and health are real. Second, some people feel everything strongly and some very little, largely because of how they were made and how they slept. Some believers have loved Christ for forty years with the emotional volume permanently low; others have had their capacity to feel flattened by depression, exhaustion or grief. Scripture never treats intensity of feeling as the measure of anything, and someone whose illness has taken his feelings has not lost the Spirit who was given to him.

The evidence is not only inward. Third, and most usefully, the presence of the Spirit shows in ways that do not depend on your feelings today. Do you call God Father, and mean it? That is the Spirit (8:15). Do you want holiness, even while failing at it? Is Christ precious to you in a way he was not at nineteen? Those are not achievements. They are signs that he is there.

Does every Christian have the Spirit, or is he a later blessing for some? Every Christian has him. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (8:9), and here Paul speaks of the Spirit as given to us: the whole church in Rome. There is no second class of believers still waiting. Christians may be filled afresh, strengthened and led more deeply as they grow (Ephesians 5:18), and you should ask for that. But you do not need to seek the Spirit as though you lacked him. You need to believe what he has already been given to do in you.

Where Christians differ: a later baptism in the Spirit? Many Pentecostal and charismatic brothers and sisters speak of a baptism in the Spirit after conversion, and their hunger for more of God is right. This commentary’s view: the New Testament gives the Spirit to every believer at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13), with fresh fillings after, and no second class of Christian.

parallels.desc: in you they trusted and were not put to shame

verseByVerse.quote: For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ died for us when we were powerless and ungodly, at the time God had chosen, and no human love has ever gone so far. Someone might perhaps dare to die for a good person; Christ died for the ungodly.

While we were still weak. Paul now proves the love he has described. Inward experience can be doubted on a bad night, so he goes outside us altogether: the proof is a death, in public, at a datable moment, and its force lies in when it happened. “Weak” (asthenōn) does not mean doing our best in hard circumstances but without strength, the word used of the sick, like the invalid at the pool who could not get himself into the water (John 5:7).

At the right time Christ died for the ungodly. The cross was no accident of history. God planned it, and it came “when the fullness of time had come” (Galatians 4:4), exactly when we were helpless. “For the ungodly” means in their place, on their behalf, and “ungodly” is the word of 4:5, where God justifies the ungodly. If Christ had died for the repentant, the cross would prove that God responds well to repentance. If he had died for the promising, it would prove that God has an eye for potential. He died for people who were at that moment incapable, opposed and guilty, which proves something about God and nothing whatever about us.

Scarcely for a righteous person, perhaps for a good one. Paul looks for the highest human love he can find, to measure God’s against it. For an upright, admirable man one will scarcely die; for a warm and generous one, perhaps someone might dare it. People do die for others: a mother for her child, a soldier for the man beside him. But almost always something in the one loved draws it out; our love responds to worth or to belonging. Hardly anyone dies for a man who has wronged him and would not be grateful. That is not cynicism; it is our ceiling. Christ died for neither the righteous nor the good, but for the ungodly.

A different kind of love. God’s love is a different kind of thing, not a larger quantity of ours. Ours is drawn out by something lovely in the person loved; his begins in himself and makes lovely what it will later delight in. So the question What does God see in me? has no answer, not because the answer is disappointing, but because it assumes his love works like ours. A love with a reason can lose its reason; a love shown to people who were at that hour helpless and hostile has nothing in us to lose.

In everyday life. When you try to believe that God loves you, notice what you offer yourself as the reason: that you have been trying, that you mean well, that you are not as bad as you might be. Set it against verse 6. Christ died for the weak and the ungodly, people with not one reason to offer. Whatever you were holding did not secure this and cannot keep it. Put it down.

Does this mean Christ died for me in particular? Paul writes “we” and “us”, telling believers what Christ did for them. But weak and ungodly are not the names of a select class you might fail to qualify for; they are the names of everyone, and the gospel is offered freely to all. No one who comes to Christ will discover that he was not included. If you are trusting him, you may say with Paul that he loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20); if you are not yet, the only qualification for coming is the one you already have: being ungodly.

Uncertain wording. Interpreters are not sure how sharply Paul distinguishes the “righteous” person from the “good” one. Most think he does: the righteous man is upright and correct, the good man generous and warm, perhaps a benefactor. Others think the second clause simply softens the first; and the Greek for “a good person” could even mean “a good cause”. On every reading the point stands: the highest human love needs something worthy in its object, and Christ died for the ungodly.

parallels.desc: when the fullness of time had come

verseByVerse.quote: but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God proves his love for us by this: Christ died for us while we were still sinners. The cross is not a clue that God was once kindly disposed, but a standing exhibit of a love that saw us at our worst and gave his Son.

God shows his love. “Shows” (synistēsin) means to exhibit, to prove by putting on display, and the tense is present: God goes on demonstrating his love in this. His kindness shows in his sun rising on the evil and on the good (Matthew 5:45); but to prove that he loved people who hated him, nothing would do but the death of his Son.

His love. Literally “his own love”, and later Paul makes plain what it cost: he did not spare his own Son (8:32). This is not a loving Son appeasing an angry Father, but the Father showing his love by giving his Son (John 3:16). The cost fell inside the Trinity. Anybody can be generous with somebody else’s son.

While we were still sinners. Christ did not wait until we had begun to change; he died for us in the middle of our sinning. The cross was aimed at your life at its worst, not at the person you have since become, and it is not waiting on the person you hope to be.

The first demonstration has never ended. The exhibit is not a memory. The hands nailed at the hour of our worst were raised with the marks still in them and shown to a doubting disciple (John 20:27), and the Lamb at the centre of the throne still stands as though slain (Revelation 5:6). The proof of the Father’s love was carried into heaven and set at the centre of everything. No second demonstration is needed, because the first has never ended.

“You are enough.” The slogan on mugs and posters is meant as medicine for a culture worn out by shame and perfectionism, and the instinct is right: we need to be accepted, not kept on probation. But who says I am enough? If the verdict is mine, it rises and falls with my week, and on the day I lose my temper with my children the slogan becomes one more standard I am failing: the old treadmill in softer clothes. Paul says something far better. You were not enough. You were weak, ungodly, a sinner, an enemy, and at that very moment God gave his Son for you. A love that took the worst into account before it acted cannot be lost when the worst comes out. The slogan asks you to keep believing in yourself. The cross asks you to believe in a love that has already seen everything and stayed.

The two moments to reach for this verse. They are opposite. The first is when you have failed badly and cannot bring yourself to pray, and the accusation says, Not after this. But the love was demonstrated when you were doing exactly this, and worse; God knew your failure when the price was paid. The second catches the respectable, who have never doubted God’s love because it seems reasonable enough: they go to church, give, pray and mean well. That confidence rests on an assessment of themselves, which can be revised. Verse 8 takes it away, which feels at first like a loss and is the only route to a peace that does not depend on how the year has gone.

How can it be loving to punish an innocent man in the place of the guilty? Put that way it sounds like a miscarriage of justice. But this verse does not describe a third party being conscripted. The Judge did not find a substitute; he became one. The one who was owed the debt is the one who paid it, in the person of his Son, by agreement within the Godhead before the world began, and the Son laid down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). That is not injustice. It is the only arrangement in which mercy costs the one who extends it, justice is fully satisfied, and the guilty are fully freed.

If God loves me like this, why does my life feel as though he does not? Because Paul points you not to your circumstances as the proof of God’s love but to the cross. Circumstances in a fallen world shift every week; read alone, they say God loves you on Monday and has forgotten you by Thursday. The cross is the fixed point from which everything else is read: the God who gave his Son for you while you were his enemy has not stopped caring because the job was lost or the treatment failed. He who did not spare his own Son will with him graciously give us all things (8:32). Read your life by the cross, never the cross by your life.

verseByVerse.quote: Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God justified and reconciled us when we were his enemies, he will certainly finish saving us now that we are his friends. The hard part is done, and the rest is safe in the hands of a living Saviour.

Justified by his blood. By his sacrificial death, which turned God’s wrath away from us (3:25). Paul now reasons from the harder case to the easier, as Jewish teachers often did. If a man has given you his house, he is not going to quibble about the key.

Much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. God’s wrath is the Judge’s just sentence against evil, stored up for the day when it will be revealed in full (2:5). We instinctively assume the hard part is still ahead: the cross is settled, but will we make it? Paul says we have it the wrong way round. The hard part was justifying enemies, and that is done. What is left is God keeping his friends safe on that day, and he will not fail at the easy end of his own work.

While we were enemies. Paul has climbed for four verses, weak, ungodly, sinners, and now enemies, hostile to God (8:7). God did not merely find us lost and pity us; he found us in arms against him and made peace at his own expense. And he took the initiative: it is God who reconciled us to himself through Christ (2 Corinthians 5:18–20). We did not come to the table. He came to us.

Saved by his life. Reconciled by his death, we shall be saved by his life. Our future rests not on something a dead man once did, but on a living Saviour who always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). So your security does not depend on the strength of your grip on Christ, but on a man alive at this moment whose present occupation is you. The Son who died for his enemies now lives for his friends, and he has never lost one whom the Father gave him (John 6:39).

Assurance and perseverance. These verses ground the perseverance of the saints: God keeps every true believer to the end. They answer a fear many serious Christians rarely voice: I might not last, because I know myself. That fear would be reasonable if the finishing depended on you. But the one who did the hard part when you were his enemy is doing the rest now that you are his child.

What it does not mean. This is no invitation to drift; chapters 6 and 12 to 16 spell out what is required. Paul is saying where the guarantee lies. The Christian is still called to endure, and he can, because the outcome does not hang on the quality of his enduring, and the Spirit given to him (v. 5) is his strength. A man rowing a boat that is also under tow rows better, not worse.

If I am already saved, what does saved from wrath mean? Scripture speaks of salvation in three tenses. You have been saved from the penalty of sin, when you were justified (Ephesians 2:8). You are being saved from its power, day by day, as the Spirit makes you holy (1 Corinthians 1:18). And you will be saved from its presence and from the wrath to come on the last day (1 Thessalonians 1:10). Paul means the third here: the final rescue when Christ returns. It has not happened yet, and it is not in doubt, because it was paid for in the first.

But what about the warnings, and people who seem to fall away? The New Testament seriously warns believers against drifting and unbelief (Hebrews 3:12–14), and some who professed faith did leave. John explains: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Their departure showed that the root was never there, not that God failed to keep one of his own. The warnings are one of the means by which God keeps his people: a believer who heeds them and turns back to Christ is persevering. If you fear you might fall away, the fear itself, and the turning to Christ it produces, are signs of life. Those who fall away are not usually worried about it.

verseByVerse.quote: More than that, we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The best gift of the gospel is God himself: through Christ, the reconciled now rejoice in God. Peace, hope and rescue all lead here, to delight in the Giver.

We also rejoice in God. Three rejoicings make a staircase: in hope of glory (v. 2), joy about the future; in sufferings (v. 3), joy in the present at its worst; and now in God himself, the top step. The goal of salvation is not a set of benefits. It is God.

Received reconciliation. Not achieved, but received. This was no settlement between two aggrieved parties who each moved some way. One party was entirely in the wrong and did not want terms; the other made peace at his own cost and handed it to the offender as a gift.

Now. The small word is Paul’s drumbeat through the section: now justified (v. 9), now reconciled (v. 10), now received (v. 11). Not at the last day, not pending review. Whatever remains outstanding in the Christian life, and chapters 6 to 8 will be honest about how much does, the relationship itself is settled.

Joy in God through a Man. The words “through our Lord Jesus Christ” belong to the whole sentence, because God is enjoyed only where he is seen, and he is seen in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). Whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father (John 14:9). So the joy at the top of the staircase is a share in the Son’s own delight in his Father: Jesus prayed that the love with which the Father loved him before the foundation of the world might be in his people (John 17:24, 26). We rejoice in God by being brought inside that joy.

The gifts and the Giver. It is possible to be glad about forgiveness, relieved about judgment and attached to one’s church, and have little appetite for God himself. That is not hypocrisy; the gifts were meant to be enjoyed. But test it: if God gave you everything you have asked and were himself absent, would it be enough? If something essential would be missing from such a world, you have found what verse 11 is about, and that preference is the surest evidence in the chapter that something real has happened to you. If your honest answer troubles you, bring the trouble to him: grieving that you want him too little is itself a way of wanting him.

What does rejoicing in God actually look like? Enjoying God for who he is, not only for what he does. It shows in praise that dwells on his holiness, faithfulness, wisdom and mercy, and not only on the week’s answers to prayer; in prayer that sometimes asks for nothing and simply stays in his company; in reading Scripture to see him, not only to find instructions; and in a quiet steadiness when the gifts are thin, because the chief good has not gone anywhere. It does not need to be loud. Asaph had watched the wicked prosper until his feet almost slipped, and he ended his psalm finding God his portion, with no one in heaven or on earth he desired besides him (Psalm 73:25–26).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Death in Adam, Life in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two men decide the standing of the human race, and the second undoes the work of the first and far more. Through Adam’s one trespass sin and death entered the world and spread to all, and death reigned even before the law was given (vv. 12–14). But the parallel is uneven: the gift outweighs the trespass, justifying after many sins and making those who receive it reign in life (vv. 15–17). Then Paul completes his sentence: as one trespass led to condemnation for all in Adam, one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all in Christ (vv. 18–19). The law only made sin increase, but grace abounded all the more, and it now reigns through righteousness to eternal life (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Federal headship

Romans 5:12–21 is the main biblical basis for the Reformed doctrine of original sin: all sinned in Adam, their covenant head (see “Federal headship” at vv. 12–13 and the box there on the two readings of “all sinned”). And the parallel with Christ is the point: as we were condemned in Adam, so we are justified in Christ, in the same way, by one man acting for all who belong to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish writers of Paul’s day already saw Adam as the one through whom ruin came to humanity, and Paul uses that shared starting point to show how universal sin is and how wide the gospel’s offer is. Now: Every generation supplies fresh evidence that something has gone wrong with the human race at its root. Romans 5:12–21 names where it began, in Adam, and offers the remedy, Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned — for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin entered the world through one man, Adam, death came in behind it, and death spread to everyone because all sinned. Paul begins a comparison between Adam and Christ here that he will not finish until verse 18.

Through one man. The one man is Adam (Genesis 3). Paul treats him as a real, historical man, and tells his story here for one reason: the Man who was to come (v. 14). Adam is in the paragraph because Christ is.

A sentence left unfinished. Paul begins, “just as sin came into the world through one man”, and breaks off; the matching “so” does not arrive until verse 18. Knowing that verses 13 to 17 are an aside makes the paragraph easier to follow.

Death through sin. Death is not natural; it is the penalty of sin (Genesis 2:17). And it is more than the grave. Warned that in the day he ate he would surely die, Adam died at once in his relationship with God, and in his body years later. So death here includes physical death, the spiritual death of being cut off from God (Ephesians 2:1), and, apart from Christ, eternal death, the wages of sin (Romans 6:23). That is why the answer at the end of the chapter is not only resurrection but eternal life (v. 21).

Death spread to all. Paul’s evidence is a fact anybody can check: death has spread to all, with no exception in the record, infants included. What could account for it?

Because all sinned. In what sense did all sin? Not merely by copying Adam, for Paul will say five times that condemnation and death came through one man’s one trespass (vv. 15–19). The Reformed tradition calls this federal headship, from the Latin for covenant (foedus): Adam stood as covenant head of the race, and his sin is counted to all his descendants, just as Christ’s obedience is counted to believers (Westminster Confession 6.3). An older view, natural headship, says we sinned in Adam because all human nature was present in him. Both reject the idea that Adam merely set a bad example, and the federal view best explains the exact symmetry Paul draws between the two men (on the Greek behind “because”, see the end of this note).

Sin is not counted where there is no law. “Counted” (ellogeitai) means charged to an account, as in a ledger. Between Adam and Moses there was no written law, so people’s sins were not charged as transgressions of a stated command, as Adam’s was (see 4:15). Yet they still died, and death is the penalty of sin, so Adam’s sin must have been counted to them. The written law did not create sin, then; it put into words what was already wrong.

He walked out holding the keys. One man opened the door, death came in after him, and no one born since has been able to shut it. Then the eternal Son took the flesh of Adam’s children, without Adam’s sin, stood where Adam stood and did not fall. He walked into the death Adam let loose, not dragged but willing, and on the third day walked out of it holding the keys (Revelation 1:18).

In everyday life. Many say death is natural, yet nobody stands at a funeral thinking this is how it should be. We grieve as though a person has been taken, and Scripture agrees with the instinct, not the theory: death is an enemy, the last to be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26). At the next graveside, let your grief say what Paul says, and then let your hope say what he goes on to say.

Is it fair to be condemned for Adam’s sin? Every reader asks it, usually as: I never voted for Adam. Several things help. Representation is how God has always related to humanity: the head acts for those in him. It is the fabric of ordinary life too. A country goes to war on the decision of a government many of its citizens did not choose; children inherit the language, debts and reputation their parents hand them. We accept inherited goods readily and object loudly to inherited liability.

Represented by Adam or by Christ. Adam was the best representative humanity could have had, in a perfect world with every advantage; no one can say he would have done better. And each of us confirms his choice: every human being has stood where Adam stood, with what God has said on one side and his own preference on the other, and has chosen as he chose. So Paul can say both that the many were made sinners by one man’s disobedience and that all sinned. Above all, reject representation and we lose the gospel, for we are saved in exactly the same way: by another man’s obedience counted to us (vv. 18–19). We cannot accept the second Adam and refuse to understand the first. The question is not whether we will be represented, but by whom.

Standing alone. Insist on standing alone, judged strictly on your own record, and you would be free of Adam’s guilt but left with your own, which this letter has spent three chapters describing. Both men acted before you were consulted. Only one acted deliberately for your good.

Does original sin mean I am not really responsible for my sins? No. Original sin explains where the disease came from; it does not excuse what you do with it. Scripture holds people accountable for their own choices (Ezekiel 18:20; Romans 2:6), and nobody sins against his will; we sin because we want to. The doctrine deepens responsibility, showing that the problem is not a few bad decisions but a heart turned from God at the root: bad news for self-improvement, good news for the gospel. You need not a better example but a new head and a new heart, and both are offered in Christ.

Where Christians differ: two readings of “all sinned”. The first, taught by Pelagius, a monk of the early fifth century, says that Adam only set a bad example, and all die because each person sins personally, following it. The second says all sinned in Adam, when he sinned as the representative head of the human race. This commentary’s view: the second, for three reasons Paul gives in the passage itself. First, death reigned even over those who did not sin as Adam did (v. 14), including infants, who have committed no personal sins, so their death must come from Adam’s sin. Second, Paul says five times that condemnation and death came through one man’s one trespass (vv. 15–19), not each person’s many sins. Third, verse 19 says that by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners: Adam’s act, not our own, is the ground of our standing as sinners. Personal sins follow, real and adding to our guilt, but the root is our union with Adam. This is original sin: we inherit Adam’s guilt, counted to us, and his corrupted nature (Psalm 51:5; Ephesians 2:3).

Where Christians differ: was Adam a real person? Some Christians, seeking to harmonise Genesis with evolutionary accounts of human origins, hold that Adam is a symbol of humanity, not a real first man. This commentary’s view: Paul’s argument requires a real, historical Adam. He sets one man against one man, one trespass against one act of righteousness, and a real history of death reigning from Adam to Moses (v. 14). Without a real Adam whose sin brought condemnation, the parallel with the real Christ whose obedience brings justification falls apart, and so does the comfort. Paul treats Adam the same way elsewhere (1 Corinthians 15:22; 1 Timothy 2:13–14); Jesus treated Adam and Eve as real (Matthew 19:4–5); and Luke traces Jesus’ genealogy back to Adam (Luke 3:38). Christians who take the symbolic view are often wrestling honestly with real scientific questions, which deserve patient answers; but the argument of this chapter stands or falls with a real Adam.

Uncertain wording. “Because” translates two small Greek words (eph’ hō) whose exact sense has long been debated. Augustine, reading the Latin translation (in quo, “in whom”), took them as “in whom all sinned”, that is, in Adam. Most scholars now agree that the Greek means “because”, as in the ESV, though a few suggest other senses, such as “with the result that”. On any reading the question remains in what sense all sinned, and the rest of the passage answers it (see above).
verseByVerse.note: “One man” is Adam.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death ruled everyone from Adam to Moses, even those who had broken no stated command as Adam had, and Adam, as head of his race, was a pattern of the one who was to come. The verse shows how far Adam’s act reached, and points to a Man whose act would reach further.

Death reigned. Death did not merely occur; it reigned, the word for a king’s dominion, which Paul uses four more times before the chapter closes. Death is not only the moment a body stops; it is a power with a territory and subjects, governing a life long before it arrives, setting the limit on every plan and giving every love its ache. It reigned over infants and kings, and not one grave escaped it. Then One came into its territory who owed it nothing, let it take him, and broke its rule from the inside.

Not like the transgression of Adam. Adam broke an explicit command knowingly. Between him and Moses there was no such published command to charge people under, and they died anyway, because of Adam (v. 13).

A type of the one who was to come. A type is a pattern, a mould, a foreshadowing (typos). All we have been told of Adam is catastrophe, yet Paul calls him a preliminary sketch of Christ: not in his sin, but in his position, one man whose one act decided the standing of all who belong to him. Two men, two heads, two families: Adam is the pattern Christ reverses (1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49).

The mechanism kept. God did not answer the disaster by abolishing the arrangement that produced it. He sent a second Man to stand at its head, so that the very thing you would have complained about in Eden is what makes your salvation possible. Adam was never merely a warning. He was a rough draft, and the finished work was already in view.

In everyday life. Watch this week how much is quietly shaped by death’s reign: the plans you make to feel secure, the fear behind the money, the dread of a diagnosis, the need to leave a mark. Name each before Christ, and say plainly that you belong to another King. Death still has its day in your body, but it has lost its throne over your life.

What about infants and those who could never sin knowingly? Many readers come here with a question that is not academic, about the infant, the stillborn, the profoundly disabled, anyone who dies before there is anything to charge, usually with a name and a date in mind. This verse says something sobering: they die. Scripture exempts no one from the ruin we share in Adam, and this passage is why infants are mortal at all. But it does not say they are condemned. Paul’s subject is death’s dominion, not the final destiny of individuals, and to read a paragraph about the reign of death as a roll of the lost is a serious mistake, one that has caused enormous grief.

The ground of hope. Scripture gives real ground for hope, without a formula. David’s child died, and David stopped fasting, washed, worshipped and said that he would go to the child, though the child would not return to him (2 Samuel 12:23): words of expectation, not resignation, from a man who looked to dwell in the house of the LORD for ever (Psalm 23:6). Our Lord took children in his arms and said the kingdom of God belongs to such as these (Mark 10:14–16). The Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), and he judges according to the light given (2:12).

What the confessions say. The Westminster Confession speaks of elect infants dying in infancy as regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (Westminster 10.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3), and many Reformed teachers, among them Charles Spurgeon, Charles Hodge and B. B. Warfield, have held that all who die in infancy are among them: saved not by an innocence this chapter denies them, but by sovereign mercy through the same Christ. Scripture does not state that in so many words, and it would be wrong to pretend it does. It is a hope resting on the character of God, the only place a hope was ever safe.

If you are reading this with a grave in mind. Hear the two halves in the right order. Yes, this passage explains why that death happened at all: death is the enemy Paul describes, and your grief is not a failure of faith but an accurate response to an intruder. And no, this passage is not a verdict on that child. The one who will decide is the one who wept at a friend’s tomb while fully intending to empty it, and who himself became an infant.

How do I know which family I am in? Not by birth, church background or feelings. Everyone begins in Adam; nobody is born into Christ. You come into the second family by being joined to its head through faith, trusting Christ himself, not your record, for acceptance with God. If you are resting on him, you are in him, whatever your past. If you are not sure, do not wait to be sure: come to him now. He has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: A “type” is a pattern or foreshadowing: Adam, head of the old humanity, foreshadows Christ, head of the new.

parallels.desc: the first man Adam, the last Adam

verseByVerse.quote: But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many. And the free gift is not like the result of that one man's sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s free gift is not the mirror image of Adam’s trespass: it is far greater, overflowing to many and bringing justification after countless sins. The pattern is the same, but the power is not.

The free gift is not like the trespass. Paul has set the two men side by side, and now twice he says the sides do not balance. If they did, Christ would merely undo Adam and we would be back where we started. But they are nothing like the same size, because God put his own Son on one of them.

Much more. Grace is stronger than sin. “Abounded” means overflowed the container. The gospel is not the restoration of Eden. Adam lost a garden; we are promised a city. Adam had innocence, a fragile thing lost in an afternoon; the believer has a righteousness that is not his own and so cannot be forfeited by him. Adam could fall. The man in Christ cannot finally fall, because he is not standing on his own record. We do not end where Adam began; we end further on, redeemed, not merely restored.

One trespass, many trespasses. The second imbalance is in the arithmetic (v. 16). Adam broke one command, and condemnation followed. Christ faced the accumulated mass of every sin of every person he came to save, and justification followed. We would assume many sins harder to deal with than one. It is the reverse: one was enough to condemn, and the countless were not too many to forgive.

The grace of that one man Jesus Christ. The gift is named twice: the grace of God, and the free gift by the grace of one man. The Father’s grace and the Son’s are one grace. And it comes through a man: the eternal Son had to become one of us to stand at the head of a new humanity, as Adam stood at the head of the old.

In everyday life. After your last serious failure, did you calculate how much ground you had lost and how many good weeks it would cost? That is Adam’s arithmetic, where everything runs on your record, and you are not in that system. There is no ground to make up, because the ground was never yours, and there is no quantity at which the gift becomes insufficient, because it was never weighed against you. Confess it, receive the gift, and get up.

Can he forgive this much? Many Christians privately fear not whether God can forgive sin, but whether he can forgive this much: the man converted at fifty who cannot stop counting the years, the believer who keeps returning to the same failure and suspects there must be a limit. The gift is not measured out to match the debt, enough for a certain quantity of sin and running short beyond it. Grace was never measured against the sin at all. It is measured against the worth of the one who gives it.

If I am forgiven, why do I still feel the weight of sins I have confessed? Because memory and conscience are slower than the verdict. God has removed your transgressions as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12); your memory has not, and it is not meant to be the judge. When an old sin returns, do not confess it again as though the first confession failed. Thank God it was forgiven, and let the memory make you humble and gentle with others. Where a wrong you did can still be put right, put it right, because God’s forgiveness does not cancel the duty of restitution; where it cannot, leave it with the Christ who bore it. Feelings of guilt over forgiven sin are not God’s voice; the gospel is.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who receive God’s abundant grace and his gift of righteousness will not merely escape death’s reign; they will themselves reign in life through Christ. Under Adam we were ruled; in Christ we are given a throne.

Reign in life. We expect the matching clause to say that life will reign through Jesus Christ. Instead the parallel breaks again, upward: not life, but people, will reign. Under Adam we were the territory being ruled. Under Christ we are not merely liberated subjects; we share his rule (2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 5:10). This is the destiny Genesis described when the creature made in God’s image was told to have dominion. Adam was made to rule and ended a subject of death; the man in Christ was a subject of death and ends by ruling. The King of kings did not merely free his people from the tyrant. He emptied the tyrant’s throne and set them beside himself.

Will reign. The verb is future, and anyone who cannot find much evidence of sovereignty in his own life is reading it correctly. But the word beside it is present: those who are receiving the abundance of grace. The receiving is now and the reigning is later, which is the shape of the Christian life: a king in exile, whose title is already granted and whose coronation is on a date he does not know.

Those who receive. One condition, in one word, the only thing in the sentence that we do, and it adds nothing to the gift. The grace is given, the righteousness is credited as a gift, not a quality we produce, and the reign is conferred. And Paul chooses his nouns to make refusal look absurd: not grace but the abundance of grace, not righteousness but the free gift of righteousness.

What it does not mean. The language of reigning has been badly misused. This is not a promise that faith gives you command now over illness, finances or other people. The verb is future; the men who wrote these letters were beaten, imprisoned and executed; and Paul is about to describe the whole creation groaning and Christians groaning with it (8:22–23). Reigning in life is a destination. What does begin now is freedom from sin’s rule, which chapter 6 will describe.

How do I receive it? By faith, the empty hand of the beggar: trusting that what Christ did is enough, and resting your whole case with God on him. It is not a feeling to work up or a prayer with the right words; it is reliance. You go on receiving the same way, coming back to him daily as the only ground of your acceptance, especially on the days you have failed. A man carried down from a burning building does not earn his rescue. He only has to stop fighting the arms that hold him and let the rescuer have him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous. — Romans 5:18–19
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Adam’s one trespass brought condemnation to all who belong to him, so Christ’s obedience brings justification and life to all who belong to him. Here Paul at last finishes the sentence he began in verse 12; everything between was an aside.

Justification and life for all men. Read alone, the phrase seems to say that everyone is saved; it means all who are in Christ, as all in Adam are condemned (see the box at the end of this note). Each head reaches every person who belongs to him with the same completeness, which is what you want to know if you fear being an exception at the edges of the second group. You are not.

The many were made sinners. “Made” here means constituted, appointed, put in the category of (katestathēsan). It is a legal word, describing where a person stands before God, not first what he is like in character. Adam’s disobedience was counted to all in him.

By the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous. Christ’s obedience is counted to all in him, and Paul names a part of his work often left untaught. He does not say here that Christ died for our sins, though he believes it, but obedience: a whole life of perfect obedience to God’s law, ending in obedience to death on the cross (Philippians 2:8). All his years count, not only the hours on the cross: the temptations refused in the wilderness, the ordinary decades in a workshop, every commandment kept in the only human life that ever kept them.

Active and passive obedience. Theologians call these his active obedience (he kept the law perfectly for us) and his passive obedience (he bore its penalty for us), and both are credited to believers. So justification is more than pardon. A pardon cancels a record and leaves the man with none. The New Testament describes an exchange: your record reckoned to him and his to you, so that you stand before God as one who has kept the law entirely. The Son lived every hour of a human life in perfect love for his Father, then gave that life up on the cross, and both the life and the death are yours. This is the believer’s rest on the days his own obedience falls short, which is every day, for we all stumble in many ways (James 3:2). Our standing never rested on our obedience; Christ’s is counted as ours, and so our imperfect obedience is accepted for his sake, offered to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5). This never excuses sin; it is what sets a forgiven child free to obey gladly.

In everyday life. Which do you actually believe: God has forgiven me, or God accepts me in the righteousness of Jesus Christ, as fully as he accepts his Son? The second may sound like presumption, but it is the plain implication of verse 19; the gap between them is how much of this verse you have not yet believed. Say the second today, and pray from it.

Is being made righteous the same as becoming good? No, though the one always leads to the other. Being made righteous here is justification: God’s verdict that you are righteous in his sight because Christ’s obedience is counted to you. It is complete the moment you believe, and it does not grow. Becoming good in heart and behaviour is sanctification: the Spirit’s lifelong work of changing you into Christ’s likeness, real and growing but never complete in this life. Confusing them is dangerous both ways. If your acceptance depends on your progress, you will never have peace. If you think acceptance needs no progress, you have not understood the grace that accepted you, as chapter 6 is about to show.

Where Christians differ: are all saved? Universalists read “justification and life for all men” as meaning that every person will be saved. This commentary’s view: Paul limits it to those who receive (v. 17), believers. In the very next sentence “all men” becomes “the many” in both halves: he uses the phrases interchangeably, contrasting two humanities, not counting heads. As in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive (1 Corinthians 15:22): the “all” is all who belong to each head. And a sentence must be read with its author: the same apostle wrote chapter 2 on the day of wrath and chapter 9 on vessels of wrath, and Scripture clearly teaches that some perish eternally (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Matthew 25:46). The longing behind universalism, that mercy should triumph, is right in itself; Scripture answers it with a multitude no one can number (Revelation 7:9), not with the salvation of all.

Uncertain wording. Verse 18 is compressed in Greek and has no verb; literally, as through one trespass to all men for condemnation, so through one act of righteousness to all men for justification of life. Translators supply “led” and “leads”. Two smaller questions follow. “One” may go with the deed (“one trespass”, as in the ESV) or with the man (“the offence of one”, as in the King James Version); either way the one act is one man’s act, so the meaning hardly changes. And the word rendered “act of righteousness” (dikaiōma) can also mean a righteous decree or requirement; most take it here as Christ’s righteous deed, which verse 19 calls his obedience. “Justification and life” is literally “justification of life”: the verdict that brings life.

parallels.desc: shall my servant make many to be accounted righteous

verseByVerse.quote: Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. — Romans 5:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law made sin increase by exposing it, but grace overflowed beyond it, so that grace now reigns where sin once reigned, bringing eternal life through Jesus Christ. The law exposed the disease; only grace could cure it.

The law came in. A strange statement of purpose: God gave the law at Sinai in order that the trespass might increase. The verb (pareisēlthen) means came in alongside, entering a story already under way. The law is not the main plot; it arrived between Adam and Christ with a defined job, a bold thing to say to people whose national identity was built around it.

How does the law increase trespass? Not by making people worse in themselves. Chapter 4 has set out the first way: “where there is no law there is no transgression” (4:15), so once the line is drawn, wrongdoing becomes the breaking of a known command, and the law shows sin as sin. The second way is more uncomfortable, and Paul will describe it from his own experience in chapter 7: a prohibition provokes (7:7–13). Tell a man “do not” and something in him wakes up, as anyone knows who never cared about a cupboard until told not to open it. The law does not create the appetite. It exposes it, and so inflames it, because the disease is rebellion, and rebellion rises when it is told no.

Why would God do that? Because a vague sin is never brought to be forgiven; nobody asks. A general sense of not being all one should be goes nowhere in particular. The law turns that fog into an itemised bill, something specific enough to bring to a Saviour. It was given not to save but to expose our need. Sin had to be made visible before grace could be seen to be enough.

Grace abounded all the more. Sin increased; grace super-abounded (hypereperisseusen), an already strong verb made stronger still, found elsewhere in the New Testament only at 2 Corinthians 7:4. Wherever sin has gone, grace has gone further, and it did not arrive with a measure in its hand.

As sin reigned in death, grace also might reign. Two kings: sin reigning in death, grace reigning through righteousness. A reign is a government you live under; you do not negotiate with it, you are transferred from one to the other, the great theme of chapters 6 to 8. The justified person is no longer defined by Adam’s inheritance or his own failures. He lives under the reign of grace, moving towards eternal life, claimed and kept by the God who abounds.

Through Jesus Christ our Lord. The refrain that closes each stage of chapters 5 to 8 (5:11, 21; 6:23; 7:25; 8:39). Ten verses on two men end on a name. The law came in alongside; he came in to reign. Not grace permits or overlooks, but grace reigns, the language of a throne. Sin had a reign too, and it ended in a graveyard the size of the world. The new King took his throne by dying, and the first thing he did with the crown was to spend it giving life away: eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

For the one who thinks he is the exception. This comfort is aimed at those who think they are outside it: the one who came late, after damage that cannot be repaired, or the one with something in his past never said aloud. Where sin went deepest, grace went further. Bring the thing by name to Christ today, and, if it would help you to be free, to one trusted, mature believer as well (James 5:16).

Is the law bad, then? No. The law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (7:12). The fault is in us: the law is a straight edge laid against a crooked wall, which does not make the wall crooked but shows how crooked it is. For the believer the law remains a good guide to the life that pleases God, and its moral commands are summed up in love (13:8–10). What it cannot do is give the life it describes. That is what grace does.

Then why not sin more, so that grace abounds more? Paul answers this abuse in the first lines of the next chapter: by no means (6:1–2). He does not soften his statement to prevent it; he lets it stand at full strength. But the answer is already here: grace reigns through righteousness, not by suspending it. A man who concludes that he may now sin freely has misunderstood the kind of king he is dealing with. Grace is not permission; it is a rule you live under, and its rule is righteous. Someone who wants grace in order to keep sinning has not yet wanted grace at all, only escape.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>2</sup>Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God.<sup>3</sup>Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance,<sup>4</sup>and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,<sup>5</sup>and hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.<sup>6</sup>For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.<sup>7</sup>For one will scarcely die for a righteous person—though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die—<sup>8</sup>but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.<sup>9</sup>Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God.<sup>10</sup>For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.<sup>11</sup>More than that, we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.<sup>12</sup>Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned—<sup>13</sup>for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law.<sup>14</sup>Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come.<sup>15</sup>But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man’s trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many.<sup>16</sup>And the free gift is not like the result of that one man’s sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification.<sup>17</sup>For if, because of one man’s trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.<sup>18</sup>Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men.<sup>19</sup>For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous.<sup>20</sup>Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more,<sup>21</sup>so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

keyVerse.quote: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
keyVerse.note: This verse turns the corner of the letter, from how a sinner is justified to what it means to live justified. The rest of the chapter unfolds what this peace contains (vv. 2–11) and what it rests on: the obedience of the one man Jesus Christ, counted to all who belong to him (vv. 12–21). It is a peace made by God and received by faith, not a feeling we have to keep up.

5.reflection:
Paul says that believers already have peace with God and stand in grace (vv. 1–2). What difference does it make to prayer and to daily life to begin from “I am right with God” instead of “I am trying to get right with God”? Which one usually describes your week?

Verses 3–5 say that suffering can produce endurance, character and hope, but it can also produce bitterness. Looking back on a hard time in your own life, what made the difference, and how does verse 5 explain it?

Paul proves God’s love by when Christ died: while we were weak, ungodly, sinners and enemies (vv. 6–10). Why is that better news than being told we are good enough? How should it shape the way we treat people who have wronged us?

Verses 12–21 say every person stands under one of two heads, Adam or Christ. Why do we object to being represented by Adam but gladly accept being represented by Christ? What does it mean for you to belong to the second family?

6.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
6.overview:
Where we are. Paul has just said that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (5:20–21). Chapter 6 answers the objection that sentence provokes; chapter 7 takes up the law.

The message. Grace never leaves a sinner where it found him. Everyone God justifies he has joined to Christ, and in Christ the believer has died to sin’s reign and been raised to a new life with God. He is no longer sin’s slave but has a new Master, whose gift is eternal life. Holiness is not a way to earn what grace gives; it is living from what is already true.

Why it was said. Paul’s preaching of free grace was being slandered as a licence to sin (3:8; see the introduction), and the charge was natural: if God justifies the ungodly apart from works, obedience sounds optional. Paul meets it not by retreating into moralism but by going deeper into the gospel.

How the chapter makes its case. Two questions, each met with “By no means!” First, shall we continue in sin (vv. 1–14)? No: baptism declares that we died, were buried and were raised with Christ (vv. 3–8), and our new life is as secure as his, who died to sin once for all (vv. 9–10). Only then come the commands, to count it true and give ourselves to God, and a promise: sin will not be master, for we are under grace (vv. 11–14). Second, may we sin now and then (vv. 15–23)? No: everyone is the slave of what he obeys (v. 16), believers have changed masters (vv. 17–18), and each service has its own slope, fruit and end (vv. 19–22), a wage or a gift (v. 23).

Where it leads. Every claim the chapter makes about us rests on Christ: he went down into death under our sin, was raised by the glory of the Father, and lives to God for ever (vv. 4, 9–10), and our dying and rising are his, shared because we are in him. The chapter ends not with a technique but with a name, “Christ Jesus our Lord” (v. 23): the Master who claims us bought us with his own blood.

For us. When temptation says this is simply who you are, Romans 6 says that man is buried. You are not a slave trying to escape but a free person refusing to go back. Count on what Christ has done, give him your eyes, hands and tongue today, and when you fail, come back under grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — United with Christ in Death and Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace does not leave believers in sin, because it has joined them to Christ, and in him they died to sin’s reign and rose to a new life. Baptism pictures that union: dying, burial and rising with him (vv. 1–5). The old self was crucified, so sin, though still present (chapter 7 is honest about that), has lost its claim (vv. 6–8). Our security rests on Christ, who died to sin once for all and will never die again (vv. 9–10). Only then come the commands, and the section ends on a promise rather than a target: sin will have no dominion, for we are under grace (vv. 11–14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ: The Foundation of Sanctification

Romans 6 grounds holiness in union with Christ, not in moral effort alone. Reformed teachers have held that justification and sanctification are distinct but never separated, because both come from being joined to Christ. John Murray, in Redemption Accomplished and Applied, argued that union with Christ is not one blessing among others but the root of them all.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The objection Paul answers, sin so that grace may abound, was a real slander against his preaching (3:8). He does not retreat into moralism; he goes deeper into the gospel. Now: The same objection still comes whenever grace is preached plainly, and Paul’s answer still stands: grace does not make people careless about sin; it joins them to the Christ who died and rose.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace gives no believer room to stay in sin, because every believer has died to sin’s reign. Paul’s answer to the objection is not first a rule but a fact about who Christians are.

What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? The question follows from 5:20: if sin gives grace more room to shine, why not sin more? Paul has heard it before: at 3:8 he reports that people were slandering him with it, as though he taught “why not do evil that good may come”. Nobody ever accused the Pharisees of encouraging sin. You only meet this objection if you have said something that sounds dangerously like “God accepts the ungodly and their record contributes nothing”, which is precisely what Paul has been saying for five chapters. A gospel that has never once been misheard this way may not yet have been stated clearly.

Continue in sin. The verb means to remain, to go on dwelling somewhere. Paul is not asking whether a Christian ever sins; chapter 7 is painfully clear about that. He is asking whether a Christian takes up residence in it: not whether you have trespassed, but whether you have built a house on the property.

By no means! Paul’s most emphatic way of rejecting a thought (mē genoito), something like “perish the thought”. Having provoked the objection, he does not retreat an inch from 5:20.

How can we who died to sin still live in it? He does not say “you must not” but “how can we?” One puts up a fence; the other says the thing no longer fits who you are. You do not tell a man released from a life sentence that he is forbidden to sleep in his old cell; you ask him why on earth he would want to.

What “died to sin” means. The key is verse 10, which says that Christ also died to sin. He never had sin in him, so for him dying to sin cannot mean that sin was rooted out; it means he passed out of sin’s realm and claim (see the note on vv. 9–10). Believers, united to him, died with him to that same reign: sin’s legal claim on us ended, and we now live under the reign of grace (5:21). And it is a past fact (we died), not a command (die to sin!): done to you, not achieved by you, dated at a cross and applied when you were united to Christ. That is why every command in this chapter comes after it.

A former employer. Think of sin as a former employer, not a feeling that has gone away. He still has your number, he still rings, and he knows exactly what to say. What he has lost is not his voice but his authority: he can make suggestions, but he cannot give an instruction you are obliged to carry out, not because you have grown stronger but because you no longer work there.

He ended the tenancy. Sin’s house was where we lived, and its rent was death. Christ came into that house, took its whole debt on himself, died there, and carried us out with him when he rose. He did not pardon us and leave us under the same roof.

What it does not mean. Not that believers no longer feel sin’s pull, or cannot sin: Paul goes on to command them not to let sin reign (v. 12), which would be pointless if they could not. Sin has not died in us; we died to its reign.

Then why do I still sin? Because sin’s reign has been broken, but its presence remains until the resurrection (treated fully at vv. 5–6). It still lives in our mortal bodies and pulls at us (vv. 12–13; 7:20–23), but it has no right to our obedience, so we resist it not as slaves trying to escape but as free people refusing to go back. The fight is real, but it is fought from victory.

What is the difference between falling into sin and living in it? Falling is being overtaken: you sin, you know it, it grieves you, and you go back to God and fight again (Galatians 6:1; 1 John 2:1). Living in it is making peace with it: you no longer call it sin, or you call it sin and have stopped resisting, and you have arranged your life so that it can continue. A believer can fall often, and badly, and still be fighting; what Paul calls impossible is the settled residence. If you are unsure which describes you, ask whether you still bring the thing to God honestly. If you are, you are not at home in it. If you have stopped, start today: the door out is still open.
verseByVerse.note: Paul answers a charge his teaching of grace invited.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baptism declares that believers were joined to Christ in his death and burial, so that, as he was raised, they too might live a new life. Paul grounds “we died to sin” in something every Christian in Rome already knew.

Do you not know? Paul is not teaching something new but reminding them of what they were told at the beginning and have evidently not been using. Most of us are short not of information but of the habit of standing on what we already have. And he can assume it in a church he had never visited (1:13): what baptism meant was taught wherever the gospel went, so he appeals to common ground, not a private theory.

Into his death. Baptism into Christ Jesus means union with him, and especially with his death: when he died, we died with him. The word that matters most is “into”: not a benefit transferred at a distance, but your being placed inside an event. What happened to Christ is counted as having happened to you, because you are in him: you died, were buried and were raised, in events in Judea before you existed.

Buried with him. Baptism pictures burial, going under the water as into the grave (Colossians 2:12), and immersion makes the picture vivid. Burial confirms that a death is real and final: a man in a coma may recover; a man in the ground has been publicly given up on. Paul leaves no possibility that the old life is merely convalescing. And Christ went down into that death first, alone, under the full weight of our sin, and lay in a borrowed grave.

By the glory of the Father. Not “power”, which is what we would have written. Glory is the weight and blazing reality of who God is, so the raising of Jesus expressed the Father’s whole character, his verdict on his Son made visible. The same glory stands behind your newness of life: the energy available for an ordinary Christian’s Tuesday is the energy that emptied the tomb.

Newness of life. Rising from the water pictures rising with Christ, and “newness” is a new quality of life, the life of the resurrection. Paul does not say we were raised in order to feel new, but in order that we might walk: daily conduct, the least dramatic verb available, ordinary and repetitive, and it gets you somewhere over time.

In everyday life. Take the sin you fight most often, and notice what you say to yourself in the moment of temptation. If it is only “I must not”, that is a fence, and fences are climbed. Paul supplies another sentence: “I am not that man any longer; that man is buried.” It is not a stronger effort; it is a truer description. Remember your baptism today.

I was baptised as an infant, or I have never been baptised. What should I do? If you trust Christ and have never been baptised, be baptised: it is the Lord’s command for every disciple (Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38). Speak to your church’s pastor. If you were baptised as an infant and have since come to faith, this commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, that baptism belongs to those who profess faith, and so would encourage you to be baptised as a believer. Do it humbly, without contempt for those who brought you as a child in love and obedience as they understood it. Either way, the main thing is not the water but the union it declares: if you are in Christ, you have died and risen with him.

Where Christians differ: what does baptism do? Roman Catholic and Lutheran Christians see baptism as the moment union with Christ actually happens: in the rite God gives new birth and joins the person to Christ (baptismal regeneration). Others, Martyn Lloyd-Jones among them, think Paul means not water baptism at all but the Spirit’s baptism into Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13). This commentary’s view: Paul means water baptism, but as the sign of a union God brings about by the Spirit through faith. He addresses believers, for whom baptism expressed their faith. Union with Christ is by faith, wrought by the Spirit (Galatians 3:26–27; Ephesians 3:17); so Colossians says we were raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God (Colossians 2:12), and Abraham’s sign followed his faith (4:11). Even when Peter says that baptism now saves you, he explains at once: not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience (1 Peter 3:21). The water does not save; Christ does. The reality is union with Christ; baptism is its God-given picture. Credobaptists, who baptise only those who profess faith, see here strong support for believers’ baptism by immersion, picturing death, burial and resurrection in a person who has already come to faith. Christians who baptise infants, many of them our dear brothers, see the sign as God’s promise to the children of believers (compare 4:11); but the dying and rising Paul describes here is something the baptised have entered by faith.

parallels.desc: buried with him in baptism

verseByVerse.quote: For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joined to Christ in his death, believers will certainly share his resurrection, because the self they were in Adam was crucified with him to break sin’s hold on them. The aim is freedom, not only forgiveness.

United with him. Paul’s word (symphytoi) is not a legal term but comes from a verb for growing together, as when a shoot is grafted into another tree and the two share one life.
