All three moves are still in use: the commandment exaggerated, the Giver’s motive questioned, and the consequence not disproved, only made to feel unreal.

Sin misinforms. Sin’s first work is not to overpower you but to misinform you, about what the sin will give and what it will cost: that this will satisfy, that it will not cost much, that you will be able to stop, that God is being unreasonable.

Holy and righteous and good. After five verses on how the commandment was used to kill him, Paul uses three adjectives where one would have done. The law is not the problem; sin is. Nor is it a set of rules God happened to choose. It comes from the Holy One and mirrors him: its demands are his own purity put into words. That is why breaking it is never mere rule-breaking but an offence against God himself (Psalm 51:4), and why the holy law is so terrible to sinners and so precious to the redeemed.

A wounded man’s verdict. Paul was wounded by the commandment and says so, yet he will not let his experience be evidence against God. We tend to do the reverse and blame the command, a conclusion that always flatters us. The problem is not in the doctor’s prescription but in the patient’s condition.

Where the serpent met his match. The holy law, which sin used to kill us, found in Christ one who loved it and kept it perfectly. The deceiver came to the last Adam in the wilderness with the same kind of lie, that God’s word could be bent and his care doubted, and this time it failed. Hungry, alone and offered every shortcut, Jesus answered each lie with a commandment from Deuteronomy, the very law sin had turned into a weapon (Matthew 4:1–11). In his mouth the word was not an occasion for sin but a sword against it. Where Adam believed the slander and died, Christ believed his Father and lived. Then he took on himself the death that sin had dealt through the commandment, and in dying crushed the serpent’s head, as was promised in the garden (Genesis 3:15).

How do I actually fight sin’s lies? As Jesus did: answer the lie with what God has said, from verses learned in advance, not hunted for in the moment. Ask the arithmetic questions sin hopes you will not ask: what will this cost tomorrow, and who else will pay? Say the truth aloud: this will not satisfy; God is not holding out on me; he gave his Son, so he will not withhold any good thing (8:32). Tell a trusted Christian friend, because lies thrive in secret. And remember that being tempted is not sinning; Christ was tempted in every way, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

In everyday life. Think of a commandment that has cost you something, or that you have failed so often you have stopped hoping. Is there a quiet sense that God asked too much, that a reasonable God would have made an exception for you? That resentment is the serpent’s second move, still working. Name it, and look at the cross: nobody who sees the Father give up his own Son for us all (8:32) can go on believing that the Giver of the commandment is mean.
verseByVerse.note: “Deceived” echoes the serpent’s deception of Eve.

parallels.desc: the serpent deceived me

verseByVerse.quote: Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good law did not kill Paul; sin did, and by turning God’s good gift into a weapon it showed itself to be sin at its worst. God gave the commandment knowing this, so that sin would be exposed for what it is.

Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? “By no means!” This is where verses 7–12 have been heading, and it answers a question that ought to trouble a thoughtful reader: if God knew the law would provoke sin rather than restrain it, why give it? Paul does not call it a miscalculation. It was the purpose.

Shown to be sin. The law was given, among other things, to make the disease declare itself. Nobody goes to a physician for a condition he cannot feel; the commandment forced a hidden thing to produce symptoms, violent enough that the patient went for help.

Sinful beyond measure. The phrase (kath’ hyperbolēn) lies behind our word hyperbole. Sin earns it not by producing something spectacular but by what it is willing to use: it took the holiest thing God had given, a good commandment designed for life, and turned it into an instrument of death.

Sin has a strategy. We think of sin as weakness; Paul describes something with a strategy, ready to turn the best things to its own use. A man may use accurate theology to avoid God, and many do. Repentance itself can become a show of sorrow that eases the guilt without ever dealing with the sin. And the man who has fought an obvious sin for twenty years is often caught by one he never thought to watch.

The best thing sin ever seized. Sin showed itself most fully when it laid hold of the best gift God ever gave. The Son of God came, holy and righteous and good, the living picture of all that the law commands, and sin used God’s own law, in the mouths of the leaders of God’s own people, to put him to death: we have a law, they said, and by that law he ought to die (John 19:7). At Calvary sin was unmasked as never before. And there God turned its masterstroke against it: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, he condemned sin in the flesh (8:3). The place where sin did its worst is the place where it received its sentence.

The other thing beyond measure. Paul uses the same phrase for the eternal weight of glory being prepared for the people of God (2 Corinthians 4:17). “Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (5:20). God’s mercy has outrun his people’s sin at every turn, and it ends in a glory that outweighs all of it together.

Do I need to feel terrible about my sin before I can come to Christ? No. The law shows us sin so that we will come, not so that we earn the right to come by feeling bad enough. Conviction is measured not by the depth of the misery but by where it sends you. Some come through long terror of conscience, others through a quiet, clear seeing that they need him, and both are the Spirit’s work. If you see enough of your sin to know that you cannot save yourself, you see enough to come. Christ invites the weary and heavy-laden, not the sufficiently weary (Matthew 11:28).

In everyday life. Ask what good thing in your life is being used against you. Your work, a gift, which has become the place you go to avoid a difficulty at home. Your theological knowledge, which is real, and has become a way of feeling superior to other Christians. Your service, which helps people, and has become how you avoid asking whether anybody knows you. Inspect one good thing this week, and ask God to show you how sinful sin is, so that you will treasure his grace.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is spiritual, but Paul finds himself still fleshly and baffled by his own actions: he does what he hates and fails to do what he wants. Here the present tense begins, and with it one of the most debated and most comforting passages in Scripture.

In the flow. Verses 7–13 cleared the law of being sin; verses 14–25 show that it cannot make a man holy either, even a man who loves it. That prepares 8:3: what the law could not do, weakened by the flesh, God did by sending his own Son.

The law is spiritual. Not vague or only inward, but from the Spirit of God, carrying his holiness. That is why a person of the flesh cannot keep it, and why those who walk by the Spirit begin to fulfil it (8:4).

I am of the flesh. Made of flesh, human, weak (sarkinos), and “I am”, not “I was”.

Sold under sin. Slave-market language (see slavery in the ancient world), and the New Testament answers it in the same market. You were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20), ransomed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). So the believer who still feels the old master’s grip in his flesh no longer belongs to the old master. The sale to sin was real, but Christ’s purchase is the one that stands. The struggle here is that of a slave bought by a new Lord, still learning to walk out of the old house.

I do not understand my own actions. Not merely that he regrets them: he cannot make sense of them. Anyone who has fought a recurring sin knows that its strangest feature is not its power but its senselessness: afterwards you cannot say why you did it. This man is not making excuses. He is baffled.

The very thing I hate. He does not do what he wants, which means he wants the right thing. This is not a show of reluctance by a man enjoying his sin; the wanting is real, and it is the source of the anguish. A man who wanted only the wrong thing would have no conflict to report.

Not ashamed to call them brothers. The holy law could only show us the gap between what we are and what we ought to be, and the Son of God came into that gap. He took our flesh, yet was never sold under sin; he always did the things that pleased his Father (John 8:29). Tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), he pities those still fighting. He remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14), and he is not ashamed to call such strugglers his brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

What it does not mean. Not a licence: a man who quotes Romans 7 to excuse a sin he has stopped fighting has turned a description of anguish into a permission slip, and the anguish is precisely what he no longer has. Nor a ceiling: chapters 6 and 8 insist that the Christian grows in holiness (6:19–22; 8:13). This chapter describes the floor of Christian experience: you may find yourself there at any time, and you are not lost because you are.

Should I expect to feel like this all the time? No. Indwelling sin remains until glory, but the experience of the conflict varies, with seasons of real victory and quiet joy and seasons when the struggle is fierce. Here the believer measures himself honestly against the law; chapter 8 shows the same believer looking at Christ and the Spirit, and finding no condemnation, real power and sure hope. A healthy Christian lives in both chapters at once, and gives more of his attention to the second.

But how can a believer be “sold under sin”? This is the strongest objection to reading verses 14–25 as a Christian’s experience, since in 6:17–18 believers have been set free from sin. Three things help. First, Paul carefully limits where this is true: “nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh” (v. 18); “with my flesh I serve the law of sin” (v. 25). He means what remains of the old nature, not the whole person, whose inner being delights in God’s law (v. 22). Second, he measures the believer against the law alone, apart from the Spirit’s help: the law can command but not enable, which is why chapter 8, full of the Spirit, follows at once. Third, captivity describes real defeats in a real war (v. 23), not surrender: losing a battle is not deserting.

The comfort survives either reading. If Paul describes the Christian, your experience of failure is normal and does not disqualify you. If he describes life under law before Christ, he shows you what you have been rescued from and where to look instead of at yourself. Either way the answer comes in the same breath: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord (v. 25).

Where Christians differ: who is the “I” of verses 14–25? Some (many early Greek fathers, Wesley, and many modern scholars) see an unbeliever under the law, or Paul before conversion. Their arguments are real: “sold under sin” (v. 14), and verse 5, which puts “living in the flesh” in the past, while these verses sound like that same condition. Others hold that Paul describes his past as a Jew under the law, seen with Christian eyes. Martyn Lloyd-Jones, in his sermons on Romans, argued for a third option: a person awakened by the law to his sin and distressed, but not yet born again and resting in Christ. This commentary’s view: with Augustine (in his later writings), Luther, Calvin and the Reformed tradition, this best describes a believer, and it is the most natural reading and the truest to what believers experience. The present tense; the delight in God’s law in the inner being (v. 22), which no unbeliever has (8:7); the hatred of sin (v. 15); the cry for deliverance and thanks for it (vv. 24–25): all fit a regenerate person who still has indwelling sin. It describes the struggle, not the whole Christian life; chapter 8 shows the victory by the Spirit. Mature believers often feel this struggle most keenly, because they love God’s law most.
verseByVerse.note: Christians have long debated whether Paul here describes life before conversion or the ongoing struggle of a believer; many, following Augustine and the Reformers, read it as the believer’s experience.

parallels.desc: the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s hatred of his own sin shows that his deepest self sides with God’s law; the sin is still his doing, but it comes from an occupant he opposes, not from who he now is.

I agree with the law, that it is good. Paul’s final evidence for the law is his own failure: his very unwillingness shows that his conscience has voted for the commandment while his hands voted against it. Guilt, uncomfortable as it is, is a person admitting that God’s law is right just after he has broken it.

Sin that dwells within me. Not an excuse, but a diagnosis. “Dwells” (oikousa): lives, makes its home. Sin is a lodger, not a visitor: it has a room, knows the layout and pays no rent, which is why sin in a believer so often looks like a habit rather than a decision. A lodger does not need to be invited each time. But sin may dwell in a believer; it does not own him. The deed of the house was bought with blood, and the Spirit of God has taken up residence in the same rooms, the stronger occupant. The believer is responsible for his sins, but they do not express who he truly is in Christ.

No longer I. Paul can speak of an “I” distinct from his sin because something has happened to that “I”. Our old self was crucified with Christ (6:6), and he says the same of himself elsewhere: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). The real Paul is the man joined to Christ, who died with him and was raised with him. Who a Christian is, is settled not by his worst day but by Christ’s death and resurrection, and knowing that gives him the courage to call his remaining sin an enemy.

Not the oldest excuse in the world. Read carelessly, the verse becomes just that. But Paul has spent a chapter accepting responsibility; if you catch yourself saying, “That was not the real me”, you are misusing it. The difference is easy to see: Paul’s sentence produces anguish and a cry for deliverance; the excuse produces relief and no cry at all.

Holding both. “I did that”, and “that is not who I am”: hold the first alone and you get despair; hold the second alone and you get evasion. Paul holds both in one sentence, full responsibility and an identity not defined by the failure. The first keeps you honest; the second keeps you standing.

Is guilt not just something to be got over? Some guilt is false, attached to rules God never gave, and the gospel frees us from that too (Colossians 2:20–23). But the guilt of this verse is conscience agreeing with a good law (v. 16), and silencing it is like disconnecting a smoke alarm because the noise is unpleasant. True guilt is cured not by denial but by having the wrong dealt with, which only a God both just and merciful can do. He does not call the sin nothing. He condemned it in the flesh of his Son (8:3), so that the guilty may be forgiven without the wrong being pretended away.

How does this fit with John’s word that no one born of God makes a practice of sinning (1 John 3:9)? John describes the settled direction of a life, not a sinless one; the same letter says that anyone who claims to have no sin deceives himself (1 John 1:8). Paul’s man hates the sin he does and fights it. What John rules out is the man who has made peace with it.

Will God punish me for the sins I commit as a Christian? Not with condemnation: every one was laid on Christ and paid for at the cross, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). But God disciplines his children, as a father and not as a judge (Hebrews 12:5–11). He may let you feel a sin’s bitterness, withdraw the felt sense of his nearness for a time, or let consequences stand, to make you share his holiness, not to make you pay. So confess freely, as a child to a father who has already forgiven the debt (1 John 1:9), and expect his correction to be love.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his fallen nature Paul finds nothing good and no power to do the good he wants: the will is there, the ability is not. So the evil he hates keeps breaking through.

Nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. Paul corrects himself mid-sentence, and the correction matters. Something good does dwell in a believer, the Spirit (8:9) and the delight of verse 22, so he narrows the statement to the flesh, which is not the whole of him. Copy the correction. To say “There is nothing good in me at all” sounds humble and is not accurate: it leaves no basis for hope, and no explanation for the fact that you mind about your sin. The flesh has not improved and cannot be improved, but the flesh is not the whole man.

What is the flesh? Human nature in its fallen state, not the physical body; the English suggests that bodily appetites are the problem while the mind is clean. But the vice lists in this letter are full of pride, envy, gossip and malice, sins with no bodily component at all (1:29–31). Flesh is the whole self as it lived without God at the centre, and what is left of that in a believer. So a man who denies himself every bodily pleasure can be entirely fleshly, and a man enjoying his dinner with thanksgiving need not be. The body is not the enemy; it will be raised.

The desire, but not the ability. He is willing, but not able in his own strength; only the Spirit gives the ability (8:4, 13). That undoes every self-improvement scheme, for most moral advice assumes that what is missing is the wanting, and supplies motivation. Paul has the motivation, and he is drowning anyway. Nobody discovers this by reading about it; he discovers it on the fifth occasion of resolving the same thing with complete sincerity and failing by Thursday.

What I keep on doing. Not that he never does good, but never as fully as he wants. The verb describes something that goes on happening: not a bad week but the shape of a lifetime, which makes the passage depressing or liberating, depending entirely on what comes next. Paul offers no technique. He states the problem in its full hopelessness and lets it stand, because the answer is not a better strategy but a person, Jesus Christ our Lord (v. 25), and he wants you to have exhausted every alternative before he names him.

Willing and doing in one man. There has been one human life in which the desire to do right and the ability to carry it out never once came apart. “My food is to do the will of him who sent me,” Jesus said, “and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). In Gethsemane the struggle was real, and still the willing and the doing held together: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). What verse 18 cannot find in us was found whole in him. By that one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (5:19), and the good he did is counted to everyone who trusts him, while his Spirit begins in them the same union of wanting and doing.

If I cannot do it, why try at all? Because the ability Paul lacks in himself is given by the Spirit, who works through your effort, not instead of it: you put to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit (8:13), working out your salvation because God is at work in you (Philippians 2:12–13). So you still pray, flee, confess and form new habits, but as someone who has given up on his own strength and leans his full weight on another. Despair of yourself is the beginning of victory, not the end of trying.

In everyday life. Take the sin you return to and ask which is true: “I do not really want to stop”, or “I want to stop and cannot”. They need different medicine. If the first, you still love the sin, and the answer is repentance. If the second, you are where verse 18 is, and your wanting is evidence that God has been at work in you: you did not manufacture it. Often you will find both at once, and the part of you that hates the sin is the Spirit’s work (Galatians 5:17).
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, not the body as such.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul repeats, word for word, that sin dwells in him as an enemy, and names the pattern he has found: whenever he wants to do good, evil is right there.

A law. Here “law” means a principle, a fixed pattern, as we speak of the law of gravity: something that always happens and makes no exceptions for people who are trying hard (but see “Uncertain wording” below). Temptation is always close; sin was crouching at the door for Cain (Genesis 4:7).

Evil lies close at hand. Evil turns up just when the good is wanted, as if the wanting had called it. You resolve to pray more, and the following week is the busiest in a year. You determine to be patient with a particular person, and within about thirty-six hours that person becomes markedly more irritating. It is easy to conclude that the resolve was insincere, or that God is not helping. But Paul calls it a law. The opposition does not show that your resolve was false; it shows that it was real. A man walking with the current does not feel the river; only the one who turns against it does.

Opposed at every step toward the good. Jesus knew this law at its fiercest, from the side of perfect obedience. At his baptism the Father declared his delight in him, and at once the Spirit led him into the wilderness to be tempted (Matthew 3:17–4:1). When he began to show his disciples that he must suffer, the opposition came through Peter, one of his closest friends, and he had to say, “Get behind me, Satan!” (Matthew 16:21–23). Every step he took toward the Father’s will was opposed, and he never once gave way. Because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

What it does not mean. Not every difficulty after a good decision is a spiritual assault; sometimes the week really was busy. Paul describes a pattern, not a key to every event, and a Christian who reads every inconvenience as warfare will grow strange and frightened, exhaust himself and misjudge his neighbours.

So what do I do when the counter-attack comes? Keep going, and do the next small right thing. Expect resistance, so that it does not surprise you into quitting. Name the resolve and the opposition to God in prayer. Shrink the resolution if necessary, from an hour of prayer to ten honest minutes, rather than abandon it. Tell another Christian, because resolutions kept alone are easily dropped. And when you fail, start again the same day, not next Monday. The evil may lie close at hand, but the Lord is closer: he is at hand (Philippians 4:5), and he is able to keep you from stumbling (Jude 24).

Uncertain wording. The Greek of verse 21 is compressed, and “the law” in it can be read two ways. Most, like the ESV, take it as a principle of experience, matching the “other law” and “law of sin” of verse 23. Some take it as the law of Moses: I find, with regard to the law, that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand. Either way the point is certain: wanting the good does not keep evil away. The ESV’s reading is the likelier.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his inner self the believer delights in God’s law, yet in his body another power fights that delight and at times takes him prisoner. Both are true at once, in different places.

I delight in the law of God. “Delight” (synēdomai): rejoice with, take pleasure in. Not mere approval but delight, the language of the psalmist (Psalm 1:2; 119:97), and precisely what the next chapter says the unconverted cannot do: the mind set on the flesh is hostile to God and does not submit to God’s law, indeed it cannot (8:7). Whatever else is disputed here, the man of verse 22 is not the man of 8:7. “Inner being” is the inner self, renewed by the Spirit (2 Corinthians 4:16; Ephesians 3:16).

Waging war. The believer is a battlefield: the flesh against the Spirit (Galatians 5:17). The verb describes a sustained campaign with strategy and objectives, not a series of accidents.

Making me captive. Not total defeat, but painful losses, like a soldier taken alive after a lost battle and marched off where the victor chooses. Paul admits not merely to being tempted but to being taken prisoner: more humiliating, and more honest.

In my members. Hands, eyes, tongue, the body with its trained reflexes. The delight is in the inner being; the defeat happens where the habits live, which is the shape of most Christian failure. A Christian rarely sins because he stopped believing the truth that morning; his beliefs were sound, but the battle was fought in his habits.

Whose delight this is. The delight of verse 22 has a source. Psalm 40 says, “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8), and Hebrews hears that psalm on the lips of Christ, “I have come to do your will”, as he comes into the world to offer his body once for all (Hebrews 10:5–10). A few verses later Hebrews quotes the new covenant promise: “I will put my laws on their hearts” (Hebrews 10:16). The order is the gospel: first the law was in the heart of the Son; then, because of his offering, it is written in the hearts of his people. The believer’s delight in God’s law is a share in Christ’s own.

Both real. A Christian who recognises himself in the captivity often concludes that his delight must be false. Paul puts both in one sentence. A prisoner of war has not changed sides. He is in enemy hands, he is still loyal, and everything now depends on whether anybody is coming for him. Somebody is. Christ has already fought the decisive battle and won it, disarming the rulers and authorities and triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15); the war is real, but the outcome was settled on a hill outside Jerusalem.

Fortify the right position. If the war is fought in the members, that is where the defences belong. Hence the New Testament’s physical, unspiritual-sounding commands: flee (1 Corinthians 6:18), cut it off (Matthew 5:30), make no provision for the flesh (13:14), with the indwelling Spirit as the strength to obey them (8:13). A man who prays about a temptation and takes no practical steps has fortified the wrong position. In practice: the phone that stays out of the bedroom, the route home that does not pass the shop, the drink not poured, the friend who has permission to ask.

What should I do straight after I have lost a battle? Go to God at once, not after a decent interval of feeling bad. Confess the specific sin plainly; he is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9), because Christ’s blood has paid for it. Do not try to earn your way back with extra devotion; you are received on the same ground as before, Christ. Put right what you have damaged, ask what made the defeat easier and change it, and carry on: the war is not lost when a battle is. The devil wants a fall to become a retreat. The gospel turns it into a return.

In everyday life. If you suspect your own delight, do not ask whether you always obey; verse 23 has answered that. Ask what you feel about the commandment you keep breaking. Does anything in you say, “That is good, and I wish I were like that”? An unconverted man thinks the standard unreasonable. If you find yourself agreeing with the very law that is currently defeating you, that agreement is not nothing. It is the deepest thing in you, and it was put there.

parallels.desc: his delight is in the law of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worn out by the war, Paul cries out for a deliverer and at once thanks God for him: Jesus Christ our Lord. Yet until the deliverance is complete, the struggle goes on.

Wretched man that I am! Not self-pity or despair, but the cry of a man worn out by a struggle that has gone on too long. The risen Christ uses it of the church at Laodicea, who did not know it applied to them (Revelation 3:17). Paul knows. This man has stopped making excuses for himself.

Who will deliver me from this body of death? “Who,” not “what”: not a technique, but a person. The Roman poet Virgil tells of the tyrant Mezentius, who bound living men to corpses, face to face and hand to hand, and left them to die in that embrace, and commentators have long recalled the image here. Whether or not Paul had it in mind, it fits: something dead, strapped to a living man, which he cannot reach round to untie and cannot outrun. He does not ask to be improved. He asks to be delivered, which is what you ask when the problem is attached to you.

Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! The answer bursts out at once; nothing stands between the cry and the answer but a question mark. The chapter is finally not about how long the misery lasts but about how near the deliverer is. Jesus Christ delivers: now in part, by the Spirit (8:2), and fully at the resurrection, when this body of death is changed (8:23; 1 Corinthians 15:57). The question looked to the future; the reply is gratitude, in the present, for something already true while he waits for its completion.

So then. After his praise Paul states the war again, because the deliverance is certain but not yet complete. Between conversion and glory the believer is both things at once: not yet sinless, but no longer sin’s slave at heart. Chapter 8 opens on that same man, and its first word to him is that there is now no condemnation.

The design of the chapter. It brings a man to the end of himself while he is still holding on to God. The cry of verse 24 is the last thing a self-reliant man will say and the first thing a rescued man remembers saying. Wretched, and thanking God in the same breath: that is a Christian.

The knot no discipline could untie. The living man was bound to a corpse and could not cut himself free, so the Son of God came and let our death be bound to him. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). He rose in a body death can never touch, and he will change our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). No discipline could have untied the knot; a Person severed it, with hands that were pierced to do it.

Is it right for a Christian to call himself wretched? As an honest cry about his remaining sin, yes; as his settled identity, no. Paul says it in the same breath as “Thanks be to God”, and he calls every believer a saint, beloved, a child of God (1:7; 8:16). The clear sight of sin behind the cry is itself a gift, but it is not the whole truth, and he does not stop there. If you find yourself saying the first half of verse 24 and never the first half of verse 25, you have taken the lament without the answer.

When will the struggle end? For the soul, at death: a believer’s soul is then made perfect in holiness and goes at once into the presence of Christ (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1; Philippians 1:23; Hebrews 12:23). There is no purgatory to finish the job; Christ’s work has finished it. For the body, at the resurrection: the very place where this war was fought will be raised imperishable and glorious, with no law of sin left in its members (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). The struggle is the last chapter of the old life, not the first chapter of the endless one.

In everyday life. Ask what you have been asking for. If your prayers about your besetting sin are requests for assistance, “help me try harder”, you are still asking “what” and not “who”. This verse is the cry of a man who has given up on himself and wants a person to come and get him. Often that prayer comes only when the other kind has been exhausted, which may be why God lets his people be exhausted. And when you next make the cry of verse 24, answer it at once with the thanksgiving of verse 25.

Where Christians differ: sinless perfection. Some holiness teachers claim believers can reach a state of sinless perfection in this life; some in the Wesleyan and Holiness traditions teach that a believer can be so filled with love that he no longer sins deliberately, and often read 7:14–25 as life before conversion or before that second blessing (a later, distinct work of grace). This commentary’s view: Paul, an apostle, still struggled. John says that if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8). Believers grow in holiness and win real victories, but sinless perfection comes only at glorification (Philippians 3:12; 1 John 3:2). Sin’s rule is broken now; its presence ends only when we are glorified. Those who hold the other view are often earnest Christians hungry for holiness, and that hunger is right; the question is only whether Scripture promises its fulfilment before glory.

Uncertain wording. The Greek can be read “this body of death” (ESV), where “this” points to the body, or “the body of this death” (KJV), where it points to the death Paul has described. Nor is it certain whether “body” means the physical body, mortal and the place where sin’s law works (v. 23), or, as in “body of sin” (6:6), the whole self as sin has claimed it. The meaning is close either way: Paul longs to be freed from a sin-ridden, death-bound existence he cannot escape, and the answer looks to the redemption of our bodies (8:23).

Textual note. The KJV has “I thank God”, the reading of many manuscripts; others, followed by most modern Bibles, read “Thanks be to God”, and the meaning is the same.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Or do you not know, brothers —for I am speaking to those who know the law—that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives?<sup>2</sup>For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.<sup>3</sup>Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.<sup>4</sup>Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God.<sup>5</sup>For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.<sup>6</sup>But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.<sup>7</sup>What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.”<sup>8</sup>But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.<sup>9</sup>I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died.<sup>10</sup>The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.<sup>11</sup>For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.<sup>12</sup>So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.<sup>13</sup>Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.<sup>14</sup>For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin.<sup>15</sup>For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.<sup>16</sup>Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good.<sup>17</sup>So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.<sup>18</sup>For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out.<sup>19</sup>For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.<sup>20</sup>Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.<sup>21</sup>So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.<sup>22</sup>For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being,<sup>23</sup>but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.<sup>24</sup>Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?<sup>25</sup>Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

keyVerse.quote: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter meets here. The law has done all it can, exposing sin and showing a man who loves it that he cannot free himself, and so he asks not “what” but “who”. The answer is a person, given with thanks in the same breath, and it opens the door to chapter 8 and its “no condemnation”.

7.reflection:
Paul pictures life under the law as a marriage to a husband who is always right and never satisfied (vv. 1–4). Where do you still relate to God as if you had to stay in credit with him, and what difference does it make that you now belong to the risen Christ?

Paul calls the law “holy and righteous and good” (v. 12) even though sin used it to kill him. When a command of God has cost you something, how are you tempted to blame the command rather than the sin, and how does the cross answer the suspicion that God is mean?

Verses 14–25 describe a man who delights in God’s law and still does what he hates. Do you recognise this struggle? How can the passage comfort a struggling believer without becoming an excuse for sin he has stopped fighting?

The cry of verse 24 asks “who”, not “what”, and is answered at once with thanks (v. 25). What would change in the way you pray about your besetting sins if you began to ask for a person rather than a technique?

8.title: No Condemnation, All Glory
8.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 8 is the summit of Romans. Chapters 5–7 have shown the justified believer at peace with God, joined to Christ, and yet still at war with remaining sin; chapter 7 ended with the cry “Wretched man that I am!” (7:24). Chapter 8 is God’s full answer, before Paul turns to Israel in chapters 9–11.

The message. Everyone who is in Christ Jesus is safe with God, from the first verse to the last. There is no condemnation for them, because God condemned their sin in his Son, and no separation, because nothing in all creation can break his love. Between the two stands the Holy Spirit, named more often here than anywhere else in the letter. He frees God’s children from sin’s rule, lives in them, makes them cry “Abba! Father!”, prays for them in their weakness, and guarantees that their bodies, and the whole creation with them, will be set free.

Why it was said. Paul’s gospel of free grace was accused of leaving people in their sins (3:8; 6:1), and the believers in Rome, a small mixed church in the capital of the empire, faced pressures that seemed to argue against God’s love (see the introduction). Anyone who had just heard chapter 7 would ask two questions: if I still struggle like this, am I really his? And if I suffer like this, does he really care?

How the chapter makes its case. First, freedom (vv. 1–11): no condemnation, because God condemned sin in his Son’s flesh and the Spirit of life has freed us; flesh and Spirit are two kinds of life, every Christian has the Spirit, and the Spirit will raise his mortal body. Second, family (vv. 12–17): led by the Spirit, God’s children put sin to death, call him Abba, and are heirs with Christ, sharing his sufferings on the way to his glory. Third, hope (vv. 18–30): creation groans, we groan, and the Spirit groans in prayer for us, while God works all things for our good and his purpose runs unbroken from foreknowledge to glory, a chain with no missing link. Fourth, security (vv. 31–39): God is for us, gave his Son, justifies us, and lets nothing separate us from his love.

Where it leads. Every part of the chapter rests on Christ: the Son sent in our flesh and condemned in our place (v. 3), raised by the Spirit who now lives in us (v. 11), the firstborn among many brothers whose likeness we are destined to wear (v. 29), the Son the Father did not spare (v. 32), and the Lord who sits at God’s right hand interceding for us (v. 34). The love that nothing can break is “the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (v. 39).

For us. This chapter was written for strugglers and sufferers, not for those who feel strong. If you are fighting sin, fight it by the Spirit, knowing you are not condemned. If you are grieving or in pain, groan honestly, knowing your groaning is labour and not death. And whatever you fear might undo you, name it, and set it against verses 38 and 39.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — No Condemnation: Life in the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who are in Christ will never be condemned, because God condemned their sin in his Son and gave them his Spirit, who makes them alive and will raise them. The verdict rests not on the believer’s life on a given day but on Christ: the Spirit of life has freed us from sin’s rule (vv. 1–2), because God sent his Son and condemned sin in his flesh, so that the law’s requirement is fulfilled in us (vv. 3–4). Flesh and Spirit are not body and soul but two kinds of life, one set on self and hostile to God, the other set on the Spirit and marked by life and peace (vv. 5–8). Every Christian belongs to the second, because the Spirit lives in him, and the same Spirit will raise his mortal body (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification and Assurance

Romans 8:1 is the foundation of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The absence of condemnation for those in Christ is total: nothing past, present or future can bring it back, because justification is not a process but a verdict, given once and not reversed. A Christian may sin grievously and be disciplined for it, but she is not in danger of condemnation. The Spirit she has received is the guarantee (v. 11) that what began in justification will be completed in glory.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's readers knew condemnation as a court's verdict of guilty, with its sentence. In the court of God, no condemnation means the case is closed, the penalty paid, and the accused free for good. Now: Many Christians hold the doctrine of justification and still live under a cloud (see the note on vv. 1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death. — Romans 8:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who are joined to Christ will never be condemned, because the Spirit of life has set them free from the rule of sin and death. Paul says this not to people who have conquered their sin but to people still fighting it.

Therefore. The word reaches back to Christ’s work (3:21–5:21) and to the cry of 7:24–25, not to a triumphant paragraph about victory over sin. It answers a man who has just called himself wretched, who cannot do what he wants and keeps doing what he hates. He has not improved or turned a corner. He has cried out, and the answer is: “There is therefore now no condemnation.” From here the chapter runs to no separation (v. 39), with the Holy Spirit as the reason in between.

Now. Already, not someday, and not when the struggle has been resolved: in the middle of it, on the same page as the groaning. If Paul had wanted to make this a reward for progress he had every opportunity, and he wrote “now” instead. The verdict of the last day has been given in advance, in our favour.

No condemnation. The Greek sentence opens with the word “no” (ouden): in effect, “None, therefore, now, condemnation.” Not reduced, not probationary. Katakrima is not merely the guilty verdict but the sentence that follows, the penalty to be served. So the charge has not only been dropped; there is nothing left to serve. A man can be acquitted and still be ruined by the costs; this is an acquittal with nothing of any kind left to pay.

In Christ Jesus. Faith has joined you to him, so that your sin was counted to him and his righteousness is counted to you (2 Corinthians 5:21). The believer does not stand in herself, where condemnation would be entirely deserved, but in Christ: hidden in him, clothed in his righteousness, sharing his verdict before the Father. The condemnation has already fallen, on the Son of God, in full, on a hill outside Jerusalem; it cannot fall again on those who are found in him.

The law of the Spirit of life. Verse 2 explains why there is no condemnation. Paul usually means the law of Moses when he says law, so why read it here as a ruling power? Four reasons. First, he has just used the word this way. In 7:21 he says, “I find it to be a law”: a fixed pattern, that when he wants to do right, evil lies close at hand. In 7:23 another law in his members wages war and makes him captive to the law of sin. A law that wages war and takes prisoners is not a written code but a power that rules, and the law of sin and death in 8:2 is plainly the law of sin of 7:23 and 7:25.

Three more reasons. Second, Paul had already stretched the word in 3:27, where boasting is excluded by the law of faith: the principle or order of faith. Third, ordinary Greek, like English, used law for a fixed rule of how things work, as we speak of the law of gravity. Fourth, the two laws in v. 2 are rival masters, one freeing from the other, and the law of Moses is holy, righteous and good (7:12); it cannot be the law of sin and death in the sense of something evil. So the law of sin and death is the ruling power of sin, which always ends in death; the law of the Spirit of life is the ruling power of the Holy Spirit, who gives life.

Has set you free. The tense marks a decisive act, done once: not a process that may or may not succeed, but a liberation that has happened in Christ Jesus, to whom we are joined. The chains were broken not by the prisoner’s effort but by the Spirit of God.

How did the one power set me free from the other? Paul answers in vv. 3–4, and the liberation has two sides. The legal side: sin ruled in death because the law’s sentence against the sinner stood. God condemned sin in the flesh of his Son (v. 3), so the sentence has been carried out and sin has no legal right left to hold us; that is why v. 2 can explain v. 1. The living side: the Spirit, who is life, now lives in us (vv. 9–11). Uniting us to Christ in his death and resurrection, he has ended sin’s reign (6:6–7, 14) and given us a new heart with new desires (Ezekiel 36:26–27), so that we now want God and can resist sin. Preachers often use a picture: the law of gravity is not repealed when an aircraft flies, but a stronger law, the lift of the wing, overcomes it, as long as the aircraft flies in that power. Sin still pulls; the Spirit is the stronger power.

What it does not mean. Not that sin is no longer present, or that the believer no longer struggles; Romans 7:14–25 and Galatians 5:17 describe that struggle honestly. Sin is no longer the master. We were slaves with no choice; now we are free people who fight, on the winning side. Nor does it mean freedom from God’s moral law as a guide for life (v. 4; 13:8–10).

Living under a cloud. This verse has to be preached to Christians, because many believers hold the doctrine and live under a cloud of something else. They cannot hear a promise of God without adding a condition. They pray as though re-applying each time. They find it easier to believe they are forgiven than that they are welcome. And when something goes wrong, their first instinct is to ask what they are being punished for. Whatever the hard thing in your life is, it is not that. It may be discipline, or consequence, or the ordinary friction of a groaning world, but it is not God collecting on a debt, because there is no debt outstanding.

Three things often confused. Condemnation is gone entirely. Discipline remains, and is evidence of sonship rather than of wrath: “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). And consequences remain, often in full: a man may be completely forgiven and still lose the marriage. Telling him his forgiveness must be doubtful because his circumstances are hard is one of the cruellest mistakes a Christian can make.

If there is no condemnation, why do I still feel guilty? Because feelings are slower than verdicts, and a conscience trained for years under the old marriage to the law (7:1–4) keeps its habits for a while. Some guilt is the Spirit convicting you of a real sin: then confess it plainly and specifically, and receive the forgiveness already bought (1 John 1:9). But much of what Christians feel is accusation, not conviction. Conviction is specific, leads to Christ and leaves you lighter; accusation is vague, drives you away from God and leaves you heavier. When the feeling persists after you have confessed, do not wait for it to lift before you believe. Answer it with this verse, out loud if necessary. God’s verdict is the fact; your feeling is weather.

Where Christians differ: does “law” here still mean the law of Moses? Some scholars (for example James Dunn, and in his own way N. T. Wright) argue that both laws are the Mosaic law seen two ways: the law used by sin to produce death (7:8–11), and the same law, empowered by the Spirit, leading to life. This commentary’s view: there is a real play on words, and Paul knows he is using his key word in a surprising way. But the most natural reading, and that of most careful commentators (Calvin, Murray and Moo among them), is that law here means the governing power under which a person lives. Two regimes, two rulers: the reign of sin leading to death, and the reign of the Spirit giving life, as in 5:21, where sin reigned in death but grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who walk not according to the flesh” to v. 1, and the King James and New King James Versions follow them. This was probably copied from v. 4, and makes “no condemnation” sound conditional on our walk. The earliest manuscripts don’t have it. No condemnation rests on being in Christ, not on our performance. In v. 2, the manuscripts vary between “set you free” (singular, as in the ESV), “set me free” (as in the King James Version) and “set us free”. The singular “you” is probably original: Paul turns from the “I” of chapter 7 and speaks directly to each reader.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who walk not according to the flesh,” and that some read “me” for “you.”

verseByVerse.quote: For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. — Romans 8:3–4
verseByVerse.commentary:
What the law could never do, God has done: in his Son he condemned our sin, so that the law’s whole demand is met in us who live by the Spirit. The “no condemnation” of v. 1 rests on a condemnation that has already fallen, on Christ.

What the law could not do. The law could tell us what is right and condemn us for doing wrong, but it could not give us the power to obey or the forgiveness we need (7:14–25). The weakness was not in the law but in us, the material it had to work with: the law failed the way a ladder fails a man who cannot climb, which is to say, it did not fail at all. Then the subject changes: “God has done”. The law could not; the man of chapter 7 could not. Everything after those words is not what must be attempted but what has been accomplished, in real flesh, by somebody else.

What Paul means by “the flesh”. The word runs through vv. 3–13. “Flesh” (sarx) can mean the body’s tissue, human descent (1:3) or human frailty (3:20). But in Romans 7–8 and Galatians 5 it means human nature as it is since the fall, living from itself and for itself, turned away from God. It is not the body as such: Christ came in flesh, and our bodies will be raised (v. 11). It includes the mind (v. 6), the will and the desires; its works include jealousy, rivalry and anger (Galatians 5:19–21), and even religion done in our own strength, “confidence in the flesh” (Philippians 3:3–6). It is the whole self organised around self. Paul also uses it for a realm, the old order of life under Adam. So to be “in the flesh” (vv. 8–9) is to be unconverted, and believers are no longer in it (v. 9); yet the flesh remains in them as a pull, which they fight by the Spirit (v. 13; Galatians 5:16–17).

His own Son, in the likeness of sinful flesh. The Son existed before he came: he was sent from heaven and became truly human, subject to weakness, temptation and death, yet without sin (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15). And Paul places the word “likeness” precisely. Not the likeness of flesh, which would make the incarnation a costume; not sinful flesh, which would put sin in the Son; but the likeness of sinful flesh: real flesh, genuinely ours, weak and mortal, without the sin. If the flesh he took was not truly ours, he did not redeem ours; as the old Fathers said, what is not assumed (taken on by the Son) is not healed. If it was sinful, he would have needed saving himself. He had to be near enough to be one of us and clean enough to be of use, and this one clause holds both.

He condemned sin in the flesh. The ESV notes that “for sin” can also be rendered “as a sin offering”, like those of Leviticus 4; Isaiah 53:10 foretold the Servant’s life made an offering for guilt. “Condemned” (katekrinen) is the verb that matches “condemnation” in v. 1. Sin was sentenced and punished in Christ’s flesh on the cross. This is penal substitution: penal, because it was the penalty God’s law pronounces on sin; substitution, because it fell on someone in our place. Christ did not merely suffer alongside sinners: he bore the sentence that was theirs, so that it is no longer waiting for them (Isaiah 53:5–6; 1 Peter 2:24).

Where the condemnation went. The condemnation of v. 1 was not waived; it was carried out, and Paul names the place: the flesh of God’s own Son. There is none in v. 1 because there was some in v. 3. And “in the flesh” names the battlefield. Sin had made its home in human nature and had never been beaten there. God did not defeat it from a distance by decree; he came into the territory sin had held since Eden and beat it there: Christ, the second Adam, winning on our ground what the first Adam lost on it.

The righteous requirement. To dikaiōma, singular: not the many commandments but the law’s one total demand. “Might be fulfilled” is passive, and it is fulfilled “in us”, not “by us”.

Who walk. To walk is to live, step by step. This is not a condition we must meet for the requirement to be fulfilled; it describes the people in whom it is fulfilled. Everyone in Christ walks by the Spirit, imperfectly but truly. Paul does not turn it into a technique, and will not say how it is done until v. 13. What he establishes here is that the resources have changed: the walking follows from the gift rather than producing it. The man of chapter 7 had the desire and not the ability; here the ability arrives from outside him. The Father sent his own Son; the Son took our flesh and bore our sentence; the Spirit now writes in us the very righteousness the law required.

In everyday life. When you face a sin you have repeatedly lost to, what do you reach for? If it is your own determination, a firmer resolve, a better system, a promise to yourself, you are working with the resources of chapter 7, and chapter 7 records how that ends. The Spirit is not a reserve to be summoned in emergencies; he lives in every Christian, all the time. So begin today’s fight by remembering that sin has already been condemned in Christ, and ask the Spirit for the walking.

Was Jesus really tempted, if he never sinned? Yes, in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15): hunger in the wilderness, the pull of an easier road, and in Gethsemane the full horror of the cup. Sinlessness does not make temptation lighter; it makes it heavier. A man who gives way at the first push never learns how strong the pressure can become; only one who never yields feels its full weight to the end. So when you bring him your temptations, you bring them to the only person who has felt their whole force and stood, and who is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

But how can it be fulfilled if my obedience is still imperfect? In Christ the requirement is fully met now, and nothing can be added to it. And even the Spirit’s work in us does not claim perfection. In 13:8–10 Paul says the one who loves another has fulfilled the law, using the same verb, without suggesting that any believer loves perfectly. A life of Spirit-produced love is genuinely, if not yet completely, the law’s fulfilment: real now, growing, and perfect at glorification, when we are conformed to the image of the Son (v. 29; Philippians 1:6; 1 John 3:2).

Where Christians differ: what does it mean that the law’s requirement is fulfilled in us? Does Paul mean the law’s demand for punishment, carried out on Christ; its demand for a righteous life, now lived by believers; or both? The first view is forensic: the law demanded perfect righteousness, and that demand is fully met for us in Christ, whose obedience and death are counted as ours. Calvin took it this way, and so does Douglas Moo: the passive verb, the singular “requirement”, the word “fulfilled” and the link with no condemnation all point to something God does, completely, rather than our partial obedience. The second is ethical: the Spirit now enables believers to live the life the law always aimed at, love for God and neighbour. C. E. B. Cranfield and Thomas Schreiner take this view, noting that the verse ends with the walk of those in whom it is fulfilled, and that God sent his Son not only to forgive us but to change us (Ezekiel 36:27; Jeremiah 31:33). The third holds both: the law’s real demand is righteousness, the punishment falls on those who fail to give it, and Christ met that demand both by his perfect obedience and by bearing the penalty for our disobedience. This commentary’s view: the two belong together, with the forensic sense as the foundation. In Christ the law’s whole requirement has been fully met for us, which is why Paul can say “fulfilled” without qualification, passive and “in us”: we are in Christ, and what is true of him is counted true of us. And the same union brings the Spirit, who begins to produce in us the very righteousness the law requires; that is why the verse ends with how we walk. Justification (the verdict, given once, that we are righteous in Christ) and sanctification (the Spirit’s steady remaking of us in holiness) are never separated: no one has the first without beginning the second.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “for sin” can also be rendered “as a sin offering.”

parallels.desc: the sin offering

verseByVerse.quote: For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What people set their minds on shows which of two kinds of people they are: the mind set on the flesh is death already, the mind set on the Spirit is life and peace. Paul is describing the unconverted and the converted, not grading Christians on their concentration.

A compass, not a moment. “Set the mind” (phronousin) covers more than thinking: what you care about and are inclined toward, the whole disposition of a person. It is not his opinion, nor the stray thought on a train; it is where he goes when nothing requires him to be anywhere: the direction the needle returns to when it is left alone.

Settings are visible in the gaps. You find out where your mind is set not at church or at work, where the agenda is set for you, but in the unstructured minutes. What do you reach for when you wake in the night? What fills the ten minutes in a queue, the drive with the radio off, the moment your hand goes to your phone before you have decided anything? A man’s mind, when released, goes where it lives.

Is death. In the Bible, death is first of all separation: of the soul from the body, and of the person from God, the source of life. A mind set on the flesh is already in that state: alive in the body, but dead toward God, unable to know, love or please him (Ephesians 2:1–3; 1 Timothy 5:6). This is not a penalty attached at the end but a condition already in effect, as drowning is not a punishment for being underwater: it is what being underwater does. Unless God intervenes, it ends in physical death and finally in the second death (6:23; Revelation 20:14), separation from God for ever.

Life and peace. Life is the life of God shared with us: knowing God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (John 17:3), begun now and completed in the resurrection (vv. 10–11). Peace is first peace with God: the war is over (5:1, 10), whereas the mind of the flesh is still hostile to God (v. 7). Then peace within, the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, a life put right (Philippians 4:7). We would have written life and holiness, or life and usefulness; Paul writes peace, the exact answer to chapter 7, a chapter of war: a law waging war, a man taken captive, a self divided. What ends the war is not a stronger will but a mind no longer set on the flesh, the very thing that was fighting against it.

The things of the Spirit. The Spirit-led mind cares about what God cares about (Colossians 3:1–2; Philippians 4:8): Christ, his word, holiness, his people, his kingdom. And the Spirit’s own work, Jesus said, is to glorify him, taking what is Christ’s and declaring it to us (John 16:14), so a mind set on the Spirit is in the end a mind set on Christ. There has been one human mind set on the things of the Spirit without a wandering minute: the Son, whose food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:34). That is why Paul can write, “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). Life and peace are his, and the Spirit turns our minds to him so that they become ours: “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). The Prince of Peace made that peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and the Spirit draws our wandering minds home to it.

A guard for the tender conscience. This verse can be turned into a whip for the wrong person. The believer whose mind wanders in prayer, who finds Scripture hard going this month, who is distractible and knows it, is not the man whose mind is set on the flesh. The proof is that it troubles him. A mind genuinely set on the flesh does not lie awake troubled by how little it wants God. Wanting to want him is already the needle pointing the right way, however unsteadily.

So how do I actually set my mind on the Spirit? By choosing what you look at, repeatedly, until the needle learns. Seek the things that are above, where Christ is (Colossians 3:1–2): give the first minutes of the day to his word rather than the news, even if only a psalm. Carry one verse with you and return to it in the gaps. Pray in sentences through the day. Think on whatever is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely and commendable (Philippians 4:8), which means also choosing what not to watch and read. Gladly give the Lord’s Day to worship with his people, because minds are set in company. And when your mind has drifted, do not scold yourself; simply turn it back. Every turning is the Spirit at work.

verseByVerse.quote: For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mind set on the flesh is at war with God: it will not submit to his law, it cannot, and nothing it does can please him. That is why the change in v. 9 must come from God.

Hostile, not merely indifferent. The unconverted mind is at war with God (5:10; Colossians 1:21). Paul is not saying that everyone outside Christ hates God consciously; many are perfectly polite about him, and some are religious. He is describing an orientation rather than an emotion, like one magnet set against another: the closer God comes, the more it turns away. Watch a conversation when God stops being a topic and starts making a claim. Discussed as an idea, he is interesting; introduced as someone with rights over the listener, the temperature changes. That shift is often unconscious, and it is the thing Paul is naming.

Indeed, it cannot. Theologians call this total inability: not that people are as bad as they could be, but that no part of fallen human nature can turn itself to God (1 Corinthians 2:14; John 6:44). The natural man is not equipped to obey, as a stone is not equipped to float, and this is what makes the Christian faith unlike every programme of moral improvement. It also bears on chapter 7: the man who delights in God’s law in his inner being (7:22) is doing what the mind of the flesh cannot, one reason to see him as a believer.

Inability is not an excuse. It is not a disability imposed from outside, so it does not reduce guilt. It is the inability of a man who cannot bring himself to love someone he has decided to despise: real, total, and entirely his own fault. And it can wear religious clothes. A person can keep God’s rules in order to keep God at a distance, obeying so that God will owe him and leave him in charge of his own life. That is the flesh too, and Paul knew it from the inside (Philippians 3:4–7).

The one Man who pleased God. Those in the flesh cannot please God (v. 8): that describes every human being since Adam, with one exception. Over the Jordan the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and Jesus could say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), in real human flesh, his will submitted to the Father all the way to the cross. So the gospel does not tell the natural man to improve until God is pleased with him. It joins him to the One with whom God is already well pleased, and makes him accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6).

A stone made to float. This bleak paragraph stands just before “You, however” (v. 9), so that you know what it cost to be able to find yourself in verse 9. Verse 8 once described you, and it was not your own effort that changed that. While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (5:10). When we could not submit, the Son submitted for us, all the way to the cross; when we could not please God, he made us pleasing to him in his Son. Every Christian is a stone that God has made to float, and the praise belongs entirely to him.

Why your arguments did not work. If unbelief were merely a shortage of information, the cleverest people would always be the first to believe, which they are not. The problem is inability, which is why conversion is described as new birth, resurrection, and a heart of flesh for a heart of stone. So when you have explained it, lived it and answered every objection to someone you love, and still they do not believe, it is not that you argued badly. The work is God’s, and the person you pray for is not a harder case than you were. Keep praying, loving and speaking; God gives new life through his word (James 1:18).

Are the good deeds of unbelievers worthless, then? Not to people: an unbelieving doctor who heals, an honest neighbour, a father who provides, all do things God commands that bless others, and by his common grace God restrains evil and gives such kindness through them. But they cannot please God in Paul’s sense, because they do not come from a heart made right by faith, and are not done in love for him or for his glory (Hebrews 11:6). The Westminster Confession says such works may be good things in themselves and useful to others, yet they cannot please God or make a person fit to receive grace (Westminster 16.7; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 16.7). So we honour the good we see in unbelievers, and we never tell them it will bring them to God.

Where Christians differ: free will. Arminian Christians (those who hold that God’s saving grace can be resisted, and that he chooses those he foresees will believe) teach that God gives everyone enough grace, which they call prevenient grace, to choose to believe. They too confess that no one comes to God without grace, and they are brothers and sisters in Christ. This commentary’s view: Paul says the fleshly mind cannot submit to God. Only the Spirit’s regenerating work makes faith possible (John 3:3–8; Ephesians 2:4–5). This is why salvation is entirely God’s work: he must give new life before we can respond.

verseByVerse.quote: You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every Christian has the Spirit of God living in him and so belongs to Christ; his body is still mortal, but the Spirit within him is life. To have the Spirit is to have Christ, and to lack him is not to belong to Christ at all.

In the Spirit. Believers belong to the realm of the Spirit, because the Spirit dwells in them. “Dwells” (oikei): lives at home, permanently. “If in fact” (eiper) is here probably not a doubt but a reminder: since, as is the case.

Does not belong to him. Paul packs three names into two verses: the Spirit of God dwells in you; anyone without the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him; and Christ is in you. The Spirit is sent by the Father and by the Son (John 14:26; 15:26), and Christ can call God’s own Spirit his Spirit only because Christ is God. The New Testament assumes the Trinity here rather than arguing for it, and the Spirit is not a lesser third party sent as a substitute while the Lord is elsewhere; he is how the risen Christ is present with his people, and with the Son comes the Father: “we will come to him and make our home with him” (John 14:23).

The body is dead. Not a corpse, but mortal, under the sentence of death that entered the world through sin (5:12). Paul does not pretend that the indwelling Spirit fixes everything now. Christians still grow old, fall ill and die, and any teaching which implies that enough faith should keep a believer well has not read this verse.

The Spirit is life because of righteousness. Translations differ over whether this is the Holy Spirit or the human spirit (see “Where Christians differ” below). “Because of righteousness” is set against “because of sin”: as sin brought death, so righteousness brings life. This is mainly the righteousness of justification, God’s verdict that we are righteous in Christ (5:17–21). Because we are justified, the Spirit gives us life.

Decaying and being renewed. The body dead, the Spirit life: both true at once, which is the shape of the whole Christian experience, a man decaying and being renewed simultaneously, who can feel both on the same afternoon (2 Corinthians 4:16). And the Lord of heaven has taken up residence in bodies that are wearing out, not because they are worthy of him, but because he has declared us righteous in his Son. He did not wait for a better house. He moved into this one, and he means to rebuild it.

Read by the wrong person. Verse 9 is one of the great dividing lines, but it is regularly read by the wrong person: the anxious believer takes it as an examination he is probably failing, while the man who ought to be searched by it reads past it without a flicker. Paul does not say “anyone who does not feel the Spirit”, or who has not had a particular experience or cannot point to a datable moment. He is describing not a sensation but a possession, and possessions are verified by their effects rather than by how vividly they are felt.

How would I know? Not by looking inward at your feelings, which mostly report on your temperament and how you slept. Look for effects. Do you call God Father and mean it, not as a formula but as an address (v. 15)? Do you find yourself loving Christian people you have nothing else in common with (1 John 3:14)? Do you mind about your sin, and mind more than you used to (chapter 7)? Is Christ precious to you in a way he once was not? None of those is spectacular. All of them are supernatural: nothing in the flesh produces them (vv. 7–8).

Is there a second experience of the Spirit that ordinary Christians lack? No. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion: in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). There are not two classes of Christians, those who merely believe and those who have the Spirit. What Scripture does call for is being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), a continual yielding to the one who already lives in you, shown in worship, thanksgiving and humble service, not in a single crisis experience. So do not go looking for the Spirit as though he had not yet arrived; ask him to fill the rooms he already owns. Many Pentecostal and charismatic believers speak of a later baptism in the Spirit, and their zeal for Christ is often real and humbling; this commentary honours them, but reads 1 Corinthians 12:13 as saying that every believer has already been given the Spirit, so that later experiences are best understood as fresh fillings of the one who has come to stay.

Where Christians differ: the Holy Spirit, or the human spirit? The 1984 NIV reads v. 10 as the human spirit (“your spirit is alive”); the ESV, the 2011 NIV (“the Spirit gives life”) and the CSB read it as the Holy Spirit. The case for the human spirit: Paul contrasts body and spirit, two parts of the person, and the believer’s body is dead while their inner self is alive. This commentary’s view: Paul means the Holy Spirit, for four reasons. First, he does not say the spirit is alive (zōn), which would suit the human spirit, but that the Spirit is life (zōē), a noun: life itself, its source. Second, the Spirit has just been called the Spirit of life (v. 2). Third, every other use of spirit in vv. 9–11 means the Holy Spirit, and v. 11, continuing the thought, says the same Spirit will give life to your mortal bodies. Fourth, Paul’s contrast is not between two parts of a person but between two powers: sin brings death, the Spirit brings life. So your body is still marked for death because of sin, but the Spirit who lives in you is life, and gives you life now, which will reach even your body at the resurrection. The two readings meet in experience: the believer is alive to God already (6:11), because the Holy Spirit, who is life, lives in him.

verseByVerse.quote: If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit who lives in every believer is the Spirit of the God who raised Jesus, and through him God will raise their mortal bodies too. The power of Easter is already living in us.

The name God is given. Paul could have named God in many ways, and he says this: “him who raised Jesus from the dead”. Not the Almighty or the Creator, but the one who did that particular thing on that particular morning. He says it twice in one sentence, fixing our attention on a single historical act, and then says that the same power is at this moment resident in our bodies. If that Spirit dwells in you, as he does in every Christian (v. 9), then the God who has already done the harder thing, raising Jesus, has placed inside you the Spirit by whom he will do the easier one, raising you. The difficult case is behind us.

Will also give life to your mortal bodies. As Jesus rose bodily, so will we: salvation includes the body (v. 23; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). Matter matters to God: he made it, his Son took it, and he will raise it in glory. The promise is not made to some refined essence of you that survives the wreck, but to the body reading this: the one with the bad knee and the scan results, the one that gets tired at four in the afternoon. Christianity does not offer escape from the body; it offers the body back, repaired.

Closer to Plato than to Paul. Ask what happens when a believer dies and most Christians will speak of the soul going to be with the Lord, which is true, but not the main thing the New Testament says. A soul leaving the body behind for ever is the hope of the Greek philosopher Plato, not of Paul. Paul’s hope is a raised body in a renewed creation, and this verse says the deposit on it is already lodged in the very flesh that is wearing out.

Through his Spirit who dwells in you. The indwelling Spirit is the guarantee of our inheritance (Ephesians 1:14). Paul’s word there, arrabōn, means a down payment: the first instalment, which binds the one who pays it to pay the rest.
