verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since God is for us, no opposition can finally succeed, and the God who gave up his own Son for us will not hold back anything else we need.

What then shall we say to these things? “These things” are not merely the golden chain of the previous verse. The phrase reaches back through the whole letter: the wrath revealed, every mouth stopped, the propitiation (the sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath) set forth in public, the ungodly justified, peace with God, the reign of grace, no condemnation, the Spirit given, the groaning, the chain. Paul has finished arguing. What follows is a challenge thrown out to the universe.

If God is for us, who can be against us? Not that no one opposes us, since many do, but that no opposition can succeed against those God is for. The “if” is not tentative: the Greek treats it as true, so it is better heard as since God is for us, the established fact of eight chapters. And “for us” does not mean God has picked our team; it means he himself is our advocate, champion and protector.

He who did not spare his own Son. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb, “did not spare”, in a scene every reader would have recalled. On the mountain, with the knife raised over Isaac, the voice from heaven tells Abraham that now he knows Abraham fears God, seeing he has not withheld his son, his only son (Genesis 22:12, 16). Paul takes the sentence God spoke to Abraham and applies it to God.

No ram in the thicket. The whole verse rests on this. Abraham was stopped: a voice, a hand caught before it fell, and a ram in the thicket so that the son could walk down the mountain alive. At Calvary there was no voice and no ram in the thicket, because this time the Son was the ram. God asked Abraham for something he did not in the end require of him, and then did it himself. Abraham climbed a mountain with his son and came down with him. God climbed the same kind of hill and came down alone, and the whole security of every Christian rests on the fact that nobody stopped him.

Gave him up for us all. The verb has run through this letter like a dark thread: “gave them up”, used three times in chapter 1 of God handing sinners over to what they had chosen (1:24, 26, 28). The letter’s most terrible verb and its most merciful one are the same verb, and here it reaches its destination. The Father handed over the Son so that he would never have to hand us over.

How will he not also with him graciously give us all things? The argument runs from greater to lesser. If God has already paid out the greatest sum he could, his own Son, no later request will strain his account. His generosity was settled publicly, at Golgotha; everything else is a smaller ask. The verb “graciously give” is built on the word for grace, and “all things” is the same phrase as in v. 28: the all things that work together for good are the all things he will freely give.

What it does not mean. Not a blank cheque, promising whatever you ask for. “All things” is bounded by what has just been defined as the good, conformity to the image of his Son (v. 29), and the chapter has already admitted that we often do not know what to pray for (v. 26). The promise is that nothing you truly need will be withheld, by a God who has already proved he does not hold back the things that cost him.

In everyday life. Name something good that you want and have quietly concluded God is not willing to give you: the healing, the child, the work, the release from the thing that has you. As evidence that he is unwilling you will generally find a long silence and a feeling. As evidence that he is willing you have the execution of his own Son, on your behalf, while you were his enemy. Whatever he withholds, he does not withhold it because he is unwilling to be good to you.

Was it cruel of the Father to give up his Son? No, and the objection misses who is giving. The Son was not an unwilling victim pushed forward by an angry Father. He laid down his life of his own accord (John 10:18), and Paul can say both that the Father gave him up and that the Son gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). Father and Son are one God with one will and one love. At the cross God did not make someone else pay; he paid himself, in the person of his Son. It is the costliest kindness there has ever been.

Then why do I lack things I ask for? Because a good Father gives what is good, which is not always what is asked, and because he sees further than we do. He may withhold a thing because it would harm us, or because something better is coming, or for reasons we will not learn in this life; but you can be sure of the direction of his heart. Ask freely and specifically; Jesus tells you to (Matthew 7:7–11). But when the answer is no or not yet, do not read it as stinginess. A God who gave his Son is not saving money on you.

parallels.desc: the LORD is on my side; I will not fear
you have not withheld your son

verseByVerse.quote: Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died — more than that, who was raised — who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No accusation against God’s chosen people can stand, because the Judge himself has justified them, and the Christ who died and rose now speaks for them at God’s right hand.

Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? A courtroom scene. Satan accuses (Revelation 12:10), conscience accuses, others accuse. The natural reply would be that there is nothing to charge, and Paul could not say that: the first three chapters of this letter were the charge sheet, and every word of it stands. So he answers a question about the prosecution by naming the judge: it is God who justifies. The charges may be entirely accurate; they have already been heard by the only court with authority to judge, and the verdict is in. The accusation is not denied but outranked.

Who is to condemn? The question takes us back to the first verse of the chapter, no condemnation, and now gives the full reason for it, in four clauses, each raising the ground higher. He died: the penalty has been carried. He was raised: the payment was accepted, publicly receipted. He is at the right hand: the one with the right to condemn is the one already seated as sovereign (Psalm 110:1). He is interceding: he is using that position, at this moment, on your behalf, pleading his finished work (Hebrews 7:25).

Who indeed is interceding for us. Christians think a great deal about what Christ did and far less about what he is doing now. He is not pleading with a reluctant Father, as though the Father needed persuading; the Father is the one who gave him. The case is permanently before the court with counsel permanently present. John puts it plainly for people who have just failed: “if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). There has not been a moment since he took his seat in which the Son of God was not speaking to his Father about people who do not deserve to be mentioned.

Who sits where. The Judge is the one who justifies. The counsel for the defence is the one who might have condemned. That is why Scripture can call the enemy the accuser of our brothers, who accuses them day and night before our God (Revelation 12:10), and still treat him as thrown down. He is not necessarily lying about you; he simply has no right to be heard in this court. And the Advocate is the one who died for your sins, which is a far more serious view of them than the accuser has. He speaks for you not out of sentiment but because he has the receipts.

In everyday life. When the accusation comes, usually at night and usually after a failure, listen to your own reply. If it begins “but I am trying”, “but I have repented”, “but I did well last week”, you have accepted the prosecution’s framing and are conducting your own defence, and your record cannot bear the weight. The reply this passage gives contains no information about you whatever: it is God who justifies; Christ Jesus died, was raised, is at the right hand, and is speaking for me now. Four facts, none of them about your week.

What do I do when my conscience accuses me of something true? Agree with it about the sin, and disagree with it about the verdict. If the charge is true, confess it to God plainly; do not argue, minimise or blame. Then take your stand where this verse stands: it is God who justifies, and Christ has died for this very sin. Even when our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything (1 John 3:20). If you have wronged someone, put it right. But do not let a true charge become a false sentence. The sin was real; so was the payment.

parallels.desc: he who vindicates me is near; who will contend with me?

verseByVerse.quote: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As it is written, "For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No hardship, however terrible, can separate us from Christ’s love, even when, as Scripture itself admits, God’s people look like sheep led to the slaughter.

Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Paul has narrowed the question, and the narrowing is the comfort. He does not ask whether these things can separate us from a sense of God’s nearness, or from peace of mind, which suffering demonstrably can disturb, but from the love of Christ. That is the thing under guarantee. Your feelings about God will be knocked about badly by famine and danger and the sword; his love for you is not among the casualties.

Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword. Seven trials, most of which Paul himself endured (2 Corinthians 11:23–28); the early church remembered that he was later beheaded in Rome. Every item had a face for him: he is reading out his diary. Nor was it hypothetical for the people receiving the letter. Within a few years of its being read aloud in Rome, Nero would be using Christians as entertainment, some torn by dogs, some crucified, some set alight in the imperial gardens. The verse is not too grand for your difficulties; it was built to bear a great deal more.

As it is written. At the summit of his argument for the believer’s security, Paul quotes not a psalm of triumph but a complaint, Psalm 44:22. The nation is being slaughtered and cannot understand why, though they have not forgotten God, and near its end the psalm cries, “Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord?” (Psalm 44:17, 23). The Christian life will often look, from outside, exactly like abandonment, sheep in a queue at the slaughterhouse, and he says so by quoting the complaint rather than answering it. Suffering has always been the lot of God’s people; they are not spared it, but they are never separated from Christ’s love in it.

For your sake. “Regarded as sheep to be slaughtered” is how it looks, not how it is. And the psalm gives three words for why: for your sake. This is not meaningless loss. Even at the slaughterhouse the sheep belong to somebody, and their being there has to do with him.

The love that went through the list. The love of Christ has a history. Before these things touched Paul, they touched his Lord: hungry in the wilderness, hunted by rulers, sorrowful even to death in Gethsemane, stripped by soldiers who gambled for his clothes, and brought to the end of the list not by the sword but on a cross. The Good Shepherd himself became the lamb that is led to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7), so that no sheep of his would ever face the slaughter alone. His love went through the whole of Paul’s list and came out the other side with nail-scarred hands still holding his own; nothing that comes to us now is a new test for it.

In everyday life. In the middle of something hard it is natural to reason from the circumstance: “if he loved me, this would not be happening”. Paul reasons the other way round, from the evidence of v. 32. The measure of Christ’s love for you is not the state of your life this year but a cross, fixed, dated, and unaffected by anything now happening to you; and the same love holds those who are being killed for his sake today, whom you can name in prayer this week (Hebrews 13:3).

Is it wrong to ask God why? No. Paul has just quoted a psalm that asks him why, and God put it in the Bible. Lament is not unbelief; it is faith that talks to God when it does not understand him, rather than turning away. The psalmist asks why and still appeals to God’s steadfast love (Psalm 44:26). Jesus himself cried out from the cross, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). So bring your questions to God, not away from him. What you must not do is turn the unanswered why into a verdict against his love. The cross has already settled that.

parallels.desc: for your sake we are killed all the day long

verseByVerse.quote: No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In all these trials, not by escaping them, believers win more than a victory, through the Christ who loved them.

More than conquerors. The word (hypernikōmen) is rare in Greek and found only here in the New Testament: it puts hyper on the front of the verb to conquer, over-conquer. And the first words are the ones to hold: “in all these things”, not out of them or after them. The sword of v. 35 is not confiscated before it falls. Paul is describing a victory that happens with the sword still in the room.

Through him who loved us. This phrase keeps the whole thing from becoming a boast about Christian resilience. The tense is past: loved, pointing at a completed act rather than a passing sentiment. The strength you conquer by is not being generated in you now; it was spent at a particular moment in history, outside a city wall, and you are living on it. That is a relief to anyone who has quietly concluded that real Christians must be stronger than they are.

What do we conquer? Not people. Paul will soon tell us to bless those who persecute us (12:14), and our enemies are to be loved, not defeated (12:20–21). What we conquer are “all these things”: the list of v. 35, the list of vv. 38–39, and behind them the accusation of vv. 33–34. Each threatens to separate us from the love of Christ, to break our faith, or to prove that God has abandoned us. To conquer them is for them to fail at that.

In what way do we conquer? Not as the world means it: sheep led to slaughter (v. 36) do not look like conquerors. We win not by escaping these things but in them, and three things happen.

1. They cannot separate us from God’s love. A persecutor can take your freedom, your health or your life, but not your Saviour (vv. 38–39). What these enemies were trying to do, they cannot do.

2. They are made to serve us. God works all things together for good (v. 28). Suffering produces endurance, character and hope (5:3–5), and our light, momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17). The enemy is turned into a servant.

3. Even death becomes gain. For Paul, to die was to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:21–23). The last enemy, which seems to win, opens the door home (1 Corinthians 15:54–57).

Why “more than” conquerors? An ordinary conqueror wins the battle but is often wounded by it, and loses something. The believer may lose much that is precious, and rightly grieve it, but he cannot lose Christ, and he gains from the very battle: adversity that would have destroyed him is conscripted into making him like the Son (vv. 28–29), which was the point of his existence. The enemy is not merely defeated; he is put to work. And the victory is secure before the battle starts, because Christ has already won it: take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33; Colossians 2:15).

The lion did not make them let go. That is why the martyrs are not tragic figures. The saints conquered the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death (Revelation 12:11): they conquered by dying faithful. The lions of the arena did not defeat them; the lion did not even manage to make them let go, and in the attempt it sent them home. That is how their Champion won before them. The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, and when John turned to look at him he saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:5–6). He conquered by being slain, and he makes his people conquerors in the same way.

What it looks like. A Christian with cancer whose body weakens while her trust in Christ grows deeper. Believers in prison for their faith who sing, as Paul and Silas did at midnight (Acts 16:25). Paul himself, in chains, writing Philippians, the most joyful of his letters. None of them escaped. All of them conquered.

What it does not mean. Not triumphalism: that Christians will be healthy, wealthy and successful, or that the church will win every battle in society. Not that we will always feel victorious: Paul once despaired of life itself (2 Corinthians 1:8–9), and our feelings may say defeat while the fact is victory. And not that the victory is our own strength or courage. Christ’s love holds us; we do not hold ourselves. A Christian weeping in a hospital corridor is not failing this verse. He is standing inside it, in the dark, carried by a love that does not need him to notice it in order to hold.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 8:38–39
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is certain that nothing in all creation, in any state, power, time or place, will ever be able to separate God’s people from his love in Christ Jesus.

For I am sure. Paul ends with a personal declaration. He has been through the catalogue of v. 35 himself, and none of it reached the thing that mattered. His certainty is not presumption: he has tested the rope and found it holds.

A list in pairs. Each pair covers a whole field by its two extremes. Death nor life: every state a creature can be in; there is no third option. Angels nor rulers nor powers: the entire unseen order, good or evil, whatever ranks it holds. Things present nor things to come: all of time, in both directions. Height nor depth: the whole of space, and also astrologers’ terms for the highest and lowest points of a star’s course. Paul is going through the ancient world’s inventory of the powers thought to decide a human fate, and crossing them off.

Nor anything else in all creation. This clause closes every remaining door. Whatever you were about to raise, your own temperament, your family history, a sin you have never mentioned to anybody, the thing you most fear will one day undo you, is in that clause. If it is part of creation, it cannot separate you. The apostle went looking for something in the universe strong enough to break the grip of God on one of his children, and came back having found nothing at all.

The one thing not on the list. There is one being who is not part of creation, and that is God himself. The only remaining threat would be God changing his mind, which is precisely what the whole letter has argued he will not and cannot do, because the love was fixed before you existed and secured at the cost of his Son.

In Christ Jesus our Lord. The last words locate the love exactly. It is not a benevolence in the sky which we hope covers us, but love held for you in a Person, who died and was raised and is at the right hand interceding. So the question “could I lose it?” is really the question “could he be dislodged?”, which is a much easier question to answer.

No condemnation, no separation. Nothing against you at the beginning of the chapter; nothing between you at the end. Because a just Judge has justified (3:26), the last word here is not a sentiment but a verdict, entered in a court, and unappealable. The love that chose us before creation cannot be overcome by anything within it. Here the gospel argument comes to rest, and so does the believer: in the love of God, in Christ Jesus our Lord.

In everyday life. Say the sentence with your own name and the thing you fear most in it: neither death, nor the diagnosis, nor what I did all those years ago, nor my father’s illness in me, nor the years I wasted, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate me from the love of God in Christ Jesus my Lord. Whatever makes that sentence hard to say is the thing you have been treating as stronger than the cross, and there is no such thing.

But could I not separate myself? First, you are part of creation, and Paul’s catch-all makes no exception for the reader. Second, and better, the chain of vv. 29–30 contains no link that depends on you. If your remaining in the love of God rested on your grip, the honest verdict on every one of us would be that we will let go, probably before Friday. The security here is not that we hold on well. It is that the holding is being done from the other end.

The warnings of Hebrews. Arminian Christians, whose concern that confidence should never breed carelessness is a fair one, answer that a believer may still turn away by his own choice, pointing to the warnings of Hebrews (Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29). The warnings are real and must be heard, but they are among the means by which God keeps his people (as at v. 13). Those who finally fall away show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19). If you fear that you have fallen away, come back to Christ, who casts out no one who comes (John 6:37).

What of a Christian who takes his own life? It is not the unforgivable sin, and Scripture never says it is; very often the mind of someone who dies this way has been darkened by illness and anguish. Suicide is still a grave sin, and no one should read this verse as making it light. A believer’s safety rests on Christ’s grip, not on the state of his mind in his last hour, and death heads Paul’s list. Those who mourn a believer who died this way may grieve with hope. And anyone tempted to it should tell someone today, a friend, a pastor or a doctor, and hold on to the love that will not let him go.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be lost? Some hold that, though nothing outside us can separate us, we can separate ourselves by turning away. This commentary’s view: “nor anything else in all creation” includes us. And the chain of vv. 29–30 ensures that all who are justified are glorified. This is the perseverance of the saints: God keeps his own, and they persevere because he keeps them (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; 1 Peter 1:5). It is not a licence for carelessness, but the ground of joyful, confident obedience.
verseByVerse.note: Paul names every kind of power, time and place, whether seen or unseen.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.<sup>2</sup>For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death.<sup>3</sup>For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh,<sup>4</sup>in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.<sup>5</sup>For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit.<sup>6</sup>For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.<sup>7</sup>For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law; indeed, it cannot.<sup>8</sup>Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.<sup>9</sup>You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.<sup>10</sup>But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.<sup>11</sup>If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.<sup>12</sup>So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.<sup>13</sup>For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.<sup>14</sup>For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.<sup>15</sup>For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”<sup>16</sup>The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God,<sup>17</sup>and if children, then heirs—heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him.<sup>18</sup>For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.<sup>19</sup>For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God.<sup>20</sup>For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope<sup>21</sup>that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.<sup>22</sup>For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now.<sup>23</sup>And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.<sup>24</sup>For in this hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees?<sup>25</sup>But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience.<sup>26</sup>Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.<sup>27</sup>And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.<sup>28</sup>And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.<sup>29</sup>For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.<sup>30</sup>And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified.<sup>31</sup>What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?<sup>32</sup>He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?<sup>33</sup>Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies.<sup>34</sup>Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died—more than that, who was raised— who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us.<sup>35</sup>Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?<sup>36</sup>As it is written, “For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered.”<sup>37</sup>No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.<sup>38</sup>For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers,<sup>39</sup>nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

keyVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter unfolds this sentence: why there is no condemnation (God condemned sin in his Son, v. 3), what life it opens (the Spirit, adoption and hope), and how long it lasts (nothing can separate us, vv. 38–39). It is spoken to strugglers fresh from the cry of 7:24, not to those who have arrived, and it rests entirely on being in Christ Jesus.

8.reflection:
Romans 8 follows straight on from the cry of 7:24, “Wretched man that I am!” Why does it matter that “no condemnation” (v. 1) is spoken to people still struggling with sin? How should it change the way you come to God after you have failed?

Paul says we must put to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit (v. 13), and that those led by the Spirit cry “Abba! Father!” (v. 15). How do these two belong together? Where do you need to fight sin as a loved child rather than as an anxious slave?

Creation groans, we groan, and the Spirit groans for us (vv. 22–27). What are you groaning over at present, and how does it help to know that this is labour leading to birth, and that the Spirit prays for you when you have no words?

Verse 28 is often quoted and often misused. What does it promise, what does it not promise, and how do verses 31–39 give you reasons to trust it when you cannot see the good?

9.title: The Sovereignty of God in Election
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 8 ended with the promise that nothing “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (8:39). Chapter 9 opens the three chapters (9–11) that face the question this promise raises: what about Israel? It is one of the most debated chapters in the Bible.

The message. God’s word has not failed. The unbelief of most of Israel does not mean God has broken his promise, because the promise never rested on descent or on human effort. It has always rested on God’s free mercy, which chose Isaac and not Ishmael, Jacob and not Esau, and now calls a people out of Jews and Gentiles alike. God is not unjust in this, for no one is owed mercy, and the creature cannot put his Maker on trial. Yet the chapter ends with the door wide open: whoever believes in the stone God has laid in Zion will not be put to shame.

Why it was said. Most of Paul’s own people had refused their Messiah, and Paul was accused of abandoning them (see the introduction). If God’s promises to Israel had come to nothing, his promises in chapter 8 could not be trusted either. And in a Roman church of Jewish and Gentile believers, Gentiles were tempted to look down on Israel (11:18–20). For Paul the question is personal before it is theological.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul begins with tears: he would be cut off from Christ for his kinsmen, to whom belong the covenant gifts and the Christ himself (vv. 1–5). Then the answer: not all Israel is Israel, for the promise ran through Isaac and through Jacob, chosen before birth so that election would rest on “him who calls” (vv. 6–13). Two objections follow, raised by Paul himself. Is God unjust? No: mercy is his to give, as he told Moses, and he raised up Pharaoh to show his power (vv. 14–18). Why then does he find fault? The clay cannot answer back to the potter, and God has endured vessels of wrath with much patience to make known his riches to vessels of mercy, “even us” (vv. 19–24). Hosea and Isaiah foretold both the Gentiles’ calling and Israel’s remnant (vv. 25–29). Last, Paul turns to Israel’s side: they pursued righteousness as if by works and stumbled over the stone (vv. 30–33).

Where it leads. Christ stands at both ends of the chapter: “the Christ, who is God over all” comes from Israel (v. 5), and Christ is the stone laid in Zion (v. 33). The line of promise narrows from Abraham to Isaac, to Jacob, to a remnant, until it reaches one Offspring, and in him it widens to take in “whoever believes”. Paul’s wish to be accursed for his people could not be granted; Christ was made a curse for his.

For us. These are the Bible’s hardest pages on God’s sovereign choice, and Paul writes them weeping, praying and ending with an invitation. Let them humble you, for your salvation rests on mercy, not on your will or exertion. Let them steady you, for a choice never based on your record cannot be undone by it. And let them send you to pray for those you love who do not yet believe, and to tell them that whoever trusts in Christ will not be put to shame.

keyVerse.quote: So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.
keyVerse.note: Verse 6 asks whether God’s word has failed; this verse gives the reason it cannot. Salvation never rested on what people want or achieve, so their failure cannot undo it: it rests on God, who has mercy. That is hard news for pride and the best news there is for anyone who knows he could never have willed or run enough.

9.reflection:
Paul writes the Bible’s hardest chapter on election with “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” for his unbelieving kinsmen (vv. 1–3). Who are the people you grieve and pray for? How does Paul’s example shape the way we should speak about God’s choice, and the way we should pray?

Verse 16 says salvation “depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.” Where do you still rely on your own wanting or trying to stand before God? How does this verse humble you, and how does it comfort you?

Paul raises the objections himself: is God unjust (v. 14), and why does he still find fault (v. 19)? Which of these questions troubles you most? What do Paul’s answers, and the place where he refuses to say more (v. 20), teach us about how to bring hard questions to God?

The chapter that speaks so strongly of God’s choice ends, “whoever believes in him will not be put to shame” (v. 33). How do God’s sovereign mercy and the open invitation of the gospel fit together in your own story, and in the way you share the gospel with others?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s grief for Israel is the measure of what they have refused: every gift God gave them, and last of all the Christ himself. Before he takes up the question, Paul calls three witnesses to his anguish (v. 1) and offers to be cut off from Christ for his kinsmen (vv. 2–3), so that the apostle who will argue for God’s sovereign choice without flinching is first seen weeping for the lost. Then he lists Israel’s privileges: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs, and last and highest the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever (vv. 4–5). The tragedy he mourns is that the Messiah came from Israel and was refused by most of Israel.
verseByVerse.theology:
Evangelistic passion and doctrinal conviction

Romans 9:1–3 shows that a firm belief in God’s sovereign choice need not make anyone indifferent to the lost (see the note on vv. 2–3). Election encourages mission: we preach because God has people everywhere (Acts 18:10), and he calls them through the preaching of the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s list of Israel’s privileges blocks any easy dismissal of Jewish unbelief, as though Israel had simply missed something obvious. Now: Someone who has grown up in a Christian home, heard the gospel from childhood and been surrounded by every means of grace, yet has never trusted Christ, stands where Paul’s Israel stood (see the note on v. 4).

verseByVerse.quote: I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit— — Romans 9:1
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul swears, with Christ and the Spirit as witnesses, that he grieves for Israel. Before he says the hardest things in the letter about his own people, he wants them to know that he speaks as one who loves them.

I am speaking the truth in Christ; I am not lying. A double oath, positive and negative; “in Christ” means as one united to Christ, speaking in his presence. Why does a man need witnesses to say he is sad? Because in every synagogue from Antioch to Corinth he is the man who went over to the other side, who eats with Gentiles and says the law cannot save anybody. To his own people he is a defector, and a defector’s tears are cheap. So before he says one word about election, he raises his hand in court.

My conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit. Conscience is the inner moral awareness that judges your own conduct, able to accuse or defend you (2:15), though never the final judge (1 Corinthians 4:4). The law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15); Paul brings three, Christ, his conscience and the Holy Spirit, for one sentence about sorrow, because he fully expects not to be believed. And the Spirit who a chapter ago was interceding “with groanings too deep for words” (8:26) now testifies to a groan that has surfaced, with names attached: brothers, kinsmen, a whole people.

The setting. Some Jews accused Paul of abandoning his people and teaching against the law (Acts 21:21, 28), and in Rome Gentile believers were tempted to look down on Jews (see the introduction). So he opens with an oath of love.

No step down from the summit. There is no transition between the chapters. The highest line in the letter, that nothing can separate us from the love of God, is followed at once by “great sorrow and unceasing anguish”. The assurance and the grief are in one man’s chest at the same hour, and neither is pretending. The love of chapter 8 does not seal a man up, safe and unbothered, at a distance from the lost. It puts him in tears over people, many of whom would gladly see him dead (Acts 23:12).

The heart of Christ. Paul swears “in Christ”, and the phrase tells you whose sorrow this is. He speaks as one joined to the Lord who looked at Jerusalem and said, “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). No one knew the Father’s purposes as the Son did, and that knowledge did not dry his eyes. Paul’s anguish is not his temperament breaking through his theology. It is the heart of Christ beating in a servant of Christ.

Why does Paul need to say this before teaching election? Because doctrine heard from someone who does not love you sounds like contempt. If he began with the potter and the clay, his Jewish readers would assume he was gloating, and his Gentile readers might be tempted to gloat themselves (11:18–20). The truth of election is not softened by love, but it can only be rightly heard where love is plainly present. Whoever teaches it with a shrug has not been taught it by Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul grieves so deeply for his unbelieving people that he would give up his own place in Christ for theirs, if that could be. It cannot, but the wish shows the measure of his love.

Great sorrow and unceasing anguish. Anguish like the pain of a wound, that never stops. Unceasing (adialeiptos) appears elsewhere in this letter only at 1:9, in its adverb form, of his praying: “without ceasing I mention you always in my prayers”. In Paul the grief and the praying are not two things; his grief is the form his praying takes. If you have prayed the same name every morning for thirty years, a son, a sister, a husband who will not come, and wondered whether the fact that it still hurts means your faith is thin, this verse says the reverse. That hurt is what unceasing prayer feels like from the inside.

Accursed and cut off from Christ. Accursed (anathema) means devoted to God for destruction, like the things under the ban at Jericho that Israel was forbidden to keep back (Joshua 6:17). Paul would take the sentence himself. Chapter 8 has just listed everything that cannot separate us from the love of Christ; with the ink barely dry, the man who wrote that list offers to be its one exception, sooner than watch his people perish.

My kinsmen according to the flesh. Fellow Jews, his own flesh and blood. In chapters 7 and 8 “the flesh” meant our sinful nature; here “according to the flesh” means nothing worse than family, by natural descent. Grace did not dissolve those ties; it made him love his own people more fiercely. If you have been made to feel that desperation over your own household is a lower love a mature Christian should have risen above, Paul puts the most intense sentence in this letter on exactly that ground.

Moses before him. Moses made the same offer after the golden calf: “please blot me out of your book that you have written” (Exodus 32:32). The answer was no, and Paul’s offer is refused for the same reason: a sinner cannot be accursed on behalf of sinners; he has nothing to spare. Only one man in history could be cut off and save anybody by it, and he has been. Christ became “a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), and the darkness at noon and the cry “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” are what Paul’s wish looks like when it is granted to someone who could carry it. So the deepest thing this verse shows is not how much Paul loves Israel, but that his love, at full stretch, is a shadow of a love that actually went through with it.

Grief, doctrine, prayer, hope. You may come to a chapter on election with a name in your throat: a child who walked away, a husband who is kind and unbelieving. Read verse 3 first, as your own permission: the man who says God has mercy on whomever he wills is weeping while he says it.

Where election must not be misused. First, election is never a diagnosis you may run on another person. Scripture never lets you conclude that because someone has not come yet, they never will. Paul’s own kinsmen are the unbelievers in question, and he spends three chapters refusing to write them off: still praying for them (10:1), still saying God has the power to graft them in again (11:23). You do not know who is elect; you know whom to pray for. Second, this is no guarantee that everyone you love will be saved, and pretending otherwise is a comfort that breaks when tested. What you are given is a warrant to keep asking a God who is free, which is exactly why the asking is worth anything.

Is it wrong to grieve this much if I trust God’s sovereignty? No. Paul held God’s sovereignty more firmly than anyone and grieved without ceasing; Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). Grief for the lost is not unbelief; it is love agreeing with God that perishing is terrible. What sovereignty adds is not numbness but hope: because salvation depends on God and not on the sinner, no one you pray for is beyond his reach. Let the grief drive you to prayer, not despair.

Uncertain wording. “I could wish” translates a past-tense form of the verb (ēuchomēn). In theory it could mean “I used to wish”, and some older interpreters took it that way. But the natural sense, followed by almost all translations, is a wish stated and withdrawn in the same breath: a thing Paul would ask for if it could be asked for. He knows it is not on offer, and says it anyway, because it is the only measure he has of what this costs him.
verseByVerse.note: “Accursed” is anathema — devoted to destruction.

parallels.desc: Moses: blot me out of your book

verseByVerse.quote: They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s privileges were real gifts from God, and they still belong to Israel. Paul lists them not to belittle them but in wonder, and his grief is proportioned to the size of the gift.

They are Israelites. Not just Jews (the word of chapter 2) but the honoured covenant name, given to Jacob when God met him in the dark and would not let him go without a new name (Genesis 32:28). Two verses on, Paul will show that the name has a wider and a narrower sense: “not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel” (v. 6).

The adoption. Israel was God’s firstborn son (Exodus 4:22; Hosea 11:1), a national sonship that was both a privilege and a picture of the sonship believers receive in Christ. Adoption means being taken into a family you were not born into and given a son’s name, standing and inheritance (Galatians 4:5–7).

The glory. God’s visible glorious presence (often called the Shekinah), in the cloud and fire, the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 40:34). Every item has a date and eyewitnesses: the day the cloud filled the house of the LORD so that the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10–11), the night the fire stood over the camp so that a child could wake in the desert and see by it.

The covenants. Plural: with Abraham, at Sinai, with David, and the promised new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31).

The giving of the law. The event at Sinai when God spoke his law to them, one Greek word (nomothesia). No other nation had statutes and rules so righteous (Deuteronomy 4:8).

The worship. The priestly service of tabernacle and temple (latreia), with the sacrifices God himself had appointed.

And the promises. Above all, the promises of the Messiah and of salvation. They were not optimism; they were sentences with names in them, spoken to particular men in particular fields. Whatever else Israel lacked, they were never guessing.

To them belong. The Greek has no verb, and the natural sense is present: belong, not belonged. A generation after the crucifixion, Paul puts no item of the list into the past. That present tense is the seed of chapter 11: “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). Paul is grieving, but he is not writing an obituary.

The words of chapter 8. Read the list with chapter 8 open beside it. Adoption: the Spirit-given cry of sons (8:15, 23). Glory: what we rejoice in hope of and are being conformed to (5:2; 8:18, 30). Covenants and promises: the whole argument of chapter 4. The words Paul used for the Christian’s highest blessings belonged first to a people who have now refused the Messiah. It is the privileges that are breaking his heart.

Six gifts with one face. Hold each gift up to the light and Christ is standing inside it. The son God called out of Egypt (Hosea 11:1) is the Son Matthew sees coming back from Egypt (Matthew 2:15). The glory of the tabernacle shines in him, “the radiance of the glory of God” (Hebrews 1:3). The covenants run on to the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20); the law he came to fulfil (Matthew 5:17); the worship of altar and priest is gathered up in the one who is both priest and sacrifice (Hebrews 9:11–14); and the promises are about him. Israel was handed six portraits of one person, and the grief of this chapter is that when he came, the family that owned the portraits did not know the face.

What it does not mean. Not that privilege damns, but that privilege does not save. What condemned Israel was refusing the Christ the covenants pointed to, and the invitation stayed open (chapter 10). If you were raised in church and read this with a cold hand on your chest, that alarm is not the verdict. It is the kindness of God, still doing what 2:4 says it is meant to do: lead you to repentance.

If privileges do not save, why are they called privileges? Because they are real gifts that bring you near the truth: the Jews’ advantage was much in every way, chiefly that they were entrusted with the words of God (3:1–2). A Christian upbringing, a Bible and a faithful church put the gospel within reach, and God often uses them. But they are means, not the thing itself. A map is a great privilege to a lost traveller, but it does him no good if he never follows it.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts read the singular, the covenant, but the plural is well supported and fits the list.
verseByVerse.note: “The glory” is God’s glorious presence among his people, as in the tabernacle and temple.

parallels.desc: Israel is my firstborn son

verseByVerse.quote: To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen. — Romans 9:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
The highest privilege of all is that the Messiah came from Israel, a Jew by descent who is also God over all, blessed forever. At the end of the list Paul’s grief breaks into worship.

The patriarchs. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the fathers to whom God made the promises, and with whom the rest of this chapter is about to deal.

According to the flesh. By his human descent (1:3), a phrase that implies there is more to him. God over all has a family tree, with names and awkward histories. Of all the privileges on the list, this is the one that cannot be revoked or repeated: one nation, out of every nation on earth, supplied the human nature of God. Whatever the church has said about Israel in its uglier centuries, it has had to say it about the relatives of its own Lord.

Who is God over all. A clear statement that Christ is God. The kinsman according to the flesh is God over all, and both halves of that sentence are true; the church has spent two thousand years learning not to drop either one. This is the ultimate privilege and the ultimate tragedy: the God of Israel came to Israel, and Israel largely did not receive him. So the one who is over all has already been on the receiving end of the very refusal you may be grieving.

Blessed forever. Amen. Paul does not stop to defend the statement. Nine chapters into one of the most closely argued letters ever written, the argument gives out and turns into praise. At the end of the worst grief in the letter he blesses Christ forever, and he will do it again when chapter 11 closes with “To him be glory forever” (11:36). The grief is bracketed by worship at both ends: sorrow not explained away, but held inside praise.

Whose hands are these? See where Paul has put this sentence. He is about to spend twenty verses defending the freedom of God: mercy on whomever he wills, a potter with rights over the clay, Pharaoh raised up for a purpose. That argument frightens people, and it should not be softened. But Paul shows who this sovereign is before he shows what he may do. So when the potter’s hands appear in verse 21, you already know whose they are: not raw power or fate, but the one who took the flesh of the very people he chooses among, and who held the clay with hands that bear the nail marks. The doctrine of election is only unbearable while God is anonymous. Verse 5 makes sure he is not.

How can Jesus be descended from Israel and also be God over all? Because the eternal Son, who is God, took a full human nature to himself when he was conceived by the Spirit in Mary (John 1:14; Galatians 4:4). He did not stop being God, and he did not merely appear to be human. He is one person with two natures, as the church confessed at the Council of Chalcedon (AD 451): truly God, truly man, without confusion and without division. So the baby in Bethlehem was God over all, and the man on the cross was “the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). That is why his death can save: a man died, and the one who died was God.

Textual note: the punctuation. The earliest manuscripts had no punctuation, so the sentence can be divided in more than one way. The ESV text reads it of Christ; its footnote gives alternatives that make it a separate praise of the Father, such as: Christ. God who is over all be blessed forever. This is a real grammatical possibility, not an invention by people avoiding the deity of Christ, and it should be admitted honestly. This commentary’s view: the ESV text is right. The natural flow of the Greek joins “who is” to the Christ just named. “According to the flesh” is a limiting phrase that calls for its counterpart, as in 1:3–4, where descended from David according to the flesh is answered by Son of God in power; cut the sentence in half and the limitation dangles. Paul’s separate blessings of God normally put “blessed” first (2 Corinthians 1:3; Ephesians 1:3; compare Luke 1:68), which here it does not. And a sudden burst of praise to the Father sits oddly in a lament, whereas a final and highest item at the end of a list of privileges sits perfectly. Most of the church fathers read it this way, and it fits the New Testament’s plain teaching that Jesus is God (John 1:1; 20:28; Titus 2:13; Hebrews 1:8). The traditional reading is not merely the pious one; it is the natural one.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes alternative punctuations, such as “Christ. God who is over all be blessed forever”; the ESV text calls Christ God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–29 — God's Sovereign Choice: Election and the Potter's Right
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word has not failed, because his promise has always rested on his free mercy, not on descent or effort. Not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel: the promise ran through Isaac, not Ishmael, and through Jacob, chosen before the twins were born, so that God’s purpose would rest on his call and not on works (vv. 6–13). Is God then unjust? No: mercy is his to give, as he told Moses after the golden calf, and Pharaoh shows the other side, hardening (vv. 14–18). Why then does he still find fault? Paul offers no theory; the clay cannot put its potter on trial (vv. 19–21). The section turns on verses 22–24: God has endured the vessels of wrath with much patience, and the vessels of mercy are named at last, us, called from Jews and Gentiles alike. Hosea and Isaiah close it (vv. 25–29): without God’s mercy no one would be left at all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Unconditional election

Romans 9:6–29 is the main New Testament passage for the Reformed teaching of unconditional election: God’s choice of individuals for salvation, made before the foundation of the world, resting not on foreseen faith or merit but on his own good pleasure. Calvin argues (Institutes III.21–24) that to make election depend on foreseen faith turns grace into a reward for human initiative. Election that rests on God’s own love, and works through human response rather than around it, gives all the glory to God and puts all the hope in him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau came from stories every Jewish reader knew: God’s free choosing was there in Israel’s own beginnings. Now: This teaching tends to draw one of two responses: “That is not fair,” or “Why me, Lord?” The second is the right one. The person who asks why he was chosen and finds no answer in himself has understood the doctrine, and is on his knees.

verseByVerse.quote: But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel, and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but "Through Isaac shall your offspring be named."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word to Israel has not failed, because his promise was never made to every descendant of Abraham but to the children he named. The unbelief of many Jews is not the promise collapsing; from the beginning it ran by God’s choice, not by descent alone.

It is not as though the word of God has failed. This is the theme of chapters 9–11. To chapter 8’s promise a reader of the Old Testament has an obvious reply: God said things like that to Israel too, and look at them now. If God’s word to them fell over, no promise of his is worth the weight you are putting on it, and your assurance is a sentiment. Paul is defending the only ground you have for believing chapter 8.

Failed. The verb (ekpiptō) is used of a ship driven off its course and onto the rocks (Acts 27:17, 26, 29) and of a flower falling from its stem: something that has come adrift. Paul is answering a reader who stands on the shoreline looking at what appears to be wreckage, and telling him he is looking at a ship still under way.

Not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel. Literally, not all who are from Israel are Israel. The same word cannot mean the same thing both times, or the sentence would contradict itself. The first Israel is the man Jacob and his physical descendants; the second is narrower, an Israel in the full sense of the promise within the nation, those chosen and called by God. Paul defines it two verses later: “the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (v. 8). He made a similar move at 2:28–29, distinguishing the outward Jew from the one whose circumcision is of the heart; here the same distinction is pressed further, to descent itself.

How do we know this is true? The Old Testament had been saying it all along. From the first generations, birth alone did not make an heir: of Abraham’s two sons only Isaac carried the promise (Genesis 17:19–21; 21:12), and of Rebekah’s twins God chose Jacob before they were born (Genesis 25:23). The prophets spoke of a faithful remnant within the nation (vv. 27, 29); in Elijah’s day God kept seven thousand who had not bowed the knee to Baal (1 Kings 19:18), and there is a remnant, chosen by grace, “at the present time” too (11:2–5). Moses told Israel to circumcise their hearts (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6), and Jeremiah called all the house of Israel uncircumcised in heart (Jeremiah 9:25–26). John the Baptist warned his hearers not to presume to say, “We have Abraham as our father” (Matthew 3:9); Jesus told some who claimed Abraham that if they were his children they would do what Abraham did (John 8:39–44), and called Nathanael “an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47).

Through Isaac shall your offspring be named. Paul quotes Genesis 21:12, from a hard page. Ishmael had been thirteen years in the house (Genesis 17:25), and when God promised a son by Sarah, Abraham pleaded for the child he had: “Oh that Ishmael might live before you!” (Genesis 17:18). I already love this one. The words Paul quotes were spoken when Sarah demanded that Hagar and the boy be sent away, and “the thing was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son” (Genesis 21:11). Paul’s claim is not that God changed his mind about Israel, but that the promise was always narrower than descent. It never ran through the son Abraham already had, but through a son who did not exist yet, born to two people long past the age of producing him. The word of God cannot fall off course, because it never depended on what Abraham had available, only on what God had said he would do.

Not cursed, not discarded. God’s answer to Abraham’s plea was no, and in the same breath he promised to bless Ishmael and multiply him greatly (Genesis 17:20). It helps to see this early in a chapter that will get much harder: being outside the line of promise is not the same as being outside God’s kindness.

The offspring who is one. Follow the narrowing and see where it ends. Not all Abraham’s children, but Isaac; not both of Isaac’s sons, but Jacob; not all Jacob’s descendants, but a remnant. In Galatians Paul names the last step himself: the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, and Scripture says offspring, not offsprings, referring to one, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). The line of promise runs down the generations until it becomes a single man, and then it widens again: “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). So the true Israel is not first a membership list. It is Christ, and everyone joined to him by faith, whose standing, sonship and inheritance are counted theirs. God’s word did not fail when the nation said no. It arrived, in person, at Bethlehem.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s promise to Israel was a trick, or that being a physical Jew counts for nothing (3:1–2; 11:28–29). Nor that the church has simply replaced Israel, so that the Jewish people no longer matter to God (11:1–2). The narrowing did not happen to Israel from outside; it was the principle operating inside Israel from Abraham onward, and in chapter 11 Paul insists it is still the same tree with the same root.

Does this apply to people who grew up in the church? Yes, the principle does. Being born into a Christian family, baptised and brought up in church does not by itself make a person a child of God, any more than being born a Jew did; each must be born again (John 3:3) and come to Christ in faith. That is no reason for alarm for those who trust him, nor for despising a Christian upbringing, which God often uses to bring children to faith. It is a reason never to assume: pray for and speak to your children as people who need Christ, not as people who already have him because of their family.

Where Christians differ: the two Israels. Dispensationalists (who see God’s dealings with Israel and with the church as distinct, with distinct promises) hold that “Israel” in Scripture always refers to ethnic Israel, so the true Israel here is believing Jews only, and God’s promises to the nation remain separate from his purposes for the church. Covenant theologians (who read the whole Bible as one unfolding covenant of grace) see in this verse the principle that runs through the whole Bible: the true people of God are the chosen and believing, Jew and Gentile together in Christ. This commentary’s view: in Romans 9:6 itself, both sides largely agree: the true Israel is the elect, believing remnant within the Jewish nation, such as Paul himself (11:1, 5). The wider truth, that believing Gentiles share fully in Abraham’s family and are grafted into Israel’s olive tree, is taught clearly elsewhere (Galatians 3:7, 29; Romans 11:17; Ephesians 2:11–22), and makes one people of God, not two; whether Paul ever calls the church as a whole “Israel” is debated (Galatians 6:16). But Paul does not therefore write off ethnic Israel. He keeps calling the nation Israel (9:31; 10:21; 11:7), says they are still beloved for the sake of their forefathers (11:28–29), and holds out the hope that all Israel will be saved (11:25–26), which many read as a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ and others as the full gathering of God’s people.

parallels.desc: through Isaac shall your offspring be named

verseByVerse.quote: This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring. For this is what the promise said: "About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s children are not produced by natural birth but by his promise, as Isaac was. Isaac was born because God said he would be, when nothing human could bring it about.

The children of the flesh. Ishmael was a child of the flesh: born by ordinary human means, when Abraham and Sarah tried to obtain the promised son by their own plan through Hagar (Genesis 16). “Flesh” here is not contempt for Jewish descent; Paul has just wept over his brothers. It means what human capacity can produce on its own: not ethnicity but ability.

The children of the promise are counted as offspring. Isaac was born by God’s promise and power, to a barren woman past age (Galatians 4:23, 28), when Abraham’s body was as good as dead (4:19). “Counted” is logizomai, the accountant’s word of chapter 4: there righteousness was credited to a man; here a person is entered into a family, from outside, in. You did not qualify for this household on the strength of your paperwork. You were counted into it. And reckoning is not pretending: God is not overlooking the fact that you are not related; he is stating what is now the case.

About this time next year I will return. Paul quotes Genesis 18:10 and 14. God put a date on his own word, in a house where the one thing that had run out was time. And the promise is not merely that a child will appear but that God will return: he does not post the miracle from a distance. The promises of God keep turning out to have God himself inside them.

Is anything too hard for the LORD? Attached to that date is the question the whole of Genesis 18 turns on (Genesis 18:14). It is a question, not an announcement: God is not asking Abraham and Sarah to ignore their age, but to add in the one who made the promise. Isaac points forward to the new birth: the children of God are born because God acts, not because nature is able (John 1:12–13). And he has done the same in you: he spoke, and a heart that could produce nothing living began to believe.

Nothing will be impossible with God. The question asked at Sarah’s tent was answered again at a door in Nazareth. When the angel told Mary she would bear a son though she had no husband, he gave her the reply of Genesis 18:14 in new words (Luke 1:37). Isaac came from a womb that was dead; Jesus from a womb that had never known a man. Both births were announced in advance. But Isaac was a child of the promise, and Jesus is the one the promise was about. Everyone counted into Abraham’s family is counted in him.

What it does not mean. Isaac is not a guarantee that God will do the particular impossible thing you have in mind: the marriage restored, the diagnosis reversed, the son home by Christmas. Sarah was given a son; plenty of faithful women in Scripture were not. Isaac establishes not a promise about your circumstances but evidence about your God: he acts where there is nothing to act with.

In everyday life. Trace your Christian life backwards: past the decision, the church you happened to walk into, the person who would not leave you alone about it, the household you were born into. Mark the point where the chain stops consisting of things you arranged. It ends somewhere you did not put yourself. And when you plan, work and strive, do it gladly, but do not mistake what your own strength produces for what only God’s word can create. The flesh did produce a son, Ishmael; what it could not produce was the one the promise had named.

My conversion was ordinary. Am I really a child of promise? Very likely, yes. Isaac’s birth was a miracle, and it still took nine months: no lightning, no voice, just a woman growing larger through a winter. So if you came to Christ with no drama at all, a friend who kept asking, a hard year, a sermon you barely remember, and one day you noticed you believed it, do not conclude you are a child of the flesh because the wiring did not show. The most supernatural birth in the Old Testament looked, from outside the tent, like an ordinary confinement. The question is not how dramatic your beginning was but whether you now trust Christ.

parallels.desc: Sarah shall have a son

verseByVerse.quote: And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac, though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad — in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls —
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chose Jacob over Esau before either was born or had done anything, so that his purpose would rest on his own call and not on their deeds. Paul’s second example removes every human reason that could be offered for the difference.

And not only so. A stronger example that closes a loophole. A reader could say the real difference between Isaac and Ishmael was Hagar. So Paul reaches for one father, one mother, one conception: twins (Genesis 25:21–26). Every variable that could be offered as the hidden reason has been removed, and the difference remains.

Though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad. Before the boys had a character or a single act to their name, the distinction was set, so God’s choice cannot have rested on their deeds. Whatever else the doctrine of election is, it is the news that the most important thing ever decided about you was settled before you were in a position to spoil it.

In order that God’s purpose of election might continue. God’s purpose is his plan (as in 8:28), carried out by his choosing, and “continue” means that it stands firm. “In order that” carries the argument: God announced his choice at the one moment when nobody could mistake what it rested on.

Not because of works but because of him who calls. The basis of election is not anything in the person but God who calls. Calling here is God’s effective summons, as in 8:30.

A frightened mother. The scene is not a seminar. Rebekah is pregnant and in pain. The children struggle together within her until she says, “If it is thus, why is this happening to me?” and goes to inquire of the LORD (Genesis 25:22). One of the most contested doctrines in the Bible arrives as an answer to a frightened woman asking why her pregnancy hurts.

Chosen in him. Paul’s fullest statement of this truth adds two words this verse leaves unspoken: “he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). Election is never a bare decision about names on a list; it is election in Christ. The Father’s first choice is his Son, “my Chosen One” (Luke 9:35; Isaiah 42:1), and every other choosing happens in him. That is why the choice could be made before the twins were born without being arbitrary, and why it stands: it rests not on Jacob, nor on you, but on the one in whom it was made, and he cannot fail. We cannot read God’s decree, but we can look at Christ and come to him.

The comfort on the underside. Turn the verse over: if nothing good you did was ever the reason, then nothing bad you do can be the disqualification. God’s choice never rested on your record, so your record cannot overturn it. That is why this doctrine, which frightens people at first hearing, has comforted so many on their deathbeds: it is the one ground of assurance that your own performance cannot erode.

What it does not mean. Not that God is arbitrary or his choice random; his reasons are hidden in his own wisdom and love (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). Not that human choices do not matter; Esau truly despised his birthright (Hebrews 12:16). And it is not a licence to sin (6:1–2): behaviour is not irrelevant, but it was never the foundation.

If election is unconditional, how can I know I am elect? Not by peering into God’s secret decree, but by looking where he has pointed you: to Christ and his promise. Do you trust Christ? Then you have been called, and those he called he predestined (8:30). Faith is the fruit of election, so the fruit tells you about the root. Peter tells believers to make their calling and election sure by growing in godliness (2 Peter 1:10), not as the ground of acceptance but as its evidence. Look first to Christ, not to yourself.

Where Christians differ: election based on foreseen faith. Arminian teachers (Christians who hold that God’s saving grace can finally be resisted) say God chose people because he foresaw that they would believe; others say election here concerns only nations or roles in history, not individual salvation. The first view deserves a straight answer, because faith is not a work, and so “not because of works” does not by itself settle it. This commentary’s view: Paul’s point excludes foreseen faith. Had God chosen Jacob because he foresaw his faith, Paul would simply say so, and the objection of verse 14 (is God unjust?) would never arise. Paul’s alternative to works is not foreseen faith but the caller, and five verses later he says it flatly: it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy (v. 16). Foreseen willing is still willing. Faith is not the cause of election but its fruit (Acts 13:48; Ephesians 2:8). And though Jacob and Esau stand at the head of nations, Paul uses them to answer a question about individual salvation: why some Jews are saved and others are not (vv. 1–6, 24, 27). This is unconditional election (Westminster Confession 3.5; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.5; Canons of Dort 1.7–10). Arminian brothers want to guard God’s fairness and the reality of human response; Paul guards both too, in his own way, in verses 14–24 and in chapter 10.

verseByVerse.quote: she was told, "The older will serve the younger." As it is written, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God freely set his covenant love on Jacob and not on Esau, reversing the expected order, as Malachi later confirmed. Esau was passed over, and the nation that came from him fell under God’s judgment for its own long record of wickedness.

The older will serve the younger. From Genesis 25:23. God reversed the normal order, in which the firstborn had the leading place (see inheritance and the firstborn). Esau was born first. This never visibly came true in the two men’s lifetimes: when they finally met, it was Jacob who bowed to the ground seven times and called his brother my lord (Genesis 33:3, 8). The oracle was fulfilled at the level of nations, centuries later, when Edom became subject to David (2 Samuel 8:14).

Jacob I loved. Malachi 1:2–3 was written more than a thousand years after Rebekah’s pregnancy, about God’s covenant love for Israel (Jacob’s descendants) and his judgment on Edom (Esau’s). Paul uses it to confirm that God’s choice of Jacob was free, sovereign love.

But Esau I hated. In Hebrew idiom, “love” and “hate” in a comparison can mean choosing one and not the other, or loving one and loving the other less. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and the next verse says Leah was hated (Genesis 29:30–31); Jesus speaks the same way of hating father and mother (Luke 14:26). So “hated” here means first of all that God did not choose Esau for covenant love.

But not merely neutral. Yet “hated” must not be softened into indifference. Malachi goes on: “I have laid waste his hill country and left his heritage to jackals of the desert” (Malachi 1:3). And the verdict lands on a real record: Edom stood at the roadside as Jerusalem burned, gloating over the ruin, cutting off the fugitives, handing over survivors (Obadiah 10–14). So verse 12 quotes what God said before the twins were born, and verse 13 his verdict, centuries later, on a nation with a long history of wickedness. Nobody should be told that God announced hatred over a foetus; that is not what the text Paul quotes says.

The man God chose. Jacob bought his brother’s birthright with a bowl of stew. He lied to his blind father’s face to steal a blessing. And when he finally had to face Esau and his four hundred men, he lined up his household in order of how much he valued them: the servant women and their children in front, Leah and hers behind them, Rachel and Joseph at the back (Genesis 33:1–2). And the brother God passed over? Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept (Genesis 33:4). If election were a reward for character, this verdict is upside down. That is exactly why Paul chose the example: no one can pretend the choice was made on merit.

A ladder for the heel-grabber. Follow the chosen man past the stolen blessing. He is running for his life from the brother he cheated, sleeping in the open with a stone for a pillow, and God does not rebuke him. He shows him a ladder set up on the earth with its top in heaven and repeats to the deceiver the promises made to Abraham (Genesis 28:12–15). Jesus says he himself is that ladder: “you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51). The love that chose Jacob was never fondness for a likeable boy, but the love that would build a way between heaven and an undeserving sinner, and the way is Christ. Twenty years on, God met Jacob in a night of wrestling, and Jacob came out of it limping and called Israel, the name this chapter is arguing about. The God of Jacob wounds and renames, and will not let his chosen go.

What if I am an Esau? Look at what actually marks Esau, because Genesis is not vague: “I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?” (Genesis 25:32), and the narrator’s summary, “Thus Esau despised his birthright” (25:34). The defining thing about him is not that he longed for God and was shut out. It is that he did not want it. He sold it for one hot meal, because the future was less interesting than his appetite. So do not ask whether you feel chosen. Ask what you actually want. A man terrified of being Esau is showing the opposite of Esau’s defining trait. Contempt is not anxious; nobody ever lay awake grieving over a birthright he despised. If you want Christ, come to him; he turns no one away (John 6:37).

Where Christians differ: individuals or nations. Some say verses 10–13 speak only of nations (Israel and Edom) and earthly roles, not eternal salvation. The case is stronger than often allowed: Genesis 25:23 says in so many words, two nations are in your womb, and Malachi means Israel and Edom, not two men. What that reading gets right is a needed corrective: Paul is arguing about how God constitutes a people, and he never hands anybody a device for sorting the individuals around him. This commentary’s view: the original prophecies did concern the nations that came from the two brothers. But Paul applies the principle to individuals and to salvation, because that is his question: why some Israelites are saved and others are not (vv. 3, 6, 22–24). Nations are made up of individuals, and Jacob and Esau themselves illustrate God’s choice of persons. Within a few verses Paul moves to two named individuals, Moses and Pharaoh, and then to “even us whom he has called” (v. 24). The objection that follows (v. 14) only makes sense if Paul is teaching unconditional individual election.
verseByVerse.note: “Hated” in Hebrew idiom can mean “loved less” or “passed over” — here, not chosen.

parallels.desc: the older shall serve the younger
I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God's part? By no means! For he says to Moses, "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is not unjust in choosing, because mercy is his to give, and no one has a claim on it. Paul answers the charge of injustice with God’s own words to Moses after the golden calf, when Israel deserved nothing but destruction.

What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? The natural objection: if God chooses one twin and not the other before either has done anything, is that not unfair? That Paul raises it strongly suggests he is teaching unconditional election, for few would accuse God of injustice for choosing those he foresaw would believe. The question is evidence that you have understood, not evidence that you are resisting.

By no means! Paul’s strongest denial (mē genoito, as in 3:4; 6:2). God cannot be unjust. Paul rejects the conclusion; he does not scorn the person who asks.

For he says to Moses. Paul answers from Exodus 33:19, a sentence that is not about justice at all but about mercy, and that switch is his argument. Injustice would mean somebody received less than he was owed. At the foot of the mountain where these words were spoken, what was owed was destruction, and everybody knew it. The question is not whether God is unjust but whether he is obliged, and the whole story, from the mountain onward, is God giving somebody far too much.

The scene at Sinai. While Moses receives the law, the people dance round a metal calf, a few months after watching the sea open (Exodus 32).
