God says he will not go up with them himself, “lest I consume you on the way” (Exodus 33:3). Moses will not accept it: “If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here” (Exodus 33:15): better no promised land than a promised land without God. Then, with the nation still smelling of the fire, he asks for something astonishing: “Please show me your glory” (Exodus 33:18).

I will have mercy on whom I have mercy. God answered, “I will make all my goodness pass before you and will proclaim before you my name” (Exodus 33:19), and then came the sentence Paul quotes. A man asks to see the glory of God, and what God shows him is not power, which had been on display for months, but his freedom to be merciful. The hardest-sounding sentence in Romans 9 is, in its own place, the definition of divine glory: mercy that answers to nothing outside itself. The sentence loops back on itself like “I AM WHO I AM” at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14): once about his being, once about his mercy, and both times nothing outside God determines it.

The glory Moses asked to see. Moses saw only the back of the glory as it passed (Exodus 33:22–23). John tells us where the rest of that request was answered: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14), full of grace and truth, the very name proclaimed on the mountain, “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). So the free mercy announced at Sinai has a face. Watch Jesus call a tax collector from his booth, or promise paradise to a dying criminal (Luke 23:39–43), and you are watching God have mercy on whom he has mercy.

Free to pay for sin himself. Everything Israel received after the golden calf was mercy, and it was never cheap. The God who proclaimed himself to Moses as merciful, and as one “who will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:7), stayed true to both when the guilty were spared: he laid their judgment on his Son. God’s freedom to have mercy is the freedom to pay for sin himself. No one can demand his mercy or exhaust it, and he has put it beyond doubt for all who come to him in Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that God has no reasons, or that he enjoys the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11); the reason for his mercy lies in himself, not in us. And nothing here entitles anyone to say to a frightened person, “Perhaps he has not chosen you.” That sentence appears nowhere in this chapter. “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy” entered the Bible as a reprieve for a nation that had earned annihilation. If you hear it as a door swinging shut, that says more about what you expect of God than about what the verse says.

Then is God fair? If fair means everyone gets what he deserves, God is perfectly fair to the lost: no one will be punished beyond his sin. But no one in heaven will be there because it was fair, only because God was merciful. Think of a judge who pays the fine of one guilty man out of his own pocket. The others have not been wronged; they received justice. The one has received a gift. Grace is not a matter of being fair, and that is the best news there is, because fairness would condemn us all.

parallels.desc: I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious

verseByVerse.quote: So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God who has mercy. For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salvation rests finally on God’s mercy, not on how much anyone wants it or strives for it. Pharaoh shows the other side: God raised him up and kept him standing so that his power and name would be made known in all the earth.

Not on human will or exertion. Literally, not of him who wills, nor of him who runs (a race): wanting it enough and trying hard enough are both excluded. Esau wanted the blessing and ran to hunt game for it (Genesis 27), but did not get it.

But on God who has mercy. We do will and run, but only because God first works in us “both to will and to work” (Philippians 2:13). What Paul denies is that willing and running are the cause. He once put both halves in one sentence: “I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own” (Philippians 3:12). The pressing on is real, and it comes second: you run because you were laid hold of.

Relief for the exhausted. If salvation depended on will and exertion, the honest question would be: how much? How much wanting is enough, how much effort clears the bar? Nobody could ever rest. Verse 16 removes a measurement no one has ever passed, and it is hard news only for the heart that would rather keep running than be carried.

For the Scripture says to Pharaoh. Now the other side: hardening. Paul writes “the Scripture says” where Exodus has God speaking: what Scripture says, God says. Read Exodus 9:15–16 whole: by now God could have put out his hand and struck Pharaoh and his people with pestilence, and they would have been cut off from the earth, but for this purpose he raised him up. So the verse explains to a man six plagues into a contest he has lost why he is still alive.

I have raised you up. God brought Pharaoh onto the stage of history and kept him standing through the plagues. His whole career was ordered by God’s purpose: not as approval of his wickedness, but as the stage on which God’s power would be displayed to the nations.

That my name might be proclaimed in all the earth. It happened. Forty years later, in Jericho, a Canaanite prostitute told two Israelite spies why she had hidden them: “we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you”, and “our hearts melted” (Joshua 2:10–11). And it saved Rahab. She and her household came out of Jericho alive, and her name stands in the first chapter of Matthew, in the genealogy of Jesus Christ. Pharaoh willed and ran harder than anyone in the story, and it moved nothing; the mercy of God reached the last person in the region anyone would have picked, by way of the hardest heart in it.

Another ruler, another purpose. The pattern returns at the centre of history. Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against God’s holy servant Jesus, and the church confessed that they did only what God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27–28). Pilate, like Pharaoh, was fully responsible in his cowardice, yet through the worst thing rulers ever did God showed his power as nowhere else. The Red Sea was the rehearsal. The empty tomb is the display of power the whole earth was meant to hear about.

If it does not depend on my will, should I just wait for God to act? No. God’s mercy does not bypass your will; it renews it. The gospel calls you to repent and believe now (Acts 17:30; 2 Corinthians 6:2), and in the next chapter Paul says that “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (10:13). If you want Christ, that desire is already the sign of God’s mercy at work. Do not sit waiting for a feeling. Call on him, read his word, go where it is preached, and pray, Lord, have mercy on me. No one who ever came to him was refused.

parallels.desc: for this purpose I have raised you up

verseByVerse.quote: So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. You will say to me then, "Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shows mercy to whom he wills and hardens whom he wills, and Paul faces honestly the objection this raises. If no one can resist God’s will, how can he still blame anyone? Paul lets the question stand at full height.

So then he has mercy on whomever he wills. The two sides of God’s sovereignty, drawn from the two quotations: mercy (Moses) and hardening (Pharaoh). They are not presented as equals: mercy is what God declares about himself (Exodus 33:19), while hardening is Paul’s conclusion from the story of Pharaoh. Scripture gives mercy the greater weight, and so does this chapter, most clearly at verses 22–23.

And he hardens whomever he wills. To harden is to make stubborn and unresponsive. Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 32) and that God hardened it (Exodus 9:12; 10:20), as God foretold before any plague (Exodus 4:21). Both are true, and the order matters: not until the sixth plague does the account say that the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart (9:12), after Pharaoh had repeatedly done it himself. God does not put evil into a good heart. He hardens by withholding the softening grace that would melt it, and by giving sinners over to the sin they already love (1:24, 26, 28). Pharaoh is Romans 1 in a single man: he freely chose his stubbornness, and God, as a judge passing sentence, handed him over to the choice he kept making.

Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will? The second objection. If God decides who is hardened, how can he blame anyone? Again, it only arises because Paul really is teaching that God decides (as at v. 14). Let it stand at full height. If God’s will cannot be resisted, and what I am is finally traceable to that will, then blaming me seems like blaming a stone for falling. Every honest reader has felt it, and Paul writes for exactly that reader: “You will say to me then.”

Paul declines to solve it. What follows in verse 20 is not a rebuttal but a question about who is asking. Paul could have distinguished what God decrees from what he permits, and does not. If you came wanting the logic resolved, you will not get it here. But declining is not evading. God did the same with Job, who asked for a hearing, got questions about the sea and the ostrich, and was satisfied, not because he received the information but because he received the one speaking. A God whose decisions you could fully audit would be a God the size of your understanding, and nobody wants that God once they are in trouble.

The chapter does not stop at the potter. Paul does eventually give a cause for Israel’s failure, and it is not a decree. It is Israel: “they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works” (v. 32). And in the next chapter God holds out his hands all day long to a disobedient and contrary people (10:21; see the note on vv. 32–33). Anyone who quotes verse 20 as though it settled the question of human responsibility has stopped reading eleven verses too early.

Jesus said it first. Jesus spoke the truth of verse 18 himself, as a prayer of joy: “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will” (Matthew 11:25–26). He rejoiced in the Father’s freedom to hide and to reveal. And in the next breath he turned to the crowd: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). No one understood the sovereignty of God better than the Son, and it did not make him sparing with his invitation. Whoever wants to know how verse 18 should sound must hear it in his voice.

In everyday life. Do not play with sin, thinking you can repent later. Repeatedly refusing God hardens the heart, and God may give you over to it: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15). Whatever is true about the eternal decree, no one has ever stood before God able to say, I wanted you and you turned me away.

Has God hardened me? If that question frightens you, look at what the fear itself shows. Pharaoh never once asked it; hardness does not lie awake wondering whether it is hard. If your struggle with sin grieves you, that grief is not hardness but the Spirit at war with the flesh in you (Galatians 5:17), and he finishes what he begins (Philippians 1:6). And the remedy was never introspection. A heart of stone is not repaired by being examined more closely but replaced, as God promised: a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:26). You do not soften your own heart; you ask God for the one thing you cannot manufacture, and he has given it to multitudes of rebels who once hardened themselves against him.

Is this not just fatalism? No. Fatalism says an impersonal force fixes the outcome whatever anyone does, so nothing you do matters. Scripture says a personal God, holy and good, rules all things and works through what people do, not around it. He ordains the end and also the means: the preacher, the prayer, the hearing, the believing (10:14–15). That is why Paul, who wrote this verse, did not shrug. He prayed for Israel (10:1), preached to them in city after city, and hoped that some would be saved (11:14). A fatalist sits still. A believer in this God gets up and prays, because the God who decides also hears.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart and that God hardened it.

verseByVerse.quote: But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, "Why have you made me like this?" Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The creature has no standing to put the Creator on trial, for God has the potter’s right over the clay. Paul does not answer the objection with a theory; he reminds the questioner who he is and who God is.

But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Paul rebukes the attitude behind the question. “O man” is the address he used at 2:1 to the reader who was enjoying chapter 1. It is not an insult but a reminder that you are a creature, having this conversation from inside the made world, not outside it. “Answer back” (antapokrinomai) means to reply against, to contradict, to talk back, as if God owed us an account. It is the posture of cross-examining, not of asking. Job learned the same lesson (Job 38–42; 40:2).

Questions are not forbidden. Paul asked two of the hardest questions himself (vv. 14, 19), and Scripture is full of hard questions put to God. Habakkuk asked how long; Jeremiah said, “Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you” (Jeremiah 12:1). So if this verse has ever been used on you to shut down an honest question, in grief or doubt, it was misused. What Paul rebukes is summoning God to the stand as a defendant and making yourself his judge.

Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?” From Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9. A clay pot has no rights against its potter: God is not answerable to his creatures.

The potter’s right. The image comes from Jeremiah 18, where the vessel spoiled in the potter’s hand was not thrown out but reworked into another (Jeremiah 18:4), and God’s application is an appeal: if a nation turns from its evil, he will relent (Jeremiah 18:7–8). That does not blunt Paul, who cites the potter for the potter’s right, and the right is real; the image can also speak of judgment, as when Jeremiah smashes a flask that can never be mended (Jeremiah 19:11). But Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9 also sit within promises of restoration, and not one of these passages shows a God who does not care.

Out of the same lump. Most Reformed interpreters take the lump as all humanity, alike sinful in Adam (5:12). From it God makes some vessels for honour (salvation) and leaves others for dishonour (judgment). The lump is not innocent clay but fallen humanity, already deserving wrath, so God wrongs no one by showing mercy to some, and the difference lies entirely in the potter’s intention, not in a better grade of clay. One caution: in a household, honourable and dishonourable use means the fine dish and the common pot; the final destinies come in verses 22–23. Elsewhere Paul uses the image and has a person cleanse himself to become a vessel for honourable use (2 Timothy 2:20–21).

God in the dock. C. S. Lewis noticed the shift in an essay of 1948. Ancient people came before God as the accused come before a judge; for modern people the roles are reversed: “He is the judge: God is in the dock.” We review restaurants and rate drivers, and it feels natural to give God one star for Romans 9. There is something honest in wanting a God whose ways can bear scrutiny. But to sit in judgment on God you would need a standard higher than God to judge him by, and a place outside his world from which to see the whole case. No creature has either.

The judge who stood in the dock. The God we summon to the dock has in fact stood in one. The Son of God stood before Pilate, made no defence (Mark 15:3–5), and accepted a sentence he had not earned, so that those who sat in judgment on him could be acquitted. The defendant we put on trial turned out to be the one taking our place.

The potter in the dust. Once in the Gospels the question of verse 20 is asked out loud, about a man born blind: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answers that it was so that the works of God might be displayed in him (John 9:2–3). Then the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3) stoops, makes clay with his own hands and gives the man his sight (9:6). The potter who formed man from the dust has taken up dust a second time, and he answers the question as the potter, with a purpose no one had guessed: mercy.

What it does not mean. Not that God is a tyrant who enjoys destruction, nor that you must be stoical: not knowing why is a real grief, and Scripture never tells you to pretend otherwise. You are not required to feel resolved. You are required not to sit in judgment on God.

Does this mean we are just pots, without dignity? No. The image is about authority, not worth: we are made in God’s image and crowned with glory and honour (Psalm 8:5). The point is the relationship: we cannot stand over God and judge him, because he made us and we did not make him. And the potter who has this right is the one who reshapes spoiled clay rather than throwing it away, and whose own Son took human clay in the incarnation. To be clay in such hands is not humiliation. It is the safest place a creature can be.

Where Christians differ: double predestination. Some say God chooses only to save, and the lost simply choose damnation without any decree. Others (hyper-Calvinists, a fringe view that most Reformed churches reject) say God creates people in order to damn them and causes their sin in the same way he causes faith. This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches that God decrees both: he elects some to life, and he passes by the rest and ordains them to wrath for their sin (Westminster Confession 3.3, 3.7; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.3 puts it more gently: the rest are left to act in their sin to their just condemnation). But the two are not symmetrical. God works faith in the elect by his Spirit; he does not work sin in the reprobate, those he passes by. The saved owe everything to grace; the lost owe their condemnation entirely to their own sin. Many believers who rejoice in grace still hesitate here, and their hesitation is a fair warning to speak of it only as Paul does. Hold the mystery with humility, as he does.

parallels.desc: shall the potter be regarded as the clay?

verseByVerse.quote: What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory —
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has patiently endured those headed for judgment so that the riches of his glory would be made known to those he has prepared for mercy. Even the display of his wrath serves the display of his mercy, and the weight of Paul’s sentence falls on mercy.

What if God. The sentence begins “What if God” and never finishes. At the hardest point in his hardest chapter Paul does not assert; he puts a question and leaves it with you. If he will not close this sentence, nobody preaching it should close it harder than he did.

Desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power. His wrath is his holy anger against sin, and his power is to be seen, as with Pharaoh (v. 17).

Has endured with much patience. Here is the phrase that ruins every caricature of this passage. The word is makrothumia, slowness to anger, the kindness that 2:4 says is meant to lead you to repentance, and it is spent on the ones headed for destruction; if the only aim were to display wrath, there would be no reason to wait. Peter uses the same word and tells you what is inside it: the Lord “is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9). Romans 9 is not describing a God in a hurry to condemn.

Vessels of wrath prepared for destruction … vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory. The first verb is passive (katērtismena), and Paul does not say who prepared them; many read it as ripe for destruction, fitted for it by their own sin. The second is active, with God as subject: he prepared them beforehand (proētoimasen), as in Ephesians 2:10. And glory is not a vague word for heaven. It is what chapter 8 promised: being glorified with Christ, made like him in body and character, and living forever in the presence of the God whose wrath we once deserved (8:17–18, 29–30).

Three differences in one sentence. Of the vessels of mercy: an active verb, God named, and a prefix meaning beforehand. Of the vessels of wrath: none of the three. Paul could have made the halves match. Do not claim more than that: a passive with no stated agent can still have God’s decree behind it, as careful readers in this tradition have said. But to present election and reprobation as identical acts, worked the same way by the same hand, is more symmetrical than the apostle and the Reformed confessions (see this commentary’s view at vv. 20–21). God is the author of salvation, not of sin. And the weight of the sentence falls on verse 23, on riches, glory and mercy: wrath is what God is said to endure; mercy is what he is said to prepare.

But why would God want his wrath to be seen? A fair question. Five reasons, from this passage and the rest of Scripture.

First, because it is true of him. God’s glory is God made known as he really is. When he showed Moses his glory, he named himself merciful and gracious, abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity, and also one “who will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:6–7). A God who hid his justice would be hiding himself, and a God who did nothing about evil would not be good: we would not call a judge good who let a child abuser walk free.

Second, because evil must not have the last word. The plagues that showed God’s power were also the rescue of Pharaoh’s slaves. The cry of every victim, how long, O Lord? (Revelation 6:10; Psalm 94:3), is answered by God’s wrath. His judgment tells the world that cruelty and injustice will not win.

Third, so that his name would reach the nations. God raised Pharaoh up so that his name would be proclaimed in all the earth (v. 17), and the report of the Red Sea reached Jericho and saved Rahab (see the note on vv. 16–17).

Fourth, so that mercy is seen as mercy. This is Paul’s own answer: “in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy” (v. 23). Mercy only means something where judgment is deserved, and the saved see the riches of grace in what they were saved from: we “were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. But God, being rich in mercy” (Ephesians 2:3–4). The one who is forgiven much loves much (Luke 7:47).

Fifth and supremely, at the cross. The place where God shows both his wrath and his mercy most fully is Calvary. God put Christ forward as a propitiation, to show his righteousness, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (3:26). Propitiation means that God’s own Son stands where the sinner stood and bears the anger the sinner deserved, so that none is left. There wrath against sin is fully shown, and fully borne, by the Son, for the vessels of mercy.

You were inside the waiting. God’s patience with the vessels of wrath gives time for mercy to reach the vessels of mercy, and every Christian was on the wrong side of that sentence for a while. The waiting was not happening around you while you stood safely elsewhere. You were inside it. The delay people demand an explanation for is the delay they were saved during.

What this does not mean. Not that God enjoys destroying: “As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (Ezekiel 33:11). Not that his wrath is a loss of temper; it is his settled, holy opposition to evil. Nor that God shows his glory out of vanity. For us, living for our own glory is pride, because we are not the greatest good; God is, so making himself known is the best thing he can give his creatures. He tells us enough to trust him, and calls us to humility where we cannot see further (v. 20; 11:33–36).

In everyday life. Work out roughly how long it was between the first thing you did that you knew was wrong and the day you came to Christ. Whatever the number, that interval is much patience, measured from the inside. You lived in it for years and were not consumed: that is not a theory but your own history. So when someone tries your patience today, remember how long God endured you.

Could the person I love be a vessel of wrath? You cannot know, and you are not asked to. The categories are not visible, and the patience described here has not run out, for the person you have given up on or for you. Paul was once a persecutor who looked for all the world like a vessel of wrath, and God showed him mercy to display Christ’s perfect patience as an example (1 Timothy 1:16). While it is called today (Hebrews 3:13), the invitation stands. Your task is not to sort people but to pray for them and tell them about Christ.

Uncertain wording. Two things in verse 22 are hard to pin down. “Desiring” can be read as “because he desired” (his patience serves the display of his wrath and power) or “although he desired” (his patience holds back wrath he could rightly show at once). Many favour “because”, but either way the patience is real and the sentence moves towards the mercy of verse 23. And the sentence has no main clause; the likely sense is: what if God has done this, who are you to object? That answers verse 20.

verseByVerse.quote: even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vessels of mercy are not an abstract category but us: the people God has actually called, out of both Jews and Gentiles. No one is carried into God’s people by belonging to a group; Jew and Gentile alike are simply called.

Even us. For twenty verses everything has been in the third person: Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Moses, Pharaoh, a potter, two vessels. Then, without warning, Paul writes us, like a hand on the shoulder. The vessels of mercy prepared beforehand for glory are the people in the room where this letter is being read aloud.

Whom he has called. God’s effectual call (8:30) is not only an invitation but a summons that brings the person: God speaks through the gospel, and his Spirit gives the hearer life to answer (John 6:44; 1 Thessalonians 1:5). The verb runs under the whole passage: “named” in verse 7 is in Greek “called”, then “him who calls” (v. 11) and “called ‘sons of the living God’” (v. 26). That matters, because you cannot observe an eternal decree, and staring at it has driven serious people to despair. But a call is a thing that happens in time, to a person, at an address. It leaves marks.

Not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles. God’s purpose never was to save every Jew, but to call out a people from Jews and Gentiles alike, as he promised Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3); the Gentiles are not a fallback plan. Notice the preposition: called out of the Jews and out of the Gentiles, so neither group is summoned wholesale. The narrowing of verse 6 runs inside the Gentile world as well. Any Gentile Christian reading this chapter with quiet satisfaction about Israel has just been included in its terms, and Paul will tell him to his face: “do not be arrogant toward the branches” (11:18).

A church with a seam down the middle. The letter went to Jewish believers expelled from Rome under Claudius who had come back (Acts 18:2; compare Romans 16:3), and Gentile believers who had, it seems, kept the church going in their absence (see the introduction). Into that room Paul sends a sentence that gives neither group first place: both were simply called. Election is the one thing that can settle an argument about who ranks where. The chapter began with a man weeping because his own people would not come; it ends its argument by naming the people who did, a mixed, quarrelling congregation in the capital of the empire that would one day kill him, called out of both halves of a divided world by the God who has been doing this since Isaac.

One new man. What joins the two halves of that church is not a treaty but a person. Paul says it to another mixed congregation: Christ “himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility”, that he might “create in himself one new man in place of the two” (Ephesians 2:14–15). Jew and Gentile are not merged into a compromise; each is brought to the same cross and risen Lord, and finds the other already there. The us is Christ’s body.

In everyday life. Did you count yourself in the word us? Romans 9 is easily read from the gallery, weighing God’s conduct; Paul wrote it as a member. If the chapter has felt like a court case you are watching rather than a mercy you are inside, this verse puts you inside it. And the same call seated beside you the people in your church you find hardest to sit beside.

How do I know if I have been called? Look not for a voice but for a summons you have answered. God’s effectual call comes through the gospel: you heard the message about Christ, and something in you, against your old inclinations, found it true and came to him (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). If you now trust Christ, want to know him, and find yourself, however unevenly, turning from sin, those are the marks of the call, whether it came suddenly or gradually. If you are unsure, do not stare at yourself. Answer the call now, and keep answering it.

verseByVerse.quote: As indeed he says in Hosea, "Those who were not my people I will call 'my people,' and her who was not beloved I will call 'beloved.'" "And in the very place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' there they will be called 'sons of the living God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promised through Hosea to make a people out of those who were not his people, and he is doing it as he calls the Gentiles. Grace takes the “not” off the names of the rejected and makes outsiders the sons of the living God.

As indeed he says in Hosea. Paul now shows that the Old Testament foretold both the calling of Gentiles (vv. 25–26) and the saving of only a remnant of Israel (vv. 27–29). He quotes Hosea 2:23 and 1:10, and he is quoting the names of a man’s children.

Lo-ammi. God told Hosea to marry a woman who would be unfaithful to him, and she was. They had three children, and God named them. The second was a daughter, Lo-ruhamah, No Mercy, or not loved. The third was a son, Lo-ammi, Not My People (Hosea 1:6, 9). The sermon was his family. So when Paul quotes “her who was not beloved I will call ‘beloved’”, he is quoting a little girl’s name being taken off her. God does not hand out replacement names; the lo, the “not”, comes off. If mercy can reach that house, the question of whether it can reach Rome, or you, is already settled.

How Paul uses Hosea. Hosea spoke of the northern tribes of Israel, who by their idolatry had become like pagans; Paul applies the words to Gentiles. This is not misuse. Israel had become like the nations, and the principle is the same: God can make a people out of those who are not a people, by sheer grace. Peter applies the same words to his readers, many of them probably Gentile believers: “Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people” (1 Peter 2:10).

In the very place. Grace reaches outsiders not somewhere new where the story is not known, but at the same address where the disowning was announced. And the promise climbs higher than my people. Hosea says “sons of the living God”: not merely readmitted, but family. The God whose sons they are is the living one, over against the dead idols they had left him for.

What did the renaming cost? Everything, and Hosea shows it. God sent him back to buy his wife out of what she had sold herself into, and Scripture records the price, down to the barley (Hosea 3:2). That is the shape of every renaming God does: somebody goes and pays for the one who left. The final price was paid by Christ, the beloved Son, who on the cross was forsaken and treated as an outcast, so that those who were not God’s people could be called sons of the living God (Galatians 4:4–5). Your new name is free to you because it was not free to him.

In everyday life. You may carry a name for yourself that surfaces when the house is quiet, often one of these two: not wanted, or not forgiven. Put beside it the name God gives everyone in Christ: beloved, my people, a child of the living God. Do not argue that the old name was never true. Agree that it was, and that God has taken the not off it. Then live today under the new name, among the very people who knew the old one.
verseByVerse.note: Hosea spoke of the northern tribes of Israel; Paul applies the words to the Gentiles too.

parallels.desc: I will say to Not My People, “You are my people”

verseByVerse.quote: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: "Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved, for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah foretold that out of all Israel’s multitude only a remnant would be saved, so Israel’s widespread unbelief is God’s word coming true, not failing. The remnant is not marked by being better but by returning to God, kept by his grace.

Isaiah cries out concerning Israel. The word is a shout: a man raising his voice about his own nation. Paul quotes Isaiah 10:22–23, mainly from the Greek translation, though his opening words, the number of the sons of Israel, are borrowed from Hosea 1:10, the verse he has just quoted.

As the sand of the sea. An echo of God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17). The multitude promised to Abraham was not cancelled; it was never going to arrive by descent. Paul goes on to speak of a future fullness for Israel (11:12, 25–26), so this verse is not his last word on it.

Only a remnant of them will be saved. A small number preserved through judgment: in Isaiah, those who would come through the Assyrian disaster and return to God. The principle runs from Noah to Elijah’s seven thousand (11:4), so the unbelief of most Jews is no surprise; the prophets foretold it. And read the sentence just before the one Paul quotes, because it defines the remnant: “A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God” (Isaiah 10:21). The remnant is not defined by having survived but by having returned to God.

A boy named Remnant. Isaiah had a son called Shear-jashub, which means a remnant shall return (Isaiah 7:3). Hosea’s children were the judgment; Isaiah’s son was the hope, and his name cut both ways. With the stress on one word, only a remnant: that is the threat. With the stress on the other, a remnant shall return: that is the promise. To a man secure in his numbers and his ancestry, the word is only. To a man who has counted the faithful and thinks he has reached the end of them, the word is a remnant: there is one.

For the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay. God will bring his word to completion and will not let it drag. There is mercy even in that: God does not leave a people suspended for centuries in a judgment that never arrives and never lifts.

In the flow. Verses 25–29 take up the two halves of verse 24 in reverse order: Hosea speaks of outsiders brought in, Isaiah of Israel narrowed to a remnant. So the unbelief of many Jews is not God’s word failing (v. 6) but coming true.

The mighty God. That title is not chosen at random. The remnant returns to the mighty God, and a chapter earlier Isaiah gave the same Hebrew name to a child: “For to us a child is born, to us a son is given”, and “his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6). The God to whom the remnant returns is the God who would be born a son of David. So the remnant has a head. Christ is the true and faithful Israel (Isaiah 49:3), who went through judgment and came out of the grave, and everyone who returns to God returns through him.

What it does not mean. Not that the remnant were saved because they were better: it is “a remnant, chosen by grace” (11:5). Remnant language is the natural vocabulary of every small, self-congratulating group that thinks everyone else has compromised. Isaiah’s remnant are survivors of a catastrophe, whose only distinction is that God kept them. The moment remnant becomes a compliment you pay yourself, it has stopped describing you.

Our church is small. Does that mean we are the faithful remnant? Not necessarily, and the question can be a trap. Size proves nothing either way: large churches can be faithful and small ones proud. A small congregation preaching Christ faithfully may take comfort that God has often worked through few, but it must never become a badge. The remnant is marked not by smallness but by returning to God, by grace alone. Be faithful, pray for growth, and leave the counting to God.

Uncertain wording. The Greek of the last line is genuinely difficult: literally, the Lord “completing and cutting short” a word upon the earth. Most take it, as the ESV does, to mean that God will carry out his sentence fully and swiftly; some hear in “cutting short” Israel cut down to a remnant. Either way, his word will be done.

Textual note. The KJV, following later manuscripts, has a longer form of the verse; the earliest have the shorter one that most modern Bibles print.

parallels.desc: only a remnant will return

verseByVerse.quote: And as Isaiah predicted, "If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God had not left Israel a seed, they would have been wiped out like Sodom; that anyone is left at all is his mercy. Isaiah’s words close the section by turning the question round: not why so few, but why anyone.

And as Isaiah predicted. Paul quotes Isaiah 1:9, the final scriptural witness of the section.

If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring. The Lord of hosts is the Lord of the armies of heaven. The sentence is not a lament about how few were kept. Everything up to here has pressed a question about the people passed over; Isaiah asks the rarer one: why is there anybody here at all? He is standing in the wreckage, one of the survivors, saying we should not be here.

Offspring. Seed (sperma): the verse turns on the word. A remnant is what is left over; a seed is put into the ground on purpose. Isaiah is not saying God salvaged a few but that he planted, and Paul closes the section on a word that means a future.

We would have been like Sodom. The cities were wiped out for their sin (Genesis 19), and Israel deserved the same. One verse further Isaiah says: “Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom! Give ear to the teaching of our God, you people of Gomorrah!” (Isaiah 1:10). He calls Jerusalem, temple and all, Sodom to its face. So on his own account the difference between them was not the behaviour, but that one had seed left in it and the other did not: ten righteous men could not be found in Sodom, and Lot was pulled out by the hand. Sodom is what a place looks like when nothing has been kept back: no seed, no next generation, no morning after.

A shoot from the stump. Isaiah keeps returning to this picture. When the land is burned and felled like an oak, “the holy seed is its stump” (Isaiah 6:13), and out of a stump comes the hope: “There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit” (Isaiah 11:1). The seed God left in Jerusalem was not kept for its own sake. It was kept because the Messiah had to come from somewhere, and God would not let the line be cut off before he came. The survivors of Isaiah 1:9 were the soil in which that shoot would one day grow.

In everyday life. Finish Isaiah’s sentence about yourself: If the Lord of hosts had not left me ______, I would have been ______. A friend who would not give up on you. A conscience that would not settle. An illness that stopped you just before the irreparable thing. Left to ourselves we count what we lack; Isaiah counts what he was spared, as someone who knows what he escaped.

Does this mean the church today is only kept alive by God? Yes, and that is a comfort, not a threat. Every generation of believers exists because the Lord of hosts has left a seed. The church has survived persecution, heresy and its own failures because Christ said he would build it and the gates of hell would not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18). When churches shrink or a nation turns from God, do not despair as though the gospel were dying out: God has never let his seed be wiped out. Pray, and keep sowing.

parallels.desc: if the LORD of hosts had not left us a few survivors

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–33 — The Stumbling Stone: Israel's Pursuit and Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s fall lies at Israel’s own door: they sought righteousness by works and stumbled over Christ. Gentiles who were not pursuing righteousness received it by faith, while Israel pursued the law and did not reach it, because they chased it as if it were based on works (vv. 30–32). They tripped over the stone God laid in Zion, which is Christ, the same stone on which whoever believes will never be put to shame (vv. 32–33). Their problem was not a lack of zeal (10:2) but its direction: a righteousness of their own instead of God’s.
verseByVerse.theology:
The stone and the two ways

The stone of Romans 9:33 is one of the New Testament’s central pictures of Christ (1 Peter 2:6–8; Matthew 21:42–44). On the one stone as foundation and stumbling block, see the note on vv. 32–33. The gospel is never neutral: to one it is a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life (2 Corinthians 2:16).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel’s pursuit of righteousness by works was not insincere; it was zealous and disciplined. Now: Misdirected zeal can be harder to reach than apathy (see the note on vv. 30–31); yet the stone is laid for the devout too, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame (v. 33).

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith; but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentiles who were not seeking righteousness have received it by faith, while Israel, who pursued it through the law, missed it. The race was won by people who never entered it, because righteousness is a gift received, not a prize earned.

What shall we say, then? Paul now turns from God’s sovereignty to human responsibility. Both are true: election explains why some believe; unbelief explains why others are lost. This section runs to the end of chapter 10.

Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it. A paradox. Pursue is a hunting or racing word; attain is to overtake and lay hold of. The Gentiles were not chasing a right standing with God, yet they caught it. The people at the finish never entered the race; they were somewhere else entirely, doing the things chapter 1 described.

That is, a righteousness that is by faith. The righteousness of chapters 3–4: God’s gift of a right standing, received by faith in Christ, which is the only way anyone has ever received it.

Did not succeed in reaching that law. The ones who tried hardest ran on the wrong track. Paul does not say Israel pursued righteousness and failed to reach righteousness. He says they pursued a law and did not reach that law. The people who studied it and died rather than break it did not get to the law, because the law was leading to a person, and they treated it as a list of requirements to complete. Paul will say it outright in a few verses: “Christ is the end of the law” (10:4).

Not a lack of zeal. The diagnosis is never insincerity: they have “a zeal for God” (10:2). Misdirected zeal is harder to reach than apathy. The indifferent man has nothing invested. The devout man has forty years invested, and every one of those years argues against the one thing being asked of him. It is often the person who has not missed a Sunday in fifty years who finds grace impossible, because to receive righteousness as a gift he has to agree that the fifty years bought him nothing.

A runner who stopped. Paul is describing his own life. He had been the fastest man on Israel’s track: circumcised on the eighth day, a Pharisee, “as to righteousness under the law, blameless” (Philippians 3:5–6). Then he met the risen Christ, counted the whole race as loss, and wanted only to be found in him, “not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith” (Philippians 3:9). That is the righteousness by faith of this verse: not a better technique but a person, Christ himself, who became our righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30). He ran the course without a stumble, and his obedience is counted to outsiders who never entered and to exhausted runners who never finished, the moment they stop running for it and receive it.

How can I tell if I am pursuing righteousness by works? Ask what you are resting on when you come to God. If your confidence before him rises after a good week and collapses after a bad one, you are probably trusting your performance. If you think God owes you something for your faithfulness, or you look down on less disciplined Christians, the same root is showing. Faith rests on Christ’s righteousness, credited to you, which does not change with your week, and that frees you to obey out of gratitude rather than fear. The remedy is not to try less but to look away from yourself to Christ every day.

Uncertain wording. Literally Israel was pursuing “a law of righteousness” and did not attain to law. The ESV reads the compressed phrase as the law viewed as the way to righteousness; others take “law” loosely, as a principle or standard. Most likely Israel pursued the law of Moses as the path to a right standing with God, and never arrived at what the law was pointing to.

verseByVerse.quote: Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written, "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel fell because they sought righteousness by works and not by faith, and so they stumbled over Christ, the stone God laid in Zion. Yet the same stone is a sure foundation: whoever believes in him will never be put to shame.

Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. Israel pursued the law like a runner chasing a prize won by effort, rather than receiving God’s promise by faith. “As if”: works were never the true way; even in the Old Testament people were justified by faith (4:1–8). And notice the first word. Paul asks for a reason, and the reason is not the potter, nor the hidden will of God. It lies squarely in Israel. Twelve verses ago he refused to answer the question of fault by argument, and that refusal stands, but it was not his last word: here he names a cause for Israel’s fall, and the cause is what Israel did.

They have stumbled over the stumbling stone. The stone is Christ. A crucified Messiah offended them (1 Corinthians 1:23). He tells them their works cannot save; that is the offence. And Deuteronomy 21:23 says that a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God, so a crucified Messiah was a contradiction in terms.

As it is written. Paul combines Isaiah 28:16 (a tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion) with Isaiah 8:14 (a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling), as Peter does (1 Peter 2:6–8). The same stone is a foundation for those who trust it and a stumbling block for those who do not. The difference is not in the masonry but in the approach: come to it as a threshold and it holds you up; come at it in the dark, looking elsewhere, and it takes your feet from under you. It was placed deliberately in Zion, where nobody could get in without meeting it. The builders could not see a use for it and threw it aside (Psalm 118:22). It is holding up everything.

The curse that saves. At verse 3 Paul wished he could be accursed and cut off for his people, and could not. The stone they tripped over is the one person who could do what Paul wanted to do, and did it. The curse he bore on the cross, which made him unthinkable to them as Messiah, is the very thing that saves.

And whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. Not put to shame means never disappointed or disgraced at the judgment. “Whoever” opens the door to anyone, Jew or Gentile, and leads into chapter 10: “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (10:13). After nearly thirty verses of narrowing, this is the widest sentence in the chapter, asking for no lineage and no proof of having been chosen; it is the one sentence in Romans 9 a frightened reader can act on directly, and Paul has deliberately put it last. Shame, the word of 1:16, is the very thing this stone takes away. Paul ends one of the most uncompromising passages on election in the Bible by throwing the door open and standing back.

In everyday life. Name your stone: the thing about Christ you have to get past rather than merely accept. His exclusive claim, the wrath in chapter 1, the cross itself, or the requirement to arrive with nothing in your hands after a lifetime of being competent. It was laid as the foundation, not as an obstruction to edge around. The thing you are stumbling over is not in front of the door. It is the door.

If God chooses, can I be sure the invitation is really for me? Yes. The promise says whoever believes, and God does not make offers he does not mean. You are never asked to find out first whether you are elect; you are asked to believe, and in believing you discover that you were chosen. Jesus said that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). Election is the reason anyone comes, not a barrier at the door. If you want Christ, nothing in God’s decree stands between you and him. Come, and you will not be put to shame.

Where Christians differ: sovereignty and responsibility. Some think that if God elects, human responsibility vanishes; others think that if humans are responsible, God cannot be fully sovereign. This commentary’s view: Paul holds both in the same chapter without apology. Israel’s unbelief is truly their fault (vv. 30–33; 10:21), and salvation is truly God’s sovereign mercy (vv. 6–24). We cannot fully reconcile them in our minds, but Scripture teaches both, and so must we (Westminster Confession 3.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1; Acts 2:23). Sovereign mercy is why anyone is in. Unbelief is why anyone is out. A reader who can only carry one of them will misrepresent Paul whichever one he keeps.

parallels.desc: a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone
a stone of offence

9.text: <sup>1</sup>I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit—<sup>2</sup>that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.<sup>3</sup>For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.<sup>4</sup>They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.<sup>5</sup>To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.<sup>6</sup>But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel,<sup>7</sup>and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”<sup>8</sup>This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.<sup>9</sup>For this is what the promise said: “About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son.”<sup>10</sup>And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac,<sup>11</sup>though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls—<sup>12</sup>she was told, “The older will serve the younger.”<sup>13</sup>As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”<sup>14</sup>What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means!<sup>15</sup>For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”<sup>16</sup>So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.<sup>17</sup>For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”<sup>18</sup>So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.<sup>19</sup>You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”<sup>20</sup>But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?”<sup>21</sup>Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?<sup>22</sup>What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction,<sup>23</sup>in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory—<sup>24</sup>even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?<sup>25</sup>As indeed he says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ’my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ’beloved.’”<sup>26</sup>“And in the very place where it was said to them, ’You are not my people,’ there they will be called ’sons of the living God.’”<sup>27</sup>And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved,<sup>28</sup>for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay.”<sup>29</sup>And as Isaiah predicted, “If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah.”<sup>30</sup>What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith;<sup>31</sup>but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.<sup>32</sup>Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone,<sup>33</sup>as it is written, “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

10.title: Faith Comes by Hearing
10.overview:
Where we are. Romans 9–11 asks whether God’s word to Israel has failed (see the introduction). Chapter 9 answered from God’s free choice of mercy and ended with Israel stumbling over the stone laid in Zion (9:30–33). Chapter 10 looks at the same unbelief from the human side, before chapter 11 shows that God has not rejected his people.

The message. God’s righteousness is not a summit to be climbed but a gift brought near. Christ has come down from heaven and been raised from the dead, so that everyone, Jew or Gentile, who believes in him and calls on him as Lord will be saved. Israel stumbled not for lack of zeal but by refusing to receive that gift on God’s terms; and God, who sends preachers so that people may hear, still holds out his hands to them.

Why it was said. Paul was charged with abandoning Israel, and Gentile believers in Rome were tempted to look down on the Jewish people who had not believed (see the introduction). Paul answers both. He prays for Israel as a grieving brother, holds Israel responsible without contempt, and shows that the Gentiles were brought in not as the better party but as the people nobody counted.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul opens with prayer and a diagnosis: zeal without knowledge, a righteousness of their own set up against the righteousness God gives, which Christ has brought to its end (vv. 1–4). Then he sets Moses beside Moses. The law says do and live (v. 5), but the righteousness of faith says that no one need climb to heaven or go down to the dead, because Christ has done both: the word is near (vv. 6–8). That near word is believed in the heart and confessed with the mouth, “Jesus is Lord” (vv. 9–10), and the promise is for everyone, with no distinction (vv. 11–13). A chain then runs backwards from calling to believing, hearing, preaching and sending (vv. 14–15). Israel had every link but one: they heard, and did not obey (vv. 16–18), as their own Scriptures foretold (vv. 19–20). The chapter ends with God’s hands held out all day long (v. 21).

Where it leads. Christ is the end of the law for righteousness (v. 4), the Lord who came down and was raised (vv. 6–9), and the bearer of the divine name on whom anyone may call (v. 13): in the quietest of clauses Paul gives Jesus the name a synagogue reader would not even pronounce. And the hands held out all day long point at last to the hands stretched out on a cross, for the very people who were refusing him.

For us. If you are trying to climb up to God, stop: he has come down. If you fear you have sunk too far for him, he has been lower still, and come back. Call on him today. Then ask who first carried this word to you, and who is waiting to hear it from you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Righteousness for All Who Call: The Nearness of the Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s righteousness is a gift brought near in Christ, and it is for everyone who calls on him. Paul begins as a grieving brother, praying for an Israel whose zeal for God was sincere but uninformed (vv. 1–2). They tried to set up a righteousness of their own instead of submitting to the one God gives, and Christ is the end of that attempt (vv. 3–4). Reading Moses in Deuteronomy 30, Paul shows that no one need climb to heaven or go down to the dead: the word about Christ is near, believed in the heart and confessed with the mouth (vv. 5–10). And “everyone” rings through verses 11–13: the gospel shuts out no nation and no class of person.
verseByVerse.theology:
The confession of lordship

Romans 10:9 makes the confession “Jesus is Lord” the central act of Christian profession. Every true confession of Christ declares a transfer of final allegiance (on Caesar’s title, see the note on vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses spoke of the nearness of God’s word (Deuteronomy 30) on the plains of Moab, just before Israel entered the land; Paul applies it to the gospel, a near word proclaimed by the apostles and received by faith. Now: Romans 10:9 is a standing rebuke to every complicated scheme of salvation. It requires no theology degree, record of achievement or elaborate ritual, only the honest confession of a changed allegiance and real faith in the risen Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul longs and prays for Israel to be saved, because their zeal for God, though sincere, does not rest on a true understanding of him. He writes not as a detached critic of their failure but as a grieving brother who once shared it.

Prayer after doctrine. Chapter 9 ended with a nation tripping over the stone laid in Zion, and the very next thing Paul does is pray for them. Grief at 9:2–3, doctrine through 9:6–29, prayer here, and by 11:23 hope: one man, and no contradiction between them.

Heart’s desire. The word (eudokia) means good pleasure, delight, the thing you would choose if you could have whatever you wanted; it is used of God’s own good pleasure (Ephesians 1:5, 9). The outcome Paul would pick above every other is not that these people should be proved wrong, which was well within his powers, but that they should be saved. He asks his brothers, by now probably mostly Gentile, to care about Israel by opening his own heart rather than by issuing an instruction. His warning not to be arrogant toward the broken branches (11:18) starts here.

I bear them witness. Courtroom language: Paul appears for the defence. He was once extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers (Galatians 1:14), and listed among his credentials, “as to zeal, a persecutor of the church” (Philippians 3:6; Acts 22:3–4). So he is describing his own younger self, and that keeps the verse from contempt: he is not a healthy man diagnosing a disease he never had, but a survivor of it, who remembers exactly how right it felt.

Not according to knowledge. Knowledge here is true, full understanding, and the verse is genuinely frightening: it is possible to be sincere, disciplined, costly, lifelong and wrong. Israel’s zeal was not a pose; it produced martyrs. Nor was Paul’s: it had him guarding the coats at Stephen’s stoning (Acts 7:58) and carrying arrest warrants to Damascus (Acts 9:1–2).

Tears learned from the Lord of Israel. Paul caught this prayer from the Lord he now serves. Jesus came to his own people and they did not receive him (John 1:11), and he answered with tears, not contempt. He wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–42), and from the cross he prayed for the men who put him there: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34; some early manuscripts of Luke lack this prayer, but many others have it and most Bibles print it). At 9:3 Paul could only wish himself cut off for his people. Christ did more than wish it: he became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and he always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). Every prayer for an unbelieving Israel is an echo of his.

“As long as you’re sincere.” It may be the most widely held article of faith in the modern West: what matters is not what you believe but how genuinely you believe it. In a society that cannot agree on what is true, sincerity looks like the one thing we can all assess. But nobody lives by it where it counts. No one boards a plane because the pilot sincerely trusts his instruments, or takes a medicine because its maker meant well. And the worst harms in history have been done less by cynics than by people utterly sure of their cause, the zeal Paul once had. Yet the gospel does not answer the cult of sincerity by crowning correct opinions instead. It sets both aside as grounds for acceptance. The most devout man in Jerusalem and the most careless pagan in Corinth come in by the same door, clothed in someone else’s righteousness (v. 4). That is the one truth that can humble the zealot without making the rest of us smug.

What it does not mean. Not that zeal is wrong, nor that sincere people are saved by their sincerity; they can be lost if they reject God’s way of righteousness. Nor does it license contempt for people of other convictions; Paul credits their zeal and wants them saved, not defeated. And the remedy for zeal without knowledge has never been knowledge without zeal. Nobody argued Paul out of his. He was stopped on a road and shown, in person, the one he had been so zealous against. Zeal without knowledge is cured by meeting the one you were serving so badly.

In everyday life. You already know you are sincere. The better question: when did you last change your mind about something in your faith because Scripture required it and not because it suited you? Zeal that is according to knowledge can be corrected, because it answers to something outside itself. Zeal without knowledge has no way of revising itself; it can only grow warmer.

If God has already chosen, why should I pray for someone’s salvation? Because God has chosen to work through prayer, and he commands it (1 Timothy 2:1–4). Election is God’s purpose; prayer, like preaching, is one of the means by which he carries it out. You do not know whom God has chosen, so you pray for everyone you love, as Paul did for a people who had rejected the gospel. And election makes such prayer hopeful: if salvation depended on the sinner’s will, praying for a hardened heart would be useless, but it depends on God, who can open any heart.

How do I pray for someone to be saved? Begin with the heart: ask God for his own desire for them, because prayer kept up only as duty soon stops. Then pray for what Scripture says must happen. Pray that God will open their eyes, since “the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 4:4). Pray that he will give them a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26) and draw them to his Son (John 6:44). Pray that someone will tell them the gospel, and that you will be ready if it is you (vv. 14–15). Pray for the means he often uses: a friendship, a hard providence, a sermon that lands. And keep naming them, for years if need be. You are not wearing down a reluctant God. You are asking the God who “did not spare his own Son” (8:32) to do for them what he once did for you, when you were the one being prayed for.

verseByVerse.quote: For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel tried to build a righteousness of its own instead of receiving the righteousness God gives, and Christ has brought that whole attempt to its end for everyone who believes. He is the goal the law was always pointing to, and so the end of law-keeping as a way to be right with God.

Ignorant. Not ignorant that God is righteous, but of the righteousness God gives, the gift of right standing revealed in the gospel (1:17; 3:21–22): God himself provides the righteousness he demands. Paul’s diagnosis comes in three verbs, in order: they were ignorant, they sought to establish, they did not submit. Ignorant is the mildest and the most surprising, for this was a people steeped in the Scriptures, read aloud to them every Sabbath (Acts 15:21), and had been entrusted with the oracles of God (3:2). It means not stupidity but failing to recognise what was in front of them.

To establish their own. Establish means set up, make stand, like a monument: a record of law-keeping they hoped would stand before God (Philippians 3:9). Set it against the last verb, submit, to place yourself underneath. One man puts up a structure with his own name on it; the other gets under something somebody else built. You cannot do both at once, and what stops the second is less a failure of understanding than pride: he has spent thirty years on the first, it is nearly finished, and he cannot admit it counts for nothing.

What it looks like from inside. Picture the man. He tithes, has never been unfaithful to his wife, looks after his mother, keeps his word, gives to people in need, and has not missed a service in eleven years, all genuinely good. Ask him what stands between him and God and he will not sneer at grace; he will simply begin, somewhere in his answer, to describe himself. That is what establishing your own righteousness looks like from the inside. It does not feel like arrogance. It feels like diligence.

The end of the law. End (telos) can mean the termination, or the goal and fulfilment. The picture that holds both is a finishing tape. It ends the race, so that nobody runs on past it, and it is also the whole reason the race was run.

For righteousness. The qualifier keeps this from becoming lawlessness: the end of the law for righteousness. What has ended is the law as the route to a right standing, not the law as God’s word. Nobody is being told to stop reading Leviticus, only to stop trying to climb it. Paul has already ruled out the other reading: “Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law” (3:31).

He ran the course. Christ did not merely stand at the tape. Born under the law (Galatians 4:4), he kept every command Israel had broken, became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:8), and at the finish bore the curse the law pronounces on those who fail it (Galatians 3:13). That is why he can be the law’s end for others: he is the only one who ever reached it.

In everyday life. Finish this sentence: I have had a good week with God if I have ______. If the answer is a list, prayed more, read more, not lost my temper on Wednesday, that list is scaffolding, the sign of a man still building his own righteousness, and the habit survives in people whose doctrine of grace is entirely correct. Christ is your righteousness. He kept the law perfectly in your place, and his obedience is counted as yours (5:19), so a bad Wednesday does not undo your standing. Let this week’s obedience, worked in you by his Spirit, be thanks, not construction.

If I am not saved by keeping the law, why should I try to obey? Because obedience is now the fruit of salvation, not its price. You do not obey in order to be accepted; you obey because you have been accepted, out of love for the one who saved you (John 14:15). The law shows a believer what love looks like, and the Spirit gives the desire and power to walk in it (8:4). God’s commands are the instructions of a wise Father, not the hoops of a suspicious examiner, and a justified person who does not care to obey has not understood what he has been given (6:1–2).

Where Christians differ: end or goal. Some take telos to mean that the law is entirely finished for Christians, with no ongoing role. Others take it to mean only that the law pointed to Christ. This commentary’s view: Both senses are present and belong together. Christ is the goal the law aimed at: its sacrifices, promises and demands all pointed to him (3:21; Galatians 3:24). And so he is the end of the law as a way to gain righteousness: for everyone who believes, the attempt to be justified by law-keeping is over. But the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains the rule of life for the believer, fulfilled by those who walk by the Spirit (8:4; 13:8–10; Westminster Confession 19.5–6; 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.5–6). This is often called the third use of the law: not a ladder up to God but a guide for those already brought home. Some faithful Christians prefer to call the law of Christ, rather than the Ten Commandments as such, the believer’s rule, and they too hold that grace produces glad obedience.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 4 can also be read “Christ is the end of the law, that everyone who believes may be justified.” “End” can mean goal as well as termination.

verseByVerse.quote: For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them. But the righteousness based on faith says, "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'" (that is, to bring Christ down)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses describes two ways of righteousness: the law’s promise of life to the one who keeps it, which no sinner can meet, and the word of faith, which forbids us to think we must climb to heaven to fetch Christ down. He has already come.

Do, and live. Leviticus 18:5, which Paul also quotes in Galatians 3:12, states the principle of law: do, and live. Moses is not offering a trick: the offer is genuine and the terms honourable. The difficulty was never the offer but the doer. Whoever kept the law perfectly would live, but no sinner can (3:20; Galatians 3:10), so as a way to life the law brings only death to sinners.

The righteousness of faith speaks. Its words come from Deuteronomy 30:11–14, where Moses told Israel that God’s word was not far off or too hard. Paul is not raiding Deuteronomy out of context, as is often charged. Chapter 30 stands after the covenant curses of chapter 28, after the exile has been described in advance, and straight after God promises to circumcise the hearts of his people so that they will love him and live (Deuteronomy 30:6). The nearness Moses speaks of belongs to a passage about restoration after failure, and about surgery performed by God on the human heart.

Who will ascend. “Do not say in your heart” echoes Deuteronomy 9:4, where Moses warned Israel not to think God gave them the land because of their righteousness, and 8:17, where he forbade them to say, “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.” It is aimed at private thoughts, the sentence nobody speaks aloud, and its modern form is short: “There must be something more I have to do.” That is the ascent: believing the gospel in principle, then quietly assembling a ladder, more discipline, more feeling, a better run of weeks, as though Christ needed fetching down and the fetching were your job.

He has already come down. The Son of God became man of his own accord, without being fetched, and came down into a stable and onto a cross, so that sinners who could never ascend could be lifted up with him. You do not have to make salvation happen.

Was anyone in the Old Testament saved by keeping the law? No. The law’s promise of life for perfect obedience was real, but no sinner ever met it. Old Testament believers were saved the same way we are: by faith in God’s promise, looking forward to the Redeemer he would send. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness (4:3), and David rejoiced in the forgiveness of sins (4:6–8). The sacrifices pointed them to the coming Lamb. Only one man ever did the commandments perfectly and lived by them: Jesus Christ, and he did it for us.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live
who will ascend to heaven for us?

verseByVerse.quote: "or 'Who will descend into the abyss?'" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one needs to go down into the realm of the dead to bring Christ up, because God has raised him; salvation is already near, in the word of faith the apostles proclaim. There is nothing left to fetch.

Who will descend. Deuteronomy 30:13 says “beyond the sea”. Paul has deliberately changed it to “the abyss”, the deep, the realm of the dead (compare Psalm 107:26; Jonah 2), and he marks each application with “that is”, applying the passage as Jewish teachers of his day often did. Over the sea is merely far; the abyss is the place from which nobody returns. Up and down are the only two directions a human being could travel to reach God, and Paul closes both, because Christ has been to both and come back.

But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart,” from Deuteronomy 30:14. Salvation is as close as the word you hear and speak: nearer than the church building, nearer than the minister, nearer than the next book or the next season when things have calmed down enough to think. The gospel is not somewhere you must get to. It is already in the room, closer than the furniture.

The word of faith. The near word is the gospel message, which calls for faith, and this clause stops nearness from becoming mysticism. The word did not drift near; somebody said it out loud, and Paul builds six verses on that (vv. 14–17). The nearness of verse 8 and the preacher of verse 15 are the same fact seen from the two ends.

The width of an open mouth. Christ came down from heaven and went down into death, and rose from both to stand beside us in the word. The whole distance a sinner now stands from God is the width of an open mouth.

The sentence from below. If the ascent says, “There must be something more I have to do,” the descent is its opposite, spoken by a different kind of reader: “What he did cannot reach as far down as I have gone.” It keeps from Christ many who would never call themselves unbelievers. It does not deny the gospel; it simply holds that this particular case is beneath its reach: the thing done at nineteen, the years nobody knows about, the marriage wrecked on purpose. Paul answers it by pointing to where Christ has been: down into death itself, and up again.

What it does not mean. The near word must still be believed and confessed. And “in your heart” does not mean the word is your own inner voice, to be found by looking inside. It is near because someone sent brought it from outside. What is inside you is where it has landed, not where it came from.

What if I feel that God is far away? Feelings of distance are real, and many believers have known them (Psalm 13:1; 42:9). But the nearness of verse 8 is not a feeling; it is a fact about the word. So when God feels far, do not try to climb up or dig down to find him. Go to the near word: read it, hear it preached, say it back to him in prayer. Feelings follow slowly. The promise does not wait for them.
verseByVerse.note: Paul applies Moses’ words about the nearness of God’s word to the message about Christ.

parallels.desc: the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart

verseByVerse.quote: Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. — Romans 10:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever trusts in his heart that God raised Jesus from the dead, and openly confesses him as Lord, will be saved. Heart and mouth are one faith, seen from within and from without.

Jesus is Lord. Confess means to say the same thing, to declare openly: to agree with God about his Son, where it can be heard. “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession (1 Corinthians 12:3; Philippians 2:11). “Lord” (kyrios) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God’s name, the LORD. To confess Jesus as Lord is to confess him as God and to bow to his rule.

God raised him. Believing the resurrection is not just accepting a historical fact but trusting the living Christ whom God vindicated (4:24–25).
