Calvin called saving faith a firm and certain knowledge of God’s kindness toward us, founded on the promise freely given in Christ, revealed to our minds and sealed on our hearts by the Holy Spirit. Why name the resurrection? Because you cannot call a dead man Lord. The raising is God’s verdict on the crucifixion: the Son declared Son of God in power (1:4), and raised for our justification (4:25). What you are asked to believe is the very ground on which you are declared right.

You will be saved. “Will be saved” is future, pointing to the day of judgment. But the verdict for that day is not kept waiting until then. It has already been given to everyone who believes: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (8:1).

Heart and mouth. In verse 9 Paul follows Moses’ order, mouth then heart (v. 8); in verse 10 he sets them in the order in which they happen. Faith in the heart receives righteousness; confession with the mouth is its outward expression: one faith seen from within, where it is trust, and from without, where it is audible. Nor are justified and saved two prizes, one for believing and a better one for speaking, but one rescue named twice: by what it does to your standing before the Judge, and to your future. Justified means that the Judge has spoken in your favour: you are not made sinless on the spot, but pardoned and accepted for Christ’s sake (4:5–6). True faith does not stay silent.

What two words cost. In Greek the whole confession was two words: Kyrios Iēsous. Around AD 112 Pliny, governor of Bithynia, wrote to the Emperor Trajan about Christians and described the test he had settled on. They were told to offer incense and wine before the emperor’s image and to curse Christ; those who did were released. A capital examination came down to one sentence, said where witnesses could hear. So the mouth is named not because God needs syllables, having read the heart, but because the mouth is the organ that costs. Kyrios was Caesar’s own title, the word for the one who held the final right over your life. To give it to a crucified Galilean was to take it from somebody else. Confession is a transfer of allegiance. Jesus now has the last word over my body, my money and my plans, ahead of any employer, government or desire of my own: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

The stopped mouth opened. The argument of this letter reached its lowest point in chapter 3, in a silent courtroom: the law speaks so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God (3:19). Seven chapters later, the first thing the gospel does with a stopped mouth is give it something to say. Not a defence, but a name. Blessed be Jesus, the Lord, whom God raised from the dead, who opens the mouths of the condemned to confess him and fills their hearts with the righteousness of God.

What it does not mean. Not that saying the words is a magic formula, or that someone who cannot speak cannot be saved. Faith receives; Christ saves. Jesus blocked the magical reading in advance: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7:21), the very words of the confession, on lips he does not know. No one can say Jesus is Lord except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). The confession is not what causes the new life. It is the first sound the new life makes.

I cannot remember a moment when I confessed Christ. Am I saved? Look at the verb. “With the mouth one confesses” is a present tense and a description, not a ceremony: not an event you may have failed to perform, but what a believer’s mouth goes on doing. Someone converted alone in a hospital bed, someone who came to faith with no date to write down, someone who cannot speak at all: none is shut out. You have confessed every time you prayed to him, called him Lord in a room where that was awkward, or told the truth about whose you are when a shorter answer was available. The question is not whether there was a moment, but whether your mouth now agrees with your heart.

Should I be baptised as part of confessing Christ? Yes. In the New Testament, baptism is the first public confession a believer makes, the moment he says with his whole body that Jesus is Lord (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:36–38). It does not save; faith in Christ saves. But it is Christ’s command to all who believe, marking you out before the church and the world as his; if you trust Christ and have not been baptised as a believer, speak to your church. Many faithful brothers baptise infants, seeing baptism, like circumcision, as the sign of God’s promise to believers and their children, and we honour them. This commentary is persuaded that in the New Testament the sign follows faith, as in the baptisms Acts describes; it is a difference between brothers who share one Lord.
verseByVerse.note: “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession. “Lord” is the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Scripture says, "Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame." For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one who trusts in Christ will be put to shame, because one Lord rules over Jew and Gentile alike and gives generously to all who call on him. The one Lord is rich toward everyone.

The added word. This is Isaiah 28:16, which Paul quoted at 9:33 without the word everyone. Isaiah does not have it (the Greek Old Testament says whoever believes); Paul put it there, builds the paragraph on it, and says it twice more.

No distinction. In 3:22–23 there was no distinction in sin; here there is no distinction in salvation. There the phrase swept away every advantage anyone had counted on; here the words that closed every door open one. Nobody is far enough in to be exempt from needing this, and nobody is far enough out to be barred from having it. The gospel can be for everybody only because the ruin was.

The same Lord. One Lord, Jesus, over Jews and Gentiles alike (3:29–30; Acts 10:36). The ground is not a warm feeling about including everyone but that there is only one God. So a Gentile calling on Jesus is not a guest of somebody else’s God; he is calling on his own Maker. One door can sound narrow. But if each people had its own god and its own way, your way in would depend on where you were born. One Lord over all means that the Jew with his Scriptures and the pagan with his idols come in by the same door, on the same terms, to the same welcome.

Rich toward all. The riches are those of his grace and glory (2:4; 9:23; 11:33). The Greek says he is “being rich” toward all who call: a continuing generosity, not a fixed sum divided among claimants. That matters to the reader who came late, or out of wasted years, and expects the reduced portion. There is none. Nobody arriving now is served what earlier arrivals did not finish.

The stone that bore the shame. The “him” of verse 11 is the stone God laid in Zion, a tested and precious cornerstone (Isaiah 28:16), and the New Testament names it: Jesus, the stone the builders rejected (1 Peter 2:6–7). Why can no one who leans on him be put to shame? Because he took the shame himself. At Calvary the Son of God was stripped, mocked and hung up in public as a criminal. He endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2). The disgrace a believer’s sins deserve has been publicly spent on Christ, with none left over for the one who trusts him.

What it does not mean. Not that everyone will in fact be saved. The riches are for all who call on him. One distinction is left standing, between those who call on him and those who do not, and no one is born on the wrong side of it.

Does “no distinction” mean the Jewish people no longer matter? No. There is no distinction in the way of salvation, but Paul still speaks of Israel’s special history and future (3:1–2; 11:28–29), and he began the letter with the gospel going to the Jew first (1:16). No one has a separate road to God, and no one is excluded from the one road; but that does not erase God’s faithfulness to Israel, and it gives Gentile Christians no ground for looking down on Jewish people.

parallels.desc: whoever believes will not be in haste

verseByVerse.quote: For "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone at all who calls on the Lord Jesus to save him will be saved. The promise Joel made about calling on the LORD is kept by calling on Jesus.

The name of the Lord. Paul quotes Joel 2:32, which Peter also quoted at Pentecost (Acts 2:21). In Joel, the Lord is the LORD, Yahweh, the name given at the burning bush: four consonants that by Paul’s day a synagogue reader would not pronounce, saying Adonai instead so that the name itself never crossed his lips. Paul applies the sentence to Jesus, whom he has just called Lord (v. 9): to call on Jesus is to call on Yahweh.

To call. To pray to him, appeal to him, trust in him, worship him (Genesis 4:26; 12:8). It is faith speaking: not eloquence, but what a person does who has no other options left and one name to say. It quickly became a description of Christians: Paul writes to “all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:2), and in Damascus the disciples knew Saul was coming to bind “all who call on your name” (Acts 9:14). One of the church’s earliest names for itself was a verb.

What does Joel’s promise save us from? The promise stands at the end of a passage about the day of the LORD, the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood before that great and awesome day comes. That is rescue with a date and a named danger. Romans has named the same danger already: the wrath revealed from heaven (1:18), and the day of wrath a hard heart is storing up for itself (2:5). This verse is the way out of that day, and all it asks is that you call.

Reasoning from it, not to it. A man trained among the Pharisees, who had handled the sacred name with that much care all his life, hands it to a Galilean executed within his own adult lifetime, and does it in passing, in a clause that begins with “for”, as proof of something else. He is not arguing that Jesus is divine; he takes it as settled and argues from it. The highest claim in the chapter is made in its quietest sentence.

Everyone. No sinner who calls will be turned away. This free offer of the gospel is real, and it fits with God’s sovereign election: the elect are those who are brought to call, and none who call are turned away (John 6:37). The clearest case in the Gospels is a man being executed, with no time to make amends, no changed life to point to, and his hands not even free. What he has is a mouth and a name, and he uses them: “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). He is told, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). The name a synagogue reader would not pronounce is the one thing a dying man can still get out, and it is within reach of any mouth on earth, in any language, at any hour, without an appointment. Paul’s everyone is at least that wide.

In everyday life. Remember not the best prayer you ever prayed but the shortest one you ever meant, two or three words at an hour you would rather not describe. That is the whole of what is asked. Pray it again today, and pray it for someone else by name.

I called on him, but I felt nothing. Did it count? Read the promise again. It says will be saved, not will feel saved. What God attaches himself to here is the calling, not the sensation that may or may not come with it. Many calls he has answered were made by people sure they had spoken into an empty room. If you called on Christ in faith, he heard you, whether your feelings agree today or not. Keep calling on him, as believers do all their lives. And let the promise, not your pulse, tell you where you stand.

parallels.desc: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — The Sent Preacher and Israel's Unbelief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God brings people to faith by sending messengers with the word of Christ, and Israel’s unbelief comes not from lack of hearing but from refusing to obey. A chain runs backwards from calling to believing, hearing, preaching and sending, and Isaiah calls the messengers’ feet beautiful because of what they carry (vv. 14–15). Not all obeyed, as Isaiah foresaw, yet faith still comes from hearing the word of Christ (vv. 16–17). Israel cannot plead that it never heard or never understood: the message had gone out everywhere, and Moses and Isaiah had foretold Gentiles brought in (vv. 18–20). The chapter ends with God’s hands held out all day long to a disobedient and contrary people (v. 21): the refusal is theirs, and the love remains his.
verseByVerse.theology:
The necessity of preaching

Romans 10:14–17 is a key New Testament text on preaching. Preaching is the means God has appointed for bringing people to faith (see the note on v. 17). And because hearing needs a preacher and a preacher needs sending, the call to mission is built into the logic of salvation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The beautiful feet of Isaiah 52:7 brought Jerusalem news that the exile was over; Paul applies the picture to the heralds of a greater exodus. Now: A kind and honest life matters, but it does not tell anyone who Christ is or what he has done. People come to faith by hearing the word of Christ, so the church must keep speaking it, in pulpits and in ordinary conversation, because faith comes from hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!' — Romans 10:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can call on Christ without believing, believe without hearing, hear without a preacher, or preach without being sent; so God’s promise to save all who call goes out through messengers he sends. That is why Isaiah calls their feet beautiful.

A chain that runs backwards. Having promised salvation to everyone who calls, Paul asks what must already have happened for anyone to call, and works upstream one link at a time. Calling requires believing. Believing requires hearing. Hearing requires a preacher (kēryssō, to herald, announce publicly). Here the promise of verse 8 is paid: the word is near, in your mouth, but it was in somebody else’s mouth first.

Unless they are sent. Preaching requires sending (apostellō, the root of apostle). God sends preachers, and the church sends missionaries (Acts 13:2–3). The chain ends not at the preacher but at the sender. Nobody in it appoints himself, and the sending does not finally begin with a committee: it is God’s own initiative arriving in ordinary shoe leather. That settles the objection often raised here, that if God has chosen his people, preaching is a formality. Paul argues the reverse. The God who appointed the harvest appointed the plough, and no farmer certain of a crop leaves the seed in the barn. Election does not make proclamation optional; it makes it worth doing, because God’s word will not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

Beautiful feet. From Isaiah 52:7, describing the messengers who ran across the mountains with news of Israel’s return from exile. Watchmen on the wall had no other way to learn how the war had gone. Feet were the filthiest part of a person, given to a slave to wash, yet Isaiah calls them lovely because of what they carry. The herald shouts peace, good news, salvation, and then the line the whole scene is built for, “Your God reigns.” There has been a change of government, and you can go home. The herald on the ridge cries “Your God reigns”; the believer at the foot of the hill says “Jesus is Lord” (v. 9).

In the flow. These verses are rightly read as a missionary text, but their first job concerns Israel, for whom every link but believing was in place (vv. 16–21). The chain clears God of any charge that Israel never had a chance, and lays the failure where verse 3 laid it, at a refusal to submit.

The first Herald and the great Sender. The chain of sending begins in heaven. The Father sent the Son, and Hebrews calls Jesus the apostle and high priest of our confession (Hebrews 3:1), the first Sent One. He came as Isaiah’s herald in person, into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God and saying that the kingdom of God was at hand (Mark 1:14–15). Your God reigns, said the runner on the ridge; the kingdom is here, said the King, and he was the news he carried. Then, risen, he sent others: “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (John 20:21). Every pair of beautiful feet since has run on his errand.

In everyday life. Who told you? Not who taught you afterwards: who first put it into words in your hearing? Perhaps someone who said it badly and said it anyway; what they carried made them lovely down to the dust on their shoes. You stand at the end of a long line of feet. Then ask who is waiting to hear it from you. Pray for those sent, give to send them, and open your own mouth: your feet can be beautiful too.

Who are the sent, and must I go? Paul has in mind heralds sent to proclaim publicly, and the church still recognises and sends such people, as the church at Antioch sent Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:1–3). Not every Christian is called to be a preacher or missionary, but none needs a commission to speak of Christ. When persecution scattered the Jerusalem church, those who were scattered went about preaching the word (Acts 8:4), and every believer is to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in him (1 Peter 3:15). Some go, many send by prayer and giving, and all speak of Christ to the people around them.

Is it fair that people who never hear of Christ are lost? No one is condemned for failing to believe a message he never heard. People are judged for what they did with the light they had, the creation around them and the conscience within them (1:20; 2:12–16), and Paul has shown that no one has lived up to that light (3:9–10). The gospel is not the reason anyone is lost; it is the rescue sent to people who were lost already. And God does not leave the question hanging; he sends. The fitting answer is not to accuse God of unfairness but to join him in the sending.

Where Christians differ: those who never hear. Some say people who never hear the gospel can be saved through other religions; this is usually called pluralism. Others, often called inclusivists, hold a wider hope, that God may save through Christ people who never heard of him but responded to the light of creation or conscience, pointing to Cornelius (Acts 10), to 2:14–16, and to Psalm 19, which Paul quotes in verse 18. Those who hold it usually do so out of real love for the unreached and concern for God’s fairness. This commentary’s view: Paul’s chain says otherwise: calling requires believing, and believing requires hearing of Christ. There is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). This is why missions matter so much. Cornelius is in fact the strongest case against the wider hope: devout as he was, an angel told him to send for Peter, who would declare a message by which he would be saved (Acts 11:14). Creation is enough light to leave a man without excuse (1:20) and not enough to save him. God may use many means to bring the word, but salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Westminster Confession 10.4; 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.4). Infants dying in infancy, and those incapable of being outwardly called, are in God’s hands and saved by Christ through the Spirit as he pleases (Westminster 10.3; 1689 10.3). Parents who have lost a little one may rest that child in the hands of the God who gave him, as David did (2 Samuel 12:23).

Uncertain wording. The Greek behind “him of whom they have never heard” can also be read him whom they have never heard. Both are grammatically possible. Most translations take the first, hearing about Christ; the second would mean that in the preaching Christ himself is heard speaking (compare Ephesians 2:17). The difference is small, since Paul elsewhere holds both, and either way the point stands: no one believes in a Christ whose word has not reached him.

Textual note. The King James Version, following later manuscripts, adds the gospel of peace in verse 15; the earliest lack it, and the sense is the same.

parallels.desc: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news

verseByVerse.quote: But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, 'Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?' — Romans 10:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s problem was not that no one told them, but that not all obeyed the good news, just as Isaiah had foreseen. The prophet expected it.

Not all. Paul writes not all, and the qualification carries weight: it leaves the remnant standing, it is why chapter 11 can ask whether God has rejected his people and answer with a flat no, and it stops this verse becoming a verdict on a whole nation. Three times in verses 11–13 Paul has said “everyone” or “all”; here the same Greek word comes back with “not” in front of it. The word that carried the promise now measures the response.

Obeyed. The gospel is a command as well as an offer: repent and believe (1:5; Acts 17:30). The Greek for obey is built on the verb hear; in use it simply means obey, but in a passage about hearing Paul surely wants the echo: hearing that submits. Nobody obeys a weather forecast, but news of a change of government puts you under someone. So unbelief in this chapter is described as refusal rather than mere error: they did not submit (v. 3), they have not obeyed (v. 16), they are disobedient and contrary (v. 21).

Who has believed. Isaiah 53:1 opens the great passage on the suffering servant, and John quotes it too, of the Jews who saw Jesus’ signs and did not believe (John 12:38). The very next lines speak of a man with no form or majesty, despised and rejected: the question prefaces a report about a crucified man. The difficulty was never poor delivery but what the message says, the same thing chapter 9 called a stone people trip over.

The servant who was not believed. Yet the servant whose report was not believed is the same servant who was wounded for the transgressions of those who did not believe, and who will yet see his offspring (Isaiah 53:10). His word is not defeated by unbelief; he bore the very rejection the prophet grieved.

What it does not mean. Not that the gospel has failed when people reject it; Isaiah foresaw it. Nor that results do not matter to God’s servants. “Results belong to God” is true, and it is also the standard excuse of the lazy and the cold. Isaiah does not shrug; he brings his grief to God: “Lord, who has believed?” And Paul’s response to his people’s unbelief, at the top of this chapter, was to pray for them.

I have shared the gospel for years and no one has believed. Have I failed? Not if you have been faithful. When God commissioned Isaiah, the commission itself described the outcome: keep on hearing, but do not understand (Isaiah 6:9). Isaiah asked how long, and was told, until cities lie waste. If faithfulness were measured by response, Isaiah failed for a lifetime. Your task is to speak truly, live consistently, and pray persistently. The opening of hearts is God’s work. Many who seemed deaf for years have believed in the end, sometimes after the one who prayed had gone to glory.

parallels.desc: who has believed what he has heard from us?

verseByVerse.quote: So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. — Romans 10:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith is born when the message about Christ is heard, because Christ himself speaks through it. God creates faith through his word.

From hearing. “So” draws the conclusion from Isaiah’s question in verse 16, where the same noun stands for the message heard: faith comes by the report. This is the theology of preaching in one verse. Faith is not finally produced by argument, emotion or social influence, though God may use them, but by the word, the Holy Spirit’s instrument.

The word of Christ. Faith comes through a specific message, not a religious mood. That is why the faithful exposition of what Scripture actually says has always stood at the centre of Reformed worship. It is the word of Christ that creates faith, and the preacher’s task is to get out of the way.

Christ still speaking. Christ preached peace to people in Asia Minor who had never seen him (Ephesians 2:17), and he still does. Next Sunday’s sermon, imperfectly delivered by a tired man with a cold, is not merely a report of a distant event but the risen Christ still speaking to people who were not born when he was crucified.

What it does not mean. Not that faith is our own achievement: the Spirit uses the word to give new birth and faith (James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23). Nor does it exclude reading. Akoē is about a message reaching a person, not about ears: the housebound believer with an open Bible, the deaf believer watching an interpreter, the prisoner reading a page in his cell all receive the word of Christ, and it does there exactly what it does in a crowded church. And sitting under preaching is not the same as receiving it; a person can do the first for forty years.

How can I get more faith? Not by squeezing harder inside. People who long for more faith usually try concentrating, resolving, trying to feel more certain. But faith is a response, and a response needs something to respond to. Faith grows as it feeds on Christ in his word. Sit under faithful preaching. Read the Gospels and let Christ speak. Memorise promises and pray them back to God. Take the Lord’s Supper, where the word is made visible. And ask God for faith; he gives it (Mark 9:24; Ephesians 2:8).

Uncertain wording. Two short phrases can be taken more than one way. “Hearing” (akoē) can mean the act of hearing or the message heard; Paul probably means both: faith comes by the message, received by hearing. And “the word of Christ” can mean the message about Christ or Christ’s own word. Here too both are likely in view, for the message is about him, and he speaks through the messengers who proclaim it.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “word of God,” as the ESV note says, but “word of Christ” is the better reading.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the word of God.”

verseByVerse.quote: But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for "Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, "I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel cannot plead that it never heard the message or was never warned: the word had gone out everywhere, and Moses had foretold that God would stir Israel to jealousy through outsiders. The problem was never access, but response.

Have they not heard? Paul is not claiming that every human being has heard; he tells the same church that his ambition is to preach where Christ has not been named (15:20–21). His point is that Israel cannot plead that the message never reached them. It had been announced in their own synagogues, in their own language, by their own countrymen, for some twenty-five years.

Their voice has gone out. Psalm 19:4 is about the heavens declaring God’s glory. Paul borrows the words to describe how widely the gospel had spread: through the synagogues across the Roman world, the message had reached Jews everywhere (Colossians 1:6, 23). He is not proving from a psalm about stars that every village has heard; the announcement has gone out the way daylight goes out. And that closes a circle from the opening of the letter, where the sky was enough to leave a man without excuse (1:20); now the message that can actually save him has travelled the same roads.

Did Israel not understand? Scripture itself had told them that God would turn to the Gentiles, and Paul calls his witnesses: first Moses, then Isaiah.

I will make you jealous. From Deuteronomy 32:21, in the Song of Moses. Israel made God jealous with idols, no-gods; so God would make them jealous with a no-people, the Gentiles: measure for measure. And the detail that makes the question unanswerable: Moses was told to teach this song to Israel and put it in their mouths before they ever entered the land, so that it would stand as a witness against them in a future they had not yet lived (Deuteronomy 31:19–21). The prophecy of their own refusal, and of the outsiders brought in over it, was in their hymnbook, put in their mouths.

Jealousy meant to win them back. This theme returns in 11:11–14. It is not spite: God does not say he will replace them but make them jealous, which is only worth doing if you intend to get somebody back.

A foolish nation. A nation without understanding, without the law. Here is a guard for the Gentile reader: the Gentiles are not chosen as the better party, but as the ones nobody counted. The branch grafted in has no grounds for looking down the trunk at the branch broken off, which is the warning Paul is about to spend a chapter delivering.

What the no-people were given. What could make Israel jealous of Gentiles? Not Gentile virtue, but Israel’s own treasure in their hands. From Israel, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all (9:5), and now men in Corinth and Rome and Galatia call on him by name, sing Israel’s psalms to him, and call Abraham their father. The words that went out to the ends of the world went out on the orders of Israel’s risen Messiah: you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (Acts 1:8). The jealousy Moses foresaw is the ache of seeing your own King loved by strangers.

What about people today who have heard the gospel many times? They are in Israel’s position. Having heard is not a safe place to stay; it is greater light and greater responsibility (Luke 12:48; Hebrews 2:1–3). But it is also a mercy, because the word is still near. If that is you, do not wait to understand it better later; you have heard enough to come now. And if you are a believer with friends or family who have heard it all before, do not stop: keep praying, keep loving, and let your life make them jealous for what you have in Christ.

parallels.desc: their voice goes out through all the earth
I will make them jealous with those who are no people

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, "I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me." But of Israel he says, "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God let himself be found by Gentiles who were not looking for him, while all day long he held out his hands to an Israel that refused him. Sovereign grace and human refusal stand side by side, and Paul softens neither.

So bold. Paul quotes Isaiah 65:1–2. The verb means to throw caution aside: the prophet knew he was saying an outrageous thing. The outrage was not that God saves Gentiles; Isaiah says that many times. It was the way he does it: he is found by people who never looked for him.

Found by those who did not seek. God took the initiative and let himself be found by Gentiles who were not looking for him (compare 9:30). For some readers this is the best sentence in the chapter. Some came away from chapter 9 frightened, quietly sure they are not among the chosen, and their evidence is nearly always the same: I did not really want this. I came to it late, or badly, or for the wrong reasons. I was not seeking. Verse 20 takes that evidence off the table. Not seeking is the very description of the people God says he was found by.

All day long. God, like a parent, stands with hands stretched out all day, pleading with his children to come home. “Disobedient” (apeitheō) means refusing to be persuaded; “contrary” (antilegō) means speaking against, answering back: exactly what 9:20 said the clay has no right to do, and exactly what Israel did. Hold your arms straight out and see how long before the shoulders burn. All day long, says God: a parent in a doorway with arms open from morning until dark while a child walks past, again and again, and does not stop.

Side by side in Isaiah. Verses 20 and 21 are Isaiah 65:1 and 65:2, consecutive. Paul did not hunt through the Scriptures for a counterweight; he simply kept reading, and sovereign grace and human refusal were already lying side by side in one paragraph. That corrects any reading of chapter 9 that stops at the potter and the clay: the same apostle ends this chapter with God’s arms out, and puts the loss down to a people who would not come. Paul softens neither, and neither should we. The Lord Jesus said the same about the same city, in the street: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Luke 13:34). He does not say they could not come; he says they would not.

He has still not lowered his hands. Chapter 10 does not end with a door bolted but with arms held open, and Paul’s next sentence asks whether God has rejected his people and answers no. Isaiah was not writing about the cross, yet a Christian cannot miss where those hands went at last: on a Friday outside the walls of the city they were held out to, his incarnate Son stretched out his own on a cross, in public, for the very people refusing him. Blessed be the God who found us when we were not looking, and who has still not lowered his hands.

What it does not mean. Not that God has given up on Israel; the next chapter answers that at once. Nor is his patience endless indifference (2:4–5). A day has an evening. All day long is a measure of extraordinary endurance, not a promise that the arms will never come down.

I have drifted from God for years. Will he take me back? Yes. Look at the posture this verse describes: hands held out all day, to people who were refusing him at the very time. Most who think of coming back picture folded arms or at best a cool, formal patience. That is not the posture the text describes. Think of the father in Jesus’ parable, who saw his son a long way off and ran (Luke 15:20). Come today. Confess plainly, return to his word and his people, and do not wait until you feel worthy.

Where Christians differ: the sincerity of the offer. Some argue that if God has elected only some, his offer of salvation to the non-elect cannot be sincere. This commentary’s view: God’s outstretched hands are real. He truly calls all who hear the gospel to come, and he is grieved by their refusal (Ezekiel 33:11; Matthew 23:37). His secret purpose in election and his revealed will in the gospel do not cancel each other. We do not fully understand how they fit together, but Scripture teaches both, and we must preach freely to all (Canons of Dort 2.5; 3/4.8).

parallels.desc: I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me
I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people

10.text: <sup>1</sup>Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.<sup>2</sup>For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.<sup>3</sup>For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness.<sup>4</sup>For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.<sup>5</sup>For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them.<sup>6</sup>But the righteousness based on faith says, “Do not say in your heart, ’Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down)<sup>7</sup>“or ’Who will descend into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).<sup>8</sup>But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);<sup>9</sup>because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.<sup>10</sup>For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved.<sup>11</sup>For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.”<sup>12</sup>For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.<sup>13</sup>For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”<sup>14</sup>How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?<sup>15</sup>And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!”<sup>16</sup>But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?”<sup>17</sup>So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.<sup>18</sup>But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”<sup>19</sup>But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, “I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry.”<sup>20</sup>Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, “I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.”<sup>21</sup>But of Israel he says, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”

keyVerse.quote: because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
keyVerse.note: Here the near word of verse 8 is spelled out: trust in the heart that God raised Jesus, and the open confession that he is Lord, the title of Israel’s God. The verse holds the chapter’s two sides together, the righteousness God gives freely to faith and the voice that faith cannot keep silent, and it leads straight into the chain of preaching by which this word reaches everyone who will call (vv. 13–17).

10.reflection:
Paul says Israel had “a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (v. 2), and he had once shared that zeal. Why is sincerity not enough before God? Where are you tempted to trust your own earnestness, or to look down on people whose zeal is misplaced?

Verses 6–8 rule out two thoughts: that we must climb up to bring Christ down, and that we have sunk too low for him to reach. Which of the two is closer to your own heart, and how does the nearness of the word answer it?

To confess “Jesus is Lord” (v. 9) once cost believers their lives. What does that confession cost you, and where would saying it aloud be awkward this week?

Paul’s chain runs from sending to preaching, hearing, believing and calling (vv. 14–17). Who first told you the gospel, and who is waiting to hear it from you? How can you and your church send, pray and speak?

11.title: The Mystery of Israel and the Doxology of Grace
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 closes the three chapters (9–11) that ask whether God’s word to Israel has failed (see the introduction). Chapter 10 ended with God holding out his hands all day long to a disobedient people (10:21); chapter 11 asks whether that is the end of them, and then the letter’s whole argument so far breaks into praise.

The message. God has not rejected his people, and he has not finished with them. He keeps a remnant chosen by grace, and the hardening of the rest is partial and temporary, serving his mercy to the nations, whose blessing is meant to bring Israel home. Gentile believers stand only by faith and have nothing to boast of. God never takes back his gifts and calling, and he has shut all people up in disobedience so that he may have mercy on all.

Why it was said. Gentile believers in Rome, now the majority, were tempted to think God had traded Israel in for them and to look down on the Jewish people (v. 18; see the introduction). And every reader of chapter 8 needed to know whether God keeps his promises when his people fail.

How the chapter makes its case. Paul himself, like Elijah’s seven thousand, proves there is a remnant chosen by grace; the rest are hardened, as Scripture foretold (vv. 1–10). Israel’s stumble is not a fall: it brought riches to the world, and their full inclusion will bring more (vv. 11–16). The olive tree warns the grafted-in Gentile against pride: the root supports him, and God can graft the natural branches back (vv. 17–24). Then the mystery: a partial hardening until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and so all Israel will be saved (vv. 25–32). The argument ends in a hymn (vv. 33–36).

Where it leads. The Deliverer from Zion who takes away sins (vv. 26–27) is Christ, the one Saviour of Jew and Gentile alike, and the root that feeds every branch is the promise that was always about him. Three chapters that began in anguish (9:2) end before a God deeper than the argument could reach: “from him and through him and to him are all things” (v. 36).

For us. If God does not take back his call to a people who refused his Son, he will not take back his call to you. So do not boast, for you stand by grace alone; do not despair of anyone, for God is able to graft them in again; and when your understanding runs out, worship.

keyVerse.quote: For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.
keyVerse.note: This verse answers the question the chapter opened with (v. 1). God has not thrust away his people, because he never takes back what he has given or whom he has called, and the unbelief of a generation cannot undo a choice that never rested on their merit. The same faithfulness is every believer’s security: the God who has no regrets about Israel has none about those he calls in Christ.

11.reflection:
Elijah thought he was the only faithful one left, but God had kept seven thousand for himself (vv. 2–4). When have you felt alone in your faith? How does God’s answer to Elijah, with its rest, food, truth and fresh work, speak to you?

Paul insists that the remnant is chosen by grace and not by works, “otherwise grace would no longer be grace” (v. 6). Where do you still explain your own faith, or someone else’s unbelief, by something in the person? How would taking this verse seriously change the way you pray and speak about them?

The olive tree tells Gentile believers, “do not become proud, but fear” (v. 20), because the root supports them. What do you owe to Israel’s root? How should this shape the way Christians think and speak about the Jewish people, and about those who have left the faith?

Paul ends three hard chapters not with every question answered but with praise (vv. 33–36). Which questions about God’s ways do you find hardest? What would it look like to bring them to him as Paul did, and to let them end in worship?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Remnant: God Has Not Rejected His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has not rejected his people: he has always kept a remnant for himself by grace, and he is keeping one now. Paul is the first proof, a Benjamite and a former persecutor who now believes (vv. 1–2a). Elijah thought he was alone, but God had kept seven thousand (vv. 2b–4), and so today there is a remnant chosen by grace, not works (vv. 5–6). The harder half follows in the same breath: the elect obtained what Israel sought, but the rest were hardened, as Moses, Isaiah and David foresaw (vv. 7–10). That is not the last word; the next verse asks whether they stumbled in order to fall, and answers no.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Remnant Principle in Scripture

The remnant runs through the whole Old Testament: the remnant of Israel in Isaiah (Isaiah 10:20–22), the remnant of Jacob in Micah, the seven thousand in Elijah’s day. That is how God has always saved (see the note on vv. 5–6). The new covenant does not change God’s way of saving; it makes it plain and fulfils it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal were invisible to Elijah. The prophet who declares the cause lost may be wrong. Now: When the church seems to be in steep decline, the statistics grim and the culture running the other way, the temptation is Elijah’s: “I alone am left.” The church is always smaller than it should be and larger than it appears, and God keeps what he has promised to keep.

verseByVerse.quote: I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has not thrust away the people he set his love on, and Paul himself, a believing Israelite, is the living proof.

I ask, then, has God rejected his people? Paul’s own argument forces the question. Chapter 10 ended with God holding out his hands all day long to a disobedient and contrary people (10:21), and any reader who has followed that far is already forming the sentence: then that is the end of them. Paul asks it aloud before anyone else can. “Rejected” (apōtheomai) means to thrust away, and the wording echoes an old promise: the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name’s sake (1 Samuel 12:22; Psalm 94:14). The form of the question in Greek already expects the answer no.

By no means! Mē genoito is one of Paul’s strongest negatives, kept for conclusions that would wreck the gospel if they were allowed to stand (3:31; 6:1–2; 9:14). It is not yet an argument. It is a man flinching.

For I myself am an Israelite. He points not at the thousands of Jewish believers in Jerusalem (Acts 21:20) but at himself, the specimen with the worst history: the young man at whose feet the witnesses laid their coats while Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:58; 8:1), and who then went from house to house dragging believers off to prison. The proof that God has not finished with Israel is a Jew who had done his level best to finish the church.

The least of the tribes. Benjamin was the smallest tribe (1 Samuel 9:21), and the one that stayed with Judah when the kingdom split (1 Kings 12:21), itself a kind of remnant. Smallness has never been evidence that God has left the building.

Whom he foreknew. Not merely that God knew in advance how they would turn out; what he saw was their unbelief, which is the very problem. To know, in the Bible’s vocabulary, is to set your love on someone: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). It is the verb (proginōskō) that began the chain of God’s saving acts in 8:29. His people here are the nation he chose in love, and within it, as the next verses show, is the elect remnant. The relationship did not begin with them, so it does not end with them: what holds Israel is the grip of the God who set his love on a people before they had done anything, and kept it through the wilderness, the judges, the kings and the exile. His faithfulness is not a reaction to ours.

An Israelite at the right hand of God. Paul is only the nearest proof. From Israel, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all (9:5). The Son of God was born a son of Abraham and of David (Matthew 1:1), circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), and raised in that same body, and he still names himself the root and the descendant of David (Revelation 22:16). God cannot have thrust away the people whose flesh his Son took up into heaven. And it was this risen Israelite who met the persecuting Israelite on the Damascus road and made him his apostle. Paul’s conversion is the Messiah of Israel refusing to give up on Israel.

What it does not mean. Not that every Jew is saved, or that God has two ways of salvation, one for Jews and one for Gentiles. There is one way, faith in Christ, for there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is Lord of all (10:12). Here Paul establishes only a remnant; the larger claim comes at v. 26, and he makes no claim about territory or politics at all.

Why does a chapter about Israel matter to an ordinary Gentile Christian? Because your own salvation hangs on the same question. If God could set his love on Abraham’s children and then quietly walk away when they failed, the promises that end Romans 8 would be worth nothing either. And your Bible, your Saviour and your promises all came to you through Israel; Paul will shortly tell you that you are a branch on their tree.

So what if I feel that God has finished with me? Paul’s subject is Israel, but his method fits your fear. He does not go inward or take the temperature of anyone’s devotion. He points to a Person and a history: something God did, at a date, to a man who was not looking for it. Consulting your feelings to learn whether God has left you is like checking the weather to find out whether you are married. Look at what God has done: the promise he made, the Son he gave, the call that reached you. Those do not move when you do.

In everyday life. Somewhere today a mother will pray again for a son who has not been inside a church for twenty years, and wonder whether she is wasting her breath. This verse is for her. If God has not given up on Israel after centuries of unbelief, and the most violent enemy of the early church became its apostle, the long, unanswered prayer is not foolish. It is in line with the way God has always worked: slowly, and then on a date nobody saw coming.

parallels.desc: the LORD will not forsake his people

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel? "Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life." But what is God's reply to him? "I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even when faith seemed to have died out in Elijah’s day, God had kept thousands for himself, and he keeps his people in the same way now.

What the Scripture says of Elijah. Where this cry falls in Elijah’s life matters (1 Kings 19). He has just come off Carmel, the greatest public victory in the Old Testament, fire out of a clear sky onto a soaked altar. Then one messenger arrives from Jezebel with a threat, and the man who faced down a nation runs for his life, sits under a broom tree in the wilderness and asks God to let him die.

After the triumph. The collapse comes after a triumph, not a defeat. The dangerous ground is the week after the thing went well, when the adrenaline drains and one small piece of bad news arrives. Anyone who has crashed on a Monday after a Sunday that went beautifully has sat under that tree.

A nap and a meal. God does not correct the theology first. He lets him sleep, sends food, lets him sleep again, and sends food again (1 Kings 19:5–8); only after forty days’ walk to Horeb come the low whisper and the number. Some of what presents itself as a crisis of faith is a body that has not been fed or rested, and God treats that first. Exhaustion and depression are not the same as unbelief, and he is gentle with both.

How he appeals to God against Israel. “Appeals” (entynchanō) is the word used of the Spirit’s intercession for the saints (8:27). A prophet was called to stand between God and the people and plead for them; Elijah stands there and accuses them. Despair rarely stays private. Given long enough it starts building a case, usually against the very people you were called to serve.

I alone am left. One chapter earlier Obadiah had told Elijah to his face that he had hidden a hundred prophets of the LORD in caves and fed them (1 Kings 18:13), and the text gives no hint that they had perished since. Despair does not merely misread the evidence; it leaves out the evidence that does not fit.

But what is God’s reply to him? “Reply” (chrēmatismos) means a divine answer, an oracle: the only entirely accurate word in the exchange.

I have kept for myself. God does not say that seven thousand have stood firm, but “I have kept for myself.” Their survival is not a report on their stamina; it is a statement about his grip.

Faithfulness in the negative. What had the seven thousand done? Nothing, visibly. Their faithfulness is described entirely in the negative: they had not bowed the knee to Baal. If your obedience feels like a series of things you did not do, the gossip you did not pass on, the compromise you did not make, that is the very kind of faithfulness God chose to count.

The one who truly was left alone. Elijah’s “I alone am left” was false. There was one man of whom it was true. Jesus told his disciples, “you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone” (John 16:32), and they did: they all left him and fled (Mark 14:50), and on the cross he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). Israel’s faithful remnant narrowed to a single servant, and he was abandoned so that none of his would be. That is why God can say “I have kept for myself” and mean it. On the night he was left alone, Jesus prayed, “I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost” (John 17:12).

He gives the broken servant work again. God’s answer did not end with the number. He sent Elijah back down the mountain with errands (1 Kings 19:15–16), answering despair with truth rather than scolding. The Shepherd knows his seven thousand by name when the prophet cannot find one.

What it does not mean. The remnant doctrine has a smug cousin. Elijah’s error was self-pity; the error next door is self-congratulation, the small faithful group that has begun to enjoy being small and reads the seven thousand as a compliment. Nobody in that seven thousand knew they were being counted, and the man who was sure he had the roll call had it wrong.

What if I really am the only Christian at work, or in my family? Then God’s answer to Elijah still holds: you see far less of the board than you think, and there are almost certainly believers nearer than you know. Meanwhile do not try to stand alone: be faithfully joined to a local church, so that the isolation of Monday is answered by the fellowship of Sunday. And even where you are visibly alone, you are not unaccompanied. The one who kept the seven thousand for himself is keeping you, and he is in the room.

parallels.desc: I, even I only, am left
seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal

verseByVerse.quote: So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. — Romans 11:5–6
verseByVerse.commentary:
Today too God keeps a remnant, and it exists only because he chose it freely, by grace and not because of anything its members did. Grace and merit cannot be mixed.

A remnant at the present time. What was true on that mountain is happening in Paul’s own decade. “Remnant” (leimma) means what is left over, and the thousands of Jews who believed in Jerusalem (Acts 2:41; 21:20) were this remnant. It is not an emergency measure but the ordinary shape of how God has always saved: never the whole nation by birth, always a kept people within it.

Chosen by grace. Literally, according to the election (eklogē, choosing) of grace: the choosing is itself an act of grace, free and not for merit. The remnant is not the group that turned out better, but the group that was chosen, by a God whose choosing is gift all the way down. Nobody in it can point to anything in himself as the reason he is there. That is what makes it a remnant rather than an elite.

No longer on the basis of works. If God chose because of works, it would be wages, and wages are a debt, not a gift (4:4). Paul closes off the compromise every religious person reaches for: mostly grace, with some contribution of our own. The two are rival accounts of where the outcome came from, and only one can be true.

Otherwise grace would no longer be grace. Grace (charis) is free, undeserved favour; mix in merit and it stops being grace. Think of being given a house and being sold one at a discount. Take the discount to ninety-nine per cent: the deed still says sold, and the buyer can still say what he paid. Grace is not a very large discount but a different kind of transaction. God did not discount salvation; he gave it. He did not meet us halfway; he came all the way, in his Son, to people who were not coming.

Chosen in the Chosen One. God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4), by a grace given us in Christ Jesus before the ages began (2 Timothy 1:9). Christ is the Chosen One himself: the Father called him my Son, my Chosen One (Luke 9:35), and Peter calls him the living stone, chosen and precious in the sight of God (1 Peter 2:4). The remnant is chosen in him, so its grace has a face. Nobody earns a place in Christ. He is the gift.

Why say something so obvious? Because the instinct to earn is inexhaustible. Grace is agreed to on Sunday and quietly renegotiated by Wednesday, and the renegotiation comes disguised as seriousness. Listen to how we explain other people’s faith. She was always a seeker. He had a good upbringing. Each sentence is a small denial of verse 6, an attempt to find something in the person that accounts for the outcome; the same instinct explains those who have not come: he was always hard. This is the seed of the arrogance Paul confronts twelve verses on, when the Gentile reader starts explaining why the branches were broken off.

What it does not mean. Not that the remnant are passive. They believe and obey, but their faith is the fruit of grace, not its cause, and the man who writes verse 6 writes chapter 12 a page later. Works are the evidence and never the ground (2:7–8). What verse 6 forbids is not effort but sending God the bill for it.

If God chooses by grace, how can I know whether I am chosen? Not by trying to read God’s secret decree, but by doing what the gospel commands: believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. Election is not revealed in advance as a list but discovered from the inside, as faith. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (10:13), and no one who comes to Christ is turned away (John 6:37). If you are coming to him, you have your answer, for nobody comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). Election is meant to comfort those who believe, not to keep people from believing. Make your calling and election sure by looking at Christ, not by looking for your name.

Is it unfair that God chooses some and not others? Paul faced that question in 9:14–24: no one is owed mercy, and that anyone is chosen is astonishing. Here election is the reason there is hope at all in a dark time: in Elijah’s day and in Paul’s the nation as a whole had turned away, and left to themselves none would have remained. The remnant exists because God chose to keep one.

In everyday life. When you feel after a good week that God must be pleased with you now, or after a bad week that he must be finished with you, say verse 6 aloud. Both feelings treat God’s favour as wages, and grace has never worked that way.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add a further sentence: if it is by works, it is no longer grace, otherwise work is no longer work. The earliest manuscripts do not have it, so most modern Bibles omit it; the meaning is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened, as it is written, "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel as a whole sought a right standing with God and missed it, while the chosen remnant received it as a gift; the rest God hardened in judgment. Scripture had foretold this numbness.

Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. Seeking: these were the people still at it, in the synagogue, keeping the calendar, with a zeal for God (10:2). They sought righteousness before God (9:31; 10:3) and did not get it, while God was found by those who did not seek him (10:20). The party that was searching missed it; the party that was not searching was found.

Where the failure happened. A person can look very hard in a direction where he has already decided the answer must lie. They pursued righteousness as if it were based on works (9:32), and would not submit to a righteousness that came as a gift (10:3). And the gift arrived in a form they had ruled out in advance: a carpenter from Nazareth, crucified. Jesus put the tragedy in one sentence to the most earnest seekers of his day: “You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life” (John 5:39–40). They were holding the map and walking past the treasure.

The elect obtained it. Paul does not say they sought better. The difference lies not in the quality of their searching but in the grace that chose and gave.

But the rest were hardened. “Hardened” (pōroō) means made callous, like hard skin over a wound, and the wording implies that God did it, as he hardened Pharaoh (9:18). The next line says so outright. It is an act of judgment: God gives over to blindness those who refuse the light, the pattern of 1:24–28.

A spirit of stupor. A blend of Isaiah 29:10 and Deuteronomy 29:4. A “spirit of stupor” (katanyxis) is numbness, deep sleep, spiritual insensibility. Isaiah pictures people who stagger, drunk but not with wine, under a spirit of deep sleep (Isaiah 29:9–10): not a blindness that knows itself, but the fog of a man certain he is thinking clearly. Jesus quoted similar words from Isaiah 6 about those who would not understand his parables (Matthew 13:14–15).

A heart that has to be given. The words from Moses say the same from the other side: to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand, or eyes to see, or ears to hear (Deuteronomy 29:4). Something is withheld, not added. A heart that understands was always a gift, never standard equipment, and the judgment at its most terrible is God declining to supply what was never owed. So if you see Christ, it is not because you had better eyesight than those around you; you were given sight. The God who could justly have left the whole race in its stupor has spoken light into hearts that loved the dark: let light shine out of darkness (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Is it fair for God to harden people? God never hardens an innocent heart that wants him; he hands people over to what they have chosen. Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 32) before we read that the LORD hardened it (9:12), though God had foretold it (4:21); and Israel had resisted the prophets for centuries. Hardening gives people what they insisted on, a life without the light they refused, and that is just. What is owed to no one is the softening, and every softened heart is a mercy. So do not accuse God: thank him if your eyes have been opened, and pray for those whose eyes are still shut.

Could I be hardened without knowing it? Whoever asks that with real anxiety is showing the opposite of the stupor Paul describes. Hardening, as Scripture paints it, is comfortable: it does not lie awake worrying about God. If you are troubled about your heart, the trouble is a sign that God is at work, and the remedy is not to analyse yourself but to come to Christ now, while it is called today (Hebrews 3:13). The real danger is hearing the gospel again and again and quietly deciding there is no hurry. The door is open to anyone who will stop continuing in unbelief.

parallels.desc: the LORD has not given you eyes to see
a spirit of deep sleep

verseByVerse.quote: And David says, "Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them; let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s prayer against the enemies of God’s anointed has come true in Israel’s hardening: the very privileges they trusted have become their trap. Paul quotes it as evidence, not as a curse for us to use.

And David says. Paul quotes Psalm 69:22–23, a psalm of the suffering righteous man, and a modern reader flinches: David asks God to darken people’s eyes and bend their backs, and an apostle quotes it with approval. It is fair to find that hard. Three things make it bearable. First, the man praying is not nursing a private grudge; it is for God’s sake he has borne reproach (Psalm 69:7, 9). Second, an imprecation, a prayer calling down God’s judgment, is the opposite of vengeance: a man hands the case to the one Judge entitled to hear it and does nothing himself. Third, Paul is not giving us a prayer to aim at our neighbours. He is producing evidence: Scripture said this would happen, and it is happening.

A snare and a trap. A snare is set not in open country but where the animal habitually feeds, on the path it takes without thinking. The table is their feasts and comforts, and above all their religious privileges and the law in which they trusted: the sacrifices, the Passover, all the means by which God had fed them for centuries. The trap is in the dining room.

Bend their backs forever. The shape of a man under a load he cannot put down: the back of a slave. That is bitter, for the law opens by reminding Israel that God brought them out of the house of slavery (Exodus 20:2); the commandments that were a rescue have become a weight. “Forever” (dia pantos) here means continually, not necessarily eternally. Paul is quoting a lament, not announcing a verdict on Israel’s last day; they can be grafted in again (v. 23).

The psalm of the cross. The New Testament applies Psalm 69 to Christ again and again: zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17), the reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me (15:3), and the sour wine on a sponge (John 19:28–29; Matthew 27:34, 48). The psalm that supplied the vinegar at Golgotha supplies the verdict here, on those who rejected God’s anointed.

Who noticed the bent back. The one the psalm was about saw that back and offered to do something about it: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light (Matthew 11:28–30). That is addressed to exactly the posture this psalm describes. And he went further: he took the curse onto his own back, was darkened under it at noon, and carried it into the grave, so that the table could become a feast again. Now there is a table spread by him, where the bread is his body and the cup his blood, and it is no snare to anyone who comes in faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may curse Jews or anyone else. David’s prayer is a cry for God’s justice against those who persecuted his anointed king, fulfilled in God’s judgment on those who rejected Christ, and Christians are told to bless those who persecute them (12:14). Nor does it justify the shameful history of Christian hatred of Jews, which this chapter, read to its end, condemns.

May a Christian pray the cursing psalms today? Yes, as the psalms themselves teach, and with care. They are God’s word, and they voice a right longing that evil will not have the last word. A Christian who prays them hands vengeance to God rather than taking it himself (12:19), and prays first against the powers of evil, sin and Satan, and against unrepentant cruelty, rather than against personal enemies. Above all he prays them at the foot of the cross, where Christ bore the curse for those who would believe (Galatians 3:13), and so joins to his cry for justice a prayer for his enemies’ repentance, as Jesus did (Luke 23:34). He must never use them to bless his own grudges.

In everyday life. What traps a settled Christian is seldom what he knows is dangerous. It is the privilege: the Bible knowledge that has made him unteachable, the church role that has become the name he answers to, the doctrinal precision that began as reverence and now runs mostly on contempt. All good; all his table. Ask which part of your religious life you have never examined because it is so obviously good, and bring it back to the Lord who gave it.

parallels.desc: let their own table before them become a snare

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–24 — The Olive Tree: Gentiles Grafted In, Israel Recoverable
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s stumble is not a fall, and the Gentiles who have been blessed through it must not boast. Their trespass brought salvation to the nations, and that salvation is aimed back at Israel to make them jealous; if their failure meant riches for the world, how much more their full inclusion, for the root is still holy (vv. 11–16). Then the olive tree, the one people of God rooted in the promises to the patriarchs: unbelieving Jews are branches broken off, believing Gentiles wild shoots grafted in against nature (vv. 17–18). They stand only by faith, so they must fear rather than boast (vv. 19–22), and God is able to graft the natural branches back into their own tree (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Olive Tree and Replacement Theology

Romans 11:17–24 is central to the debate over supersessionism (the view that the church has simply replaced Israel, so that God has no further purpose for the Jewish people). The text resists that reading: unbelieving Jews are broken branches, not dead stumps, and can be grafted back in (on Israel and the church, see the box “Where Christians differ: Israel and the church” in the note on vv. 17–18). Verses 25–29 take this further.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some Gentile believers in Rome were in danger of looking down on Jewish unbelief. Paul’s answer is immediate: you stand only by faith, and the God who broke off natural branches can break off wild ones too. Now: The church has too often fallen into exactly the arrogance Paul warned against (see the note on vv. 17–18). God has not abandoned the people he foreknew.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous. Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s stumble is not a final fall: God has used it to bring salvation to the Gentiles in order to win Israel back, and their return will bring the world greater blessing still.

Did they stumble in order that they might fall? The whole hope of the chapter sits in the gap between two verbs. A stumble happens on the way somewhere; the man who trips is still going where he was going. A fall, in the sense denied here, is going down and not getting up. Paul does not deny that the stumble had a purpose, only that the purpose was the fall. What they tripped over has been named already: the stone laid in Zion, a refuge to the one who trusts in it and a stumbling stone to the one who will not (9:32–33). Then the chapter’s second mē genoito: by no means.

In the flow. Verses 1–10 answered whether God has rejected his people by pointing to the present remnant. Verse 11 asks whether the stumble of the rest is final, and Paul answers step by step until verse 26: all Israel will be saved.

Through their trespass. God brought good out of Israel’s sin, city by city, for a decade. Paul goes to the synagogue first, is thrown out, and turns to the Gentiles: at Pisidian Antioch, at Corinth, and later in Rome itself (Acts 13:46; 18:6; 28:28).

So as to make Israel jealous. The purpose comes from Deuteronomy 32:21, quoted at 10:19. You cannot be jealous about a stranger: for the provocation to work, the affection must still be there underneath. So the very emotion God means to stir is evidence of a bond never cut. You cannot make someone jealous of a house he was glad to leave.

Their full inclusion. Literally their fullness (plērōma), the word Paul uses again at v. 25 of the Gentiles: two fullnesses, one at each end of the mystery. If their loss brought such blessing, their fullness will bring far more, whether that is a great future turning of Israel to Christ, as many read it, or the full number of believing Jews gathered in through the age. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater, as in 5:9–10.

Riches from a rejected King. The trespass at its sharpest was Israel handing over its own Messiah to be crucified, and that is where the riches came from. Rejected by his own, Christ bore the sins of the world, and the gospel of a crucified and risen King went out to the nations. Paul calls it the unsearchable riches of Christ (Ephesians 3:8): not a consolation prize won from Israel’s loss, but Christ himself, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The riches for the world are a Person, given to the world by the people who refused him.

If God brings good out of sin, does that make the sin less bad? No; Paul says trespass and riches in one breath. Many of us have an episode we can no longer name honestly because good came out of it: the marriage that ended, the betrayal, the failure that redirected a life. We call it a blessing in disguise, and something in us knows that is not true and quietly stops trusting the whole account. The biblical way is to say both sentences, in order: that was wrong; God brought this out of it. That is the guard Romans 8:28 needs. God working all things for good never turns evil into good. It means evil does not get the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul gives himself wholeheartedly to his mission to the Gentiles partly so that his own people, seeing God’s blessing on them, will want their Messiah, and some will be saved.

Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Paul turns to face one part of the room. Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2), and when the edict lapsed, probably at his death in AD 54, many returned to a church that had become largely Gentile (see the introduction). These Gentile believers needed to see that Israel’s story is their story too, and were in danger of despising the Jewish believers sitting near them.

I magnify my ministry. Magnify (doxazō) is glorify: he honours his work among the Gentiles and gives himself to it fully, and at once says why. He wants it to look like something worth having, because some who are watching will be reached by no argument.

To save some of them. “My fellow Jews” is literally my flesh. His Gentile ministry had a Jewish goal: as Gentiles came to faith, some Jews would be stirred to seek their Messiah. “Save” means to be God’s instrument in saving them (1 Corinthians 9:22). Then the most quietly moving word in the two verses: some. The man who wished himself accursed for his people (9:3) has a working expectation of a few. Both belong to a healthy servant of God: a hope with no ceiling on it, and an estimate with no fantasy in it.

A light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel. Paul can magnify this ministry without vanity because it is not finally his (15:18), and its double aim is the aim of Christ himself. When old Simeon took the infant Jesus in his arms, he called him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel” (Luke 2:32). Paul’s mission is that sentence at work, city by city: the light going out to the nations so that Israel might yet see its own glory in the face of its own Messiah.

Should Christians still share the gospel with Jewish people? Yes, gladly and humbly, as Paul did. Some say it is unkind or even anti-Jewish, because Jewish people have their own covenant. Paul, a Jew, says the opposite: his heart’s desire and prayer was that they might be saved (10:1), and he shapes his whole ministry round that hope. It would be a strange love that kept from Jewish friends the Messiah who came from their own people. But do it in Paul’s spirit: with grief over the church’s history of contempt, with respect and patience, and with lives that make the gospel look like the fulfilment of their Scriptures rather than a foreign religion.

In everyday life. Paul’s hardest audience was people who had grown up with the faith and concluded they knew exactly what it was. Their counterparts today are the one raised in church who is finished with it, the minister’s son who has had all the arguments. What reaches them is people visibly better off for the thing they walked away from: not a performance of happiness, which they will detect at once, but lives changed by grace over years. Think of the friend who has heard it all, and ask what has passed between you recently: argument, or evidence?

verseByVerse.quote: For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel’s rejection brought reconciliation to the world, their acceptance will bring something greater still, for the people as a whole remains set apart to God through its holy root.

The reconciliation of the world. Their rejection (apobolē, casting away) is God’s setting aside of Israel for unbelief. Through it the gospel went to the nations, and the world was reconciled to God, who in Christ was reconciling the world to himself (2 Corinthians 5:19): enemies made friends, not because God overlooked sin, but because Christ took it away by his death (5:10–11). The setting aside of one people became the bringing near of every people.

What will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? Their acceptance (proslēmpsis, being received back) will be like a resurrection. The precise reference is uncertain (see the box at the end of this note), but the tone is not, and a parable of Jesus shows it. A father tells a resentful elder son why there is music coming from the house: “It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (Luke 15:32). Not a chart of the last things so much as a door opening on a feast that somebody had stopped expecting.

The firstfruits and the lump. From Numbers 15:17–21, and the picture is domestic. A woman making bread from the new harvest gives a cake from the first batch to God before any is eaten, and from then the whole batch is holy, set apart to him, because the first piece stood for the rest. The firstfruits are probably the patriarchs, or perhaps the believing remnant. Because God consecrated them, Israel as a whole remains set apart in his purpose.

If the root is holy. The root is the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to whom the promises were made: Israel is beloved for the sake of their forefathers (v. 28).
