Behind them stands the God who swore by himself because there was nobody greater to swear by (Hebrews 6:13). The change of metaphor prepares for the olive tree. A lump of dough is inert; a root is alive, and what flows through it is not merely a status but sap. God keeps a root alive through centuries of winter, and he has never yet failed to bring spring.

Life only the risen Christ can give. Whatever the phrase finally means, such life comes from one place only. Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25), and the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead gives life to mortal bodies (8:11). Israel’s acceptance, whenever and however it comes, will be Israel receiving her own risen Messiah. The phrase points past every strategy of the church to an empty tomb outside Jerusalem.

What it does not mean. Not that every Jew is personally holy or saved. “Holy” here means set apart by God’s covenant purpose, as the children of a believer are called holy in 1 Corinthians 7:14: belonging to a people God has marked as his own, not personally born again. Each branch must still be joined by faith, as the next verses show.

I came to faith late, with no Christian family. Is my faith second-hand? No. The holiness in view never came up out of any branch; it comes through the root. A branch attached last Tuesday draws on the same sap as one that has been there sixty years. Some believers quietly feel their faith is not quite the real thing: no heritage, converted out of nothing much. But nobody in God’s family is there by pedigree, and nobody draws life from his own history. Everyone draws it from Christ and the promise. Your family tree does not hold you up. His tree does.

Uncertain wording. Paul does not explain “life from the dead”, and careful readers take it two ways. Some take it as the final resurrection: Israel’s turning stands so close to the end that the general resurrection follows it. Others take it as the strongest figure available for a great spiritual quickening in the world, far beyond ordinary revival, like the dry bones of Ezekiel 37 standing up in a valley. For the second: Paul does not use his usual phrase for the resurrection, and the riches for the world of v. 12 suggest new life among the nations. For the first: the phrase is very strong, and Paul links Israel’s salvation closely with the Deliverer’s coming (v. 26). Hold the question with an open hand; either way, Israel’s return will be wonderful.
verseByVerse.note: The first portion of dough was offered to God, and it made the whole batch holy. The “root” is the patriarchs.

parallels.desc: a loaf from the first of your dough

verseByVerse.quote: But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree, do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you. — Romans 11:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentile believers have been grafted into Israel’s tree and live from its root, so they have no ground for looking down on the Jewish branches that were broken off.

The olive tree. Israel is often pictured as God’s olive tree, green and beautiful with good fruit (Jeremiah 11:16; Hosea 14:6). There is one tree, the one people of God, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs, not Israel as one tree and the church as another.

Some of the branches. Unbelieving Jews. Mark the restraint: not the tree felled, but some branches. Paul is exact about quantities (vv. 14, 25) where readers on both sides reach for totals.

A wild olive shoot. Gentile believers, wild by nature, once strangers to the promises and without God in the world (Ephesians 2:11–12), now grafted in by faith among the believing Jews. The odd horticulture is deliberate. Ordinary practice ran the other way: you joined a cultivated cutting onto hardy wild stock. (Ancient writers do mention grafting a wild shoot into a tired old tree to revive it, but that was the exception.) Paul is not mistaken about farming; he points at what nobody would do on purpose, which is what makes it grace. God did not plant a new tree for us; he grafted us into the old one, wild shoots from a barren hillside set, against all good gardening, into the richest root on earth.

The nourishing root. Literally the root of fatness, the rich sap of the tree: in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles (Galatians 3:14, 29).

Do not be arrogant toward the branches. “Arrogant” (katakauchaomai) is to boast against, to crow over, and the form of the command means “stop doing this”: the boasting was already under way in Rome. The broken branches are kinsmen to be mourned and prayed for, and Paul’s own posture at the start of chapter 9 is the model: grief, not gloating.

The root that supports you. Salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). A branch held up by a root it did not make, and could not survive ten minutes without, has nothing to boast of. Name something in your faith that you invented. The Scriptures came through Israel. The God you pray to introduced himself to Abraham, Moses and the prophets. The words you use when you have none of your own are usually a psalm by a Jewish king. The Messiah you belong to was a son of David, born under the law (Galatians 4:4). All of it arrived down the trunk.

The sap has a name. The promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, and the offspring, Paul says, is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Every promise in the root was a promise about him, so to be grafted into this tree by faith is to be joined to Christ, and to draw from him everything God swore to the fathers.

The church did not heed this. It must be said plainly. The sin Paul forbids here, Gentile Christians holding Jewish people in contempt, became over the centuries a settled habit of Christendom, dressed in theological language and eventually in far worse: expulsions, forced baptisms, massacres, and the ground prepared for the horrors of the twentieth century. Whatever else Romans 11 is, it is a warning given early, in writing, by an apostle, and disregarded. A commentary that expounds the metaphor and passes over that in silence has not really read the verse.

In everyday life. Never speak of the Jewish people with contempt, and do not laugh along when others do; if you have Jewish friends or neighbours, love them and pray for them by name.

Should Gentile Christians keep Jewish feasts or customs, then? They are free to learn from them but not required to keep them, and must never make them a badge of a higher Christianity: the feasts and food laws were a shadow, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). Christ is our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), and the Lord’s Supper, not the Seder, is the meal he commanded his church to keep. Studying the feasts, or sharing a Passover meal to teach children about the Last Supper, can deepen your grasp of the gospel. But Paul fought hard against Gentiles being told they must take on the law to be full members (Galatians 5:1–6). Honour the root by trusting the Messiah it bore, not by adopting its shadows.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Classic dispensationalists (who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, or dispensations, and expect a future national restoration of Israel) teach that God has two distinct peoples with two programmes, Israel and the church. Others teach that the church has simply replaced Israel, so that ethnic Israel has no further place. Both are held by Christians who love the Scriptures, and Paul plainly shares the dispensational concern that God keep his promises to Israel. This commentary’s view: the olive tree shows one people of God across both testaments, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs. Gentiles do not form a new tree, nor grow beside the old one; they are grafted into it. So there are not two peoples. But neither has God finished with ethnic Israel: the natural branches can be grafted back into their own tree whenever they believe (vv. 23–24), and many Reformed teachers read verses 25–26 as promising a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, while others read all Israel there as the whole people of God. The church is the continuation and fulfilment of Israel, not a separate plan, which is how Paul can tell Gentile believers that they are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Ephesians 2:19).
verseByVerse.note: Israel is often pictured as God’s olive tree.

parallels.desc: a green olive tree

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will say, "Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in." That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is true that branches were broken off and Gentiles grafted in, but the reason was unbelief, and the Gentile stands only by faith, so the right response is reverent fear, not pride.

Then you will say. Paul puts the boast into the Gentile’s mouth: they were removed to make room for me.

That is true. Paul grants the fact and refuses the conclusion. So correct doctrine is no protection: a man can have the doctrine of election exactly right, defend it from the text, and still draw from it a conclusion Paul answers with the word fear.

Through faith. The reason was unbelief, not ethnicity, and you stand only by faith, not merit. Not because of your faith, as though faith were the qualification that replaced their lineage, but through it. Faith is the empty hand that receives, and it gives no ground for boasting (3:27). Nobody stands on his own grip. He stands because of what he is gripping.

So do not become proud, but fear. Literally, do not think high thoughts. Fear here is reverent awe and humble watchfulness (Philippians 2:12; Proverbs 3:7). Three chapters ago Paul told these readers they had not received a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear (8:15), and there is no contradiction. The fear he forbade is a slave’s, who does not know whether he is owned; the fear he commands is the alertness of someone standing somewhere high who has understood exactly what is holding him up. Not the swagger of a branch that thinks it chose the tree, but the awe of a branch that knows it was chosen, cut and joined by a hand that did not have to reach for it.

The one who did not fall. What faith grips is a Person who stood where Israel fell. In the wilderness the generation of the exodus was cut off through unbelief (Hebrews 3:19); in the wilderness Jesus stood, answering each temptation with Moses’ words from Deuteronomy (Matthew 4:1–11), and where the branches proved faithless he was faithful to the point of death. To stand through faith is to stand in him, in a faithfulness never ours yet counted to us. He is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24). No grafted branch has ever stood on any other ground.

How can I fear God and still be sure of my salvation? Because the fear Paul commands is aimed at pride, not at God’s promises. The one who stands by faith looks away from himself to Christ, which is exactly where assurance comes from. What you are to fear is the thought that you stand in your own strength, or are better than those who fell. A child holding his father’s hand near a cliff edge is both perfectly safe and very careful, and the carefulness is part of the safety. If your fear drives you to Christ, it is the right kind. If it drives you into anxious self-inspection, it is the wrong kind: look at his grip, not yours (John 10:28–29).

In everyday life. Take a position you hold and are confident is biblically right: about who is in and who is out, about a group that has gone wrong, about the tradition you left. Ask what it makes you feel toward the people it excludes. If you find anything like satisfaction, Paul’s reply is verse 20: yes, that is true, and now be afraid. Then let the fear turn into prayer for those people, and into thanksgiving that you stand at all.

parallels.desc: let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God's kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s kindness and his severity are both real: the God who cut off unbelieving Israel will not spare proud Gentiles either, so they must go on trusting his kindness.

Neither will he spare you. Once-flourishing churches have been cut off: those of North Africa, home of Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine, and of Asia Minor, where all seven churches of Revelation stood. The risen Christ warned Ephesus that he would remove its lampstand unless it repented (Revelation 2:5), and in time there was no lampstand there.

Note then the kindness and the severity of God. “Note” is literally “look”: Paul makes the reader look at both. Kindness (chrēstotēs, goodness, generosity) is the word of 2:4, the kindness meant to lead to repentance. Severity (apotomia) is a rare word related to the verb to cut off; its adjective could describe a sheer face of rock.

Provided you continue in his kindness. A conditional warning. To continue (epimenō, remain, persevere) in God’s kindness is to go on trusting it rather than yourself, and the warning is against the very unbelief that broke the natural branches. The “you” is singular throughout the olive tree: Paul addresses the Gentile reader as one representative branch, so the warning reaches each person who reads it.

A God who is only one of them. It is easy to have a God who is one of these and not the other. The man whose God is all kindness has a religion that cannot account for a cross: no crisis was grave enough to require it. The one whose God is all severity cannot account for his own continued existence, and lives braced for the blow. Neither is the God who is there. You see both at full strength at Calvary: severity toward sin, poured out on the Son; kindness toward sinners, poured out from him. Here is a God severe enough to cut off his own branches and kind enough to graft in wild ones; holy enough that sin must be judged, and loving enough to bear the judgment himself.

How do I know I am continuing in his kindness? Not by a perfect record, but by where you keep returning: through falls and dry seasons you come back to God’s mercy in Christ as your only hope, rather than drifting into self-trust or indifference. The signs are simple: you still want him, still grieve over sin and confess it, still hold to the gospel, and stay among his people and under his word. A believer may be weak in all of these and still be continuing. The danger sign is not struggle but settled carelessness, the life that has stopped caring whether it is near God at all.

Could my own church be cut off? A local church or a whole denomination can lose the gospel and cease, in any real sense, to be a church of Christ. It rarely happens by a dramatic decision. It happens when the church begins to stand on something other than faith in God’s kindness: its tradition, respectability, size, culture or moral campaigns. The remedy is not panic but what Christ gave Ephesus: remember, repent, and do the works you did at first (Revelation 2:5). Pray for your church’s leaders, love the gospel at the centre of its life, and do not assume that a faithful past guarantees a future.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be cut off? Some take this verse to show that a truly saved person can lose salvation, as Arminian Christians (who hold that grace can be finally resisted and a real believer can fall away) often do; they take the warning seriously, and that is to their credit. This commentary’s view: Paul speaks here mainly of Gentiles as a group, a branch of the tree, not of each individual’s election, and the warning is one of God’s means of keeping his elect. Those truly in Christ will continue, because God keeps them (8:30, 38–39; John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). Those who fall away show that they were not truly of us, for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and true believers heed it. This is the perseverance of the saints (the Westminster Confession 17.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.1). Romans 11:22 is not meant to frighten a trusting believer out of the kingdom; a good many drowsy ones have been woken up by it.

verseByVerse.quote: And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again. For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unbelieving Jews will be grafted back in as soon as they stop refusing to believe, and the God who did the harder thing in grafting in Gentiles can surely restore the natural branches. Unbelief, not ancestry, cut them off, and unbelief is the one thing that can end.

God has the power. Humanly, a broken branch cannot be put back, and we quietly assume a hardened person has become too difficult a case. But the real doubt was never about the person; it was about God’s power, and God is able. The gardener here is not a man coaxing reluctant wood; he is the God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist (4:17). He did it for you when you were wild.

Contrary to nature. In bringing Gentiles in God did the unnatural thing, and that quietly demolishes Gentile confidence: the Gentile believer has already granted the harder of the two miracles. Putting a branch back onto the tree it grew on is not the astonishing operation. His own presence there is.

Their own olive tree. If God did the unnatural thing, how much easier the natural one. And anyone inclined to arrogance should read this phrase slowly: their own olive tree. The tree still belongs to them. The guest has been given a great deal; he has not been given the deeds.

Coming home to Israel’s King. A natural branch grafted back is a Jew coming to Jesus, and that is not leaving Israel’s tree but coming home to its fruit. Jesus called Nathanael an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit, and within minutes Nathanael answered, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” (John 1:47–49). To receive Israel’s own King is to receive what the tree was always growing.

If they must believe, what does God’s power have to do with it? Everything, because the faith that grafts them in is itself God’s gift. A branch cannot graft itself back. When someone who has long resisted Christ comes to believe, it is because God has given him new eyes and a new heart, as he did for Paul on the Damascus road. He is fully responsible and fully willing in it, but it is God who makes the dead branch willing. That is why we pray for unbelievers and do not merely argue with them, and why prayer for the hardest case is never wasted: it is addressed to the only one with the power.

Someone I love was raised in the faith and has left it. May I hope? Yes, and this verse gives you reason. Perhaps a quiet verdict has been reached about someone who grew up inside the faith and is now outside it: too far in, too long out. Read verse 24 with that person in view. The branch that once grew on the tree is the case Paul calls easier. He is not promising an outcome, and it would be cruel to pretend he is; some never return. But he tells you this is the easier kind of case, and that God is able. So keep praying, keep loving, keep the door open without nagging, and let your own life be the kind of evidence that makes them jealous.
verseByVerse.note: Growers normally grafted a cultivated branch onto wild stock; grafting a wild branch into a cultivated tree is, as Paul says, “contrary to nature.”

parallels.desc: when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–36 — The Mystery, the Promise, and the Doxology
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has revealed how his mercy will finish the story, and the revelation ends in worship. Israel’s hardening is partial and lasts only until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved by the Deliverer who takes away sins (vv. 25–27). Israel is at once opposed to the gospel for the Gentiles’ sake and loved for the patriarchs’ sake, for God never takes back his gifts and calling (vv. 28–29). He has shut all up in disobedience in order to have mercy on all (vv. 30–32). Then the argument turns to praise of the God whose ways no one can trace or advise, from whom, through whom and to whom are all things (vv. 33–36).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Irrevocability of God’s Covenant Purposes

Verse 29 is the capstone of chapters 9–11: God does not change his mind about what he has given and whom he has called. For Israel, whatever “all Israel will be saved” finally means (v. 26), it means at least that God will not abandon the people he chose. For the individual Christian, the calling God has given her will not be revoked either (see the note on vv. 29–30).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The doxology of verses 33–36 was Paul’s own response to the argument he had just made (see the note on v. 33). Now: When we want every mystery resolved into a tidy system, these verses remind us that we are not God. The depths of his wisdom and knowledge are beyond what our minds can hold, and the fitting posture before the mystery of election and salvation is Paul’s: to him be glory forever.

verseByVerse.quote: Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, "The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob"; — Romans 11:25–26
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has revealed that Israel’s hardening is partial and temporary, lasting until the full number of the Gentiles has come in, and that in this way all Israel will be saved by the Deliverer. Paul discloses it to humble the Gentile believers, not to hand them a timetable.

Lest you be wise in your own sight. The phrase echoes Proverbs 3:7. The greatest disclosure about the future in the letter is given to stop Christians thinking too well of themselves. It is medicine for conceit, and a reader who comes away with a firmer grip on a timetable and no change in how he regards anybody has taken the medicine and kept the disease.

This mystery. A “mystery” (mystērion) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God (16:25; Ephesians 3:3–6): not a puzzle for clever readers, but a secret God has chosen to tell. It crowns the olive tree. In verses 23–24 Paul argued that God is able to graft Israel back in; now he reveals that God will, the fullest answer to the question of v. 1.

A partial hardening has come upon Israel. Partial, for the remnant believes: all through this chapter Paul writes in fractions, not totals. And the hardening is limited in time.

Until the fullness. The most important word in the sentence is “until”. The clause that announces the hardening also sets its limit, which a permanent rejection would not have. The fullness of the Gentiles is the full number of elect Gentiles that God intends to save, coming into the people of God.

In this way. “In this way” (houtōs) means in this manner, by this process: through the hardening of part of Israel, the coming in of the Gentiles, and the jealousy that provokes Israel to faith. Some hear a sense of sequence too, but the stress falls on how God brings it about.

The Deliverer will come from Zion. From Isaiah 59:20–21, with words from Isaiah 27:9. The Deliverer is Christ: Paul’s word (ho rhyomenos, the one who rescues) is the one he uses of Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10). What the Deliverer does is the gospel itself (compare Acts 3:26): ungodliness is banished, and sins are taken away. That rules out the popular idea that Israel has a separate way of salvation, by its covenant alone and without Christ. The hope of v. 26 is enormous, and it is the same hope, by the same Saviour, as everybody else’s.

What it does not mean. It gives no ground whatever for anti-Jewish hatred. Nor does any modern political state fulfil this prophecy: Paul speaks of conversion to Christ, and what he promises is forgiveness (v. 27), not territory. Christians may pray for the Jewish people and judge the policies of the modern state as they would any other nation’s.

Does all Israel mean every Jewish person who has ever lived? No. In the Old Testament the phrase usually means the nation as a body, not every single person (1 Samuel 7:5; 2 Chronicles 12:1). So on the reading that expects a future turning, Paul’s hope is that the Jewish people as a people, in great numbers, will turn to Christ; on the reading that takes all Israel as the whole people of God, it is the full number of the saved, Jew and Gentile. It does not mean that Jews who die rejecting him are saved, any more than Gentiles who reject him are.

When will this happen, and should we watch for signs? Paul gives no date: only God knows when the fullness of the Gentiles is complete, so do not read it off the news or treat events in the Middle East as a countdown. Scripture names things that come before Christ’s return, such as the gospel reaching the nations (Matthew 24:14) and a final rebellion (2 Thessalonians 2:3), and on many readings this turning of Israel is one of them; but none is given us as a date (Matthew 24:36). Our task is the one this chapter gives: preach the gospel to the nations, love and pray for Jewish people, and stay humble. His people will be ready by being faithful, not by being well informed about a timetable.

Where Christians differ: who is all Israel? Three main views are held among Reformed Christians. First, all Israel is the whole church, Jew and Gentile, the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16); this was Calvin’s view. Second, all Israel is the total of elect Jews saved throughout history, the remnant in every generation, as in vv. 1–10. Third, all Israel is the Jewish people as a whole, who will turn to Christ in large numbers in the future, before his return. Dispensationalists (who divide history into distinct eras and keep God’s plan for Israel distinct from his plan for the church) add a separate future plan for national Israel in a thousand-year kingdom; many of them are earnest Bible readers whose love for the Jewish people this commentary shares. This commentary’s view: it does not press one reading, because godly Reformed teachers have held each. Many find the third the most natural reading of verses 25–26, and it is held here with humility: in verse 25 Israel means ethnic Israel, distinguished from the Gentiles, and it would be strange for the word to change meaning in the next sentence; and the contrast of now and then (vv. 12, 15, 23–24, 30–31) and the full inclusion of v. 12 seem to look for something greater than a remnant. Those who hold the first view answer that in this way describes the manner and not the time, and that Paul has already widened the name Israel in 9:6 (not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel); those who hold the second stress that the remnant is how God has always saved Israel. On every reading, any Jew is saved exactly as any Gentile is: through the gospel, by faith in Christ, into the one olive tree, the church. It is not a separate plan of salvation, and it does not require a rebuilt temple or a thousand-year earthly kingdom. It fits the amillennial view, which this commentary holds: the thousand years of Revelation 20 picture Christ’s present reign, and the church age ends with his one visible return, the resurrection and the judgment, with no secret rapture (an unseen coming to remove believers before a final tribulation). Premillennial Christians, who expect an earthly reign after his return, read the order of events differently, and they are honoured brothers. The Westminster Larger Catechism teaches us to pray for the calling of the Jews (Q. 191), and no reading permits contempt.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s quotation does not match Isaiah exactly. In the Hebrew of Isaiah 59:20 the Redeemer comes to Zion, and the Greek Old Testament has for the sake of Zion; Paul says from Zion. Readers differ over whether he means Christ’s first coming, whose gospel went out from Jerusalem, or his return from the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22), and the text does not settle it. Either way the Deliverer is Christ, and his work is to take away sins.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God. Interpreters differ over whether “all Israel” means the Jewish people as a whole before the end, or the whole company of God’s people, Jew and Gentile. The more natural reading in context is the first: a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ.

parallels.desc: a Redeemer will come to Zion

verseByVerse.quote: "and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins." As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s covenant promise to Israel is the forgiveness of sins, and though unbelieving Israel now stands opposed to the gospel, God still loves them for the sake of the patriarchs.

When I take away their sins. Isaiah 59:21 joined with Isaiah 27:9, echoing the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33–34. What God guarantees is not territory or a political settlement but forgiveness of sins in Christ, the heart of the new covenant (Hebrews 8:8–12), the same thing Paul has offered everybody since chapter 3.

Enemies for your sake. In relation to the gospel, unbelieving Israel stands opposed to the message and under God’s displeasure, and their rejection opened the door for the Gentiles. “For your sake” ought to stop a proud Gentile reader: the hostility he might feel superior to is what opened the door he walked through. No posture is left him but gratitude, and gratitude cannot be combined with contempt.

Beloved for the sake of their forefathers. God loved the fathers and chose their offspring after them (Deuteronomy 4:37; 7:8). They are loved on somebody else’s account: not for anything in the present generation, but because of promises made to men dead for nearly two thousand years. Our God does not lose track of a promise or let a covenant lapse.

Loved for another’s sake. If that seems arbitrary, it is the only way anyone in this letter is loved. Every Christian is loved for the sake of another: by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (5:19). Israel’s case is no exception to the gospel but the gospel applied to a nation, and the promises made to its fathers were always promises about Christ.

How can people be God’s enemies and beloved at the same time? God’s relation to people has more than one side. While someone rejects Christ he stands under God’s displeasure; that is the enemy side. Yet God may have purposes of love toward him not yet carried out, as he had toward every believer before conversion: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (5:10). Every Christian was once both. So this verse keeps us from two errors: pretending unbelief does not matter, and writing off those presently against the gospel. God has not written them off.

In everyday life. Paul holds two true things about the same people in one sentence and lets neither cancel the other. Take the person you are most tangled with and put both halves in one line, joined by and rather than but: what is actually wrong, and what is actually true of them and of your bond. Paul managed it about people who had tried to have him killed, because God had held both halves about him: once an enemy, and beloved.

parallels.desc: when he takes away his sin

verseByVerse.quote: For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God never takes back what he has given or whom he has called, so his choice of Israel still stands. And the Gentiles’ own story shows how his mercy can overtake disobedience.

Irrevocable. “Irrevocable” (ametamelētos) is built on the verb to regret, with the negative in front: without regret, never taken back. The gifts are the privileges of 9:4–5, the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the promises; the calling is God’s choosing of Israel as his people.

No regret in God. Everyone knows what it is to give generously and regret it afterwards; there is none of that in God. Someone may object that the LORD regretted making Saul king (1 Samuel 15:11). He did, and the same chapter adds that the Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret, for he is not a man (15:29). The first speaks of God’s real grief over sin as it unfolds in history; the second of his purpose, which never changes. God can be grieved by what his people do. He is never caught out by it.

You were at one time disobedient. Paul reminds his Gentile readers of their own past (Ephesians 2:2; Colossians 3:7): they received mercy because Israel’s disobedience sent the gospel their way. Their own story proves that disobedience need not be the last word, and verse 31 applies the same logic to Israel.

He loved them to the end. The clearest picture of gifts given without regret is an upper room. Jesus knew that one of the twelve had already agreed to betray him and the boldest would deny him before dawn. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (John 13:1), and he knelt and washed their feet. He called Peter knowing about the courtyard and the fire, and after the resurrection came looking for him by the lake to give him his commission again (John 21:15–17). That is irrevocable calling with a human face.

A comfort for every believer. In context the sentence is about Israel, but extending it to the individual believer is legitimate, because the same logic produced the chain of 8:29–30. If God does not take back his calling of a nation that refused his own Son, he will not take back his call to you on the day you fail him. Before the foundation of the world he knew every failure and betrayal of his people, and chose them anyway. He did not regret Abraham, or Jacob, or David, or you. His Son went to the cross knowing exactly whom he was dying for, and he does not look back on it with regret.

Does irrevocable mean a minister who falls into serious sin keeps his calling to office? No. Paul speaks of God’s saving call, not of church office. Scripture sets qualifications for elders (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9), and a man who disqualifies himself must step down, whatever his gifts. God may restore such a man to fellowship and use him again, but the church must not quote Romans 11:29 to shield a leader from discipline or to protect the institution at the expense of those he has wronged.

In everyday life. If you carry a private theory about what would finally exhaust God’s patience, some specific thing you suspect would be the end of it, name it. Verse 29 does not weigh whether it would be bad enough. It says that for those God has called there is no such thing. Bring it to him in confession, and leave it with the God who has no regrets about you.

parallels.desc: God is not man, that he should lie

verseByVerse.quote: so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy. For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mercy to the Gentiles will in turn bring mercy to disobedient Israel, for God has shut up Jew and Gentile alike in disobedience so that he may have mercy on both.

That they also may now receive mercy. The pattern reverses: Jewish disobedience brought mercy to Gentiles, and mercy to Gentiles will bring mercy to Jews. Neither group is the senior partner. If the second “now” stands (see the textual note), the time of mercy for Israel is the present gospel age.

Consigned all to disobedience. “Consigned” (synkleiō) means to shut in with no way out. Luke uses it of fish trapped in a net (Luke 5:6), and Paul of the Scripture imprisoning everything under sin (Galatians 3:22). The picture is not a courtroom but a cell with the whole human race in it, Jew and Gentile together, every exit tried and found locked.

That he may have mercy on all. God closed every other door so that the only one left would be the one that opens from outside. “All” here means all kinds, Jew and Gentile alike.

The door into the cell. Paul’s other use of the word shows who that door is: the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe (Galatians 3:22). Jesus said, “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9). God sent his Son into the cell to carry the sentence and walk out with the key. Not one prisoner comes out by his own merit, so not one can boast; every one comes out by mercy, so every one can sing.

In the flow. Verse 32 retells the whole letter so far. God has consigned all to disobedience is the verdict of 1:18–3:20; that he may have mercy on all is the message of 3:21–8:39; and the Jew and Gentile held together in that all have been the subject of chapters 9 to 11. The only place left to go is worship (vv. 33–36).

Did God make people disobey? No. God is never the author of sin, and no one is forced to disobey against his will (James 1:13). The disobedience was ours, freely chosen, as chapter 1 showed. What God did was shut the doors: he gave the law, which exposed sin, let Jew and Gentile prove what was in them, and closed off every route to salvation by merit. A doctor may show a patient the full results of the tests before he offers the cure, not because he caused the disease, but so that the cure is received as a cure.

Where Christians differ: universal salvation. Some read “mercy on all” as meaning that every human being will finally be saved. This commentary’s view: the context is about two groups, Jews and Gentiles, not every individual. Paul has just spoken of branches cut off and of God’s severity (v. 22), and elsewhere of eternal destruction (2 Thessalonians 1:9). He hopes to save some of his countrymen (v. 14), and he opened chapter 9 in anguish over people he expects to be lost. The two alls are the same width, and the whole argument since chapter 9 has told us what that width is: two categories, not every person. God shows mercy on both groups without distinction, but not all individuals are saved. Hell is real and conscious and eternal (Matthew 25:46).

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, omit the second “now”, as the ESV notes.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the second “now.”

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s argument ends in worship of a God whose riches, wisdom and knowledge are too deep to fathom, and whose ways no one can trace. Doctrine is meant to lead to doxology, from doxa, glory.

Oh, the depth! Three depths: the riches of his grace and mercy (2:4; 9:23; 10:12); the wisdom of his plan, which uses even sin and hardening to bring salvation to the world; and the knowledge by which he foreknew his people and sees all things. Eleven chapters of close reasoning do not end in a conclusion. They end with a man running out of language in front of God and saying so.

How unsearchable are his judgments. “Unsearchable” (anexeraunētos) means what cannot be fully investigated. You can follow God’s decisions a long way, as Paul has just done, but you will not reach the bottom.

And how inscrutable his ways! “Inscrutable” (anexichniastos) is built on ichnos, a footprint: his ways cannot be tracked. You can see where he has been, and you cannot reconstruct the route. Israel’s own hymnbook said so of the greatest thing God ever did for them: “Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen” (Psalm 77:19). The defining act of the nation’s history left no tracks.

A depth with a name. The wisdom of this plan is a Person: Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). And the word for untraceable is the one Paul uses for “the unsearchable riches of Christ” (Ephesians 3:8), so the depth that cannot be traced has a name. God made a path through the sea and left no footprints, and he made a path to the cross that no one could have predicted and no one can now undo.

What it does not mean. Not that God is irrational or that we can know nothing about him. He has revealed much, as Romans shows, and what he has revealed opens onto a depth no creature can fathom. The verse is often used to shut down hard questions, but nobody reasons harder than the man who wrote chapters 9 to 11. The doxology stands at the end of the argument, not instead of it.

A depth, not a muddle. Paul leaves some questions standing: why these and not those, how hardening and human responsibility fit together, what life from the dead means. He calls the unexplained remainder depth, a word of praise. A muddle is something you have failed to sort out; a depth is something you have come to the edge of. We will never reach the bottom of him, and that is our joy: we will spend eternity discovering that he is more than we thought.

Is it wrong to be troubled by chapters 9 to 11? No. Paul himself began this section with great sorrow and unceasing anguish (9:2). Hard questions here are not a sign of unbelief, and you need not pretend to feel no difficulty. But look where Paul’s troubled mind went. He took the questions to Scripture, reasoned as far as God had revealed, and then, at the edge of what he could see, worshipped rather than accused. The same road is open to you. Ask honestly, study, talk to mature believers, and when you reach the limit, let the remaining mystery make God bigger in your eyes, not smaller.

parallels.desc: my thoughts are not your thoughts

verseByVerse.quote: "For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ever seen into God’s mind or advised him, so his plan of salvation is his own wisdom alone, and that is a comfort before it is a rebuke.

The mind of the Lord. From Isaiah 40:13, in the great chapter on God’s incomparable greatness. The verse is usually quoted to silence people who question God, but Isaiah spoke it to comfort exiles, a beaten, deported people whose complaint is quoted a few verses later: “My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God” (Isaiah 40:27). They are not complaining that God is too free. They are afraid he has lost track of them.

Or who has been his counselor? No one advised God when he planned salvation; his plan comes from his own wisdom alone (Job 15:8; Jeremiah 23:18). To those exiles that is comfort, not rebuke: his handling of their case has not been delegated, or advised, or worked out from partial information. And there is a quieter mercy still. If nobody has ever been God’s counsellor, nobody has ever successfully briefed him against you. No one got to him first; there is no version of your file that someone else gave him. And this is the mind that decided, without anyone needing to suggest it, to save the ungodly at the cost of his own Son. No one could have advised it; no one would have dared.

One who has known. Among creatures the answer is no one. But there is one exception, and he is not a creature: “no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27), and “No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). The mind no creature could search came to us in a Person who has always known it from within, and so Paul can say, astonishingly, we have the mind of Christ (1 Corinthians 2:16).

Built, not blurted. The three questions of vv. 34–35 answer the three nouns of v. 33 in reverse order: his knowledge (who has known his mind), his wisdom (who has been his counsellor), his riches (who has given to him). Paul is no less careful in worship than in argument.

If no one advises God, why pray? Because God has ordained prayer as one of the means by which he carries out his plans, and he delights to hear his children. You are not informing him or persuading him to be kinder than he was; you are a child bringing his needs to a Father who has promised to act through the prayers of his people (James 5:16; Matthew 7:7–11). Prayer changes things because God has decided that it will, and it changes the one who prays, bringing his will into line with God’s. Pray boldly, and leave the counsel to him.

parallels.desc: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: "Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ever put God in his debt, so nothing we receive from him is a payment: it is all gift. In one line this is the message of Romans: salvation is by grace, not earned.

Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid? From Job 41:11 (see also Job 35:7), where God speaks out of the whirlwind, near the end of one of the longest and least comfortable answers in Scripture: “Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Whatever is under the whole heaven is mine.” No one can claim that God owes him salvation. Everything we have, including the faith we give him, he first gave us: what do you have that you did not receive? (1 Corinthians 4:7).

The ledger nailed to a cross. There is a ledger in the gospel, but it runs the other way. God was never our debtor; we were his, with a debt no one could pay. And he dealt with it himself, cancelling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). The only one who ever gave God everything he owed was the Son, obedient to the point of death, and he gave it not to put the Father in his debt but to clear ours. No one can make God owe him; at the cross God chose to pay what we owed. He needed nothing from us, and yet he gave us his Son, his Spirit, his kingdom and himself.

The background hum. The instinct this verse kills is rarely admitted aloud: the faint sense, after a stretch of obedience, that something is now owed, that faithful service has bought a measure of protection. It is not usually a belief but a background hum, and it becomes audible the moment life goes wrong.

What if God did owe you? You would have a claim. But a debt paid is not a gift given, and a God who was settling an account with you would not be loving you. Think of the friend who visits because he owes you and the friend who visits because he wanted to see you: what makes the second visit worth anything is the absence of obligation. Verse 35 is about God’s independence, and it is also the guarantee that nothing you have ever received from him was a payment.

But do we not give to God when we give money, time or service? We do, and he receives it gladly; but every gift we bring was his before it was ours. When Israel gave lavishly for the temple, David said: all things come from you, and of your own have we given you (1 Chronicles 29:14). Giving to God is not a deposit that puts him in our debt but a small part of what he lent us, returned in thanks and love, and so cheerful, not calculating (2 Corinthians 9:7).

In everyday life. The hum is loudest on the day something goes wrong after a good stretch, and the question rises by itself: after all I have done? Nothing you did put God in your debt, so nothing that happens to you is God defaulting on one. And everything good in your day came without a ledger, so you are free to give that way too, to someone who cannot repay you.

parallels.desc: who has first given to me, that I should repay him?

verseByVerse.quote: For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything that exists comes from God, is kept by him and exists for his glory, so the only fitting end to the argument is praise.

From him, through him, to him. The whole of reality in one sentence, salvation included: planned by him, carried out through him, and ending in his praise. Each preposition closes a door. From him: nothing that exists brought itself. Through him: nothing that exists keeps itself going. To him: nothing that exists is its own point.

The frame of three chapters. Chapter 9 opened with Paul in grief, breaking off to bless the Christ who came from Israel: God over all, blessed forever. Amen (9:5). Here at the far end he says Amen again. He does not arrive at praise because his difficulties dissolved, but because the God he could not fully trace turned out, when the argument was finished, to be more merciful than the argument had made him fear: a God who shut everyone in so that he could let everyone out, and who has not taken back a single thing he ever gave.

To him be glory forever. Amen. Glory (doxa) is honour, praise, weight. The Westminster Shorter Catechism begins here: our chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him forever (Q. 1). Amen means so be it, truly; it is Paul putting his name to everything God has done.

Christ at the centre. Paul gives these same prepositions to the Son: one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things (1 Corinthians 8:6); all things were created through him and for him, and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16–17).

There is no fourth preposition. From him, and through him, and to him, are all things. Every galaxy and atom, every hour of every life ever lived, the election of Abraham, the hardening of Pharaoh, the seven thousand, the remnant, the olive tree, the cross and the empty tomb, the fullness of the Gentiles and the salvation of all Israel: it began in him, it is being carried by him, and it is going home to him, and nothing anywhere falls outside the three. To him be glory forever. Amen.

A universe going somewhere. The modern West has mostly been taught a different story. In 1903 Bertrand Russell, in an essay called “A Free Man’s Worship”, told it with bleak honesty: we are the product of causes that never foresaw what they were making, and all the labour, devotion and genius of the ages is headed for extinction in the death of the solar system. The only honest foundation for life, he said, was “unyielding despair”. Almost no one lives like that: we go on loving our children and doing our work as though they mattered, borrowing meaning from a story we say we no longer believe. Paul gives the story that fits the way we actually live. Everything comes from someone, is held by someone, and is going home to someone, and the One at the end of the road is not blind matter but the God who locked everyone in so that he could have mercy on all (v. 32). The universe does not end in a vast death. It ends in a doxology.

Does all things include evil and suffering? Yes, in the sense that nothing happens outside God’s rule and purpose, but not in the sense that he does evil. God ordains whatever comes to pass, yet in such a way that he is not the author of sin, and the responsibility of creatures is not taken away (the Westminster Confession 3.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 3.1). Joseph’s brothers sold him, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The cross was the greatest evil ever done, and it was through him and to his glory. So when suffering comes, you are not in the hands of chance or of the devil, but of the God from whom, through whom and to whom all things are, who is working even this toward his glory and your good.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin.<sup>2</sup>God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel?<sup>3</sup>“Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.”<sup>4</sup>But what is God’s reply to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”<sup>5</sup>So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace.<sup>6</sup>But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.<sup>7</sup>What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened,<sup>8</sup>as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day.”<sup>9</sup>And David says, “Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them;<sup>10</sup>let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever.”<sup>11</sup>So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous.<sup>12</sup>Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!<sup>13</sup>Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry<sup>14</sup>in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.<sup>15</sup>For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?<sup>16</sup>If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.<sup>17</sup>But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree,<sup>18</sup>do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you.<sup>19</sup>Then you will say, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.”<sup>20</sup>That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.<sup>21</sup>For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.<sup>22</sup>Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.<sup>23</sup>And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again.<sup>24</sup>For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.<sup>25</sup>Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in.<sup>26</sup>And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, “The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob”;<sup>27</sup>“and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins.”<sup>28</sup>As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.<sup>29</sup>For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.<sup>30</sup>For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,<sup>31</sup>so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy.<sup>32</sup>For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.<sup>33</sup>Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!<sup>34</sup>“For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”<sup>35</sup>“Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?”<sup>36</sup>For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.

12.title: The Transformed Life
12.overview:
Where we are. Romans 12 opens the last main part of the letter (chapters 12–16). After eleven chapters on what God has done in Christ, ending in praise (11:33–36), Paul’s first word is “therefore”: the life he now describes grows out of that gospel.

The message. God has been merciful to you beyond measure, so give yourself back to him, body and mind, every day. That offering looks like a sober view of yourself, your gift used for others in the one body, and a love that is real, warm and humble, that refuses revenge and overcomes evil with good. This is not a turn from doctrine to duty but the gospel believed.

Why it was said. The Roman church mixed Jewish and Gentile believers, slaves and free, and the strain between them lies behind much of the letter (see the introduction). Such a church needed humility more than gifts, and love more than opinions. It had already felt the capital’s hostility in the expulsion under Claudius, and worse was coming: hence the stress on blessing persecutors and leaving vengeance to God.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–2 are the hinge: the mercies of God call for a living sacrifice and a renewed mind. Verses 3–8 put the renewed mind to work on how you see yourself and your place among the varied gifts of the one body. Verses 9–21 unfold one heading, “Let love be genuine”, in widening circles: within the church (vv. 9–13), towards persecutors and the lowly (vv. 14–16), and at last towards enemies (vv. 17–21).

Where it leads. Christ’s face is in every line. He received a body in order to offer it (Hebrews 10:5–10). His was the mind that stooped (Philippians 2:5–8). He hands out the gifts as spoils of his victory, and met the persecutor Saul with mercy instead of a curse. Above all, at the cross he overcame evil with good, bearing the vengeance due to his enemies and then feeding them. The chapter is a portrait of the Son being formed in his brothers.

For us. Begin each day where Paul begins, with the mercies, and then hand yourself over again: your body, your gift, your grievances. Ask where the age is pressing you into its shape, whom in your church you have not yet honoured, and which enemy you could feed this week.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Living Sacrifice and the Renewed Mind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because God has been so merciful, the only reasonable response is to give him your whole self and let him remake your mind. Paul appeals by the mercies of chapters 1–11, not by obligation, and asks for your body: an ordinary life handed over day by day as a living sacrifice (v. 1). Then he names the two forces at work on that life, the mould of the present age and the renewing of the mind, which makes a believer able to recognise and approve the will of God (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body as Instrument of Worship

Romans 12:1 refuses to divide life into a sacred part that belongs to God and a secular part that does not. The body presented to God as a living sacrifice is itself where worship happens, so daily work, rest, eating and drinking, money and marriage can all be offered to God in faith. The Reformers drew much of their teaching on the holiness of ordinary callings from passages like this. John Calvin saw the whole creation as the theatre of God’s glory; Paul places that vision in the offered body of the believer.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish and Gentile readers alike knew what a sacrifice was: an offering brought to an altar and given up to God. Now the Christian’s whole life is the offering, brought to God day by day. Now: Every culture, including the church’s own subculture, presses its assumptions on us about worth, success and meaning. The renewal of the mind is God’s answer to that pressure: learning to see life through Scripture and the mercies of God until the world’s measures lose their hold.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. — Romans 12:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has shown you such mercy, give him your whole self, and let him remake your thinking instead of letting the world shape it. This is the gospel of chapters 1–11 being lived: the only reasonable answer to mercy.

I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God. “Therefore”, a word easy to step over, ties everything that follows to all Paul has said, and “appeal” (parakaleō) is a pastor’s pleading, not a cold order. He grounds it not in the law or in what you owe but in eleven chapters of mercies: justification as a free gift (3:24), no condemnation (8:1), a Spirit who prays when praying is beyond us (8:26), nothing able to separate us from his love (8:39).

The mercies. The plural is deliberate. Oiktirmoi is the Greek Old Testament’s word for God’s compassions, translating Hebrew words related to the word for a womb: the ache of a parent over a child. It is God’s settled attitude, not one act of pardon, and every one of these mercies is given in Christ, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood (3:24–25), so that his righteous anger no longer falls on us. The mercies also set the order of obedience, which most of us reverse. Very little is asked of anyone in this letter until chapter 12 (the appeals of chapter 6 are the main exception): mercy comes first, and obedience follows as a response, never as a way to earn it. A Christian life that begins with the appeal and treats the mercies as background music will not run for long.

To present your bodies as a living sacrifice. “Present” (paristēmi) is the regular word for bringing an offering to the altar, as at 6:13 and 19, now with the whole letter behind it. What is brought is your bodies: your whole self as you live in the world, eyes, hands, tongue and time. Intentions can be offered from an armchair and cost nothing. Your body is the one part of you that has to turn up, and it leaves a record.

A living sacrifice. Old Testament sacrifices were killed. Ours is offered alive, not to atone, for that was finished once for all (Hebrews 10:14), but in thanksgiving. A dead sacrifice stays where it is put; a living one has legs, and can get up and walk off the altar, usually without deciding to. So the offering is not one moment but a daily presenting, in an ordinary life.

Holy and acceptable to God. Set apart for God, and well-pleasing to him. An animal once set apart for the altar could not be exchanged or taken back, for it belonged to the LORD (Leviticus 27:9–10); a life presented to God is not ours to reclaim on Monday. Our offerings are never without blemish, yet they are “acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:5): the Father receives a stammering, half-hearted life because it comes through his Son, who offered the one unblemished life in our place and whose obedience is counted as ours (5:19).

Which is your spiritual worship. “Worship” (latreia) is the priestly service of the temple (9:4), and “spiritual” here means fitting, reasonable (see “Uncertain wording” below). After such mercies, giving your whole life to God is not extreme devotion but the only reasonable response, and worship is the whole of life, not only Sunday.

Do not be conformed to this world. “Conformed” (syschēmatizō) means pressed into a shape, like dough in a mould, and “this world” is literally this age (aiōn), the present evil age (Galatians 1:4). You cannot escape an age by moving house or joining a smaller church. The mould is made of what everyone around you assumes without ever arguing for it: that you are what you earn, that your body is your own, that a good life is a comfortable one. And that world is passing away (1 John 2:17).

But be transformed by the renewal of your mind. “Transformed” is metamorphoō, used of Jesus transfigured on the mountain (Matthew 17:2) and of believers changed into his image “from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18): not improvement but a change of form. Both verbs describe something that keeps on being done to you by the Spirit. Yet you are not idle: you decide what you put your mind under, what you read, whose company you keep, what you rehearse while driving. Nobody drifts into a renewed mind. They drift into the world’s shape.

That by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. “Testing” (dokimazō) is to approve after testing, as metal is assayed. It closes a circle: those who did not see fit (on testing, did not approve) to acknowledge God were given up to a debased mind, adokimos, failed metal (1:28). The judgment lost there is given back here. The will of God is his moral will revealed in Scripture, not secret guidance: good, pleasing to him, and perfect, lacking nothing.

A body prepared for him. Before God asked for our bodies, he had received one. Hebrews hears Christ coming into the world with the words of Psalm 40, “a body have you prepared for me” and “I have come to do your will, O God”, and adds: “by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:5–10). (Hebrews follows the Greek translation of Psalm 40:6; your English Old Testament reads “you have given me an open ear”.) His whole bodily life was presented: hands laid on lepers, feet set towards Jerusalem, a back given to those who struck him, and at last a body on the cross. Our living sacrifice is not a second atonement but the response his offering makes possible: bodies that belong to God because his body was given for them.

The rebels all dress alike. We prize being ourselves; nobody wants to be conformed. Yet any photograph from twenty years ago shows a generation of rebels in near-identical clothes, holding near-identical opinions. Alexis de Tocqueville noticed nearly two centuries ago, visiting America, that a society of equals, with no king or established church to tell it what to think, could be ruled by something more insistent: the pressure of what everyone else already thinks. Religious people have their own mould too. “Be yourself” cannot free anyone, because it sends you inward to find a self, and you come back with whatever the age has put there. What breaks the mould is a self given from outside: someone who has heard what God thinks of him in Christ has nothing left to prove to the crowd, and can afford to be different.

What it does not mean. Not withdrawal from the world: Jesus prayed not that his Father would take us out of the world but that he would keep us from the evil one (John 17:15). The change happens from the inside, in the middle of ordinary life.

How do I make a big decision, like a job, a move or whom to marry? Verse 2 promises not a signal, an impression or an opening door, but a competence: a mind remade to weigh a situation and recognise what is good. God’s usual answer to “What should I do?” is not an instruction; he changes the person deciding. So begin with what he has revealed: marry only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39), take no job that requires you to sin, keep your promises. Within those bounds he usually gives freedom. Pray for wisdom (James 1:5). Ask which option will help you love God and others, use your gifts, and stay under good teaching in a faithful church. Take counsel from mature believers who know you (Proverbs 15:22). Then decide, and trust God with the outcome. If you honestly sought to please him, you have not missed his will.

What does renewing my mind look like in practice? It is slow and ordinary. Read Scripture to let it reshape what you love, not only for information. Sit under faithful preaching and carry one truth into the week. Memorise a few verses for anxious or tempted moments. Notice which voices fill most hours of your week, phone, news, entertainment, friends, and change the balance. Pray Scripture back to God. Change is like a tree’s growth: you rarely see it happen, but you see that it has happened.

In everyday life. Offer yourself to God, body, work and words, before the day claims them. When you wonder whether anything is changing, look back rather than in: seeing now what you could not see five years ago is this verse at work. And where change is slower than you hoped, the offering still stands, for the Father receives it for his Son’s sake, not for its quality.

Uncertain wording. “Spiritual worship” translates logikē latreia. Latreia is clearly worship; logikos is harder to put into English. It comes from logos (word, reason) and usually meant rational or reasonable, which is why the ESV note offers “rational service” and older versions read reasonable service. Others hear in it worship of the inner person rather than of animal sacrifices (the same word describes the spiritual milk of 1 Peter 2:2). The senses are close: worship that fits what God has done and engages the whole person, mind included, which is why Paul turns at once to the renewal of the mind.
verseByVerse.note: “Therefore” builds on chapters 1–11: the mercies of God come first, then the response. The ESV notes that “spiritual worship” can also be rendered “rational service.”

parallels.desc: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–8 — Gifts of Grace: Sober Self-Assessment in the Body
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A renewed mind sees itself soberly and serves gladly, because every gift is grace. Paul begins with an honest view of yourself, neither pride nor false modesty, measured by what God has given (v. 3). The church is one body with many members, where difference is the design and not a defect, and each belongs to the others (vv. 4–5). So use the gift you were given, and use it well: the gifts of vv. 6–8 are a sample, not a full list, and most of them come with a manner, generosity, zeal, cheerfulness.
verseByVerse.theology:
Charismata: Gifts of the Spirit for the Common Good

The gifts of Romans 12 are what Paul elsewhere calls charismata, gifts of grace. Each is given for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7), not to make its owner more admired (on gifts left unused, see v. 6).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The first churches mixed slaves and free, Jews and Greeks, the educated and the unlettered, and the Spirit’s gifts crossed every one of those lines: a slave might teach, and an educated Greek might serve tables. Now: Churches still drift toward two opposite errors: prizing the visible, up-front gifts until a hierarchy forms, or overlooking the ordinary gifts until people conclude they have nothing to give. Romans 12:6–8 holds the balance: every gift, faithfully used, is grace from God and service to the body.

verseByVerse.quote: For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. — Romans 12:3
verseByVerse.commentary:
A renewed mind sees itself truly, neither inflated nor running itself down, because everything it has was given by God. This is Paul’s first application of verse 2, and he addresses it to everyone.

For by the grace given to me. Paul’s apostolic authority was itself a gift of grace (1:5; 15:15): he speaks from the grace he is commending.

Not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think. Paul uses words built on the verb think (phroneō) four times in one line: do not over-think yourself (hyperphroneō) beyond what you ought, but think so as to be sound-minded (sōphroneō). The first fruit of a renewed mind is a right view of yourself, and it is said to everyone, not only the leaders or the gifted, because Paul expects pride in every person in the room. Pride is often the last thing renewed and the first to corrupt everything else, and a body cannot function if every member has privately concluded it is the head (v. 4). The same verb returns at v. 16, so humility frames everything Paul says about the church in verses 3–16.

But to think with sober judgment. A sober mind is sound and sensible: not solemn, but realistic, an estimate of yourself that is not under the influence of anything. The man who says he is no good at anything is not being humble but inaccurate, and often he is fishing for a compliment. False modesty is still pride: it has learned that running yourself down wins more praise than boasting. A sober mind can say “I am good at this” in a level voice, because the sentence is a fact about a gift rather than a claim about a person.

Each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. “Measure” (metron) is a portion, an allotment (see “Uncertain wording” below). Whatever you have was given, which leaves no room for boasting, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7), or for comparing yourself with others (Galatians 6:4). The measure was assigned to you. Nobody else was issued yours.

The mind that was in Christ. Paul’s verb is the one he reaches for to describe the mind of Christ himself: “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:5–6). There is sober thinking in its perfect form. Christ alone could have thought of himself as highly as possible without exaggeration, and his true knowledge of himself made him stoop, all the way to the cross. And the cross makes sober thinking possible for us. Whoever has stood there knows what he was worth without grace and what he was worth to God, and those two facts kill pride from opposite sides.

Does God give different amounts of saving faith? No. Saving faith is not graded: the weakest faith in Christ saves as surely as the strongest, because it is Christ who saves, not the strength of your grip on him. The measure in this verse concerns service, which is why Paul goes straight on to the gifts. So never conclude that because your faith feels small you are less saved than someone else. You may be less mature, and should want to grow; you are not less justified.

How can I tell healthy confidence from pride? Pride needs to be noticed and compared; sober confidence does not. When someone else is praised for the thing you do well, are you glad or stung? When corrected, do you listen or defend? Do you use your gift to serve, or to be seen? Can you thank God for your ability without needing anyone to mention it? Healthy confidence knows its gift, uses it, and is happy for others to have greater ones; pride is restless until it is ranked. The cure for both pride and false modesty is the same: look at what you have as given, and at the Giver as worthy.

Uncertain wording. “The measure of faith” is compressed, and its exact sense is debated. Some take it as one standard for every believer, faith itself or the gospel believed, by which each measures himself. Others take it as the portion of faith God gives each believer for the service he is called to (1 Corinthians 12:11). The second fits best with what follows, where gifts differ “according to the grace given to us” (v. 6), and this commentary reads it that way.
verseByVerse.note: A play on the verb “think” (phroneō): not to think too highly (hyperphronein) but to think with sober judgment (sōphronein).

verseByVerse.quote: For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is one body in Christ, whose many members do different work, and each member belongs to the others. Difference is the design, not a defect, and no member can live detached from the rest.

For as in one body we have many members. One of Paul’s favourite pictures of the church (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 4:15–16), and it carries a bluntness we tend to soften: parts of a body are not detachable. A hand that leaves the arm does not become an independent hand with its own plans; it becomes a dead hand, quite quickly, and the arm does not do well either. Separation is an injury to two parties.

And the members do not all have the same function. “Function” (praxis) is activity, work: an eye sees, a hand works. Say that to the person who has quietly concluded he is peripheral. Almost everything keeping your body alive at this moment is something you have never thought about, could not point to, and would not miss until it stopped.

So we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another. Our unity is real, because we are all joined to the same Christ, and the Supper makes it visible: “we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17). And the last phrase is stranger than it sounds. Paul does not say we are members of the body, which would be tidy, but members of one another. The belonging runs directly between people: you need them, and they need you.

One body, because one body was given. The church was gathered round a broken body, not shared interests. Christ did not die for a club but for a body he means to keep whole, so no member may write off another. He did not save us one by one and leave us to find our own way; he made us his body, with his life running through every member.

Do I really need to join a local church? Yes, if you can. The New Testament knows nothing of Christians who belong to Christ but to no congregation. Believers were baptised and added to a church (Acts 2:41–42), had elders who watched over them (Hebrews 13:17), and met together, which we are not to neglect (Hebrews 10:24–25). Online sermons can feed you, but they cannot know you, visit you, correct you, or receive your gifts. Commit to a faithful local church where the gospel is preached, the ordinances are kept, and members care for one another. If illness or circumstances keep you housebound, ask the church to bring its fellowship to you.

What if a church has hurt me? Then you are not alone, and your pain is real. Some churches have wounded people badly, and where there was abuse it must be named, reported where it is a crime, and never covered up. But the answer to a sick body is not to live as a severed hand; it is, in time, to find a healthy body. Take your time, pray, and look for a church where the gospel is clear, leaders are accountable, and people are gentle. Tell a pastor there what happened. Christ has not given up on his church, and he has not given up on healing you within it.

In everyday life. The useful question is not whether you are one of the parts people can name, but whether anything would stop if you did.
