In most congregations there are two or three people nobody thinks about, without whom nothing would happen by Thursday. Find out who they are in your church and thank them this week. And if you are one of them, take heart: the body knows what it would lose, even if it never says so.

verseByVerse.quote: Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has given each believer a different gift by his grace, and gifts are given to be used. Even prophecy, the most striking of them, is to be exercised within limits set by faith.

Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us. “Gifts” (charismata) come from “grace” (charis): a gift is a piece of grace, made specific and handed to a named person for building up the body, neither earned nor chosen by us (1 Corinthians 12:11). The ability you have is not a reward for the grace you received. It is more grace.

Let us use them. The Greek has no verb, but the sense is clear: gifts are for using, not admiring. A gift never exercised is a failure of stewardship, like the servant who buried his master’s money (Matthew 25:25).

If prophecy, in proportion to our faith. Prophecy (prophēteia) in the New Testament was speaking a message revealed by God for the church (1 Corinthians 14:3, 29–31), and even it was to be exercised within a limit (see “Uncertain wording” below).

Spoils from an ascended King. “When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8). In Psalm 68 the conqueror goes up and receives tribute; Paul sees the risen Christ, having won, handing the spoils out, and still giving them, so that no congregation lacks what it needs to be built up. Every gift in a church is a piece of the victory of Easter. The deacon who mends the boiler and the woman who knows which widow needs a visit were given by a Lord who gives because he has conquered, not because we have earned.

How do I find my gift? Not chiefly by a questionnaire, but by serving. Begin where there is need: the crèche rota, the welcome team, visiting the sick, the washing-up after church. Notice what bears fruit and what others recognise in you, and keep going: gifts are given to “serve one another, as good stewards of God’s varied grace” (1 Peter 4:10), so they are found in the serving. And notice what is not on Paul’s list: no gift of being impressive. Serving, teaching, encouraging, giving, leading, being kind to people in trouble: most of it happens where nobody is watching. If you have concluded you have no gift, check whether you have been searching the wrong list.

Are natural talents spiritual gifts? Often God uses the abilities he gave you at birth, for he is Creator as well as Redeemer, and the Spirit may take up an organiser’s or a carer’s abilities for the church. But a talent becomes a gift to the body when it is given over to Christ and used in love to build others up. Some abilities appear only after conversion, and some talents are never meant for church use at all. The test is not where the ability came from, but whether it is used to serve the body by grace, in humility.

Where Christians differ: does prophecy continue today? Continuationists (Christians who believe all the gifts of the New Testament church continue today) believe prophecy continues, giving new messages from God, usually understood as words prompted by the Spirit, to be weighed by the church (1 Corinthians 14:29) and never equal to Scripture. This commentary’s view: The gift of prophecy, in the sense of new revelation from God, belonged to the foundation period of the church, laid by apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20). With the completion of Scripture the canon is closed, and no new revelation is to be added (Hebrews 1:1–2; the Westminster Confession 1.1, 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.1, 1.6). Continuationists answer that New Testament prophecy was a fallible human report of the Spirit’s prompting; but a word truly from God cannot be fallible, and a church that receives new words alongside Scripture will soon be ruled by them. The prophetic function continues in a secondary sense through faithful preaching, which applies Scripture with power, as one who speaks oracles of God (1 Peter 4:11). This view is held charitably: many continuationist brothers and sisters love Christ, and their churches are often marked by warm prayer and evangelistic zeal; and all agree that any claimed word must be tested by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21).

Uncertain wording. “In proportion to our faith” is literally according to the analogia (proportion, agreement) of the faith, and it is not certain which faith Paul means. It may be the measure of faith given to the prophet (v. 3), so that he speaks no further than God has given him; or the faith, the body of truth already revealed, which no prophecy may contradict. From the second reading Reformed interpreters drew the principle that Scripture interprets Scripture. Either way the gift stays under an authority outside the gifted person.

verseByVerse.quote: ...if service, in our serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching; the one who exhorts, in his exhortation; the one who contributes, in generosity; the one who leads, with zeal; the one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness. — Romans 12:7–8
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever your gift, give yourself to it, and use it in the right spirit: give generously, lead earnestly, show mercy gladly. The manner in which a gift is used matters as much as the gift itself.

If service, in our serving. “Service” (diakonia) is practical help, the root of our word deacon. The first items simply repeat themselves, the one who serves, in his serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching, and that is a correction. Much activity can gather around a gift without being the gift: meetings about the serving, and opinions about it. Get on with the thing itself.

The one who teaches; the one who exhorts. Teaching explains and applies God’s truth (1 Timothy 4:13; 2 Timothy 2:2), not to perform or be admired. “Exhorts” is parakaleō, the word of the appeal in v. 1. Teaching informs the mind; exhortation moves the will. The church needs the one who comes alongside and says, now do it, and I will help you.

The one who contributes, in generosity. “Generosity” (haplotēs) is simplicity: a gift with one motive in it and no second agenda folded underneath (2 Corinthians 8:2; 9:11).

The one who leads, with zeal. “Leads” (proistēmi, stands before, presides) is used of elders (1 Thessalonians 5:12; 1 Timothy 5:17): lead with diligence and earnestness, not laziness (see also “Uncertain wording” below).

The one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness. Caring for the sick, poor and suffering. “Cheerfulness” (hilarotēs, from which hilarity comes, though it means gladness, not laughter) is a glad, willing heart; Paul uses its cousin in “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Mercy done with a martyr’s air does more harm than good.

The manner can cancel the gift. The last three items do not repeat themselves. Each names a manner, and this is where gifts most often go wrong: a person can exercise the right gift in a way that damages the one receiving it. Everyone has met the merciful helper who leaves you feeling like a case, or the giver whose gift arrives with strings. The gift was real; the manner cancelled it.

The manner of the Lord. Every gift on this list was exercised first, and perfectly, by Christ, in the very manner Paul names. He was a servant (diakonos, 15:8). He gave, not a portion with strings attached, but himself (Galatians 2:20). He leads his flock as “the great shepherd of the sheep” (Hebrews 13:20). And his mercy never wore a martyr’s air: the shepherd who finds the lost sheep “lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing” (Luke 15:5). So a gift exercised grudgingly does not only disappoint the person receiving it; it misrepresents the Lord whose gift it is.

He will dress himself for service. Nothing on this list needs a stage: the Son of God did most of his work with a towel and a basin. And he has not finished serving. When the master comes home and finds his servants awake, Jesus said, “he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them” (Luke 12:37). That is the Lord whose gifts we hold: the King of glory, who means one day to wait on his servants at his own table.

What it does not mean. Not that this is a complete list of gifts (compare 1 Corinthians 12; Ephesians 4:11; 1 Peter 4:10–11). Nor that those without a particular gift are excused: all must serve, give and show mercy, and the gifted do so in a special way.

What if I serve but feel no cheerfulness? Do not stop serving; ask God to change the heart behind the hands. Cheerfulness grows from remembering why you serve: Christ “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life” (Mark 10:45), and he served you first. Sometimes the lack of joy is tiredness, and you need rest or to share the load; sometimes it is serving to be noticed, and the remedy is to serve where no one will see. Pray before you serve, think of the person rather than the task, and give thanks afterwards. Joy often follows obedience rather than preceding it.

Uncertain wording. “The one who leads” (ho proistamenos) can mean one who presides, or one who protects and gives aid; a noun from the same root describes Phoebe as “a patron of many” (16:2). Because the word stands between giving and acts of mercy, some take it here as caring for those in need. The usual sense of leading, as of elders, is more likely, and either way Paul asks for the same earnestness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–21 — Love in Action: The Ethics of the Transformed Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genuine love is the shape of the transformed life, and it reaches all the way to enemies. Verse 9 is the heading: love without a mask, hating evil and clinging to good. Then the circle widens: family affection, honour, zeal, hope and hospitality within the church (vv. 10–13); blessing for persecutors (v. 14); shared joy and grief and a humble mind (vv. 15–16); no repayment of evil, peace wherever possible, and justice left to God (vv. 17–19). It ends with an enemy fed and evil overcome by good (vv. 20–21). The burning coals of v. 20 are not a promise that kindness will make your enemy suffer more (see the note on vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ethic of the Cross in Daily Life

Romans 12:9–21 shows what the cross looks like in daily life. The crucified Christ did not retaliate; he prayed for those who crucified him and overcame evil by giving himself. The believer who blesses his persecutor is not merely keeping a rule. He knows he was once God’s enemy and has been loved into the family, and he is doing to others what was done to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman church held slaves and freedmen, members of Caesar’s household (Philippians 4:22), wealthy patrons and poor migrants, and friction between them was a daily danger. Now: Churches are still divided by income, education, race and status. The question is not whether a church approves of diversity in principle but whether its members weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice across every line the world draws.

verseByVerse.quote: Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor. — Romans 12:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christian love must be real, not acted: it hates evil, clings to good, and treats fellow believers as family to be honoured first. Verse 9 heads the rest of the chapter, which widens ring by ring from the church to the enemy: the mercies of God (v. 1) passed on to other people.

Let love be genuine. Paul moves from gifts straight to love, as in 1 Corinthians 12 and 13, because gifts without love are noise. “Genuine” (anypokritos) comes from the theatre: a hypokritēs was an actor speaking his lines from behind a mask. This is love with the mask off: not love that is always warm, which no one can manage, but love that is not performing a warmth it does not have.

Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. This keeps love from turning into a mood, and both verbs are violent. “Abhor” (apostygeō) is to loathe, to shudder at; “hold fast” (kollaō) is to cleave, the word used of a man holding fast to his wife (Matthew 19:5). Love as universal acceptance cannot abhor anything, and so cannot hold fast to anything either. Real love hates what harms the beloved, and a love with no hatreds in it is not deep enough to hold anybody.

Love one another with brotherly affection. Two family words: philadelphia, love of brothers and sisters, and philostorgos, built on storgē, the unchosen affection of people who belong to each other by birth. The church is asked to have not the feel of a pleasant society but the texture of a family, including the part where you did not pick them.

Outdo one another in showing honor. The verb can also mean to go first, or to prefer one another in honour (Philippians 2:3). In a status-conscious culture Paul does not tell the church to stop competing. He changes the contest: the winner is the one who honours others first, before anyone has earned it.

Brothers of the firstborn. There was once a love entirely without a mask. The Son of God never performed a warmth he did not have: every word to the leper, every look at Peter, every tear at Lazarus’ tomb was real. And the church can be asked for family affection because in him it really is a family. God predestined his people “to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (8:29), and the Son “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). He did not choose us for our compatibility; he brought each of us, unlikely and unlovely, into his Father’s house by the same door. To withhold warmth from the person in the next pew is to treat as a stranger someone Christ calls his brother.

How can I love people in church I do not naturally like? Begin with what love does, not with what you feel. Love here is not liking but willing and doing someone’s good. You can pray for him, speak well of him, greet him warmly, ask about his week and help him when he needs it while your feelings lag behind, and very often they follow. He belongs to you by the same blood of Christ, and God chose you both knowing exactly what you are like. If there is a real wrong between you, deal with it honestly (Matthew 18:15). If he simply grates on you, he is probably one of God’s chosen tools for making you more like Christ.

Does hating evil mean hating people who do evil? No: what is evil, not who. A Christian hates sin most of all in himself, and hates what sin does to those he loves, while loving his neighbour and even his enemy (vv. 14, 20). A doctor hates cancer because he loves his patient. Love that refuses to hate evil cannot help anyone, and hatred of evil without love becomes a kind of evil itself.

In everyday life. Find someone in your church today and be the first to honour them: a word of thanks, a note, a meal, a real compliment. And if, when a friend is praised for the very thing you also do, you catch a flicker of something sour before you have arranged your face, that flicker is what the mask in this verse covers. Confess it, for Christ has already forgiven it, and then go and honour that friend.

parallels.desc: hate evil, and love good

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord. Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep your zeal for the Lord burning and go on serving him; in trouble, hold on with joyful hope, endurance and persistent prayer. Love that lasts needs a heart kept warm and a grip that will not let go.

Do not be slothful in zeal. Two words that ought not to fit: “slothful” (oknēros: hesitant, sluggish), Proverbs’ word for the sluggard, and “zeal” (spoudē), eagerness. How is a person lazy at zeal? Very easily, and it is common in long-standing Christians: nothing renounced, no doctrine abandoned, the effort simply stopped, gradually, without a decision. This is not the same as exhaustion, grief or depression, which can drain a faithful believer of all feeling while his faith holds; those call for rest, care and help, not rebuke.

Be fervent in spirit. “Fervent” (zeō) means to boil (on “spirit” or “Spirit”, see below). Luke uses the same words of Apollos as he taught accurately the things concerning Jesus (Acts 18:25). The opposite is not coldness. Most people who need this command are lukewarm, a temperature that takes no energy to maintain, and which the risen Christ finds sickening (Revelation 3:16).

Serve the Lord. As slaves (douleuō) of the Lord Jesus, not of our own projects. Zeal without this direction can be dangerous; Paul himself had once been zealous for God in persecuting the church (Philippians 3:6).

Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer. One situation, trouble, handled three ways. Rejoice in hope looks to how it ends: the hope of glory (5:2; 8:24–25). “Patient” (hypomenō) is to remain under the load, not merely wait for it to pass; tribulation (thlipsis, pressure) is to be expected (5:3). “Constant” (proskartereō) is to persist, stubbornly not letting go, the word for the first church devoting itself to the prayers (Acts 2:42). Prayer brings the trouble to God throughout, and keeps hope and patience alive.

The Lord who never cooled. In one person every clause of these verses was true without a lapse. When he cleared the temple his disciples remembered, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17; Psalm 69:9), a psalm Paul applies to Christ (15:3). For the joy set before him he endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2): hope rejoicing, and patience under the heaviest tribulation ever carried. He prayed in Gethsemane while his friends slept. So Christian zeal is not a temperament but likeness to a Master who was never lukewarm for one hour, and who served us before he asked us to serve him.

A coal from that fire. The fire that keeps a Christian warm was not lit by the Christian. John the Baptist said the One coming after him would baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire (Matthew 3:11), and the exalted Christ poured out the promised Spirit on his church (Acts 2:33). Every tired saint still praying in the dark carries a coal from that fire, and the One who kindled it tends it still: a faintly burning wick he will not quench (Isaiah 42:3; Matthew 12:20). Our fervour runs low; his love for us never has.

How do I stay under the load? A day at a time. Take today’s portion only, “Sufficient for the day is its own trouble” (Matthew 6:34), and do not carry next year’s fear on top of this morning’s pain. Tell God the truth, complaint included: “pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us” (Psalm 62:8). Keep to the plain means of grace even when they feel flat. Let someone take a corner of the weight, for “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2) assumes you will let them. And when you are ready to give up, “Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted” (Hebrews 12:3). He did not walk out from under the cross, and he has not walked out on you; he is interceding for you now (8:34). You are not holding on alone. You are being held.

What do I do when my zeal has gone cold? Do not wait to feel fervent before you return. Go back to the means God uses to light the fire: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, and warm believers. Zeal is fed by the mercies of verse 1, not by guilt. Ask whether something has cooled you, an unconfessed sin, an idol, exhaustion or a grievance, and deal with it. Christ told a cooling church to remember from where it had fallen, repent, and do the works it did at first (Revelation 2:5). Embers can be fanned into flame (2 Timothy 1:6).

What if prayer feels dead? Keep praying: constancy, not feeling, is the command. Use the Psalms, which give words to the dry seasons too (Psalm 42; 63). Pray short, honest prayers through the day, and pray with others, whose warmth can carry you. Prayer is measured not by how it feels but by who hears it: your Father hears, the Son intercedes (8:34), and the Spirit helps you when you do not know what to pray (8:26).

Uncertain wording. “Fervent in spirit” may mean your own spirit, boiling with zeal, or the Holy Spirit; the ESV note allows “fervent in the Spirit”, and the Greek, written without capital letters, cannot settle it. Both are true and belong together: a believer’s spirit burns because the Spirit has set it alight.

Textual note. A few manuscripts read “serve the time” instead of “serve the Lord”, but “serve the Lord” is the better reading.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “fervent in spirit” can also be read “fervent in the Spirit.”

verseByVerse.quote: Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Share with fellow believers in need, go out of your way to welcome strangers, and answer those who persecute you with blessing, not curses. Love opens its purse and its door, and it will not speak evil even of its enemies.

Contribute to the needs of the saints. “Contribute” (koinōneō) is to share, to have fellowship (Acts 2:44–45; Galatians 6:10); Paul himself was collecting for the poor believers in Jerusalem as he wrote (15:25–26). A boiling spirit (v. 11) shows itself in an open purse.

And seek to show hospitality. “Seek” (diōkō) is to pursue, to chase, the same word as “persecute” in the next clause: some are hunting you, and you are to be out hunting for strangers to feed. Hospitality (philoxenia) is literally love of strangers, not of friends; the stranger is the test. In a world of poor and dangerous inns, opening your home to travelling believers was vital and costly (Hebrews 13:2; 3 John 5–8). It is the hospitality of God, who did not wait for us strangers and enemies to turn up, but came looking for us and set a table for us in his house.

Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them. Paul turns toward outsiders, echoing his Master: “bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you” (Luke 6:28; Matthew 5:44). To bless (eulogeō) is to speak well of, and to ask God’s good for. Jesus prayed for his executioners (Luke 23:34), and Stephen did the same as the stones fell (Acts 7:60). There is mercy in the verb: because to bless is to speak well, the command is first about what you say, not what you feel, and you can do it this afternoon while feeling nothing appropriate whatsoever. Say something true and good about them to God, and leave unsaid what you were going to say about them to somebody else.

The setting. The Roman believers did not need persecution explained. Jewish believers among them had been driven out of the city under Claudius only a few years before (Acts 18:2), and Nero’s persecution would fall on the church there within a decade (see the introduction).

The persecutor who was blessed. Paul knew this command from the receiving end. Diōkō is the verb the risen Christ used on the Damascus road: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Christ did not curse the man hunting his church. He left him blind for three days, then sent Ananias to lay hands on him, call him brother, and give him back his sight (Acts 9:17). Every time Paul told a church to bless its persecutors, he was describing how he had been treated, and a Christian who blesses an enemy is passing on the kindness that found him.

What it does not mean. Not ignoring injustice or refusing legal protection. Blessing a persecutor is something you do with your mouth about a person; it is not a requirement to stay within his reach or to call what was done acceptable (see vv. 17–18).

How does this fit with the psalms that call down curses on enemies? Those prayers hand the enemy over to God’s justice rather than taking revenge, exactly what Paul commands in v. 19. The Christian may still pray that God will stop the wicked and cry out for justice for the oppressed. What he may not do is wish evil on a person in his own name. His word about his persecutor is blessing, and his deepest prayer is that he will repent and be saved, as Saul was.

Does hospitality need a big house or a lot of money? No: an open heart, not a large kitchen. A pot of soup, a lift to church, a seat beside you after the service, or a place at your family’s ordinary meal can all be hospitality, and the Macedonians gave out of extreme poverty (2 Corinthians 8:2). Invite the newcomer, the international student, the widow, the single person who goes home alone. The aim is not to impress, which turns hospitality into entertaining, but to welcome, as Christ has welcomed you (15:7).
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to travelling believers was vital in a world of poor, unsafe inns.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Enter into other believers’ joys and sorrows, be of one mind with them, and drop every pretension: seek out the lowly, and never think yourself wise. Love takes its cue from someone else’s life and refuses to look down on anyone.

Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Weeping with the weeping is often called the harder half, but there is a case for the other order. Grief invites sympathy, which we are practised at, and there is even a quiet satisfaction in being the one who sat with someone. Good news invites comparison, and it usually arrives exactly where you wanted news of your own: the pregnancy, the job, the child doing well. Rejoicing with the rejoicing can be the harder half, and nobody notices you doing it. Both ask you to take your emotional cue from someone else’s life rather than your own (1 Corinthians 12:26).

Live in harmony with one another. Literally, think the same thing toward one another: be of one mind, not in every opinion, but in shared purpose and care.

Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. “Haughty” is literally thinking high things. “Associate with” (synapagō) means to be carried along with, the word used of Barnabas carried away by others’ hypocrisy (Galatians 2:13). Paul turns it into a virtue and points it downward: not being kind to people beneath you, which leaves you above them, but letting yourself be carried into their company and concerns until “beneath you” stops meaning anything.

Never be wise in your own sight. From Proverbs 3:7. Paul used the phrase a chapter ago so that Gentile believers would not be wise in their own sight about Israel (11:25). There it guarded the church against contempt for outsiders; here, against contempt for the people in the next seat.

The setting. In Rome this was a concrete instruction about dinner. Hosts commonly seated guests by rank, and a generation later Pliny the Younger complained of a host who served the best wine to himself and his favourites and poorer wine to his lesser friends and freedmen. In a church that ate together, it meant whom you sat beside and what you put on their plate; today, whom you invite home, whom you sit with after the service, whose company you seek when nobody is keeping score.

The friend of the lowly. Every clause here describes Christ before it describes us. He kept a wedding’s joy from running dry (John 2:1–11), and had compassion on a widow following her only son’s coffin (Luke 7:13). He did not think high things. He let himself be carried into the company of fishermen, tax collectors, lepers and children, until his enemies’ sneer, “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19), became one of his truest titles. A church that will not sit with the lowly has not yet understood whose body it is.

What do I say to someone who is grieving? Often very little. Job’s friends did best in the first seven days, when they sat with him in silence (Job 2:13), and worst when they began to explain. Go, sit, listen, and let them talk about the one they have lost. Say you are sorry and that you love them. Do not explain the loss, compare it with your own, or tell them how to feel. Weep if you weep; Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus though he was about to raise him (John 11:35). Then keep coming back when everyone else has moved on: a meal, a lift, a note on the anniversary often speaks more than words.

What if I cannot feel glad about someone else’s good news? Tell God honestly; envy confessed is already losing its grip. Then act in love before the feeling arrives: congratulate them, thank God for their blessing, pray for them. It was not taken from you; God is not poorer for giving to them, and his plans for you are not smaller. Envy is a quiet complaint against his generosity (Matthew 20:15), and the more you rest in Christ as your treasure, the freer you are to be glad for others.

Uncertain wording. “The lowly” (tois tapeinois) can mean lowly people or lowly things; the ESV note offers “give yourselves to humble tasks”. Set against “haughty”, literally thinking high things, the second has a real claim, but “associate with”, and a church that ate together, make people the more natural reading. Either way the direction is down, towards humble company and humble work.

parallels.desc: be not wise in your own eyes

verseByVerse.quote: Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never pay back wrong with wrong; plan ahead to do what everyone can recognise as good, and do all you can to live at peace with everyone. Peace with some people may prove impossible, but the failure must not be yours.

Repay no one evil for evil. The instinct to pay back is strong; the Christian breaks the cycle (Matthew 5:38–39; 1 Thessalonians 5:15; 1 Peter 3:9). What is forbidden is repayment, not the pursuit of justice, which Paul will soon place in the hands of the magistrate. Confusing the two has done real harm to people told that reporting a crime was unchristian.

But give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. “Give thought” (pronoeō) is to plan ahead. Honourable means what even unbelievers recognise as good (Proverbs 3:4; 2 Corinthians 8:21), and such conduct commends the gospel. It is arranged beforehand, by someone who has decided in a calm hour what he will do in a hot one.

If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. Two careful limits, given out of kindness. If possible: sometimes peace is impossible without betraying truth. So far as it depends on you: you can control only yourself. Some relationships cannot be at peace, and sometimes that is not your fault, which matters enormously to the person who carries the weight of every broken relationship. Your responsibility ends where your conduct ends. It cuts the other way too: if peace fails, ask honestly whether you first did everything that depended on you.

When he was reviled. Peter sets this command in front of the cross: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). In the next breath Christ “himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24): he could absorb evil without returning it because he was carrying it away. God did everything that depended on him, and more, making peace by the blood of the cross (Colossians 1:20), and repaid our evil with the good of his Son. So we can refuse to settle accounts. Ours was settled at the cross, and every other will be settled by the One who judges justly.

Does living at peace mean I must reconcile with someone who abused me? No, not in the sense of restoring closeness or trust. Forgiveness, letting go of revenge and handing the case to God, is commanded of every Christian. Reconciliation, the rebuilding of a relationship, takes two, and it requires real repentance and changed behaviour on the other side. With someone who has abused you, safety comes first, and it may be right to keep your distance permanently, to report what happened, and to involve the authorities. As far as it depends on you means you do not seek his harm and you do not stir up conflict; it never means you must put yourself or others back in harm’s way. Abuse is never to be tolerated in the name of peace.

What about conflicts in church, especially over truth? Seek peace earnestly, but never by abandoning the gospel: Paul opposed Peter to his face when it was at stake (Galatians 2:11–14). Most church conflicts, though, are about preferences, personalities, money and hurt pride, and call for humility, patience, speaking to the person rather than about him (Matthew 18:15), and a readiness to give way. Ask: is this a matter of Scripture, or of my preference? Hold the first firmly and the second lightly.

In everyday life. Is there someone you are at odds with? Apologise for your share, plainly, without adding a but, and leave the rest to God; the Spirit whose fruit is peace (Galatians 5:22) lives in you for exactly this.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." To the contrary, "if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never take revenge: leave justice to God, who will repay, and meet your enemy’s needs with kindness instead. The wrong is not too small to matter but too serious to be left with you, and the aim is to win your enemy, not to crush him.

Beloved, never avenge yourselves. The only word of affection in these thirteen verses lands immediately before the hardest thing Paul asks. People are not argued out of revenge; affection can do what argument cannot.

But leave it to the wrath of God. Step aside and make room, like someone in a doorway told to move because something else is coming through. The wrong is not small enough to absorb. It is too serious to be left with the injured party, the one person guaranteed to judge it badly: far too harshly or, just as often, far too leniently, because he wants it all to stop. It is moved to a competent court, for justice belongs to God, and he will do it perfectly, in part through the governing authorities of the next chapter.

For it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.” From the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:35), already used at 10:19, the song in which God told Israel its own future: it holds both the mercy to the Gentiles that provokes Israel to jealousy and the vengeance that lets the wronged leave justice with God.

To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink.” From Proverbs 25:21–22, and this is where most people quietly stop reading. Food and drink, what a body needs today. Paul does not ask for a change of heart first. He asks for a meal, which you can give while your heart is still exactly where it was.

For by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head. Probably the burning pain of conscience, shame and repentance brought on by unexpected kindness (see “Uncertain wording” below). Proverbs ends the couplet not with the enemy’s ruin but with the promise that the LORD will reward you. The goal is not an enemy outmanoeuvred by your virtue but an enemy who stops being one.

Where the vengeance goes. God does not say vengeance will be dropped. He says it is his, and the New Testament tells what he has done with it. For everyone who trusts Christ it has already fallen, on the Son whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood (3:25), so that every wrong a believer has done, including every wrong done to another believer, was paid for at the cross. For the rest it waits for the day when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven in flaming fire (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). No one escapes justice because you held back; the only question is whether his sin is answered at Calvary or at the judgment seat, and you are free to pray that it will be Calvary. So you can let go.

A meal instead of a sentence. We were his enemies once, hungry and thirsty and without excuse, and God did to us what this verse says. He did not starve us out. He fed us with the bread of life and gave us living water (John 6:35; 4:14), and the coals of that kindness burned until we turned to him in shame. Every believer is an enemy who was given a meal instead of a sentence. The vengeance that was his by right, he kept in his own hands, and then he opened those hands to feed us.

What it does not mean. Not that crime should go unpunished (see the note on vv. 17–18).

How do I actually leave it with God? Not by pretending it did not hurt. Name the wrong to God exactly, as the psalmists did; he can bear the truth. Then hand it over in so many words: this is yours to judge, not mine, as Christ “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). Expect to do it again, for the grievance will come back, often at night. Starve the private trial: stop rehearsing the speech, stop gathering allies. Where a crime has been done, take it to those God has appointed (13:4). Then pray for the one who wronged you, even in one thin sentence. Timothy Keller, in The Reason for God, drew on the Croatian theologian Miroslav Volf, who had watched his homeland torn apart by war, to make the point that it is not disbelief in God’s judgment but belief in it that makes it possible to lay down the sword. If no one will ever put it right, you must. Because God will, you need not.

Is a God who takes vengeance not a cruel God? No: he is a God who refuses to shrug at evil. To overlook the murder of a man’s family would be not kindness but indifference, leaving the victim alone with his rage. And his vengeance is never spite. It is the holy Judge doing right (Genesis 18:25), slow to anger, taking no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), who has already borne its full weight himself, at the cross, for everyone who will come to him.

Must I forgive someone who has not said sorry? In your heart, yes: lay down revenge and wish him good, as Jesus prayed for those crucifying him; full reconciliation waits on his repentance (Luke 17:3).

Where Christians differ: does this forbid self-defence? Some Christians, from the Anabaptists (the radical wing of the Reformation, whose heirs include the Mennonites) to modern pacifists, hold that a follower of Jesus must never use force, citing our Lord’s command to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:39). This commentary’s view: Vengeance comes after the harm, to pay it back; defence comes during it, to stop it. The law allowed a householder to strike a thief breaking in at night (Exodus 22:2), and Scripture commands us to rescue those being taken away to death (Proverbs 24:11). In Matthew 5 Jesus speaks of an insult, a slap on the cheek, not an attack on life. So Christians may use proportionate force to protect themselves and especially others, and the state may wield the sword. What they may not do is retaliate. Christians who hold the pacifist view are to be respected as brothers trying to follow Christ’s word.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are not certain. “Leave it to the wrath of God” is literally give place to wrath, without saying whose. The ESV supplies “of God”, as most interpreters do, because the quotation that follows names the Lord as the one who repays; some have read it as stepping out of the way of the enemy’s anger. “Heap burning coals on his head” comes from Proverbs 25:22, and the origin of the picture is unknown. Most likely it means the burning shame and remorse that unexpected kindness brings, leading to a change of heart; some connect it with an Egyptian ritual in which a penitent carried a pan of coals on his head as a sign of remorse. Others read the coals as heavier judgment stored up for the enemy, but the call to bless (v. 14) and to overcome evil with good (v. 21) tells against it.
verseByVerse.note: Heaping burning coals probably means bringing the enemy to shame and a change of heart through kindness.

if your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let evil done to you win by making you like it; defeat it by doing good. This is how Christ won, and it gathers up the whole chapter.

In the flow. Verse 21 gathers up verses 14–21 and reaches back to verse 2: the call not to be conformed to this age ends in the refusal to be conformed to your enemy. Good and evil return at once in 13:3–4, where God appoints public hands to restrain evil (12:19; 13:4). The chapter that opened by asking for a body on an altar closes by asking for a body that does not hit back, both by the mercies of God.

Do not be overcome by evil. “Overcome” is conquer (nikaō), twice in one line, and in the first half you are the one conquered. The danger named first is not that you will do wrong but that a wrong done to you will go on working in you after the deed is over. Being wronged is not defeat; becoming like the wrongdoer is. The man who was genuinely wronged, and right about it, and is now permanently harder, sharper with his family, quicker to assume the worst, unable to speak about a whole category of people without an edge, has not been defeated by an argument. He has been overcome: the wrong done to him has done a second wrong, and changed him.

But overcome evil with good. Goodness is the weapon that defeats evil. This is not a retreat into niceness: return evil and you have agreed to fight on ground the enemy chose.

The victory of the cross. This is how Christ conquered: by suffering, forgiving, and doing good to his enemies. God did not overcome the world’s evil with mere force but with sacrificial love, for while we were still sinners, while we were enemies, Christ died for us (5:8, 10). The cross is not only the supreme example of this; it is the victory itself. Evil threw everything it had at Christ and was overcome, not by a greater violence but by a greater love.

When the wound becomes the identity. This condition is hard to leave. In a culture that has lost most other sources of moral standing, having been wronged is one of the few that remain. A grievance gives us a story, a side, and the quiet assurance that whatever else is true of us, we are in the right. Letting it go can feel like letting go of ourselves, or admitting that what happened did not matter, so we keep the wound open, and it keeps us. The ancient blood feud and the endless online call-out run on the same fuel. Paul does not ask anyone to pretend the wrong was small; he offers a different place to stand. The Christian’s deepest identity is not what was done to him but what was done for him. Christ was wronged more than anyone who has ever lived, and he did not build an identity on it; he turned the worst injustice in history into the means of pardoning those who did it. Someone loved like that can put down a grievance without losing himself, because his self was never kept there.

What if the evil keeps going and good seems to change nothing? Keep doing good, and leave the outcome with God. Good does not always change the other person; sometimes it only keeps evil from changing you, and that is already a victory. The cross looked like defeat on Friday, and Joseph waited years to see what God had done with his brothers’ evil (Galatians 6:9). Where the evil is ongoing harm, doing good may mean protecting the vulnerable, telling the truth and calling in the authorities. Good is not the same as giving in.

In everyday life. When someone does you wrong today, ask what good you can do in return. And bring the older wrongs to Christ as well: name one way the worst thing done to you has changed you, and ask him whether it is a wound to be healed or a hold to be broken. He does both, and he does not wait for you to have sorted out which it is before he begins.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.<sup>2</sup>Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.<sup>3</sup>For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned.<sup>4</sup>For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function,<sup>5</sup>so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.<sup>6</sup>Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;<sup>7</sup>if service, in our serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching;<sup>8</sup>the one who exhorts, in his exhortation; the one who contributes, in generosity; the one who leads, with zeal; the one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness.<sup>9</sup>Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good.<sup>10</sup>Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor.<sup>11</sup>Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord.<sup>12</sup>Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.<sup>13</sup>Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality.<sup>14</sup>Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.<sup>15</sup>Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep.<sup>16</sup>Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.<sup>17</sup>Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all.<sup>18</sup>If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.<sup>19</sup>Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.”<sup>20</sup>To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head.”<sup>21</sup>Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

keyVerse.quote: I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.
keyVerse.note: Everything in chapters 12–16 hangs on this verse. Its “therefore” and its “mercies of God” gather up the first eleven chapters, and what it asks in return is not a list of duties but a whole self handed over, day by day. It is the only reasonable worship, because Christ first offered his own body for us.

12.reflection:
Paul appeals “by the mercies of God” before he asks for anything (v. 1). Which of God’s mercies in Romans 1–11 moves you most? How does starting there change the way you obey, and where do you tend to start with the demand instead?

Verse 2 warns against being pressed into the mould of this age. What does our culture assume without ever arguing for it? What in your ordinary week, such as reading, screens or company, does most to shape your mind?

Verses 3–8 call for sober judgment about ourselves and our gifts. Is your temptation more to pride or to false modesty? What gift have others recognised in you, and how could you use it this month, in the manner Paul describes?

Verses 14–21 ask us to bless persecutors, refuse revenge and feed our enemies. Where is a grievance shaping you? What would it look like to leave it with God and overcome evil with good, while still seeking safety and justice where they are needed?

13.title: Citizens of Two Kingdoms
13.overview:
Where we are. Romans 13 continues the life of the “living sacrifice” (12:1). Chapter 12 left wrath to God (12:19); chapter 13 shows one way he carries it out in this age, through the governing authorities, and then returns to love.

The message. Give everyone what you owe, because you belong to the God who stands over every throne and to the Lord who is coming. The state is owed submission, taxes, respect and honour, as God’s servant for good. Your neighbour is owed love, the one debt never paid off. And because the night is almost over, wake up and put on Christ himself.

Why it was said. The Roman Christians confessed Jesus, not Caesar, as Lord, in the capital of the empire that had crucified him (see the introduction). Did belonging to another kingdom release them from this one? Paul, writing under Nero, rests good citizenship on God, not on the emperor; and to a church strained between Jewish and Gentile believers he says that what they owe each other is love, and that the day is too near for quarrelling and envy (v. 13).

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–7 ground civil authority in God: every authority is from him (vv. 1–2); the ruler is his servant, commending good and bearing the sword against evil (vv. 3–4); so submit for conscience’ sake (v. 5) and pay taxes, respect and honour as debts (vv. 6–7). The word “owed” carries Paul into verses 8–10, where the debt that never clears is love. Verses 11–14 set it all in the light of the coming day: cast off the night’s works and put on the Lord Jesus Christ.

Where it leads. The chapter that begins with Caesar on his throne ends with Christ as the believer’s clothing. Every throne in it was made through the Son (Colossians 1:16), yet he submitted to Pilate’s unjust court and a Roman cross so that rebels against heaven could be pardoned. He is the one man who owed nothing and paid our debt, who alone loved his neighbour without flaw, and who is the morning that is coming. To put him on is to be dressed already for the day of his appearing.

For us. This chapter will not let you make the state your saviour or your enemy, or let love become a feeling with no commandments in it. Ask what you owe, and to whom, and pay it as someone who knows what time it is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Governing Authorities: God's Servant for Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Civil government is God’s servant, so Christians submit to it, for conscience’ sake and not only from fear. Every authority exists because God set it in place, so to range yourself against the order itself is to range yourself against him (vv. 1–2). Its work is to commend good and punish evil, bearing the sword the wronged Christian has laid down (vv. 3–4; 12:19). So believers submit from conscience (v. 5) and pay what is owed: taxes, respect and honour (vv. 6–7). Paul is not asking the Romans to approve every policy of the emperor, and the rest of Scripture sets the limits (Acts 5:29); but citizenship in God’s kingdom is no licence to ignore the order God has set up, and the whole case rests on God, not on Caesar.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kingdoms and Civil Authority

The Reformers taught the doctrine of the two kingdoms as a framework for passages like Romans 13: the kingdom of God’s left hand (civil government) and of his right hand (the church). God governs civil life through natural law (the sense of right and wrong he has given all people) and common grace (his kindness to believer and unbeliever alike), and the church through his Word and Spirit. The two are distinct but not separate, and the Christian belongs to both: Caesar has his domain, Christ has his, and the two must never be confused.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman Christians had obvious reasons to view the imperial state with suspicion: it had crucified their Lord and would one day persecute them. Paul’s command to submit was not naive but grounded in God. Now: In a democracy, Romans 13 means paying taxes, respecting lawful authority, and working through lawful channels for justice (see the note on vv. 1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every Christian is to submit to the governing authorities, because God himself set them in place. Belonging to Christ’s kingdom does not release you from the order he has appointed.

Be subject. “Every person” is literally every soul, apostles included. Paul writes not hypakouō, obey, his word for children and slaves, but hypotassō, a word about rank and order: to take your place under an arrangement. You can be truly subject to an arrangement and still decline a particular command inside it, as the martyrs did who would not offer incense to the emperor. They raised no hand against the arrest, the court or the sentence; they simply would not sin.

Instituted by God. “Instituted” (tassō, appointed, set in order) shares its root with “be subject”: God set the authorities in place, and we take our place under them. All human authority is borrowed. Jesus told Pilate, who boasted of his power to release or crucify, that he would have no authority over him unless it had been given him from above (John 19:11); Nebuchadnezzar had to learn that the Most High rules the kingdom of men (Daniel 4:32). Even a state that ignores God serves his purposes by keeping order and justice: that is common grace, his kindness to believer and unbeliever alike. On order as God’s gift in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Whoever resists. “Resists” (antitassō) is a military word, to draw up in battle order against: the opposite of the ordering in verse 1. Paul does not mean the citizen who campaigns or votes against the government, or refuses one unjust demand, but settled hostility to ordered authority itself: my citizenship is in heaven, so these arrangements have no claim on me. That temptation is found on the political right and left alike. Paul answers that the arrangements have a claim because they have an Author, and that the alternative to imperfect order is not freedom but the strong doing as they please with the weak.

Will incur judgment. Judgment comes in two ways: from God, whose order has been opposed, and through the state’s own punishment, which is one of the means he uses.

The setting. Paul wrote under Nero, in the better early years of his reign (see the introduction). A small congregation in the capital that confessed Jesus, not Caesar, as Lord, some of them lately expelled with the Jews under Claudius (Acts 18:2), could easily be seen as a nest of rebels. Paul shows that the gospel does not make Christians revolutionaries, without flattering Rome for a moment: his whole argument rests on God, not on the emperor.

Thrones made through the Son. All things, thrones and authorities included, were created through the Son and for him (Colossians 1:16), and he now sits far above all rule and authority (Ephesians 1:20–21). So the order Paul tells us to respect is not a rival to Christ’s kingdom but a lower office within it, and the magistrate himself has a Master. Yet the Lord who told Pilate that his power came from above did not use his own power to escape him. He submitted to an unjust court, a corrupt governor and a Roman cross, so that rebels against the throne of heaven could be pardoned. So the Christian can be the calmest citizen in the land: not because the rulers are good, but because the King is.

Why do we either worship the state or fear it? Some look to government, without quite saying so, to do what only God can do: make us good, heal our divisions, shield us from every risk, so that the right election becomes a kind of salvation. Others see it as the great enemy, so that resisting it becomes a kind of holiness. Paul’s one word, servant (v. 4), cuts it down to size from both sides. It is God’s servant, so it is not the devil, and it is owed our taxes, respect and prayers. It is only a servant, so it is not God, and it cannot carry our hopes. Augustine, writing after Rome had been sacked, asked what kingdoms are without justice but great bands of robbers, and showed in The City of God that no earthly city can give what the heart wants. Only one government is strong enough for that weight: “the government shall be upon his shoulder” (Isaiah 9:6), and that shoulder first carried a cross out of Jerusalem (John 19:17). Because we already have a King, we can let rulers be rulers, neither saviours nor monsters.

What it does not mean. Not that every ruler is good, that every command must be obeyed, or that rulers are above God’s law; nor that Christians may not criticise a government, vote it out, take it to court, protest lawfully or work to change its laws.

Scripture refuses the absolutist reading. The Hebrew midwives disobeyed a royal order to kill baby boys, and God dealt well with them (Exodus 1:17–20). Three young men refused to bow to the king’s image and told him so to his face (Daniel 3:18). Daniel went on praying against an explicit statute (Daniel 6:10). The apostles told their nation’s supreme council, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). None of these is treated as a lapse. And in Revelation 13 the same kind of power appears as a beast rising out of the sea, making war on the saints (Revelation 13:7). A state is an ordinance of God and can become a monster, and the Christian must know which he is looking at.

Even wicked rulers? Was Nero instituted by God? Was a tyrant? Paul speaks of two things at once. The office: government as such is God’s ordinance, his gift to restrain evil in a fallen world; anarchy is never his will. And providence: no ruler comes to power apart from the God who sets up kings and removes them (Daniel 2:21; 4:17), and who sometimes gives a nation a wicked ruler as a judgment, as he used Assyria and Babylon (Isaiah 10:5; Jeremiah 27:6). That does not mean he approves what the ruler does with his power, any more than he approved of Pilate condemning Jesus (John 19:11). The ruler will answer to God for every abuse.

A guard that must be said aloud. This passage has been used by slaveholders against abolitionists, by governments against the people they were crushing, and, more often and closer to home, by someone telling a person under his power that resistance is a sin. The text itself refutes this. Verse 4 defines authority by its service to your good, and the order Paul tells you to submit to is one whose own laws forbid what is being done to you. A husband, a pastor or an employer who abuses is not the governing authority of Romans 13; he is its wrongdoer. Reporting a crime is not resisting the ordinance of God. It is using it.

In everyday life. Take the thing you are angriest at your government about and ask which it is: something you dislike, something unjust, or something that requires you personally to sin. The first is politics. The second calls for every lawful means you have. Only the third is the martyr’s question, and a Christian who treats the first as though it were the third has spent the credibility he will need if the third ever arrives.

How do I know whether a law actually requires me to sin? Ask whether it commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands, not merely whether it is foolish, costly or unfair. A tax you think wasteful does not require sin. An order to sign a false statement, to stop telling people about Christ, to deny him, to help harm the innocent, or to abandon the gathering of God’s people altogether would. The hard cases are rarer than our rhetoric suggests. When unsure, search the Scriptures, talk to your elders and pray before you act; and if you must refuse, refuse openly and respectfully, ready to bear the cost as Daniel was.

Does this still apply in a democracy, where the people choose the government? Yes, and in some ways it is easier to keep. There the governing authority is the whole lawful order: constitution, courts, parliament and the officials it appoints. Voting, lobbying, campaigning or going to court is not resisting that order but using the means it gives. What Paul forbids is treating the order itself as having no claim on you, whether in quiet law-breaking, in contempt for those elected, or in refusing to accept a lawful result because your side lost.

Where Christians differ: obedience and resistance. Some say Christians must obey the state in everything; others, that they may overthrow any unjust government. This commentary’s view: Christians must submit to the governing authorities in all lawful things, even when rulers are unbelievers or unjust (1 Peter 2:13–18). But no human authority can command what God forbids or forbid what God commands, and then we must obey God rather than men (Acts 4:19; 5:29; Daniel 3; 6). Such disobedience should be open, peaceful and willing to accept the consequences, as the apostles accepted their beating and went away rejoicing (Acts 5:40–41). Reformed tradition has also taught that when rulers become tyrants who destroy the very purpose for which God gave them authority, lesser lawful magistrates may lead lawful resistance. Calvin allowed that lower magistrates, such as estates and parliaments, have a duty to restrain a king who savagely oppresses his people (Institutes 4.20.31), and later Reformed writers such as Samuel Rutherford built on that to justify resistance led by lawful authorities. Private Christians are not to take up arms against their government on their own authority. But lawful authorities who resist a ruler who has turned against the good he exists to serve (v. 4) are upholding God’s ordinance, not resisting it. Such cases are rare and grave, a last resort, and never a private person’s revenge; the Westminster Confession (23.4) insists that even an unbelieving ruler’s lawful authority stands. Paul wrote these words under Nero, and his point here is the normal duty: submission.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote under the emperor Nero, in the early, better years of his rule. Jesus had said, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.”

parallels.desc: by me kings reign

verseByVerse.quote: For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval, for he is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruler is God’s servant for your good, appointed to commend what is right and to punish wrongdoing, even with the sword. The wrath the wronged Christian lays down (12:19) is not cancelled; part of it is entrusted to him.

Not a terror to good conduct. Paul says what government is for: to restrain evil and protect good, as even a bad government usually does when it punishes theft and murder. A ruler who becomes a terror to good conduct is doing the opposite, and this passage, which tells us where authority comes from, cannot be stretched to shield his abuse of it.

You will receive his approval. The way to live without fear of the police is to do right. And “approval” (epainos) is praise, the half of the sentence nobody quotes: the state is to commend good as well as punish evil, with the award for bravery, or thanks to the citizen who hands in what he found. An account of government that produces only fear has read half the sentence.

God’s servant for your good. “Servant” is diakonos, the word used of deacons and of Paul himself (1 Corinthians 3:5). The ruler is God’s minister whether he knows it or not, as the pagan Cyrus was (Isaiah 45:1), and his work is for your good: peace and justice, the safe street and the honest market, the conditions in which families can be raised and the gospel preached (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

Not in vain. The sword stood for the power to punish, including the power of death (Genesis 9:6; Acts 25:11): God gave the state real authority to use force. And Paul wrote this about the government that, by the church’s consistent tradition, later executed him with that very sword, on no just charge, under the same emperor. The sentence was never a compliment to Rome. It was a claim about God.

An avenger. In 12:19 the wronged Christian was told never to avenge himself but to leave it to the wrath of God. Here the magistrate is an avenger (ekdikos), the same word family and the same wrath. Wrath was not cancelled when it was taken out of your hands; some of it went to the courts and the police, who have an address, a payroll and an office in your own city. The state may do what the individual may not: justice is real, it matters enormously, and you personally are not the one authorised to administer it.

The sword and the innocent man. Once the servant of God bore the sword against the only innocent man who ever stood in his court. Pilate found no guilt in him and sentenced him anyway, the very opposite of verse 4. Yet under that injustice God was carrying out a deeper justice. The wrath the magistrate carries out only in part fell in full on God’s own Son, so that it would never fall on those who trust him (3:25; 8:1). At the cross the sword of earthly justice and the wrath of heaven met in one body, and both were turned into mercy: there God showed himself both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (3:26).

What it does not mean. Not that the state may use the sword to compel faith or punish true worship. Its sphere is civil justice, not the conscience before God: the magistrate may punish the thief, but has no authority to tell the church what to believe or whom to worship. The long history of Christians persecuting Christians in the name of this verse is a history of the sword used in vain.

If I have forgiven someone, should I still go to the police? Yes, if a crime has been committed; Paul has just called that officer God’s servant. Forgiveness gives up your own right to repay, hate or punish. It does not shield the wrongdoer from the authority God has appointed, still less leave others in danger. Above all where a child or a spouse has been abused, the church must never hide it, and the victim must never be told that silence is the Christian thing. You are not taking the matter into your own hands; you are handing it to the hands appointed for it.

May a Christian serve as a soldier or police officer? Yes. If the ruler bears the sword as God’s servant, a believer may serve in that office. John the Baptist did not tell soldiers to leave the army but to stop extorting and be content with their wages (Luke 3:14), and Jesus praised the faith of a centurion above any he had found in Israel (Matthew 8:10). Pacifists cite the warning that all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52), but that rebuked Peter for resisting God’s plan; it was not a ruling on lawful office. Hence the Christian teaching on just war: force used by lawful authority, for a just cause, as a last resort. A Christian in uniform must still refuse an unjust order, and serve with the restraint of a man who knows whose servant he is.

What if the police or the courts themselves are corrupt? Then they are failing at the very thing they exist for, and Christians may say so and work for reform by lawful means: complaint, appeal, the press, the ballot, the higher court. Corruption in an office does not abolish the office. Meanwhile keep doing good, keep your own hands clean, and remember that every corrupt judge has a Judge, who holds judgment in the midst of the rulers (Psalm 82:1).

Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some Christians believe the death penalty is always wrong, reading the sword more generally as the state’s power to punish, and pointing out that courts make mistakes and that Christ calls us to mercy. This commentary’s view: Scripture gives the state the right to use the sword, including the death penalty for the gravest crimes such as murder (Genesis 9:6; Acts 25:11). Behind it stands God’s word to Noah, given before Moses and to the whole human race: whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. The penalty rests on the dignity of the human made in God’s image, not on contempt for it. Christians may disagree on whether a given country, with its legal system, should use it, given the risk of error and injustice; Scripture permits it rather than requiring it in every case, and requires that it be done justly. But it is not wrong in principle. It is not personal revenge, which is forbidden, but God’s justice carried out by lawful authority.
verseByVerse.note: The sword stood for the government’s power to punish, including capital punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience. — Romans 13:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians submit to the authorities not only to escape punishment but because conscience knows that God has placed those authorities over them.

Not only to avoid God’s wrath. “Must” (anankē) is necessity, and Paul gives two reasons, the second deeper than the first. The first is wrath, the punishment the state carries out on God’s behalf (v. 4). Fear of consequences is a real motive, but on its own it produces a citizen who keeps the law only when he might be caught: a man who is calculating, not obeying.

But also for the sake of conscience. Conscience (syneidēsis) is the inner sense of right and wrong that accuses or excuses us (2:14–15). A Christian’s conscience knows that government is God’s ordinance, so he keeps the law when no one is watching.

The empty junction. An empty road at three in the morning, a red light, no cameras and no other car within a mile. What you do at that junction is one of the few completely honest facts you have about yourself, because there is nobody to perform for. Conscience produces the same conduct at the empty junction as at the busy one.

The same conscience sets the limit. This verse and Acts 5:29 (“We must obey God rather than men”) rest on one principle. Peter could refuse the council for the same reason Paul can tell you to pay your taxes unwatched: each man answers to Somebody who is not in the room. So conscience makes the best citizen, and the one citizen who cannot be bought or bullied into sin.

There is a Witness at every empty junction. He sees three in the morning as clearly as noon, for darkness is not dark to him (Psalm 139:12). One man lived his whole life in that light with nothing to hide: Jesus could say of his Father, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), in the unseen hours as in the temple courts. Our obedience is patchy, but by his obedience the many are made righteous (5:19): his obedience is counted as ours, and ours is accepted for his sake. So the eyes that see everything look on the believer and see the obedience of the Son, and the empty road at three in the morning is not a place of exposure but of fellowship.

Is it really a sin to break a small law, like going a little over the speed limit? In principle, yes, because Paul ties obedience to conscience, not to the size of the penalty: God has placed you under this order, whether or not anyone would mind. That does not call for anxious scrupulosity over every unclear regulation, or for treating a genuine accident as a crime. It means making no private exceptions for laws you find inconvenient. If you have been careless here, confess it simply, receive his forgiveness, and keep the rule cheerfully, as a small daily act of worship.

What if my conscience objects to something other Christians think is fine? Do not act against your conscience, but do bring it to Scripture. Conscience is not infallible; it can be too tight or too loose, and it must be taught by God’s Word. Where a matter is a genuine question of sin, obey God. Where it is personal scruple, follow your conscience without condemning brothers who see it differently, the subject Paul turns to in the next chapter (14:5, 22–23). Talk it through with a wise older Christian or an elder.

verseByVerse.quote: For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing. Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed. — Romans 13:6–7
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the authorities are God’s servants, Christians pay them what is owed: taxes and duties, respect and honour. These are debts, not gifts, and “what is owed” also marks the limit of what Caesar may claim.

You also pay taxes. Because government is God’s servant, it has a right to be funded. Jesus had already settled the principle with a coin (Mark 12:17).

Ministers of God. In verse 4 the authorities were diakonoi, servants; here they are leitourgoi, the word behind our liturgy. It meant anyone who performed a public service, but the Greek Old Testament often uses it of priests and Levites, and Paul of his own gospel ministry (15:16). A word with the temple in it: the clerk processing a tax return is rendering, without knowing it, a service to God.

Attending to this very thing. To devote yourself to, to persist at: the verb (proskartereō) is the one used in 12:12 of the Christian constant in prayer. It is an extraordinarily high view of an extraordinarily dull job.

Pay to all what is owed. “Pay” (apodidōmi) is to render what is due: a debt, not a gift. Yet “what is owed” implies that not everything demanded is owed. The saying of Jesus behind it is usually quoted only halfway: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” is followed by “and to God the things that are God’s”, which sets a limit on the first. Caesar may have the coin with his image on it. He may not have the man made in the image of God.

Taxes and revenue, respect and honour. “Taxes” (phoros) were direct taxes on land and persons; “revenue” (telos) meant customs, tolls and duties. Pay both honestly. “Respect” is literally fear, reverence (phobos); “honour” (timē) is the regard due to a position. These are harder than taxes, because they are owed to a person, sometimes one you did not vote for and do not admire. Peter, probably under the same emperor, put it in three words: honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:17). Paul does not say honour those who deserve it, but pay what is owed to the office.

The setting. Tacitus records serious public complaint over indirect taxes in AD 58, when Nero considered abolishing them, within a year or so of this letter. Paul tells a small, suspect congregation to keep paying into a treasury that funded the games, the temples of the gods and, in time, the machinery that would kill them.

The Son who paid what he did not owe. Collectors once asked Peter whether his teacher paid the temple tax. Jesus answered that the sons of a king are free; yet so as not to give offence he paid it, with a coin from a fish’s mouth, for himself and for Peter (Matthew 17:24–27). The One to whom every tribute in the universe is owed paid what he did not owe, and then paid in full at the cross the debt we could never pay. So the Christian can hand Caesar his due without resentment, and keep his unreserved honour for the Lamb who was slain, worthy to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honour and glory and blessing (Revelation 5:12).

In everyday life. Honour is mostly kept or broken in private: in how you speak about the people in power among people who agree with you, in the car, at the meal table, in the group chat. Speak of them there as people you pray for.

Must I pay taxes that fund things I believe are wrong? Yes. Jesus and Paul both told believers to pay taxes to Rome, knowing what Rome funded and what it would soon do to the church. The responsibility for how a lawful tax is spent rests on those who spend it. You remain free, and often obliged, to speak, vote and campaign against what is wrong, but withholding the tax is not one of the means Scripture gives you.

Is it wrong to reduce my tax bill? Not if you do it honestly. Using the allowances and reliefs the law provides is not cheating; they were meant to be used. Evasion is wrong: hiding income, inventing expenses, taking cash to keep it off the books, bending the truth on a form because no one will check. Could you explain what you did, plainly, to the tax inspector and to your Lord? If you would rather not, you probably know the answer.

How can I honour a leader I believe is doing real harm? Honour the office and treat the person with basic dignity, while telling the truth about his actions. You may disagree firmly, criticise his policies and vote him out. You may not mock, sneer, invent or speak of him with contempt, for he bears God’s image and holds God’s appointment. Above all, pray for him, as Paul told Timothy to pray for kings under Nero (1 Timothy 2:1–2). It is very hard to go on despising someone you are honestly praying for.
verseByVerse.note: “Taxes” were direct taxes; “revenue” meant customs and tolls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Love Fulfils the Law: Put on Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one debt you never finish paying is love, and the day is too near to waste. The move from taxes to love is not a change of subject: “Pay to all what is owed” (v. 7) becomes “Owe no one anything, except to love” (v. 8), and that love fulfils every commandment about our neighbour (vv. 9–10). Then Paul tells the time. The night is almost over, so wake, and take off the works of darkness, a list that ends not with the drunken procession but with quarrelling and envy (vv. 11–13). Put on the Lord Jesus Christ himself, and refuse the flesh its supplies (v. 14). The Christian life is not moral self-improvement but being clothed in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

Romans 13:8–10 sums up the second table of the law, our duties to our neighbour: love your neighbour as yourself. The Reformed tradition has insisted that love and law are not opposites: love is the motive, and the law is the guide (see the note on vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Verse 14 was the sentence Augustine read in the garden in Milan in AD 386 (see the note on vv. 13–14), and it still convicts, commands and strengthens. Now: The urgency of verses 11–14 belongs to every age: this life is short, Christ’s return is certain, and the works of darkness are not fit clothing for children of light. The way back from a wasted day is open today, through confession to the Christ who is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, "You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet," and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leave no debt unpaid except love, the debt you never finish paying, because love is what every commandment about your neighbour requires.
