Owe no one anything, except to love each other. The move from taxes to love is not the change of subject it seems: “Pay to all what is owed to them” (v. 7), “Owe no one anything” (v. 8). Paul has been speaking of debts all along, and now names the one that never clears. Every other obligation here can be discharged; this one is charged again every morning, to the same people, at the same rate. Augustine called it the debt we always pay and always owe. It never clears because it answers a love that never ran out: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

Has fulfilled the law. Love does what the law requires toward others. The law is like the plans of a building; love is the building itself, standing in the shape the plans described.

For the commandments. Paul lists the seventh, sixth, eighth and tenth commandments, our duties to our neighbour (Exodus 20:13–17). He is not reducing the faith to being good to people: our duty to love God is simply not his subject here, and Jesus called it the first and great commandment (Matthew 22:37–38).

You shall not covet. The list ends with the one commandment nobody can see you break, the one that undid Paul himself (7:7–8). You can keep the other three by not doing things; you cannot keep this one without something happening inside. Love, like coveting, lives in the heart before it reaches the hands.

Summed up. “Summed up” (anakephalaioō) means brought together under one head, the word Paul uses of God uniting all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:10): every duty to your neighbour has one heading. The words come from Leviticus 19:18, tucked among practical laws about harvests and wages. Jesus lifted them out as the second great commandment, on which, with the first, hang all the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 22:39–40; Galatians 5:14).

The one man who owed nothing. There was once a man who owed no one anything: he kept the whole law and left nothing unpaid. And he chose to become the greatest debtor in history. Though he was rich, for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9), taking on himself the debt of sin we owed to the justice of God and paying it in full. So we can never finish paying the debt of love, because we pay it out of what he gave; and it can never ruin us, because the debt that could have ruined us has been cleared.

What it does not mean. Not that love replaces the commandments, leaving us to decide what love requires. Love does not commit adultery, take a life, steal or covet, whatever anyone says it permits. The commandments tell love where to go, and love supplies the power to go there.

In everyday life. Think of the person in your church you find hardest: not an enemy, just the one you would rather not sit near. The debt is owed to him this week at the same rate as to the people you like, and unlike a tax it is paid in person. It is easy to arrange a life so that this invoice rarely arrives; arrange this week so that it does, paying out of the love Christ first gave you: a call, a meal, a word of thanks.

Does “as yourself” command us to love ourselves first? No. It assumes the care for ourselves that everyone already has: no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it (Ephesians 5:29). We feed ourselves, defend our reputation and excuse our faults without being told. That care becomes the measure of what we owe our neighbour: not a call to build up self-love, but to give others what we naturally give ourselves, the golden rule in a single word (Matthew 7:12).

Who is my neighbour? Jesus answered with the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37): anyone whose need God puts in your path, beginning with the nearest and reaching to the stranger and the enemy.

Does loving my neighbour mean I must always say yes? No. Love seeks the other person’s real good, and sometimes that means saying no: refusing to fund an addiction, to cover up a lie, or to go on enabling sin. Love does not require you to stay in danger. A person suffering abuse is not failing to love by getting safe and seeking help; the abuser is the one breaking the law of love. What love rules out is the cold no that protects only my comfort. Ask which answer genuinely serves this person before God.

Where Christians differ: is borrowing wrong? Some take “owe no one anything” to forbid all borrowing, including mortgages and loans. This commentary’s view: Scripture does not forbid borrowing as such; it regulates it (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–8; Psalm 37:21; Matthew 5:42). Jesus told his disciples not to refuse the one who would borrow from them, which would be strange if borrowing were sin. The context here is paying what is due, and what Scripture condemns is failing to repay: the wicked borrows but does not pay back (Psalm 37:21). It also warns that the borrower is the slave of the lender (Proverbs 22:7), so wisdom avoids unnecessary debt. A Christian may take a mortgage or a loan he can repay, should keep its terms exactly, and should be slow to borrow for what he cannot afford.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “You shall not bear false witness” to the list; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it.

parallels.desc: love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love never does a neighbour harm, and so love is what the whole law was asking for.

Love does no wrong: a floor, not a ceiling. The commandments of verse 9 are negative, and the negative form is a mercy. Positive definitions of love are hard to check, but the question whether I have done this person wrong has a plain yes or no. Yet it is only a floor, the least that love does: a man can go a whole year wronging no one and loving nobody. Paul set the ceiling a chapter earlier, where love blesses the persecutor and feeds the hungry enemy (12:14, 20), and love is patient and kind, bearing, believing, hoping and enduring all things (1 Corinthians 13:4–7). Verse 10 tells you where love starts, not where it stops.

The fulfilling of the law. “Fulfilling” (plērōma) is fullness, the complete expression of a thing: love is what the law looks like lived from the heart, the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). To fulfil the law is not to set it aside but to do what it was always asking for.

Fulfilled in Christ, and in us. There has been one perfect fulfilment of the law of love on the earth. Christ never did his neighbour wrong, and he did not stop at the floor: he touched lepers, ate with sinners, washed the feet of the man who would betray him and prayed for the soldiers driving the nails. And he came so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk according to the Spirit (8:3–4). When a believer does his neighbour no wrong, and then does him good, the law is not being kept by a moral achiever. It is being fulfilled by the Spirit of Christ in someone Christ has bought.

What it does not mean. Not that a feeling of love is enough; love shows itself in keeping God’s commandments (John 14:15). Nor can we earn God’s favour by loving well: love is the fruit of our justification, not its root.

How can I love someone I feel no affection for? Begin with what love does, not with what it feels. A feeling cannot be commanded, but actions can: do this person no wrong, speak well of him, ask God’s blessing on him, and do him one concrete good. Feelings very often follow obedience rather than leading it. And you are not left to manufacture this alone: God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (5:5). Ask him for it, honestly, about this particular person.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. — Romans 13:11–12
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s day is coming closer all the time, so wake up, take off the habits of the night and put on the armour of light.

Besides this you know the time. “Besides this” ties the coming day to the love of verses 8–10. “Time” (kairos) is not clock time but the decisive season between Christ’s first coming and his return. Paul says you know it; his readers are living as though they did not. Christians who know the day is near have no time for contempt (14:10).

Wake from sleep. Sleep here is spiritual drowsiness: carelessness, ease in the world, drifting with the culture (1 Thessalonians 5:6–7; Ephesians 5:14). Nothing in the room changes when a person wakes; Paul is not asking for new circumstances, but for someone awake inside them.

Salvation is nearer. Salvation here is its completion: the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body and final glory (8:23–24). The Christian does not walk away from his salvation as the years pass; he walks toward it. That puts nothing in doubt. Scripture speaks of salvation in three tenses: we have been saved from sin’s penalty (justified, 5:1; Ephesians 2:8), are being saved from its power (sanctified, 6:22), and shall be saved from its presence when Christ returns (8:23; Philippians 3:20–21). Paul means the third, as certain as the first, since those he justified he also glorified (8:30).

The night is far gone. The night is this present evil age; the day is Christ’s return. The Christian lives in the overlap of the ages: the old age of darkness and death is passing, and the new age of light and life has already broken in with the resurrection of Christ. To live in the works of darkness is to dress for a night that is already ending.

Cast off and put on. Both are clothing verbs, like taking off night clothes in the morning, or a soldier arming for the day (Ephesians 6:11–17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8). “Put on” is the verb of verse 14: to put on the armour of light is to put on Christ himself. The word for armour (hopla) is the “instruments” of 6:13. The Christian is given not a costume for the daylight but equipment for a fight.

Salvation with a face. What draws nearer each day is not only an event but a person. Christ, offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time to save those who are eagerly waiting for him (Hebrews 9:28). The night began in a garden when the first man hid from God. But there has been a light on the horizon since another garden, where a tomb was found empty at early dawn, and the morning that began there cannot be stopped. Christ is the bright morning star (Revelation 22:16), herald of a day with no night in it, when God himself will be our light (Revelation 22:5). So this verse is not a scolding but a summons: a sleeper woken for an arrival, and no one wants to sleep through the arrival of the One he loves most.

In everyday life. Look at two stretches of the day nobody plans and nobody sees: the last hour before you sleep and the first minutes after you wake. That is where the dressing of verse 12 actually happens. Tomorrow, give the first minutes of the day to the Lord who is coming, before the phone gets them.

Should I be afraid of the day? Not if you are in Christ. For the unbeliever the day is judgment; for the believer it is dawn, the Bridegroom coming for his bride. The right fear is the sober fear of being found asleep, which wakes us; the dread of rejection Christ has removed (8:1). If you are trusting him, the day drawing near is the best day of your life.

So what do I actually do differently because the day is near? Keep short accounts: do not leave sin unconfessed or quarrels unreconciled, as if there were all the time in the world. Spend your life on what will last: people, the gospel, faithfulness in your calling, rather than things that will burn. And hold everything else loosely: possessions, ambitions and grievances look very different in the light of morning. Nearness is a reason not for panic but for wakefulness and joy.

Where Christians differ: was Paul wrong about the timing? Some say Paul expected Christ to return within his lifetime and was mistaken. This commentary’s view: Paul taught that the day is near in the sense that it is the next great event in God’s plan, with no date given, so that every generation must live ready; he did not claim to know the date (1 Thessalonians 5:1–2). He also says that a final rebellion and the man of lawlessness will come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3), so near does not mean that no prophecy remains, though those things are not a timetable to calculate. Since Christ’s first coming we have been in the last days (Hebrews 1:2), and the time is short whether he returns tomorrow or in a thousand years, for with the Lord a thousand years are as a day (2 Peter 3:8). The sentence is not a calculation but a comparison, true every time it is read: salvation is nearer now than when we first believed, and truer for you than for Paul. For each of us the day arrives at our own death if not before, and no one has ever had grounds to think that far off. His return will be one visible, public event, not a secret rapture, followed by the resurrection of all the dead and the last judgment. Many earnest Christians expect a secret rapture first (an unseen coming to take believers away before a final tribulation); this commentary reads the passages on his coming (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17) as one loud, visible return, and honours those who read them otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires. — Romans 13:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live as people of the day: refuse the sins of the night, the respectable ones as well as the scandalous, and clothe yourself in Christ, giving the flesh nothing to work with.

Walk properly. “Properly” (euschēmonōs) means decently, becomingly, fit to be seen in daylight with nothing to hide. There are things people do at one in the morning that they would not do at eleven, in the same street. The Christian is a person for whom it is always, in effect, eleven in the morning.

Not in orgies and drunkenness. Three pairs of night sins follow, and the sting is in the order. First, excess: “orgies” (kōmoi) were the drunken processions through the streets that were a familiar feature of Roman nights.

Not in sexual immorality and sensuality. Second, sexual sin: koitai, literally beds, and aselgeia, unrestrained lust, the shamelessness that no longer even bothers to hide.

Not in quarreling and jealousy. Third, strife and envy. The list begins where a first-century reader would expect, and then, without any change of tone, ends with arguing and envy. That is aimed at the respectable. The man who has never been drunk and whose sexual conduct is beyond reproach, but who cannot let a disagreement go, keeps score and needs to be right, is named in the same breath as the drunk in the street. Paul does not grade them. We do.

Unpaid love on a Friday night. Every one of these is a social sin, done in company or needing a second party. The argument about the debt of love (v. 8) is still running: the vice list is what unpaid love looks like on a Friday night, using people for pleasure or resenting them for what they have.

But put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Believers put on Christ once for all at their conversion, signed in their baptism: as many of you as were baptised into Christ have put on Christ (Galatians 3:27). Now they must put him on daily: take on his character, live consciously in union with him, and let him be the clothing others see (Colossians 3:10–14). You do not put on a set of values but a Person: the Lord who rules you, Jesus who saves you, the Christ promised from of old. There is hardly a stranger instruction in the New Testament, that a man should wear another man and be recognised by him rather than by anything of his own. It completes 12:1–2: there the body was presented to God; here it is dressed in Christ.

Make no provision. “Provision” (pronoia) is forethought, from the same root as the verb of 12:17, give thought to do what is honourable. We plan for the flesh in calm hours too, usually without admitting it: the route home that passes the place, an app left installed, the second bottle bought just in case, the evening arranged so that being alone is inevitable. Most falls are not decided at the moment of temptation but prepared days earlier, when the provisioning felt like nothing at all. “The flesh” is not the body but our fallen nature with its sinful desires, which still pulls at the believer made new in Christ (7:22–23).

Augustine in the garden. In the late summer of AD 386 a North African professor of rhetoric sat weeping in a garden in Milan, thirty-one years old, long convinced of Christianity in his mind and unable to break with a sexual habit. As a young man he had prayed: give me chastity and self-control, but not yet. Now he heard a child’s voice from a neighbouring house chanting what sounded like a game: tolle lege, take up and read. He opened the book of Paul’s letters he had left nearby and read the first passage his eye fell on. It was this one. He writes in his Confessions (8.12) that he neither wished nor needed to read further: at the end of the sentence it was as if a light of certainty flooded his heart, and all the darkness of doubt vanished.

Which clause did it. Not a doctrine he lacked, but obedience to a plain command. Augustine had been saying not yet; Romans 13:14 is God’s answer: now. And behind the child’s voice and the open book was the sovereign grace of God, which does not wait for a man to be ready but makes him ready, and which turned that weeping professor into one of the greatest teachers of grace the church has known.

Something for the guilty to wear. He was stripped so that there would be something for the guilty to wear. The soldiers gambled for the last thing he owned while he was in the act of clothing the world. The Son of God hung in the daylight, bearing the shame of every work of darkness ever done in the night, so that sinners could be dressed in his righteousness and stand unashamed in the light of God. He has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness (Isaiah 61:10). And the One we put on is the One who is coming, so that on the day of his appearing he will find his people already dressed in himself.

What it does not mean. Not that all celebration or wine is sinful. Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding (John 2:1–11), and Scripture speaks of wine that gladdens the heart of man (Psalm 104:15); what is forbidden is excess and the loss of self-control. Nor does “make no provision” mean the body or its desires are evil in themselves; God made them good. It means refusing to plan for their misuse.

In everyday life. Name one arrangement in your life whose only real function is to keep a door open: an app, a habit, a place, a route home, a friendship that always ends the same way. Close that one thing this evening. You do not do it by willpower alone, for the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you (8:11) and is at work in you as you do it.

How do I actually put on Christ, day by day? Begin each day by remembering who you are: united to Christ, forgiven, clothed in his righteousness. Fill your mind with him in his Word, so that you know what he is like. Pray for his patience, purity and kindness in the particular situations ahead. When temptation comes, ask what the Lord Jesus looks like here, and do that, by his strength. Meet with his people and come to his table, where he feeds his church with himself by faith. Putting on Christ is not a technique but a relationship lived in the open.

What if I have removed the provisions and still fall? Then come back to Christ at once. Removing provisions is wise, but it does not save you; Christ does. The Christ you put on was never your own good record, so a fall does not strip him off you. Bring it straight to him, for the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin, and we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 1:7; 2:1). Then look honestly at what led to it, since there is often a provision you had not noticed, and tell a trusted Christian friend, because sin grows in secret and weakens in the light. Falling again does not mean you are not a Christian; making peace with the sin and no longer fighting it would be the danger sign.
verseByVerse.note: Augustine was converted on reading these verses in a garden in Milan in AD 386.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.<sup>2</sup>Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.<sup>3</sup>For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval,<sup>4</sup>for he is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer.<sup>5</sup>Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God’s wrath but also for the sake of conscience.<sup>6</sup>For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing.<sup>7</sup>Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed.<sup>8</sup>Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.<sup>9</sup>For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet,” and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”<sup>10</sup>Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.<sup>11</sup>Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed.<sup>12</sup>The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.<sup>13</sup>Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy.<sup>14</sup>But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.

keyVerse.quote: Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge of the chapter. Its “owe” gathers up the debts of verse 7, taxes, respect and honour, and then names the one debt no Christian ever finishes paying, the love that fulfils every commandment about our neighbour and that the coming day makes urgent (vv. 11–14). We can keep paying it without being ruined, because Christ, who owed nothing, paid the debt we could never pay.

13.reflection:
Paul calls the ruler “God’s servant for your good” (v. 4). Are you more tempted to look to government to fix what only God can fix, or to treat it as the enemy? How does seeing it as God’s servant, and only a servant, correct both?

Paul tells every person to submit (v. 1), yet Scripture honours the midwives, Daniel and the apostles, who refused to sin at a ruler’s command. How would you tell the difference between a law you dislike, a law that is unjust and a law that requires you to sin? How do you speak about leaders you disagree with when you are among friends?

Paul calls love the one debt we never finish paying (v. 8). Who in your church or family do you find hardest to love, and what would paying that debt in person look like this week?

The night sins of verse 13 end with quarrelling and jealousy, and verse 14 calls us to put on Christ and make no provision for the flesh. Which “respectable” sins do we excuse most easily, and what provision might you need to remove?

14.title: The Weak and the Strong: Liberty and Love
14.overview:
Where we are. Romans 14 opens the last great application of the letter (14:1–15:13). Paul has called the Romans to offer themselves to God (12:1) and to the love that fulfils the law (13:8–10); now that love meets its hardest test, a church divided at the dinner table.

The message. On matters God has left free, Christians are to welcome one another, not judge or despise one another, because each believer belongs to Christ, who died and rose to be Lord of them all and before whom they will all kneel. And those who know they are free must be ready to give up their freedom rather than lead a brother, for whom Christ died, to sin against his conscience. To settle a quarrel about menus and calendars, Paul reaches for the largest things he knows: God’s welcome, Christ’s death and rising, and the judgment seat.

Why it was said. The Roman church held Jewish believers who still kept the food laws and holy days of Moses, whom Paul calls the weak, and believers, mostly Gentile, who knew themselves free of them, whom he calls the strong; the strain between them had a history (see the introduction). Each side had its typical sin: the strong despised the scrupulous as narrow, and the scrupulous condemned the free as worldly. The particular questions have changed since, but the tension has not: what I am free to do, and what love asks me to do for my brother.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–12 forbid both sins. Welcome the weak, without arguing him out of his scruples (vv. 1–2); God has welcomed both, and the Lord will hold up his own servant (vv. 3–4); each must be settled in his own mind and act for the Lord with thanks (vv. 5–6); none of us is his own, for Christ died and rose to be Lord of all (vv. 7–9); and all of us will kneel at the same judgment seat (vv. 10–12). Verses 13–23 turn to the strong. Nothing is unclean in itself, yet it is unclean to the man who thinks it so (vv. 13–14); so do not ruin by your food the one for whom Christ died (v. 15), for the kingdom is righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (vv. 16–18). Pursue peace and building up, and give up anything that would make a brother stumble (vv. 19–21). Keep your freedom between yourself and God, and never act against your own conscience, for whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (vv. 22–23).

Where it leads. Paul counts himself among the strong (15:1), yet his concern throughout is to protect the weak, and the reason comes in the next chapter: “Christ did not please himself” (15:3). The Lord of every table, who had authority over every food law, used it to serve; the one who will sit on the judgment seat first gave his life for the brother we are tempted to look down on, and he holds up both of us.

For us. Ask which you are more prone to, the raised eyebrow or the verdict, and where you have turned a matter of conscience into a test of fellowship. Then give up something small, gladly and quietly, for a brother Christ died for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Welcome the Weak: Do Not Judge or Despise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers who disagree over matters God has left open are to welcome one another, because each belongs to Christ and answers to him alone. Paul names the typical sin of each side: the strong despise the scrupulous, and the weak condemn the free (vv. 1–3). Then he gives four reasons to stop. Each believer is another Master’s servant, and that Master will hold him up (v. 4). Both sides act in honour of the Lord and give thanks to God (vv. 5–6). Christ died and rose to be Lord of the dead and the living (vv. 7–9). And all will stand side by side before the same judgment seat (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Things indifferent and the conscience

Reformed writers use the term adiaphora (things indifferent) for matters that Scripture neither commands nor forbids, the ground Romans 14 covers. In them Christian liberty is real: what God has declared clean is clean, and a conscience the gospel has freed need not be bound again. But liberty is not the highest value; love is. Calvin insisted that the strong must use their freedom with care for the weaker conscience, not yielding to every scruple for ever, but never using freedom as a weapon against the brother Christ died for.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In Rome the tension was between Jewish and Gentile believers over food laws and the calendar. Paul does not end it by naming the winners; he points both groups to the lordship of Christ (v. 8) and the coming judgment (v. 12). Now: Every generation has its own version: alcohol, entertainment, dress, styles of worship. The principles hold: welcome the brother whose scruples differ; do not despise; do not judge; each will give account to God, not to you.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Welcome the believer whose conscience is stricter than yours as fully as God welcomed you, and do not turn the welcome into an argument. On matters Scripture leaves open, such as food, the scrupulous brother belongs at the table, not on probation at the edge of it.

In the flow. Here the love that fulfils the law (13:8–10) meets its hardest test. If God justifies Jew and Gentile alike, by faith (3:29–30), the church cannot divide them over the menu.

Weak in faith. Everything depends on getting this straight. It does not mean weak in trusting Christ for salvation, nor lax or half-hearted. It means not yet persuaded of the freedom the gospel gives in such matters: the man with more rules, not fewer, whose conscience objects if he eats the meat or ignores the day. We instinctively call the strict Christian the strong one; Paul’s labels run the other way. Read the chapter with the usual assumption, and every instruction in it lands on the wrong person.

Welcome him. “Welcome” (proslambanō, take to oneself) means accept fully into fellowship, not merely tolerate. Paul uses it four times in this section: here; in verse 3, where the reason is that God has welcomed him; and twice at 15:7, “welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you”. It is not politeness at the edge of the room but the welcome God has already shown to the person you find difficult.

But not to quarrel over opinions. “Opinions” (dialogismoi) are reasonings, debatable thoughts. Do not welcome someone in order to argue him out of his scruples. Hospitality can be a tactic, and the person being worked on can always tell.

Only vegetables. The strong believe all foods are clean (v. 14; Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). The weak probably included Jewish believers who kept the food laws and holy days of Moses, and perhaps Gentiles who feared meat offered to idols (as in 1 Corinthians 8 and 10). A scrupulous believer in Rome could not easily tell how an animal had been slaughtered or whether the meat had come through a temple, so the only certain course was to eat none, as Daniel did in Babylon (Daniel 1:8–12). A tender conscience usually over-corrects, because it cannot bear the risk. And after the expulsion under Claudius, the shared meal at the heart of the church’s fellowship had become a place of tension (see the introduction).

A bruised reed he will not break. Christ does not break the bruised reed or snuff out the smouldering wick (Matthew 12:20), and a weak conscience is such a reed. Years after Pentecost, Peter still could not bring himself to eat what the law called unclean, and said so to the Lord himself (Acts 10:14). Christ did not despise him; he showed him the vision three times, patiently, until Peter understood that God had made clean both the food and the Gentiles who ate it. The strong are asked to treat a scruple the way the Lord treated Peter’s.

He wanted them. God welcomed us first, with our wrong opinions, wrong history and a great deal of sin, without waiting for us to agree with him about everything. The Lord who receives sinners and eats with them (Luke 15:2) has set a table where the scrupulous and the free sit side by side, both there for one reason only: he wanted them. His welcome is wider than our opinions and warmer than our hearts, so sit with the brother whose scruples you do not share, and let the conversation be about Christ, not the scruple.

How do I tell a disputable matter from a real sin? Three questions sort them. Does Scripture command it or forbid it? Is the gospel itself at stake? Is anyone being told he must do this to be right with God? If all three answers are no, this chapter governs. Where Scripture calls something sin, no appeal to liberty can make it disputable. And where the gospel is at stake, the strong must not yield: when false brothers wanted Titus circumcised as a condition of acceptance, Paul did not yield to them even for a moment (Galatians 2:5). On a scruple that tries to rule the church, see v. 15.

What are the disputable matters today? Rarely temple meat. More likely alcohol, Christmas and Easter, styles of worship music, Bible translations, schooling, dress, diet, films and novels, social media, or how strictly to keep Sunday, on which sincere believers reach different conclusions. The list changes; the principle does not. Where God has not spoken, no Christian has the right to speak as though he had.

I think I am the weak brother. Is that an insult? No. It says nothing about your sincerity, your salvation or your love for Christ; the man Paul describes is scrupulous because he fears displeasing God. And nearly every command in this chapter is aimed at the strong, on your behalf. Paul does not spend a single verse telling you to hurry up.

Where Christians differ: what counts as a disputable matter? Some apply this chapter to every disagreement, including doctrine and morality. This commentary’s view: Romans 14 concerns things that Scripture neither commands nor forbids, matters indifferent in themselves (the Greek term is adiaphora). It does not cover the gospel itself, which Paul defends fiercely (Galatians 1:8–9), or clear moral commands such as sexual purity (13:13). Where God has spoken plainly, we do not treat it as an opinion. Where he has not, we give liberty, for God alone is Lord of the conscience (the Westminster Confession 20.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 21.2).
verseByVerse.note: The “weak” probably include Jewish believers who kept the food laws, and others who avoided meat that might have been offered to idols.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The free must not look down on the scrupulous, and the scrupulous must not condemn the free, because God has welcomed each of them and the Lord holds each of them up.

Let not the one who eats despise. “Despise” (exoutheneō) is to count as nothing. Each side is assigned its own sin. Freedom does not tempt a person to condemn; it tempts him to find the other man faintly ridiculous: the raised eyebrow, the anecdote told later about how strict so-and-so is.

Let not the one who abstains pass judgment. “Pass judgment” (krinō) here means condemn, writing off the free as worldly. Scruple does not tempt a person to sneer; it tempts him to convict. Neither party is usually in danger of the other’s sin, which is why each so easily believes himself innocent.

For God has welcomed him. What unites Christians is not agreement on secondary matters but the same God’s welcome: the brother you are tempted to despise or condemn sits at your table because God himself pulled out the chair. Underneath both sins lies one hunger, to feel secure by being better than somebody: the scrupulous man rests on his strictness, the free man on his insight, and religion has become a pedestal. The gospel takes the pedestal away. God’s welcome rests on Christ, not on anyone’s menu, so no one at the table needs to stand on anyone else.

Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? “Servant” (oiketēs) is a household servant. You may think another family’s arrangements peculiar, but you do not walk into their kitchen and correct their staff: it is not your household, and they do not take their orders from you. Every believer is Christ’s servant, not yours.

He will be upheld. Paul’s confidence runs toward the very person you were worried about. The Master is Christ, who died and rose to be Lord of his people (v. 9). On the night Peter would deny him, Jesus told him that he had prayed for him, that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32). Peter fell, and stood again, because he was held. Every believer is upheld at this moment by hands that do not tire and do not let go.

The relief hidden in this verse. Much of our anxiety about other Christians is a quiet doubt whether God is managing them properly. He is. You may pray for your brother, love him and talk with him. You do not have to hold him up.

In everyday life. Think of a believer whose practice differs from yours on something Scripture does not settle, and notice which reflex arrives first: the urge to laugh, or the urge to convict. That tells you which group you are actually in. Confess it to the Lord who welcomed you both, and find something kind to say about that brother to someone else.

Does this mean Christians must never judge? No. Paul forbids condemning a brother over matters God has left open. He commands the church to judge sin among its members (1 Corinthians 5:12–13), pronounces a curse on those who preach another gospel (Galatians 1:8–9), and at the end of this letter tells the Romans to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine they have been taught (16:17). The question is not whether to judge but what: sin and false teaching, yes; another believer’s conscience on a disputable matter, no.

verseByVerse.quote: One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On days God has left open, each believer must be settled in his own mind and act for the Lord; the one who keeps the day and the one who does not can both honour him and thank him.

One day as better than another. The days were probably the Sabbath and the Jewish feasts and fasts (Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16). Some believers still kept them as special; others counted all days alike.

Fully convinced in his own mind. “Fully convinced” (plērophoreō) means filled up to full assurance. Paul does not say the matter is unimportant, or do as you please. Whether you use the freedom or keep the scruple, you must have thought it through, not merely inherited it from your upbringing or your church. He asks not that everyone reach the same conclusion, but that each reach his own, which is more demanding than it sounds.

Paul’s restraint. Paul is not neutral; he is persuaded that nothing is unclean (v. 14). Yet he defends a man’s right to reach the opposite practical conclusion and act on it before God. He will argue for his view; he will not make it a rule for others. That is apostolic authority used with great gentleness, and a model for every pastor and parent.

In honour of the Lord. The test is not what a person does but whom he does it for. The Lord in this chapter is Jesus (v. 9), who said that the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28). So the Jewish believer who still keeps the seventh day keeps it in honour of its Lord, and the Gentile believer who does not is free because that same Lord has given the rest the day pointed forward to: rest from trying to earn God’s favour, because his work is finished (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). Both are standing before the One the day was always about.

He gives thanks to God. The common ground is not agreement but thanksgiving: two men do opposite things at one table, both say grace over it, and Paul treats that as the decisive fact about both.

Two kinds of tolerance. Tolerance used to mean bearing with views you believed wrong; increasingly it means believing no view is wrong. D. A. Carson, in The Intolerance of Tolerance, pointed out the irony: the new kind is strangely intolerant of anyone who still thinks some things are true. Romans 14 is the older kind at its best, and more. Everyone is fully convinced, and nobody pretends the question does not matter, yet they eat at one table, held there not by a shrug but by a welcome. Each was received by God while still wrong about a great many things, and stands because the Master holds him up (v. 4). People who know that can hold their convictions firmly and their brothers more firmly still. Relativism can only leave people alone. The gospel makes them family.

In everyday life. Before any choice in a disputed area, ask: can I thank God for this specific thing, out loud, without the sentence going strange in my mouth? If you can thank him, go ahead with a clear conscience. Liberty that cannot say grace over what it is doing has stopped being liberty, and scruple that cannot thank God for the freedom it is declining has become something other than conscience.

What it does not mean. It does not mean regular gathering for worship is optional (Hebrews 10:25). The day may be a matter of conscience; meeting with the Lord’s people is not.

What about Christmas and Easter? They belong to this chapter. A church may keep them gladly, rejoicing in the birth and resurrection of the Lord. Others, especially in some Reformed traditions, keep no holy day beyond the Lord’s Day, wanting nothing in worship that Scripture does not command. Both can act in honour of the Lord; neither may treat the other as compromised or as a killjoy.

How do I become fully convinced? Not by waiting for a feeling. Read what Scripture says on the matter, and what it does not, and ask whether you could give a reason from God’s Word for what you do. Talk it through with mature believers, including some who disagree, and pray for wisdom (James 1:5). Then reach a conclusion you can thank God for, and live by it while remaining teachable. Being fully convinced does not mean you can never change your mind, only that you act from conviction now, not from pressure or confusion.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day. Some say this verse proves no day is special for Christians. Others hold that the fourth commandment, given at creation (Genesis 2:3) and part of the moral law, binds Christians to a strict Sabbath observance, now on Sunday, and that this verse speaks only of Jewish ceremonial days; this is the view of the Westminster Confession (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), which call the Lord’s Day the Christian Sabbath. This commentary’s view: the Old Testament Sabbath was a shadow fulfilled in Christ, who is our true rest (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10; Matthew 11:28). In Colossians Paul lists Sabbaths among the shadows whose substance is Christ, and here he lets a believer treat every day alike, which many find hard to square with a binding weekly Sabbath. Christians are not bound by the Sabbath laws of Moses, and Paul leaves Jewish days to conscience. But the first day of the week, the day of Christ’s resurrection, was the day the early church gathered for worship (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). Gathering with God’s people on the Lord’s Day, resting from ordinary work where possible and giving the day to worship, is a great privilege and a wise rhythm, gladly set apart out of joy and wisdom, not a binding law with rules about work; and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (v. 5; Colossians 2:16–17). Those who hold the Westminster and 1689 view are godly brothers who keep the day in honour of the Lord, and deserve respect, not contempt.
verseByVerse.note: The days in question were probably the Sabbath and Jewish festivals.

verseByVerse.quote: For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No Christian belongs to himself: in life and in death we are the Lord’s, so even our smallest choices are made for him.

None of us lives to himself. This is the principle beneath the chapter. The verse is often quoted to mean that no one is an island, which is true but not Paul’s point; the next words say to whom we live: the Lord. Every choice, from what to eat to every life decision, is made in his presence.

To the Lord. All of life, and death itself, is lived toward Christ, under his eye. “To the Lord”, “to the Lord”, “the Lord’s”: three times in a single verse. Both parties keep claiming to be right; Paul keeps answering that neither of them is his own. That settles a dispute between equals without deciding which of them is correct. It decides who has the right to rule them both.

We are the Lord’s. This is our great comfort. The Heidelberg Catechism opens with this truth and cites this passage for it: my only comfort in life and in death is that I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ (Question 1).

Into your hands. The Lord to whom we live and die first walked this road. He did not please himself (15:3). He lived to do the will of the One who sent him (John 4:34), and he died to the Father too, with the words of Psalm 31 on his lips: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). So the Christian who dies to the Lord is not stepping into the dark alone. He dies into hands that were pierced for him.

Where this sentence has ended up. “Whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s” is read at gravesides and said in hospital rooms at three in the morning, and Paul wrote it about a disagreement over vegetables. That does not make the verse smaller. He puts the largest thing he knows under the smallest quarrel, which shows how seriously he takes the damage it can do.

What does it look like to live to the Lord on an ordinary day? It means asking, about ordinary things: whom am I doing this for? Work done honestly when no one checks (Colossians 3:23), money spent as a steward, time and rest received as his gift, people treated as his. It is not religious thoughts every minute, but no private zone where he has no say, and that is not a burden but a freedom: you no longer have to be your own god.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ died and rose again for this very purpose, to be Lord of all his people, living and dead, so no believer may take Christ’s place over another’s conscience.

To this end. To settle a dispute about dinner, Paul goes to the cross and the empty tomb, not as an illustration but as the argument: Christ died to purchase those enslaved to sin and death, and rose to rule them as the living, reigning King.

Lord both of the dead and of the living. Christ’s rule reaches beyond the grave. Believers who have died are still his (1 Thessalonians 4:14–16), as are those alive now; by dying and rising he won the right to rule over all (Philippians 2:8–11; Acts 2:36). Christ went into the one country from which no ruler had returned, and came back holding the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). He rules both countries, because he has lived in both.

Both sides disqualified. If the cross was meant to make Christ Lord, then taking charge of another believer’s conscience in a matter God has left open intrudes on what Calvary secured. The strong man imposing his freedom and the weak man imposing his scruple both are trying to sit on a throne that was bought with blood for someone else.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ became Lord only at his resurrection, as if he were not God before. He was always God the Son; as the God-man and Redeemer he received the lordship he won by dying and rising.

Where are believers who have died? With Christ, consciously, now, not unaware and not in some place of further cleansing: Paul longed to depart and be with Christ, which he called far better (Philippians 1:23), and he spoke of being away from the body as being at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Their bodies rest in the grave awaiting the resurrection; their souls are with him, under his rule and in his joy. Scripture calls their death sleep because it is temporary and peaceful, not because they have ceased to know.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God; for it is written, "As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stop judging and despising your brother, because all of us will kneel before the same judgment seat, and the Judge’s seat is not ours.

Why do you pass judgment on your brother? To the weak: why judge? To the strong: why despise? In Greek both questions begin with an emphatic “you”: Paul turns to each party in turn, like a man pointing. And “brother”, twice: you are not arguing with an opponent but with family.

The judgment seat. The bēma was the raised stone platform in a Greek city from which a magistrate gave his ruling. Paul had stood before one himself, in Corinth, when Gallio dismissed the case against him (Acts 18:12–16). In 2 Corinthians 5:10 he calls it the judgment seat of Christ, for God judges through Christ (John 5:22; Acts 17:31). We will not be judges there but judged, the strong and the weak exactly level, so we should not take the judge’s seat now.

Every knee shall bow. The words come from Isaiah 45:23 (with “as I live” from Isaiah 49:18), spoken by the God who has just said there is no other. Paul elsewhere applies the same verse to Jesus, at whose name every knee bows (Philippians 2:10–11), a sign of how fully he counts Jesus as the one God of Isaiah. You will bow before him beside the brother you were correcting. That is the argument: the judge’s seat is already taken. Every act of judging another believer over an open question is an attempt to sit somewhere that already has someone in it.

The Judge who stood trial. The same Lord who will sit on the judgment seat once stood before Pilate’s, silent, condemned for us. The One we will bow to is the One who bowed his head on the cross and gave up his spirit.

What it does not mean. Every knee bowing does not mean that all will be saved. Believers will bow in worship and joy; the rest will bow because they must, acknowledging too late the Lord they refused, and will go away into eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46). The bowing is universal; the salvation is not.

Will believers be judged? Yes: we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). But not to decide whether they are saved. That was settled when they believed: whoever believes does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life (John 5:24; Romans 8:1). What is examined is their life and service. Some will receive reward, and others will suffer loss, though they themselves are saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

Textual note: in verse 10 some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “the judgment seat of Christ” instead of “of God”. The meaning is the same, for Paul uses both phrases (2 Corinthians 5:10), and God judges through his Son.

parallels.desc: to me every knee shall bow

verseByVerse.quote: So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each of us will answer to God for his own life, not for his brother’s.

Give an account. “Account” (logos) is a reckoning, like an account book. “Each of us”: personally, individually. “Of himself”: not of others. Whatever else is asked, you will not be asked about your brother’s choices in matters of conscience (Matthew 12:36; Hebrews 4:13).

No comparisons in court. This removes a defence many of us have quietly prepared. Nearly every account we give of ourselves is comparative: I am not as strict as him, I am not as careless as her. It works in conversation, where someone is always available to be worse. It will not work on that day, when the other party will be busy giving his own account.

The Judge who is also the advocate. The One who receives the account is the Lord Jesus, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5:22). That is the comfort folded inside the warning. We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:1–2), the one whose sacrifice has met God’s just anger against them in full. The account is real. But it will be read in the presence of the One who bore its worst lines on the cross, and who speaks for the one giving it.

In everyday life. Try describing your spiritual condition to God without mentioning another Christian, a church you left or a generation you think has gone wrong: just yourself, before the Lord who has already answered for you. What remains is what you will give account of.

If I am justified, why should the account concern me? Because it is real, and your Father cares how his children live. It is not a trial to decide whether you will be condemned (see vv. 10–11), but more like a son showing his father what he did with what he was given: it should make you serious, not afraid of rejection. And it frees you from comparison, because you are not being measured against your brother, only seen by your Lord, who knows your frame and remembers that you are dust (Psalm 103:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Do Not Cause a Brother to Stumble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who are free must never use their freedom to lead a brother into sin against his conscience. Nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for the man who thinks it so (vv. 13–14), and the weak brother is one for whom Christ died (v. 15). The kingdom of God is not food but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (vv. 16–18), so pursue peace and build one another up, giving up even meat and wine where they would make a brother stumble (vv. 19–21). Keep your freedom between yourself and God, and never act against your own conscience, for whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.theology:
Christian liberty and the law of love

Freedom is real, but love is higher. The freedom the gospel gives is freedom from the bondage of sin and law, for the service of God and neighbour. To use freedom as a weapon against a brother’s conscience misuses it as surely as legalism does; it is just as self-centred, only pointed in another direction.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Much of the meat in a first-century market had passed through a pagan temple (compare 1 Corinthians 8–10). The strong knew the idol was nothing; the weak felt defiled. Paul’s principle: your knowledge does not give you the right to wound your brother’s conscience. Now: The strong Christian is tempted to treat freedom as a badge of maturity to be displayed rather than a gift to be handled with care. Maturity shows itself less in using freedom than in being willing to limit it for love.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother. I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. — Romans 14:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stop passing verdicts on one another and pass one on yourself: never trip a brother into sin, for though no food is unclean in itself, it is unclean to the man who thinks it so. Paul turns from the judgment seat to the dinner table, and from the weak to the strong, asking the strong to take responsibility for the spiritual welfare of the weak.

But rather decide. Verse 13 uses the same Greek verb (krinō) twice, which the English hides: let us no longer judge one another, but judge this instead. Paul does not ask them to stop making judgments, but to make one about themselves: resolve never to put an obstacle in a brother’s path. The urge to pass verdicts is turned on ourselves.

A stumbling block or hindrance. The first word (proskomma) means the thing your foot catches on; the second (skandalon) first named the trigger of a trap, and in the New Testament it means whatever trips a person into sin. Neither means giving offence in the modern sense. The damage is not that the weak brother is annoyed by your steak. It is that he eats one, against his own conscience, because you made it awkward not to, and something inside him gives way.

Persuaded in the Lord Jesus. Paul sides with the strong, by Jesus’ authority, not personal preference. Behind it very probably stands the day Jesus said that nothing entering a man from outside can defile him, to which Mark adds the comment, “Thus he declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). (The KJV reads that phrase as part of Jesus’ saying; most modern Bibles take it as Mark’s comment.) The food laws, which had marked Israel out as holy for centuries, were fulfilled in Christ. “Unclean” (koinos) means common, ritually impure.

Unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. Our care for the weak hangs on this half of the verse. In itself the food is clean; for that man, eating it really does defile. Conscience creates obligation, not reality: believing meat unclean does not make it so, but a man who acts against his conscience has done wrong even when the act was harmless, because he did what he believed God forbids.

He has made the unclean clean. The Lord Jesus spoke one sentence, and every table became a place where Jew and Gentile could sit together. He has made the unclean clean: lepers, sinners, Gentiles, us. And he teaches the people he sets free to use their freedom tenderly, for he had authority over every law and every table, and he used it to serve rather than to be served (Mark 10:45).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that sin is whatever someone thinks it is, so that morality is relative. Paul speaks only of matters indifferent, like food. Murder is unclean whatever anyone thinks.

So how do I help a brother with a weak conscience? Never by pressure. The only real remedy is that he come to think otherwise, through teaching, time and the example of people he trusts; getting him to do the thing while he still believes it wrong only teaches him to ignore his conscience. So be patient, open the Scriptures with him when he wants to, live your own freedom gently, and leave the timing to the Spirit. Some people never change their mind on the matter, and that is all right; Paul never says the weak must become strong before they are welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If your freedom draws a brother into wounding his conscience, you have stopped loving him; do not ruin over a meal someone Christ died to save.

If your brother is grieved by what you eat. “Grieved” (lypeō) means pained: his conscience is wounded, because he is drawn into doing what he thinks wrong, or watches a brother do what he believes dishonours God.

You are no longer walking in love. The strong man here has broken no rule; his theology is correct and his dinner lawful. He has simply stopped walking in love somewhere between being right and being at the table. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up (1 Corinthians 8:1).

Do not destroy. “Destroy” (apollymi) is the word used across the New Testament for ruin and perishing. Paul could have said upset, or set back. He chose the word for wreckage, and attached it to a plate of food. The wreckage is rarely one catastrophe: a man acts against his conscience once, in company, to avoid looking foolish, and a conscience overridden once is easier to override again. What has been damaged is the very thing by which he says no to any sin.

The one for whom Christ died. Christ gave his life for this brother; will you not give up a meal for him? He died, by name, for the scrupulous believer with his long list and for the free believer who finds him tiresome, and he will lose neither.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the weak can control the strong by complaining. The concern is a brother who might be led to sin against his conscience, not one who merely disapproves. A Christian who uses his scruples to rule the church, or who demands that his preferences become everyone’s law, is no longer the weak brother of this chapter. He is closer to the false brothers to whom Paul would not yield for a moment (Galatians 2:5).

How do I know whether my freedom is actually hurting someone? Watch and ask. Is there a believer present whose conscience forbids this, and who might follow your example against it? A new Christian, or someone fighting alcohol or gambling, for whom your freedom could reopen an old door? If unsure, ask him privately and gently. Usually the answer is clear, and the cost of restraint small: an evening, a meal, a glass. The brother is worth far more.

Where Christians differ: can someone for whom Christ died be destroyed? Some Christians, often called Arminian, use this verse to argue that Christ died for people who will finally perish, and that a true believer can be lost; they want the warning heard at full weight, and in that they are right. This commentary’s view: Paul is warning the strong about the real tendency of their actions: what they do could lead a brother into sin and spiritual ruin. The warning is real, and God uses such warnings to keep his people. Elsewhere Paul is clear that those for whom Christ died will certainly be saved (5:8–10; 8:32–34). Christ died effectively for his sheep, and none of them will be snatched from his hand (John 10:11, 28). This is definite atonement (Christ’s death actually secures the salvation of those for whom he died) and the perseverance of the saints (all who truly believe will be kept by God to the end). The man who wrote that nothing can separate us from the love of God (8:39) is not contradicting himself over dinner; Scripture names real dangers at full strength to those in a position to cause them. The point here is ethical: treat your brother as someone precious to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let your good freedom get a bad name, because God’s kingdom is not about food but about righteousness, peace and joy given by the Holy Spirit.

Spoken of as evil. The good in danger is the liberty itself, a true gift of the gospel. Used carelessly it will be slandered (literally blasphemed), and a right thing handled without love becomes evidence that the doctrine produces bad men.

Not a matter of eating and drinking. The kingdom of God is his rule, present now in Christ and coming in fullness, and its heart is not food. A kingdom is simply wherever a king’s word is obeyed, and every table has one. Whatever must win at your table, your menu, your scruple, your being right, is what reigns there. See also Kingdom of God in the Theological Dictionary.

Righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Righteousness: right standing with God and right living. Peace: with God and with one another. Joy: delight in God. All three are the Spirit’s work (Galatians 5:22), so his power, not the strong man’s resolve, makes such love possible. Nor are they only private inward states. Peace is between the two parties at the table, joy is that of a brother not trampled, righteousness is doing right by him: Paul describes what a room looks like, not only what a soul feels.

All three through our Lord Jesus Christ. Each has already come in this letter through Christ: the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ (3:22), peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (5:1), and rejoicing in God through our Lord Jesus Christ (5:11). So the kingdom is life under the King who died and rose, the Spirit bringing his gifts to the very table where two believers disagree. And this King did not come to win the menu. At his last meal he claimed nothing and gave everything: “This is my body, which is given for you” (Luke 22:19). Where he reigns, people no longer need to win.

The new dietary laws. Quarrels about food do not belong to a religious past: our secular culture keeps food laws with near-religious seriousness. A rich dessert is “sinful”, a salad is “guilt-free”, an indulgent weekend calls for a “detox”, and a strict regime allows “cheat days”. The vocabulary of sin and cleansing has moved from the soul to the plate, and, as in Rome, the menu shows who is pure and who is not. Eating carefully is no sin, and often simple wisdom. But a righteousness you can eat your way into is one you can eat your way out of, and it never lets you rest. Paul knew both the man whose diet is his holiness and the man whose god is his belly (Philippians 3:19; 16:18), and the kingdom answers both. Its righteousness is not consumed but received, from the One whose flesh is true food (John 6:55), given for people who could never be made clean by anything they ate or refused.

In everyday life. When a meal or a church decision turns into a contest, ask who is King at this table, and let the small thing go for your brother’s sake. Or suppose someone watched your congregation for a month without its statement of faith: from what generates heat after the service, what would he conclude it was about? How people vote, what they watch, the precise vocabulary for things we already agree on? If the answer is not near righteousness, peace and joy, it is near food and drink, whatever the modern equivalent has turned out to be.

Does this mean our freedom does not matter? No. Christian liberty is precious; Christ bought it, and Paul fought for it (Galatians 5:1). But it exists for love, worship and joy, and used to wound a brother or win an argument it has forgotten what it is for. Prize your freedom enough to protect its good name.

Uncertain wording. In verse 16 the Greek says simply “your good”; the ESV’s “what you regard as good” is an interpretation. Most take it, as this note does, to be the strong believer’s freedom. Some take it more broadly as the good of the gospel itself, or the church’s whole life in Christ, which outsiders would slander if believers tore one another apart over food. The two are close: the freedom is part of the gospel’s good, and either way careless use brings it into disrepute.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men. So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who serves Christ in this way pleases God and wins the respect even of outsiders, so make peace and building one another up your aim.

Whoever thus serves Christ. “Thus” means by living for righteousness, peace and joy rather than for food; “serves” (douleuō) is a slave’s word. Such service is acceptable to God not because it is flawless, but because it is offered through the Son: spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5).

Acceptable to God and approved by men. “Approved” (dokimos) means tested and found genuine, like a coin that has been weighed. Even the watching world (12:17), which understands little of our doctrine, recognises that kind of love when it sees it.

Pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding. “Pursue” (diōkō) is a word for chasing hard: peace does not come simply by keeping out of arguments. And upbuilding (oikodomē) is a builder’s noun. A congregation is a site with work going on, where every action adds a row of bricks or removes one (1 Corinthians 14:12).

The approved Servant. There was one Servant whom the Father fully approved (Matthew 3:17), who laid aside what he was entitled to for others (Philippians 2:6–7). The believer who gives up a freedom for a brother walks in his steps, and is accepted in him. And a church that pursues peace is only echoing the God who pursued it first, and who came looking for us when we were his enemies (5:10).

The better question. The instinctive question is: am I allowed? Here the answer is usually yes, which is why it is useless. Paul asks instead: what will this build? A thing can be entirely permitted and still take a wall down.

What mutual upbuilding looks like. It is slow, ordinary work, one row at a time, and every member is on the site: a specific encouragement, not “good sermon” but “what you said to my son on Sunday has stayed with him”; asking what God has been teaching someone, then praying for him by name; passing on a verse without lecturing; quietly changing plans so a weaker brother can join in; speaking well of people not in the room, for gossip is demolition done in a whisper. “Mutual” means it runs both ways, so let others build you up too. And remember whose building it is. Christ said, “I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18). We carry his bricks, and the stone that everything rests on is already laid.

Does pursuing peace mean I should never disagree? No. Paul himself has just told the strong that he agrees with them (v. 14). It means disagreeing in a way that builds: speaking the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), at the right time, listening first, refusing to caricature, and never letting a difference on a secondary matter turn into a break in fellowship. Some peace is false, bought by silence about sin or the gospel, but most church quarrels are not about the gospel, and on those the person who makes peace is called a son of God (Matthew 5:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No meal is worth wrecking what God has built in a brother: all food is clean, but it is good to give up meat, wine or anything else that would trip him into sin.

Do not destroy the work of God. The work of God is your brother, or the church God is building in him and around him. “Destroy” (katalyō) is the builder’s opposite of verse 19: to demolish what has been put up. Someone else has been building in that man for years; do not walk onto the site with a hammer over a question of lunch.

Everything is indeed clean. Paul never takes back his view to keep the peace, but he adds at once that “it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats.” Being right is not enough; how you use your rights matters.

Not to eat meat or drink wine. Love may mean giving up a right altogether, at least in certain company; wine perhaps because it too was used in pagan offerings. Quoted, especially since the nineteenth century, as a standing rule about alcohol, the verse turns the chapter upside down. Paul does not say wine is unclean; he has just insisted that everything is indeed clean (v. 20). What he says is that abstaining is good where it prevents a brother stumbling: freely chosen, for that occasion, and for somebody else’s sake.

Created in Christ Jesus. The work has a name: we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus (Ephesians 2:10). Whatever God has done in that scrupulous believer, he has done in Christ, and he means to finish it on the day of Christ (Philippians 1:6). The strong believer who presses his freedom on a weak brother swings a hammer at something Christ built at the cost of his own life. Is any dinner worth that?

Why the restraint cannot become a law. Once the strong man’s self-limitation is made a law for every believer, it has stopped being love and become what this chapter forbids: a scruple imposed on another man’s conscience. The free are asked to restrain themselves, never to make their restraint everyone’s rule.

Should I tell people that I am holding back for their sake? Usually not. The practical form of this verse is smaller and harder than a policy: the quiet decision that at this table, with this person, you will not have what you are entitled to, and will not announce it, which is the part most of us fail. A sacrifice that is advertised turns into a rebuke, and makes the weak brother feel like a burden. If he asks, answer simply and kindly. Otherwise let love work in silence.

What if a friend is fighting an addiction? Then this verse applies in full. If someone near you is recovering from alcohol, gambling or any other bondage, lay down your freedom in that area gladly whenever you are with him, probably for longer than you think necessary, without making him ask. Do whatever makes it easiest for him to stand, without fuss. That is not legalism but love carrying a brother’s burden (Galatians 6:2).

Where Christians differ: alcohol. Some say this verse requires total abstinence from alcohol for all Christians. Others say Christians can drink freely regardless of others. This commentary’s view: Scripture presents wine as a gift of God (Psalm 104:15; John 2:1–11) and forbids drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18; 13:13). Drinking in moderation is a matter of Christian liberty. But love will gladly give it up where it would cause a brother to stumble, for instance around someone struggling with alcohol. Those who choose to abstain may do so for the Lord, and should not judge those who drink moderately.

verseByVerse.quote: The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hold your freedom before God without parading it; happy is the person whose conscience does not accuse him over what he does.

The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. The faith here is your conviction about liberty. Enjoy it before God, without making it a test of fellowship. Paul is not telling the strong to hide their convictions; he has just stated his own (v. 14). He forbids the display: liberty that satisfies fully only when the scrupulous are watching.

Blessed. “Blessed” means happy, in God’s favour. A clear conscience is a great gift (Acts 24:16). The happy man can do the thing and get on with the evening, without wondering at midnight whether it was all right. That is a mercy for the many sincere Christians who conduct a running trial of themselves over things God has not forbidden: God counts a settled conscience a gift, not laxity.

The Son who paid the tax. Jesus did exactly this. Asked whether his teacher paid the temple tax, he explained to Peter that kings do not tax their own sons, so the sons are free. Yet, so as not to give offence, he sent Peter to find a coin in a fish’s mouth and paid for them both (Matthew 17:24–27). He held his freedom without surrendering it or parading it, and the strong believer is to keep his liberty the same way.

Not innocent, but forgiven. We could never have given ourselves a clear conscience; ours had every reason to condemn us. Then the blood of Christ cleansed our consciences from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14), and there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (8:1). So the believer can lie down at night in peace, not because he is innocent but because he is forgiven.

In everyday life. Ask whether there is any freedom you enjoy more when someone disapproving is watching. If so, quietly drop the display. The freedom was Christ’s gift to be enjoyed before God, not a point to be scored.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith in Christ should be kept private. Paul speaks only of convictions about matters indifferent. The gospel itself is to be confessed with the mouth before the world (10:9–10).

Can a quiet conscience be wrong? Yes. The sentence must not be read as: if you feel fine, you are fine. Paul means a conscience taught by the gospel, not one that has gone quiet because it has been ignored long enough, seared (1 Timothy 4:2). Quiet that comes from clarity is a blessing; quiet that comes from numbness is a symptom, usually visible to everyone but the man himself. So keep your conscience under the Word, and listen when wise friends raise a concern.

Isn’t keeping my convictions private a kind of hypocrisy? No. Hypocrisy is pretending to be what you are not. Paul does not ask you to feign scruples or deny your view when asked, only not to parade your freedom where it would wound. Not ordering a drink beside a brother who struggles is not lying but loving, and you can explain your convictions gently to anyone who sincerely asks.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. — Romans 14:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
To do what you believe is wrong is sin, even when the thing itself is harmless, because whatever is not done from faith is sin.

In the flow. The chapter began with the one who is weak in faith and ends with the rule that whatever does not come from faith is sin, fitting a letter about a righteousness that is by faith from first to last (1:17). And 15:1 picks the argument up at once, climbing to Christ, who did not please himself (15:3).

Whoever has doubts. To doubt is to waver, to be divided in mind (diakrinō): the root Paul used for judging in verse 13, here turned inward on a person at war with himself. He is eating the thing while one half of him objects, and Paul says the verdict on that is already in.

Because the eating is not from faith. Faith here is a settled conviction before God that this is right. The food was not wrong (vv. 14, 20). He is condemned for acting against his own conviction, not for what was on his plate.

For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. If you cannot do something in confidence that it pleases God, do not do it, for acting against conscience trains you to ignore God’s voice. Augustine used the sentence against the idea that the virtues of unbelievers are truly virtuous, and the Reformers took it up as proof that no act, however decent, pleases God apart from faith in Christ (Hebrews 11:6; the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, both 16.7). The principle really does reach that far.

The one life lived wholly from faith. Why should faith decide whether an act is sin? Because faith is the hand that rests on Christ, and God is pleased with what we do only as we are in him. Only one human life has been lived wholly from faith: Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:2), who never once acted against his Father’s will.
