We never obey like that, even at our best, but his obedience is counted as ours, and failure does not undo our standing in him. So the question at the table is never only whether the food is clean. It is whether I can do this as one who rests in Christ.

Does this mean I am sinning whenever I am unsure? No. The terror this verse causes usually comes from reading it out of its room. It does not mean every action needs a conscious act of faith first, or you would sin every time you changed gear. It does not mean you must feel certain before acting; feelings of certainty are not faith, and often accompany foolishness. Nor is being unsure about a hard question sinful; Paul has just spent a chapter making room for the unsure. What it does mean, in context, is this: do not do the disputed thing while you believe it to be wrong. The man who eats what he thinks is unclean, because the company made it awkward not to, has acted on the pressure of the room rather than on his conviction before God, and the eating is a small act of unbelief.

The cure is not paralysis. Verse 5 already gave it: each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The answer to doubt is not to stop acting but to stop being divided: to be taught, reach a settled position and act from it, which is more work than either abstaining or complying. The Lord does not drive his children; he leads them. He teaches the conscience he has cleansed, and he is willing to take years over it.

So are the good deeds of unbelievers worth nothing? Not worth nothing to people. When an unbeliever feeds the hungry or tells the truth, his neighbours are truly helped, and God blesses the world through such kindness. But those deeds are not done from faith or for God’s glory, and so they cannot make the doer right with God or earn his favour (Westminster 16.7; 1689 16.7). That is no sneer at decent people, for it is the verdict on every one of us; even the believer’s best works are accepted only because he is accepted in Christ. No one, religious or irreligious, stands before God on his own record; all alike need a righteousness that is not their own (3:21–22).

How do I train my conscience? By putting it under God’s Word. Learn both what God commands and what he leaves free; many tender consciences are bound by rules from a family, a church culture or a past fear rather than the Bible. Ask of each scruple: where does God say this? Learn from mature Christians, and pray. And be patient: a conscience grows the way a person grows, slowly. Never force it to go faster than conviction, and never let it fall asleep.

Textual note: the doxology. Many later manuscripts, the majority of surviving copies, place 16:25–27 here, at the end of chapter 14; one early papyrus places it after 15:33; the oldest and best manuscripts have it at the end of chapter 16, where the ESV, the KJV and most Bibles print it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert 16:25–27 here, at the end of chapter 14. Others place it after 15:33, and a few omit it. The variation probably shows that the letter circulated in more than one form in the early church; but the doxology is found in almost all manuscripts, and its natural place is at the close of the letter, where the ESV prints it.

keyVerse.quote: For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the floor beneath the whole chapter. Because every believer belongs to the Lord, no one may rule another’s conscience (vv. 4, 9), and because my brother belongs to the Lord, I may not spend his conscience on my freedom (v. 15). Paul wrote about vegetables the sentence Christians still say at gravesides: the Lord who owns us in life does not let go of us in death.

14.reflection:
Paul calls the believer with more scruples “weak in faith”, yet aims nearly every command at the strong (vv. 1–4, 13–21). Which way do you tend to fail: the raised eyebrow of the strong, or the verdict of the weak? What does each reveal about where we look for security?

Verses 7–12 answer a quarrel about food with Christ’s death, his resurrection and his judgment seat. How does knowing that you and your brother both belong to the Lord, and will both give account to him, change the way you disagree?

What are the disputable matters in your church today? How can you tell them apart from matters of sin or of the gospel, where Paul would not give way (Galatians 2:5)?

Is there a freedom you could lay down, quietly and without announcing it, for the sake of a particular brother or sister (vv. 15, 20–21)? What would it cost you, and why is he or she worth it?

15.title: Unity, Hope, and the Mission of Paul
15.overview:
Where we are. Romans 15 finishes the argument about the strong and the weak begun at 14:1, closes the teaching of the letter with a prayer (v. 13), and turns to Paul’s mission and plans (vv. 14–33), taking up the threads of 1:8–15.

The message. Christ did not please himself but welcomed the unworthy, Jew and Gentile alike, so his people must carry and welcome one another until a divided church praises God with one voice. That welcome is going out to the world: Christ came as Israel’s servant to keep God’s promises, so that the nations, who had no promise, might praise God for his mercy. Paul spends his life carrying that mercy where Christ has never been named, and asks the Romans to share the work.

Why it was said. The Roman church was strained between Jewish believers who kept the food laws and mostly Gentile believers who knew themselves free, and Gentiles were tempted to look down on Israel (see the introduction and chapter 14). And Paul needed a church he had never visited to trust his gospel, pray for his dangerous journey to Jerusalem, and back his mission to Spain.

How the chapter makes its case. The strong must carry the weak, as Christ bore the reproaches meant for God (vv. 1–3); Scripture gives hope, and God gives one mind and one voice (vv. 4–6). Then the summit: welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you (v. 7), for Christ served Israel and showed mercy to the nations, as the Law, the Psalms and the Prophets foretold (vv. 8–12). A prayer to the God of hope closes the argument (v. 13). Paul then explains his bold letter (vv. 14–15), describes his mission as priestly service (vv. 16–21), sets out his route by Jerusalem and Rome to Spain (vv. 22–29), and asks for prayer (vv. 30–33).

Where it leads. The strong who carry the weak are not doing something heroic; they are following their Lord, who did not please himself (v. 3). He is the servant of Israel and the root of Jesse in whom the nations hope (vv. 8–12). Paul frames it all in prayer, because the God of endurance, of hope and of peace (vv. 5, 13, 33) gives the unity he asks for, and the song beginning in a quarrelsome Roman house church will be sung by every nation around the throne.

For us. Ask whom you are merely tolerating instead of carrying, and whom you would keep from your table though Christ has welcomed them to his. Then lift your eyes: pray for those who carry the gospel to the unreached, give to send them, and ask whether God would have you go.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Example of Christ and the God of Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ’s welcome of us is both the pattern and the power for welcoming one another, so that Jew and Gentile praise God together. The strong owe it to the weak to carry them and build them up (vv. 1–2), because Christ did not please himself but bore the insults aimed at God (v. 3, quoting Psalm 69:9). Scripture written long ago gives hope, and the God who gives it can give one mind and one voice (vv. 4–6). Verse 7 is the summit of everything since 14:1: welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you. Christ served Israel to keep God’s promises and the nations to show them mercy (vv. 8–9), as the Law, the Writings and the Prophets all foretold (vv. 9–12), and the section ends in prayer to the God of hope (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ, the pattern for bearing with the weak

Paul grounds the duty of the strong in Christ himself (15:3). This is more than copying a good man’s example. Christ is Lord, he rules by serving, and his self-giving is the source of ours. When Paul tells the Galatians to bear one another’s burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2), that law is this pattern: the One who bore what he did not owe, so that we might be released from what we could not pay.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The unity Paul prays for in vv. 5–6 was not an abstract hope. The Roman church was divided: Jewish and Gentile believers, strong and weak, people of different classes and nations. Now: Believers who have every reason to be divided, by race, class, culture or politics, worshipping together with one voice, still commend the gospel powerfully.

verseByVerse.quote: We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers whose consciences are free owe it to those whose consciences are tender to carry them, seeking their good instead of their own pleasure. Strength in the church is not a privilege to enjoy but a debt to pay.

Who are the strong and the weak? The weak, probably many of them Jewish Christians, still kept the food laws and holy days in conscience (14:2, 5); the strong knew that in Christ nothing is unclean in itself (14:14; see the note on 14:1). Both trust the same Saviour; the difference is how much freedom a conscience has grasped on matters God has left free. And the weak are not the people with the worst morals. They are often the most careful people in the room.

We who are strong have an obligation. Paul counts himself among the strong, and at once makes strength a duty. The word (opheilō) is a debt word that runs the length of the letter: Paul a debtor to Greeks and to barbarians (1:14), owing no one anything except love (13:8), and here the strong owing the weak. They thought their knowledge made them creditors. It makes them debtors.

To bear with the failings of the weak. “Bear with” is too polite for the verb. Bastazō means to pick up and carry, the word for carrying one another’s burdens (Galatians 6:2) and for Jesus carrying his own cross (John 19:17). Not tolerate: carry. The strong are to get underneath the weak and take the weight.

Their failings, not their convictions. What is carried is their failings (asthenēmata): weaknesses, scruples, tender consciences. Paul does not soften his opinion to be kind; he has said plainly that nothing is unclean in itself (14:14), and he calls the scruple a weakness. But he refuses to treat being right as permission to leave the man behind. He neither pretends the other man is right to keep the peace, nor tells him he is wrong and considers his duty done. He thinks the weak brother mistaken and picks him up anyway.

Not to please ourselves, but our neighbour for his good. Every gift God gives, whether knowledge, maturity, health, money or a robust conscience, comes with a direction attached, and the direction is outward. Pleasing the neighbour is not flattering him but seeking his real good, building him up (oikodomē, the word for putting up a house). Paul is not commending the anxious habit of becoming whatever people want; if he were still trying to please people, he would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). Pleasing aimed at his growth is love. Pleasing aimed at his approval is fear, and from outside the two look alike.

Carried first. The strong are asked nothing Christ has not first done for them. Matthew says of Jesus healing the crowds, “He took our illnesses and bore our diseases” (Matthew 8:17), with this verb for carrying, and he went on carrying until “he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). The Lord who promised to carry his people to grey hairs (Isaiah 46:3–4) kept that word in Christ, and has never set them down. That is the glory of God in Christ: omnipotence that bends low, owes us nothing, and carries us anyway. Every strong believer in Rome had first been a weak thing picked up by Christ. Paul is asking a man who has been carried to carry someone else.

In everyday life. Picture the person in your church whose conscience is tighter than yours, and ask what carrying him would look like, as opposed to merely managing him: a meal planned around what he can eat with a clear conscience, a joke about his scruples left unmade.

What if the weak brother is using his scruple to run everyone else? Bearing with a tender conscience is different from surrendering to a man who turns his scruple into a rule for the church or a test of salvation. When false brothers demanded that Titus be circumcised, Paul did not yield for a moment, “so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved” (Galatians 2:3–5). A weak brother says, I cannot do this with a clear conscience. A legalist says, you cannot be right with God unless you live as I do. The first you carry gently, often for years. The second you resist, kindly and firmly, because the gospel itself is at stake. Both are to be loved.

Does this mean I can never use my freedom? No. The strong need not live permanently by the weakest conscience in the church; they must never use their freedom in a way that wounds a brother or draws him into sinning against his conscience (14:15, 20–21). Most of the time your liberty harms no one, and you may enjoy God’s gifts with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4). The question is not whether this is allowed, but who is at the table and what it will do to him. Keep your freedom between yourself and God (14:22) when using it would hurt someone, and use it freely when it would not.

parallels.desc: bear one another’s burdens

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, "The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The strong must not please themselves, because Christ did not please himself but took on himself the insults aimed at God. Paul reaches for his supreme example in the middle of a discussion about vegetables: no question is too small to be settled at the cross.

For Christ did not please himself. He came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45), and emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:5–8). Put flesh on the phrase: crowds arriving when he had gone away to be alone, and compassion on them anyway (Mark 6:31–34); a conversation at a well when he was tired and thirsty (John 4:6–7); no place to lay his head (Luke 9:58); washing the feet of men who would run away that same night (John 13:5). The interruption was never treated as an interruption, because the people who caused it were the reason he had come.

The reproaches fell on me. Paul quotes Psalm 69:9, a psalm of the suffering righteous one which the New Testament applies to Christ again and again (John 2:17; 15:25; 19:28–29; Romans 11:9–10). The “you” is God; the “me” is Christ. The insults aimed at the Father landed on the Son: the mockery at the foot of the cross, the spitting, the crown of thorns. And at Calvary he bore far more than the world’s scorn: the curse our sin deserved (Galatians 3:13). No burden the strong are asked to carry comes near it.

Motive, measure and covering. The cross is both the motive and the measure of Christian self-giving. Where we fall short of that measure, as we all do (James 3:2), his perfect obedience stands in our place (5:19), so our halting self-giving is accepted for his sake. Psalm 69 supplied the judgment in 11:9–10 and the example here: the one who bore the reproach is either your pattern or your judge.

What it does not mean. Not that Christ had no joy: he went to weddings and dinners, and “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2). Nor that Christians must say yes to every request: Jesus withdrew to pray and refused to be made king by a crowd (John 6:15). He did not please himself, but neither did he please everyone. He pleased his Father, with the good of others always in view.

How can a psalm of David be about Christ? David wrote Psalm 69 out of his own suffering, as a king hated without cause. But he was the anointed king through whom God had promised a greater Son (2 Samuel 7:12–16); his sufferings were a sketch, and Jesus is the finished portrait. The disciples saw it the day he cleared the temple and remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17), the first half of the very verse Paul quotes. The Spirit who spoke through David knew whose voice would finally fill the psalm (Acts 2:30–31; 1 Peter 1:11), so Paul reads it the way its Author meant.

parallels.desc: the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me

verseByVerse.quote: For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Old Testament was written for us, to give us hope through the endurance and encouragement it produces, and the God who gives these through it can make a divided church think as one. Paul has just settled a dispute by quoting a psalm; here he says what he is doing every time he reaches back into the Old Testament.

For our instruction. The whole Old Testament was written for Christians too (1 Corinthians 10:11; 2 Timothy 3:16). David, describing his own misery in Psalm 69, was also writing for a mixed congregation in Rome a thousand years later, readers God already knew by name.

Endurance, encouragement, hope. “Endurance” (hypomonē) is steadfastness under weight; “encouragement” (paraklēsis) is comfort and exhortation together, the voice of one who comes alongside. Both come through the Scriptures, and their goal is not knowledge, or even obedience, but hope, because of what the Scriptures record: occasion after occasion on which God did what he said, generally later and stranger than anyone wanted. Abraham waited twenty-five years for a son; Israel waited four centuries in Egypt and seventy years in Babylon. Every time, God kept his word. So endurance comes before hope. You do not read the Bible and instantly feel hopeful; you find that the waiting in it is nearly always longer than seems reasonable, and slowly become someone who can wait, and that endurance grows into hope (5:3–5).

Written about him, for us. Paul’s own use of Psalm 69 (v. 3) shows how the Old Testament instructs: not mainly by giving us heroes to copy, but by showing us the One every page is leaning towards. When the risen Jesus opened the Scriptures on the road to Emmaus, the disciples’ hearts burned within them (Luke 24:32). Every promise God kept through those long waits was a step on the road to the cross and the empty tomb, and the God who kept those promises in Christ will keep the rest.

May the God of endurance and encouragement. Scripture gives endurance and encouragement, and Paul calls God the God of endurance and encouragement: the book gives what its Author is. That is also a caution, for a person can read the words without ever meeting the God they reveal (John 5:39–40).

One mind about Christ. To live in harmony is literally to think the same thing, as in 12:16, and “in accord with Christ Jesus” means by his pattern and under his rule, the Christ of verse 3. Unity is not uniformity of opinion on food. The strong and the weak will go on disagreeing about the menu; Paul prays that they will be of one mind about the Lord who welcomed them both, so that their shared praise is louder than their disagreement.

Why should a modern person live by an ancient book? C. S. Lewis called the instinct behind this question chronological snobbery, and observed that every age has blind spots it cannot see from inside; old books have mistakes too, but not the same ones as ours. That is why Scripture feels abrasive to every generation at a different point: too strict about sex for one, too soft on enemies for another, too hard on money for a third. A book that offends every age in a different place is not simply the product of any of them. We do not finally sit in judgment on it. It reads us, and then it hands us hope.

If the Old Testament was written for us, do all its laws still bind us? Everything in it is for our instruction, but not everything is a command addressed to us. The ceremonial laws, sacrifices, food laws and festivals, were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1), which is exactly why the strong in Rome were right that foods are clean. The civil laws governed Israel as a nation and teach us their underlying justice. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still shows God’s will for every person (13:8–10; the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, both 19.3–5). Read every page asking what it shows of God, of Christ and of his promises, and even Leviticus instructs.

What if I read the Bible and still do not feel hopeful? Keep reading, and change what you are looking for: hope here is not a feeling but a settled expectation that grows as you watch God keep his promises page after page. Read the long stories, not only the comforting verses: Joseph, Ruth, the exile and return, and above all the Gospels, where the darkest Friday is followed by Sunday. Pray the psalms of lament, which are there for people who cannot feel hope yet (Psalm 42; 88). And read with others, because encouragement often reaches us through a brother’s voice reading the same words.

verseByVerse.quote: that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ welcomed you when you had nothing to commend you, so welcome every fellow believer in the same way, that the whole church may praise God with one voice. The goal of unity is worship, and its standard is Christ.

With one voice. “Together” (homothymadon) is Luke’s word for the first believers praying and breaking bread (Acts 1:14; 2:46), and “with one voice” is literally with one mouth. Two chapters of conflict end not in agreement but in a room of people who still disagree, making one sound. That is the sound the cross was meant to make: one family, praising one Father, through one Son.

The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is not a general deity to whom Jews and Gentiles bring their separate religions; he is the Father of Jesus, known through Jesus. The strong and the weak share what matters most.

Welcome one another. Verse 7 is the summit of an argument climbing since 14:1. “Welcome” (proslambanō) means to receive someone into your company, your home and your table. In 14:1 the strong were told to welcome the man whose conscience was tighter than theirs, because God has welcomed him (14:3). Here the word comes twice in one verse, and now it runs in every direction, “welcome one another”, with Christ himself as the standard.

As Christ has welcomed you. This letter has already spelled out that standard. Christ welcomed you while you were ungodly (4:5), weak (5:6), a sinner (5:8), an enemy (5:10). He did not welcome the promising or the nearly persuaded. He opened the door to us when we were barring it from the inside, and did not wait for us to become presentable. That removes the last excuse: nobody in Rome was being asked to welcome someone worse than they had been when they were welcomed. Nobody since has been.

For the glory of God. The welcome is not first for the comfort of the person received but for God’s reputation. A church where people who would never otherwise sit together eat together is a living advertisement for the grace that brought them there.

What welcoming looks like. More than a nod at the door. Notice the person on their own, and sit with them rather than with your friends. Learn names and use them the next week. Ask questions of people unlike you, and listen. Bring people to your table, because in Scripture welcome nearly always means a meal. Keep welcoming after the first visit: the hardest weeks for a newcomer are often the third and the tenth, when the novelty has worn off and they do not yet feel they belong. Make room for one person this Sunday the way Christ made room for you.

Does unity mean we have to agree about everything? No. Paul prays for one voice, not one opinion on every question. Christians must agree on the gospel itself: who Christ is, what he has done, and how a sinner is made right with God (Galatians 1:8–9). On secondary matters, such as the questions of conscience in chapter 14, schooling, styles of music or whether to drink wine, believers can hold different convictions and still worship side by side. Even where churches must decide their own practice, as on baptism, we can honour those who differ as true brothers. Maturity is not having no convictions, but not letting them stop you singing with someone who holds different ones.

Who counts as someone Christ has welcomed? Anyone who credibly confesses Jesus as Lord, trusts him alone for salvation, and is not living in open, unrepentant sin. You do not have to see into his heart; you receive what he professes and how he lives. That includes the socially awkward, the one from a very different background, the new convert whose life is still a mess but who is fighting, and the one whose politics you find hard to bear. If Christ has received him, the table belongs to Christ, and you are not its doorkeeper.

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God's truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, "Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ came as a servant to Israel to prove God true to his promises, and so that the nations, who had no promise, might praise God for his mercy. This is how Christ has welcomed both: to Israel he brings promises kept, to the nations sheer mercy.

A servant to the circumcised. Christ became not only the Jewish people’s teacher but their servant (diakonos), a word often used of someone who waits at table, born under the law and sent first to them (Matthew 15:24; Galatians 4:4). Paul is writing to a mostly Gentile congregation already warned against arrogance toward Jewish believers (11:18): the Lord they worship became a servant to the very people they are inclined to look down on.

To show God’s truthfulness. Truthfulness (alētheia) here is God’s faithfulness to his word. By coming to Israel, Christ proved God true to his promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (2 Corinthians 1:20). The oath sworn two thousand years before Bethlehem was kept to the letter, in the land, the tribe and the line God had named.

For his mercy. Israel had promises to be kept; the nations had none, for they were strangers to the covenants of promise (Ephesians 2:12). Blessing for the nations was always God’s plan, sworn to Abraham (Genesis 22:18), but sworn to him, not to them. So the Gentiles receive as people with no claim: by mercy alone.

Praise among the Gentiles. Paul quotes Psalm 18:49 (also 2 Samuel 22:50), David’s song of victory. In Christ, the Son of David, the line becomes his own: the Messiah stands among the nations and leads their praise, “in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise” (Hebrews 2:12). When a Gentile church sings, it joins a song its King is already singing.

Where faithfulness and mercy meet. God is truthful, for he kept every word he swore. God is merciful, for he gave what he never swore. Christ is the place where both meet, the faithfulness of God to Israel and his mercy to the world joined in one servant, who now leads every nation in praise of his Father.

A rebuke and a comfort. To the Gentile believer tempted to feel like the main story: you are here on mercy, and mercy by definition was not owed. To the Jewish believer watching his people’s privileges seem to pass to strangers: the promises were not cancelled but confirmed, and Christ took the servant’s place to do it. Both have reason to praise, and neither has reason to boast.

Were the Jews not saved by mercy too? Yes. Paul’s contrast is about the route, not the ground. The promises themselves were mercy, given to a people who did not deserve them (Deuteronomy 7:7–8), and Israel’s salvation rests on God’s gracious choice (11:5–6). But Israel had the promise in advance, so Christ’s coming showed God keeping his word; the Gentiles had no word to hold, so his coming to them could only look like sheer kindness. One is mercy keeping a promise; the other is mercy with nothing to keep.

Uncertain wording. Paul’s Greek in verses 8–9 is compressed, and it is not certain how the clause about the Gentiles joins what comes before. It may be a second purpose of Christ’s servanthood, as the ESV takes it, or a second thing Paul declares (I tell you that Christ became a servant to Israel, and that the Gentiles glorify God for his mercy). The sense is the same either way: Israel’s promises kept and the nations’ praise both flow from Christ’s work as servant.

parallels.desc: I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again it says, "Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people." And again, "Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses and the psalmist had long ago called the nations to praise Israel’s God alongside his people.

Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people. The words come from Deuteronomy 32:43 in the Greek translation, the end of the Song of Moses, which Paul has quoted twice already (10:19; 12:19). The song about Israel’s unfaithfulness and God’s faithfulness turns out to contain the Gentiles too, and not instead of Israel or in a separate room: with his people, in the same congregation, singing the same thing. It is the picture Paul has been trying to produce in Rome for two chapters, and Moses got there first.

Psalm 117. The second quotation is Psalm 117:1, the shortest chapter in the Bible, whose two verses call the nations to praise the God of Israel for his steadfast love toward us, that is, toward Israel. What God does for his people is meant to set the whole world singing.

The whole Old Testament agrees. Paul takes one quotation from the Law (Deuteronomy 32), two from the Writings (Psalms 18 and 117) and one from the Prophets (Isaiah 11, in v. 12): every division of the Hebrew Bible. A hope once held by one nation on a strip of land between the desert and the sea is now sung on every continent, by people whose ancestors bowed to idols of wood and stone.

Why the nations can sing. Moses and the psalmist summoned the nations, but could not bring them; for centuries only a few, like Ruth and Naaman, came. What turned the summons into a song was Christ, the servant who came so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy (vv. 8–9). In him the steadfast love of Psalm 117 took flesh and its faithfulness was kept, and through his blood the nations who had no promise were brought near (Ephesians 2:13).

In everyday life. Pray Psalm 117 today, slowly; it takes less than a minute. Then pray for a nation where Christ is not yet praised. The Son of David, who by his blood ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Revelation 5:9), is still gathering that choir: ask him to raise up a church there that sings Psalm 117 in its own language.

Does “with his people” mean there are two peoples of God? No. There is one olive tree, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs, into which believing Gentiles are grafted alongside believing Jews (11:17–24), and in Christ there is one new man where once there were two (Ephesians 2:14–16). Gentiles join Israel’s worship, praising Israel’s God through Israel’s Messiah. What God will yet do for the Jewish people as a whole is a question Christians answer in different ways from chapter 11, and Paul leaves room for a future mercy to Israel (11:25–32). But there is only ever one family of faith, and one song.

Textual note. If you look up Deuteronomy 32:43 in the ESV, you will find “Rejoice with him, O heavens” rather than Paul’s words. Ancient copies of that verse differ, and so do English Bibles; older versions read Rejoice, O ye nations, with his people. Paul quotes the line as the Greek translation gives it, and the standard Hebrew text also calls on the nations, so the call to the nations is not in doubt.
verseByVerse.note: Paul cites the Law, the Psalms and the Prophets to show God always intended Gentiles to praise him.

parallels.desc: rejoice with him, O heavens
praise the LORD, all nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again Isaiah says, "The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah foretold a king from David’s line who would rise to rule the nations and be their hope, and Jesus is that king. The last of Paul’s four quotations, from Isaiah 11:10 in the Greek translation, is the one the others lead to.

The root of Jesse will come. Jesse was David’s father; the root of Jesse is the promised king from David’s line (Isaiah 11:1). Isaiah’s picture was a dynasty felled like a tree at ground level, and a green shoot coming up out of the dead wood. Jesus is that root and offspring of David (Revelation 5:5; 22:16). By the time he was born, David’s line had dwindled to a carpenter in Nazareth; nobody looking at Joseph’s workshop would have seen a throne. A shoot from a stump is not a rescue of the old tree but life on the other side of the loss, from the same root, and the tree God grows from it will never be cut down again.

He who arises to rule the Gentiles. “Arises” (anistamai) is one of the New Testament words for resurrection. In Isaiah it means to rise up to rule, but Paul may well have heard more in it: the shoot from the stump rose from the dead, and the risen Christ rules the nations. Where the Hebrew of Isaiah says the nations will inquire of him, the Greek says they will hope in him; both mean the nations will turn to this king.

In him will the Gentiles hope. To hope in him is to rest your whole future on him, looking to Christ for what the nations once sought from their idols: safety, meaning and life beyond death (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10). Paul ends the chain of quotations on the word “hope”, and his prayer takes it up at once: “May the God of hope fill you” (v. 13).

In everyday life. Look at the stump in your own life: the plan that failed, the family line or the ministry that seems finished. God has often brought a shoot out of exactly that kind of dead wood. Do not demand that he repair the old tree. Ask him for life from the root.

Why is Jesus called the root of Jesse, not just a branch? Both are true. Isaiah 11:1 calls the coming king a shoot from the stump of Jesse: he grows out of David’s family as its descendant. But Isaiah 11:10 calls him the root of Jesse, and Jesus himself says, “I am the root and the descendant of David” (Revelation 22:16). He is David’s offspring according to the flesh (1:3), and David’s source and Lord as the eternal Son (Matthew 22:41–45). He comes from David, and David came from him.

How can Christ rule the nations now, when the world looks so godless? His rule is real now but mostly hidden, like a seed in the ground or yeast in dough (Matthew 13:31–33). He reigns over all things for the sake of his church (Ephesians 1:20–22), restraining evil, overruling the plans of rulers, and gathering his people from every nation through the gospel. Every new believer in a closed country is a sign of his rule. One day it will be visible to everyone, when he returns and every knee bows (Philippians 2:10–11). Until then the headlines are not the measure of his reign.
verseByVerse.note: Jesse was David’s father; the “root of Jesse” is the promised king from David’s line.

parallels.desc: the root of Jesse, of him shall the nations inquire

verseByVerse.quote: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope. — Romans 15:13
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends the argument by praying that the God of hope will fill believers with joy and peace as they trust him, so that by the Spirit they overflow with hope. The case that began at 1:16 with the gospel as the power of God for salvation ends not in a conclusion but in a benediction, a prayer of blessing.

May the God of hope. Not the God who recommends hope or requires it, but the God whose own name it is, and out of whom it comes. Hope is not a mood he asks his people to work up; he has it in himself without limit, however dark things look.

Joy and peace in believing. Joy and peace are marks of the kingdom (14:17), and the verb is fill: not trickle, but fill, with all joy. They come “in believing”: not afterwards, as a reward for having trusted well enough, but as we trust.

Abound in hope. “Abound” (perisseuō) means overflow: more hope than circumstances justify, by the Spirit’s power (5:5; 8:24–25). This is not optimism, a temperament, but expectation grounded in fourteen chapters: a verdict passed, a Spirit given, a Son raised, a love nothing can separate us from (8:38–39).

Hope has a name. The prayer follows straight on from Isaiah’s promise that the Gentiles will hope in the root of Jesse (v. 12). The God of hope fills his people by giving them his Son: “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27). Christian hope rests on a Person who already holds the future and lives in those who trust him. The grave was the strongest argument against hope that has ever been made. God answered it on a Sunday morning, and he has not needed to argue since.

A mercy for the reader in a dark season. Paul does not command them to abound in hope. He asks God to do it to them. The verse is not a standard you are failing to meet. It is a prayer someone is praying for you.

In everyday life. Pray this verse for yourself and for someone you love, by name. Then write down one fact from Romans that is true of you whether you feel it or not: no condemnation (8:1), nothing can separate (8:39), all things for good (8:28). Read it aloud when the day gets hard. You are not manufacturing hope; you are standing where the Spirit pours it.

How is Christian hope different from wishful thinking? Wishful thinking says, I hope it will turn out well, with no particular reason to think so. Christian hope says, I know how it will turn out, because God has promised it and Christ has already risen. Hope in the New Testament is certainty about what is not yet seen (8:24–25), with a definite object, the return of Christ, the resurrection and the new creation (5:2; 8:18–23), and a definite ground, the character of God and the finished work of his Son. It may not tell you how next month will go. It tells you how everything will end, and that you will be there.

What if I believe but do not feel joy and peace? Then you are in the company of many faithful saints, and this verse is still for you. Feelings can be dimmed by illness, grief, exhaustion, depression or long trial, and none of those mean your faith is false. Keep looking to Christ, hearing his word and praying even when the words are thin; joy and peace come in believing, but not always on our schedule, so ask God for them plainly, as Paul did. If darkness lingers, speak to a pastor or a trusted believer and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; medicine a doctor prescribes is no failure of faith, and you need not be ashamed of the help God gives. If hopelessness ever turns to thoughts of ending your life, tell someone and get help that same day. The Spirit’s work is often deeper than our feelings can register.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–33 — Paul's Priestly Ministry and His Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s mission is worship: he offers the nations to God, and he asks the Roman church to share in it. He has written boldly only as a reminder, because of the grace that made him the Gentiles’ apostle (vv. 14–15), a priest whose offering is the Gentiles themselves, made holy by the Spirit (vv. 16–17). Christ has worked through him from Jerusalem to Illyricum (vv. 18–19), and his ambition is to go where Christ has not been named (vv. 20–21). So he looks to Spain by way of Rome (vv. 22–24), but first he must take the Gentile churches’ gift to Jerusalem (vv. 25–29), and he asks the Romans to strive with him in prayer for that dangerous journey (vv. 30–33).
verseByVerse.theology:
Mission as priestly worship

In 15:16 Paul pictures his mission as priestly service: the nations offered to God, made acceptable and holy by the Holy Spirit. Evangelism is therefore not merely a strategy or a duty but an act of worship. That vision has moved many missionaries, from the pastors Geneva sent into France to William Carey in India.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ministry from Jerusalem to Illyricum took perhaps fifteen years of hard labour (see the note on vv. 18–19). Now: There are still peoples and places where Christ has not been named, and the whole church shares Paul’s concern that the unreached should hear, by sending, giving and praying until all nations have heard (see vv. 20–21).

verseByVerse.quote: I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is confident about the Roman Christians, and has written boldly only to remind them, because God’s grace has made him the apostle to the Gentiles. With verse 14 the argument of the letter is complete, and Paul takes up again the threads of 1:8–15: their faith, his calling, his longing to visit.

Satisfied about you. “Satisfied” (peithō) means persuaded, confident. Paul has told this church not to be arrogant (11:18), not to think too highly of itself (12:3), not to despise or judge (14:3), and not to please itself (15:1). Now he says he is persuaded about them, and that they can instruct each other without him.

Able to instruct one another. Goodness (agathōsynē) is moral excellence and kindness. To instruct (noutheteō) is to admonish, to set someone’s mind right by warning and teaching. Ordinary members, with the Spirit and the Scriptures, can counsel each other from God’s word.

By way of reminder, because of the grace given me. Paul admits he has been very bold, but calls the letter a reminder, treating them as people who already know the heart of it (2 Peter 1:12–13). We do not usually drift because we have never heard the truth, but because we have stopped hearing it. His apostleship is a gift of grace (1:5; 12:3), and it obliges him to speak even to those who already know, because the gospel is too important to take for granted.

The word of Christ dwelling richly. What equips ordinary believers to counsel one another? Christ himself: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom” (Colossians 3:16), with the same verb for admonishing. The knowledge that fills the Roman church is knowledge of the Son who died and rose (1:3–4), and Paul’s reminder is fourteen chapters about what he has done. That is why the church never outgrows reminders. The Lord gave his people a meal to keep eating in remembrance of him (1 Corinthians 11:24), because the cure for drift is never a new truth. It is the same Christ, held up again.

The hard thing, and then the honest praise. Most of us, having said the hard thing, either apologise for it or leave it there with no kind word. Paul says it at full strength and then names the good he sees in them, and he means it, or the sentence would be worth nothing. Consider the last difficult thing you told a fellow Christian. Could you, that same day, have named three genuine strengths in him out loud? If not, the correction may still have been true, but it was not coming from where Paul’s came from.

If members can instruct one another, why do we need pastors? God gives both, for different work. Christ gives pastors and teachers to equip the saints for the work of ministry (Ephesians 4:11–12), and elders are charged with teaching, guarding the flock and answering for souls (Acts 20:28; Hebrews 13:17). But the goal of their teaching is a church in which everyone can speak the truth in love to everyone else (Ephesians 4:15–16). A healthy church is one where a believer struggling on Wednesday is helped by a friend who opens the Bible with him, long before the problem reaches the pastor’s study.

I do not feel able to counsel anyone. Where do I start? Smaller than you think. Instructing one another is not lecturing but bringing God’s word to bear on a friend’s life with goodness and knowledge. Listen first and ask what is really going on; remind them of the gospel; point to a promise or command that fits; pray with them there and then; be honest about your own struggles. And know when to say, this is beyond me, let us ask the elders together. Most faithful counsel in the church’s history has been given over kitchen tables by people who would never have called themselves counsellors.

verseByVerse.quote: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s mission is a priest’s work: through the gospel he brings the Gentiles to God as an offering the Holy Spirit has made holy, and his only boast is in what Christ has done. The whole sentence is written in the language of the altar.

A minister in priestly service. Paul puts three temple words into one sentence. He is a leitourgos, a minister in public, priestly service; he serves the gospel as a priest (hierourgeō); and what he brings is an offering. His altar is the gospel and his offering is people: not his preaching or his sufferings, but the converts themselves, the very living sacrifice he told them to make of themselves (12:1).

Acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. Isaiah foresaw the nations bringing Israel’s scattered brothers as an offering to the LORD (Isaiah 66:20); here the nations are themselves the offering. Once unclean in Jewish eyes, they are now “sanctified”, set apart for God and made fit for his presence, not by circumcision but by the Spirit. God once refused the blind and lame animals Israel brought to his altar, because he is a great King (Malachi 1:8, 14); only the Spirit could make former idolaters an offering such a God would receive, and so fulfil his promise that his name would be great among the nations (Malachi 1:11). This also answers the scruples of the weak: if God accepts the Gentiles as a holy offering, no Christian may treat them as unclean.

Reason to be proud. “Proud” (kauchēsis) is boasting, glorying: not vanity but the joy of a craftsman whose work has been effective, grounded entirely “in Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

The man who could never be a priest. Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin (11:1; Philippians 3:5), not of Levi, the priestly tribe (see priests and Levites). The one role closed to him by birth is the one he uses for his life’s work. In that he follows his Lord, who was from Judah, a tribe of which Moses said nothing about priests (Hebrews 7:14), yet is the great high priest who offered himself. Paul can carry the Gentiles to God only because Christ has already brought them near by his own blood, and the offering is acceptable because it is presented through him. Christ is the priest who offered himself; the Spirit is the fire that sanctifies the offering; the Father receives it with delight.

What it does not mean. Not that ministers are priests offering sacrifices of atonement, as in Roman Catholic teaching on the Mass. Christ’s sacrifice was once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). Paul’s priestly language is a picture of evangelism, and all believers are a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices (1 Peter 2:5).

In everyday life. If bringing people to Christ is a duty, it competes with other duties and loses to most of them. If it is priestly work, carrying an offering to God, it belongs with worship, and the question stops being whether you have time for it. Think of one person you long to see brought to God; pray for them as a priest would, and look for one opening to speak of Christ.

Is evangelism only for missionaries and pastors? No. Paul’s apostolic calling was unique, but every believer belongs to the royal priesthood that proclaims the excellencies of him who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9). Not everyone is a preacher, but everyone is a witness, ready to give a reason for the hope within, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). For most of us that means people we already know, prayed for by name, loved patiently, and told the gospel plainly when the door opens. And everyone can support those who are sent, by prayer and giving, as Paul is about to ask the Romans to do.

Is it wrong to feel proud of something God has done through me? Not if the pride is Paul’s kind: glad, grateful and pointed at Christ. Sinful pride says, look what I did; holy gladness says, look what Christ did, and he let me be there. If you can rejoice as much over fruit in another person’s ministry as in your own, your boasting is in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Paul pictures his mission as priestly work, offering the believing Gentiles to God.

parallels.desc: they shall bring your brothers as an offering

verseByVerse.quote: For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience — by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God — so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will speak only of what Christ has done through him: by word, deed and the Spirit’s power, Christ has brought Gentiles to obedience across the eastern Mediterranean. Paul has arranged the sentence so that he cannot be its subject.

What Christ has accomplished through me. Christ acts; Paul is the one he works through. This is not false modesty, which would refuse to mention the work: Paul reports it place by place. He simply makes sure Christ is named as the one who did it. Christ spoke through his servant’s mouth and opened hearts in Lystra, Philippi and Corinth that no preacher could open.

To bring the Gentiles to obedience. The obedience of faith (1:5; 16:26): the letter opens and closes with the phrase, and it names the goal of all mission. Not decisions recorded, but nations brought to bow to Christ in trust and obedience.

By word and deed, signs and wonders. Paul’s message was spoken, and his life embodied it, as he worked with his own hands and cared for the churches. He also did miracles that confirmed his message (Acts 14:3; 19:11–12). But the final phrase matters most: the power of the Spirit of God, behind word, deed and sign alike, who opens hearts and brings the nations to obedience.

From Jerusalem to Illyricum. Illyricum lay along the eastern shore of the Adriatic (modern Albania, Croatia and nearby). Jerusalem to Illyricum is the whole eastern Mediterranean, well over a thousand miles, covered on foot and by ship over years that also held the beatings, shipwrecks and sleepless nights he lists elsewhere (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). None of that appears here. He names the two ends of the journey and moves on.

I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel. Not that everyone in the region had believed, but that he had fully preached the gospel there, planting churches in key cities that could reach their own territory. Paul’s definition of a finished job is not a converted population. It is a living church in place, doing what he would otherwise have stayed to do.

Does God still heal today, then? Yes, and Christians should ask him to. What has ceased is the apostolic sign gift (see the box below), not God himself, who hears the prayers of his people. James tells the sick to call the elders to pray over them and anoint them, and “the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick” (James 5:14–15). Sometimes God heals, quickly or slowly, with or without medicine, which is also his gift. Sometimes he does not, and gives grace to bear the weakness instead, as he did for Paul (2 Corinthians 12:7–10). Either way, pray boldly and leave the answer with him.

Where Christians differ: signs and wonders today. Some teach that signs and wonders like those of the apostles should accompany all gospel preaching today. This commentary’s view: Paul calls signs and wonders the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). They confirmed the apostolic message as Scripture was being given (Hebrews 2:3–4). With the apostles gone and the canon complete, the miraculous sign gifts have ceased as a regular part of ministry. God still answers prayer and can heal and work wonders as he pleases, but the gospel is now confirmed by the written word. This is held charitably toward continuationist brothers and sisters (those who believe all the gifts continue today), many of whom love Christ deeply and read 1 Corinthians 12–14 as a pattern for every age.
verseByVerse.note: Illyricum lay along the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, north-west of Macedonia.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else's foundation, but as it is written, 'Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.' — Romans 15:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s ambition is to preach Christ where he has never been named, because Isaiah foretold that those who had never been told would see. He does not apologise for having an ambition; he points it at the places where the name of Christ has never been said out loud.

My ambition. “Ambition” (philotimeomai) is built from the words for love and honour: to make something your aim and point of pride (2 Corinthians 5:9). Ambition is not the problem in a Christian; ambition pointed at the wrong thing is. The builders of Babel wanted to make a name for themselves (Genesis 11:4). Paul wanted to make Christ’s name known where it had never been heard: the same energy, aimed at a different name, is the difference between an idol and a calling.

Not where Christ has already been named. Others could water where he planted (1 Corinthians 3:6, 10). His gift was to take the gospel where no one had yet preached it, rather than build on someone else’s foundation, and to leave behind a church that would reach its own region.

Those who have never been told of him will see. Paul quotes Isaiah 52:15, the verse just before Isaiah 53, the passage about the one wounded for our transgressions, by whose stripes we are healed. He lifts his mission statement out of the song of the suffering servant, from the very place where the nations who were never told finally see. That is the God we worship: one who does not wait for the nations to seek him, but sends his word to the ends of the earth, to people who had no idea anyone was looking for them.

What it does not mean. This verse has been used to make settled ministry look second-rate. Paul describes his own calling, not a universal rule; he himself stayed in Ephesus three years (Acts 20:31). Somebody has to stay, as Timothy did at Ephesus, doing the long, unnoticed work of a pastor. The ambition commended is that the unreached should be reached, not that every Christian should be restless.

In everyday life. Ask what your ambition is: not your plan for the week, but the thing you would most love to see happen before you die. If the name of Christ is nowhere in it, ask God to reshape it.

What are unreached peoples, and what can I do from here? An unreached people is a group, usually defined by language and culture, with no church strong enough to evangelise the rest without outside help; many have no Bible in their language and have never met a Christian. Most of us will not go to them, but all of us can share Paul’s ambition. Learn about one such people and pray for them regularly and specifically. Give to missionaries working among them. Welcome internationals in your own town, since many come from places where the gospel is hard to hear. Encourage the young people in your church who sense a call. And ask God whether he might be calling you.

parallels.desc: that which has not been told them they see

verseByVerse.quote: This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
This pioneer work is why Paul has so long been kept from Rome, but now that it is finished in the east, he can come at last. He names the reason without complaint, though the delay has lasted “many years” (v. 23; compare 1:13).

So often hindered. The verb (enkoptō) means to cut in, often explained from the breaking up of a road so that no one can pass. Something has been across the road, repeatedly, for years.

No longer any room for work in these regions. A sentence that would be absurd from anybody else. The eastern Mediterranean is finished in the sense already given (v. 19): planted with churches that can do the rest.

The Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. Luke shows who stood across Paul’s road at least once. On his second journey the Holy Spirit forbade them to preach in Asia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them into Bithynia (Acts 16:6–7). The closed road led to Troas, the man of Macedonia, and the churches of Philippi and Thessalonica. Even when Satan hindered him (1 Thessalonians 2:18), the risen Lord was ruling his servant’s steps. Paul could wait for Rome because he knew whose hand was on the map.

How do I know whether God is hindering me, or I am just giving up? Ask what is actually across the road. Paul was hindered not by fear or idleness but by faithfulness: there was gospel work in front of him that had to be done first. If what keeps you from the thing you long for is a real duty God has placed in front of you, the delay is his, and you can wait without guilt. If it is fear, comfort or sin, call it by its name and repent. Either way keep the desire alive in prayer, as Paul kept praying for Rome for years (1:10). God often brings a long-held desire to pass at the moment it can do the most good.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul plans to visit Rome on his way to Spain, and hopes the church there will send him on with its support. He names the end of the earth in the same breath as a request for travelling expenses.

Spain. Not just another destination. Spain was the far western end of the Roman world: beyond it the map ran out and the Atlantic began. When Paul says Spain, he is naming the end of the earth as his generation understood the phrase.

Helped on my journey there by you. “Helped on my journey” (propempō, send forward) was almost a technical term for missionary support: supplies, money, companions (Acts 15:3; 3 John 6). Part of Paul’s purpose in writing was to win their support for Spain (see the introduction), and he evidently thought the way to raise support for a mission was to explain the gospel at length.

Once I have enjoyed your company. Literally, once I have been filled with you (empiplēmi). Paul expects the Roman Christians to do him good; they are not only a supply base.

To the end of the earth. The goal was not Paul’s invention. It was the risen Lord’s last word before he ascended: “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). Christ had told Ananias that Paul was his chosen instrument to carry his name before the Gentiles (Acts 9:15). Behind both stands Isaiah 49:6: Simeon, holding the infant Jesus, called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32), and Paul applied that promise to his own mission (Acts 13:47), the Servant’s light carried by the Servant’s servants. The gospel has since gone to continents Paul never imagined, because the God who sent it intends to be worshipped there. Whether or not Paul reached Spain, Christ did.

Did Paul ever reach Spain? We do not know. Acts leaves him under house arrest in Rome and stops. Clement of Rome, writing about AD 96, says Paul reached the limits of the west, which many take to mean Spain, and it may. The last plan in the letter is the one whose outcome the New Testament never reports. Most faithful lives end that way, with the accounting done elsewhere, by a Lord of the harvest who records every faithful plan, finished or unfinished.

Is it right for missionaries to ask for money? Yes, when it is done openly and for the sake of the gospel. Paul asks plainly here, and the New Testament commends churches that send gospel workers on their way in a manner worthy of God, since they go out for the sake of the name (3 John 6–8). Paul sometimes refused support where it would have hindered the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12, 15–18), but he never thought supporting missionaries second-class work; those who give become partners in the mission (Philippians 1:5; 4:15–17). When a missionary asks for help, do not hear it as begging. Hear it as an invitation to share in the work.
verseByVerse.note: Spain was the western edge of the known world. Whether Paul ever reached it is uncertain; early tradition says he did.

verseByVerse.quote: At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he goes west, Paul must first go east to Jerusalem with the gift the Gentile churches of Greece have gladly given for the poor believers there. He is postponing the mission of his life to hand over a relief fund.

Going to Jerusalem. Paul is almost certainly writing from Corinth (16:1, 23; see the introduction). He means to go west, and first he will travel some eight hundred miles the opposite way, carrying money, to the city where he asks prayer to be delivered from the unbelievers (v. 31).

A contribution for the poor. The collection took years to gather (1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9). “Contribution” is koinōnia, fellowship, sharing. The Jerusalem church had been through famine (Acts 11:28–30) and was probably cut off from much of the society it had left. The unity of Jew and Gentile that Paul has argued for across this letter was about to arrive in Jerusalem in a bag, carried by representatives of the nations chapter 11 said had been grafted in.

Have been pleased. His word for the givers, twice in two verses. The Macedonians gave out of extreme poverty, begging for the privilege (2 Corinthians 8:1–4). The gospel had made poor Greeks glad to give to poorer Jews.

Setting his face toward Jerusalem. Luke tells this journey in a way that recalls another. Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). Paul, carrying this gift, went constrained by the Spirit, knowing that imprisonment and afflictions awaited him (Acts 20:22–23), and his friends said, “Let the will of the Lord be done” (Acts 21:14), words that echo Gethsemane. Christ went up to Jerusalem to give himself for his people; Paul goes to serve them, carrying the fruit of that self-giving. “Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9): that is the fountain the collection flowed from. Greek believers gave gladly to Jewish believers they would never meet, because a Jewish Saviour had given everything to make them rich.

Should Christians help poor believers first, or the poor in general? Both, with a particular care for the church: “Let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians 6:10). A family looks after its own members first, not because it does not care about the neighbours, but because they are family. So churches should make sure no believer among them, or in poorer churches elsewhere, goes without, as this collection did. And Christians should also be known for mercy to the poor around them, whoever they are, like the good Samaritan (Luke 10:29–37). The order is especially, not only.
verseByVerse.note: The collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem was a major project of Paul’s later ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gentile churches gave gladly, yet they also owed it: having shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings, they ought to serve Israel’s poor with material ones. Glad giving and a real debt are not opposites.

They owe it to them. The last appearance of a theme that runs through the letter (1:14; 8:12; 13:8; 15:1), and once again the debt is owed to people the debtor might have looked down on.

Their spiritual blessings. The gospel, the promises, the Messiah, the Scriptures all came to the Gentiles from the Jews (9:4–5; 11:17–18). “Share” is koinōneō, from the same root as “contribution” in verse 26. This deflates Gentile self-importance, Paul’s target since chapter 11: the nations did not generate their own faith. A Gentile church sending relief to Jerusalem is a congregation admitting in public where it got what it has.

Material blessings. Literally, fleshly things: here simply bodily needs such as food and money, with no thought of sin. “Be of service” is leitourgeō, priestly service, the word family of verse 16: giving money is a form of worship (Philippians 4:18). The exchange is deliberately uneven. You cannot return a gospel; you can send money, as the fitting response to a gift that cannot be repaid.

Salvation is from the Jews. Jesus said it himself, to a Samaritan woman at a well (John 4:22), and moments later told her he was the Messiah (John 4:26). The greatest of Israel’s spiritual blessings was not a book or a rite but a Person, a Jewish man from Nazareth, through whom the riches of God came to the nations.

What it does not mean. Not a general rule that teachers must be paid by those taught; Paul argues that elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:11–14). Here the debt is owed by the whole Gentile church to the mother congregation.

In everyday life. Name three people who carried the gospel to you: who taught you, baptised you, wrote what fed you. Then give something back, gladly: money to a ministry like theirs, a letter of thanks to one still living, or time given to pass on what they gave you.

Do Gentile Christians today owe something to the Jewish people? A debt of gratitude, certainly. Every Gentile believer worships Israel’s God, reads Israel’s Scriptures and trusts Israel’s Messiah. That rules out every trace of contempt for Jewish people, which has disgraced the church too often in its history (11:18–20), and should move us to love, to pray for their salvation as Paul did (10:1), and to share Christ with them humbly. The particular debt in this verse was owed to Jewish believers in need, so its closest application is generous care for Jewish Christians and for the poor among God’s people. Christians differ on how this relates to modern politics, and the verse does not settle those questions.

verseByVerse.quote: When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you. I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once the gift is safely delivered, Paul will set out for Spain by way of Rome, sure that he will come with the full blessing of Christ. Every word of that prediction held; none of the travel arrangements did.

What has been collected. Paul calls the gift fruit: the fruit of the gospel, grown in Greek soil and brought home to the root. He means to see it safely into their hands himself.

The fullness of the blessing of Christ. The blessing of Christ is everything Christ gives (Ephesians 1:3), and Paul expects to bring it in full because he brings Christ himself in the gospel. He is right, and he has no idea what it will cost. He was arrested in Jerusalem within days (Acts 21), spent two years in custody at Caesarea, was shipwrecked off Malta, and came into Rome in chains some three years later (Acts 28:16). Even as a prisoner he came in the fullness of Christ’s blessing (Philippians 1:12–13).

Unhindered. Paul has twice said he was hindered (1:13; v. 22). Luke ends Acts with Paul in Rome under house arrest, teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, and the last word of the narrative in Greek is unhindered (Acts 28:31). The obstruction was to the man, never to the message.

In everyday life. Think of a plan of yours that went wrong in the last few years and ask honestly what came through it anyway. Not everything that went wrong was secretly good. But the blessing of Christ was not one of the things you lost.

Is it a lack of faith to make plans? No. Paul planned carefully: routes, timing, support, a three-stage itinerary across the Mediterranean. Scripture commends forethought (Proverbs 21:5; Luke 14:28). What it forbids is the arrogance that plans as though tomorrow belongs to us: “Instead you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that’” (James 4:15). So plan, pray over the plans, and hold them with open hands. Paul’s confidence was not in the itinerary but in Christ’s blessing, which no change of route could remove.

Uncertain wording. Behind the ESV’s “delivered to them what has been collected” lies an unusual phrase, literally having sealed to them this fruit, and its exact sense is not certain. A seal marked something as genuine and complete, like goods signed for on delivery, so most take it, as the ESV does, to mean that Paul will see the gift safely and properly handed over. Others think he means he will confirm it to the Jerusalem church as the true fruit of the Gentile mission. Either way, he means to finish this task properly before he turns west.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begs the Romans to join his struggle in prayer, that he may be kept safe from unbelievers in Judea and that the believers in Jerusalem may accept the gift. The apostle who wrote chapter 8 is frightened, and he believes he needs the prayers of ordinary believers he has never met.

By our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit. The love of the Spirit is the love the Spirit produces in believers, binding them together across the miles. The whole Trinity is present in verse 30: Christian prayer is to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit.

Strive together with me. Synagōnizomai means wrestle together. The root is agōn, a contest, from which we get agony; Paul uses its relatives of Epaphras, “always struggling on your behalf in his prayers” (Colossians 4:12). Prayer here is hard work, done alongside somebody, on their behalf, at a distance.

Delivered from the unbelievers. Many in Jerusalem hated Paul as a traitor to the law (Acts 20:22–23; 21:10–14). He also feared the Jewish believers might refuse a gift from Gentiles out of suspicion about his ministry (Acts 21:20–21), so that the gift meant to show unity would be rejected.

Watch with me. Paul is not the first to walk toward Jerusalem asking friends to pray. In Gethsemane Jesus told three disciples his soul was very sorrowful, even to death, and asked them to remain and watch with him (Matthew 26:38). Luke adds that, being in agony, he prayed more earnestly (Luke 22:44); these verses are missing from some early manuscripts, so some Bibles bracket them. His friends slept. He wrestled alone and said to the Father, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). Because he went through that struggle unaided, Paul can appeal by our Lord Jesus Christ for a struggle shared. The Lord who had no one to strive alongside him has made a people who strive alongside one another.

How God answered. He asked to be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea. He was seized in the temple and would have been beaten to death had Roman soldiers not taken him into custody (Acts 21:30–33), and later the Romans protected him from a plot to kill him (Acts 23:12–35). He was delivered, into arrest. He asked that his service be acceptable to the saints. Luke says the brothers received him gladly (Acts 21:17), and mentions the money only once, in passing, in Paul’s defence before Felix (Acts 24:17). And he asked to come to Rome with joy. He came in chains, at the empire’s expense, and Luke’s last picture is of him welcoming all who came to him, preaching for two years (Acts 28:30–31). He got the joy, but not in the shape he asked for.

Not a glib answer. This is not the cheap, even cruel, assurance that every unanswered prayer is secretly a better answer. Paul lost years to that arrest, and the man asking here for a safe journey did not get one. What the passage shows is narrower and more honest: God answered every one of these petitions, none of them in the manner requested, and Paul’s ministry was not diminished by the difference. Several of his letters are traditionally dated to his imprisonment.

In everyday life. Take a prayer of your own that you consider unanswered, and ask what actually happened next: not to your circumstances, but to you and the people around you. Sometimes the honest answer is still that it was a loss and you are waiting; Paul wrote chapter 8 about groaning. But sometimes the answer arrived under a different name and was not recognised.

How do I strive in prayer for someone? Paul’s request shows the way. Pray specifically: he names the danger, the place and the outcome he wants, so ask missionaries and friends what to pray for, and pray for exactly that. Pray persistently: wrestling is not one quick mention, so write the names down and return to them on set days. Pray with others: a prayer meeting is where a church gets into the struggle together. Pray for their faithfulness as well as their safety, as Paul asks that his service be acceptable, and elsewhere that he may speak boldly (Ephesians 6:19–20). Then find out how God answered, and give thanks. You come “by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit”: the Son intercedes at the Father’s right hand (8:34), and the Spirit helps us in our weakness (8:26). You are joining a prayer that is already being prayed.

If God has already planned everything, why pray? Because God has planned the prayers too. He ordains not only what will happen but the means by which it happens, and prayer is one of his chosen means (the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, both 5.3). Prayer does not change God’s mind; it is the way he has chosen to bring his good purposes to pass, and to draw us into his work. When you pray for a missionary’s safety, you are not interfering with providence. You are one of the means providence is using.
verseByVerse.note: These prayers were answered in unexpected ways: Paul was arrested in Jerusalem and reached Rome as a prisoner.

verseByVerse.quote: so that by God's will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company. May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul hopes, if God wills, to reach Rome with joy and rest among them, and he blesses them with the presence of the God of peace. The letter that began in a courtroom ends with peace.

By God’s will. All Paul’s plans depend on it (1:10). He wanted to arrive rested, on his way to Spain. The will of God would bring him there by a road of violence, prison and the sea. He wrote the words anyway, and the words held.

Refreshed in your company. “Refreshed” (synanapauomai) means to rest together. The man who has carried the churches on his heart for twenty years wants nothing more from Rome than to sit down with them and be renewed.

The God of peace. The God who made peace with us through Christ (5:1). Peace with God is more than a calm feeling: it means the war is over. We were his enemies, under his just anger (5:9–10); now, justified by faith, we are reconciled and welcome. He also gives peace within the church, between strong and weak, Jew and Gentile (14:19; 16:20).

The names of God in this chapter. The God of endurance and encouragement (v. 5), the God of hope (v. 13), the God of peace (v. 33). Three times Paul names God by the exact thing his readers need: a divided and weary church needs the God of endurance and encouragement, a discouraged one the God of hope, an anxious one the God of peace. Paul addresses God as the one who already is what the situation lacks. So the last thing the argument of Romans leaves in the room is not a doctrine but a presence.

Peace is the right last word. The letter began with wrath revealed from heaven, every mouth stopped, the whole world accountable to God (1:18; 3:19). It arrives at “the God of peace be with you all”, and “all” matters: the strong and the weak, Jew and Gentile, the ones who eat and the ones who do not. The hostility has been dealt with in both directions, between God and man and between people sitting in the same room, and both in the same place: Christ “himself is our peace”, who reconciled Jew and Gentile to God in one body through the cross (Ephesians 2:14–16). He made peace with enemies, at the cost of his Son’s blood. And he did not make it and leave: on the night before the cross the Son said, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:27). He has never taken it back.

What if church drains me rather than refreshes me? Then you are not alone, and the verse still shows the goal. Paul expected to be refreshed by Christians, and God means his people to be that for one another (Philemon 7, 20). But churches are made of forgiven sinners, and some seasons are hard. Look for it where it can be found: one or two believers to pray with honestly, a friendship around the Bible. Ask whether you come expecting only to give, or only to receive; both starve a soul. If something in your church is genuinely harmful, speak to the elders. But do not give up meeting together (Hebrews 10:24–25), because the God of peace usually sends his refreshment through his people.

Textual note. One early copy of Romans places the closing doxology (16:25–27) straight after this verse; see the textual note at 16:25–27.
