15.text: <sup>1</sup>We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves.<sup>2</sup>Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up.<sup>3</sup>For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.”<sup>4</sup>For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.<sup>5</sup>May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,<sup>6</sup>that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>7</sup>Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.<sup>8</sup>For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God’s truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs,<sup>9</sup>and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, “Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.”<sup>10</sup>And again it says, “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people.”<sup>11</sup>And again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him.”<sup>12</sup>And again Isaiah says, “The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope.”<sup>13</sup>May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.<sup>14</sup>I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another.<sup>15</sup>But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God<sup>16</sup>to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.<sup>17</sup>In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.<sup>18</sup>For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience—by word and deed,<sup>19</sup>by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God—so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ;<sup>20</sup>and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else’s foundation,<sup>21</sup>but as it is written, “Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.”<sup>22</sup>This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you.<sup>23</sup>But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you,<sup>24</sup>I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while.<sup>25</sup>At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints.<sup>26</sup>For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem.<sup>27</sup>For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.<sup>28</sup>When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you.<sup>29</sup>I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.<sup>30</sup>I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf,<sup>31</sup>that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,<sup>32</sup>so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company.<sup>33</sup>May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

keyVerse.quote: Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the summit of the argument that began at 14:1, and it sums up one of the reasons Paul wrote the letter (see the introduction). Its standard is Christ, who welcomed us while we were ungodly, weak and his enemies, and its goal is God’s glory: a church of people who would never otherwise sit together, praising one Father with one voice.

15.reflection:
Paul says the strong must “bear with the failings of the weak” (v. 1), a verb that means to pick up and carry. What is the difference between carrying a fellow believer and merely tolerating or managing him? Whom might you be called to carry?

Verse 7 makes Christ’s welcome the standard for ours. Recall how he welcomed you (5:6–10). Is there a believer, or a kind of believer, you find hard to welcome, and what would welcoming them look like this month?

Paul calls his evangelism priestly service and the converted Gentiles an offering to God (v. 16). How does seeing mission as worship change the way we think about speaking of Christ and about supporting those who go to people who have never heard?

All of Paul’s requests in vv. 30–32 were answered, but none in the way he expected. How should that shape the way you pray, and the way you look back on prayers that seemed unanswered?

16.title: Greetings, Warnings, and the Final Doxology
16.overview:
Where we are. Romans 16 closes the letter. The argument is finished and Paul’s plans are set out (15:14–33); what remains is greetings, a last warning, and praise.

The message. The gospel of Romans makes a family, and God knows every member of it by name. The doctrine of fifteen chapters now has faces: a patroness, a tentmaking couple, slaves and freedmen, a man linked to Herod’s family, a city official and a man called Fourth, all greeted as brothers and sisters. That family must be guarded from those who would divide it for their own ends, and everything returns at last to glory to the only wise God through Jesus Christ.

Why it was said. Paul had never visited Rome, and was about to ask its congregations, Jewish and Gentile believers still learning to welcome one another, to back his mission to Spain (see the introduction). Greeting so many who knew him showed he was no stranger, and the warning protected a welcoming church (15:7) from people who would exploit its welcome.

How the chapter makes its case. Phoebe, who very probably carried the letter, is commended (vv. 1–2). Twenty-six people are named, with households besides: co-workers, fellow prisoners, women who toiled, members of great houses, and at last names with nothing attached (vv. 3–15), all made one family by the holy kiss (v. 16). Then the warmth turns sharp: mark and avoid those who divide the church against the doctrine you were taught, and trust the God of peace to crush Satan under your feet (vv. 17–20). Paul’s companions add their greetings, the scribe Tertius among them (vv. 21–23), and the doxology gathers up the gospel, the mystery now revealed to all nations, and the obedience of faith with which the letter began (vv. 25–27; compare 1:1–5).

Where it leads. Nearly every name is greeted “in the Lord” or “in Christ”. What they share is not class, race or usefulness but union with the one who became a servant, laid down his life for his friends, and will crush the serpent under the feet of those he has freed. The letter that opened with the gospel concerning God’s Son (1:3) ends with glory to God through that Son, for ever.

For us. God does not love his church in bulk; he remembers the unnoticed worker, the unnamed mother, the slave the world counted as property. Ask whom you would not naturally greet as family, guard your church against flattering voices that divide it, and let the end of Romans be your end too: worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — A Network of Saints: The Social World of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gospel makes one family out of people the world kept apart, and God knows each of them by name. Paul commends Phoebe, who very probably carried the letter, as a servant of her church and a patron of many (vv. 1–2). Then he greets the church in Rome person by person: co-workers who risked their lives, the first convert of Asia, women who worked hard in the Lord, slaves and freedmen, believers in great households, and at last clusters of names with nothing attached (vv. 3–15; see the note on vv. 14–15). The holy kiss, a greeting that belonged chiefly to family, declares these strangers family in Christ (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
The church as the new humanity

Romans 16:1–16 puts names and faces to the argument of chapters 1–15. The lack of distinction between Jew and Greek (10:12), the olive tree into which Gentiles are grafted (11:17–24), the command to welcome one another as Christ has welcomed us (15:7): all are visible in the list. The doctrine of justification by faith produces a new kind of community.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: By the standards of the first-century world the mixing in Romans 16 was startling. Social boundaries in Rome were sharply kept, and eating with inferiors could bring shame. Now: A church whose members all share one race, class or income, especially by design, has a question to ask itself (see the note on vv. 8–9).

verseByVerse.quote: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. — Romans 16:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks the Romans to welcome Phoebe, who served her church and supported him, as a sister in the Lord, and to help her in whatever she needs.

Why should I read a list of names? Because here the doctrine becomes visible. For fifteen chapters Paul has argued that God justifies the ungodly (declares guilty people righteous for Christ’s sake, 4:5), shows no partiality, and makes Jew and Gentile one family in Christ. Chapter 16 is that family on the ground: a wealthy patroness, a tentmaking couple, slaves with common names, a city treasurer and a man called Fourth, all greeted as brothers and sisters, by a God who remembers people the world forgets. And since Paul was about to ask a church he had never visited to back his mission to Spain (15:24), greeting so many who knew him was in effect naming his references.

Our sister Phoebe. A letter of commendation (synistēmi, to recommend) let travelling believers be trusted and received (2 Corinthians 3:1). There was no post for private letters, and the roll containing Romans very probably went to Rome in her luggage. The bearer commonly read the letter aloud and answered questions about it, so the Romans very possibly first heard of the potter and the clay, and of the love nothing can separate them from, in Phoebe’s voice.

A servant of the church at Cenchreae. Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth (Acts 18:18). “Servant” is diakonos; the ESV notes that it can be rendered deaconess. Because Paul ties the word to a particular congregation, it points to a recognised role there, not just to a helpful person.

A patron of many. “Patron” (prostatis, found only here in the New Testament) means benefactor, protector: probably a woman of means who used her wealth and influence to support Paul and others with money, housing and introductions. The apostle to the Gentiles is on record as somebody’s dependent, and is not embarrassed to say so.

A servant like her Lord. A chapter earlier Paul used the same word of Christ, who became a servant (diakonos) to the circumcised (15:8). Whatever Phoebe’s office, her service bore her Lord’s family likeness. And the Romans are to welcome her “in the Lord”, as Christ has welcomed them (15:7), not for her wealth or standing; every name in this chapter is greeted on that ground.

He saw every coin she gave. God did not send this letter by angel, but in the hands of a sister from a harbour town who had spent her money on his servants, and he has kept her name in his book ever since. He saw every coin she gave and every traveller she sheltered. He is a God who notices, and remembers.

What it does not mean. Not that women’s service is second-class. Paul’s greetings begin with a woman who held a recognised place of service, funded the apostle, and was trusted with what may be the most important letter he ever wrote.

In everyday life. Think of one missionary or gospel worker who is a stranger somewhere, or carries a heavy load, and ask what a patron would do with what God has given you: a room, a meal, a gift, an introduction.

What do deacons actually do? They care for the practical needs of the church so that the elders can give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word, a pattern usually traced to the seven appointed so that widows were not neglected in the daily distribution of food (Acts 6:1–6). Today that means caring for the poor and sick, organising practical help, looking after buildings and finances, and welcoming newcomers. Their qualifications are mostly about character, and it is no lesser calling (1 Timothy 3:8–13).

So how can women serve in my church? In more ways than most churches use. In the New Testament women host churches (Lydia, Acts 16:15), fund the mission (Luke 8:1–3), carry apostolic letters (Phoebe), labour in the gospel alongside Paul (Philippians 4:2–3), explain the faith privately to men and women alike (Acts 18:26), train younger women (Titus 2:3–5), and pass the faith to children (2 Timothy 1:5). In a complementarian church they can lead ministries of mercy, teach women and children, counsel, organise, show hospitality, pray in the gathering, and serve in recognised roles; what is reserved for qualified men is the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church. A church that keeps that boundary but leaves its women’s gifts unused has obeyed half the chapter.

Where Christians differ: Phoebe and women in church office. Some argue from Phoebe that women may hold any office, including elder or pastor; others deny she held any office at all. Among those who agree on the eldership, some take her title in its general sense, some see her as a deaconess serving especially among women, and some as a deacon in the office of 1 Timothy 3:8–13, reading 1 Timothy 3:11 as speaking of women deacons. This commentary’s view: Phoebe was an honoured servant of her church, and she may well have held a recognised role of service, which some Reformed churches call deaconess (compare 1 Timothy 3:11). The office of deacon is one of practical service and mercy, not of governing or teaching the church with authority. The New Testament reserves the office of elder or pastor, with its authority to teach and rule, for qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). This is the complementarian view: men and women are equal in worth and in Christ (Galatians 3:28), with different callings in the church and home. Egalitarian Christians, who hold that every office is open to women, read these texts differently out of a real desire to honour women’s gifts, and are to be respected as brothers and sisters. Phoebe shows how highly Paul valued women’s ministry, and churches should honour and use women’s gifts fully within Scripture’s pattern.
verseByVerse.note: Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. The ESV notes that “servant” can also be rendered “deaconess.” Phoebe probably carried this letter to Rome. A patron was a benefactor who supported others with her resources.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets Prisca and Aquila, his fellow workers, who risked their lives to save his, so that every Gentile church owes them thanks.

Greet Prisca and Aquila. Prisca is a form of Priscilla. She and Aquila, tentmakers like Paul, had returned to Rome after Claudius’ expulsion of the Jews (Acts 18:2) was lifted. Paul met them in Corinth and took them to Ephesus, where they taught Apollos the way of God more accurately and hosted a church (Acts 18:18–26; 1 Corinthians 16:19). The wife is named first, as in four of the six places the couple appears (here; Acts 18:18, 26; 2 Timothy 4:19). In a world that ordered such things carefully, she was probably the more prominent, by standing or by gift. Paul notices, and does not mind.

My fellow workers. Fellow workers (synergoi), not his helpers: they served the same Lord, and the work was his.

Risked their necks. Literally, laid down their own necks: the posture of a man on an executioner’s block. We do not know when; it may have been the riot in Ephesus (Acts 19:23–41). Paul does not explain, so his readers evidently knew the story. By saving him, they served all the churches he founded: every Gentile believer reading Romans owes something to a couple who were willing to die for the man who wrote it.

Greater love has no one than this. Jesus said, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13), and then he laid down his own. A tentmaking couple who put their necks under the blade for a friend were showing, in a small way, the love first shown to them at the cross.

How does Priscilla teaching Apollos fit with 1 Timothy 2:12? Egalitarian Christians (who hold that every church office is open to women) see her as proof that Paul placed no limit on women’s teaching. But look at what Luke says she did: with her husband she took Apollos aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:26). That was private instruction by a couple, not the authoritative teaching of the gathered church that 1 Timothy 2 reserves for qualified men. The complementarian reading honours both texts: women may and should teach the faith, in the ways listed at vv. 1–2 and in private conversation like this with men too, while the office of elder and the preaching of the church belong to men. And Paul’s greeting shows how highly he valued her.

What does it look like for a married couple to serve together? Priscilla and Aquila worked the same trade, opened the same home, taught the same young preacher and risked the same danger. Their marriage was not a retreat from ministry but a base for it. Today that might mean a Bible study in your home, students or lonely people at your table, a younger couple to mentor, a ministry worked side by side, and prayer for the church, not only for yourselves: a husband who leads with self-giving love and a wife honoured as his fellow worker, both looking outward.
verseByVerse.note: Prisca is a form of Priscilla. She and Aquila had returned to Rome after Claudius’s expulsion of Jews ended.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets the church that meets in Prisca and Aquila’s home, and Epaenetus, whom he loves, the first person in the province of Asia to come to Christ.

The church in their house. Buildings set apart for Christian worship appear only in the third century; Rome probably had several house churches (vv. 5, 14, 15). The church (ekklēsia) is the people: a whole congregation in someone’s front room, with no sign and no address anybody would recognise, and from such rooms the gospel spread through the empire.

My beloved Epaenetus. Paul greets not a congregation in the abstract but a man he loves. Asia was the Roman province in western Turkey, with Ephesus its chief city. “First convert” is literally firstfruits (aparchē), a sacrificial term: the first of the harvest brought to God as the pledge that the rest is coming. It fits Paul’s picture of himself as a priest bringing the Gentiles to God as an offering (15:16). Epaenetus may have been converted through Priscilla and Aquila in Ephesus, which would explain why he is greeted next to them.

Firstfruits for Christ. The harvest is Christ’s. A generation later the risen Lord appeared to John standing among the seven golden lampstands, the churches of Asia (Revelation 1:12–13, 20). The province where Epaenetus once stood alone had become a place where Christ himself walked among his churches.

The loneliness of being first. Somebody in every place has to be first, with no church to join and nobody gone before. Epaenetus was that man in Asia, which became one of the great centres of early Christianity. When God sows a single seed in a pagan province, he means the whole field. If you are the only believer in your family, your street or your workplace, remember Epaenetus, and pray for the harvest of which you might be the firstfruits.

Is a small church meeting in a home a real church? Yes, if it has what makes a church a church. It is defined not by building or size but by its marks: the gospel truly preached, baptism and the Lord’s Supper rightly administered, and a people under the care of qualified elders, gathering regularly for worship and holding one another to account in love (Acts 2:42; 14:23; Hebrews 10:24–25). A dozen people in a living room with these things are a church; a thousand in an auditorium without them are not. Whatever its size, a church should be in fellowship with other faithful churches, as the house churches of Rome were with each other and with Paul.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes; there were no church buildings.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul honours Mary for her hard work, and Andronicus and Junia, fellow Jews who shared his imprisonment and belonged to Christ before he did.

Mary, who has worked hard for you. “Worked hard” (kopiaō) means toiled to the point of weariness, the word Paul uses of his own apostolic work (1 Corinthians 15:10). It appears three times in this chapter, each time of women: Mary here, and Tryphaena and Tryphosa, and Persis (v. 12). Paul does not say what any of them did, only how hard they did it, and that he noticed and wanted a church across the Mediterranean to know their names.

Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen. “Kinsmen” here means fellow Jews (9:3). The two were probably husband and wife. The ESV notes that the name may be read Junias, a man’s name, but Junia, a common Roman woman’s name, is more likely: the early church read it as a woman’s name almost without exception, John Chrysostom among them, and the masculine Junias has not been found in any ancient inscription or writing. They had been in prison with Paul at some point, or for the same cause (2 Corinthians 11:23), and however “well known to the apostles” is taken (see below), the church’s founding leaders held them in high regard.

They were in Christ before me. They were believers before Paul’s conversion (around AD 33–34), among the very first, perhaps from Pentecost (Acts 2:10 mentions visitors from Rome). And the two words “in Christ” hold the whole of salvation: joined to him by faith, so that his death counts as yours and his life becomes yours, and there is no condemnation (8:1). While Paul was still breathing threats against the church, these two were already in Christ, perhaps among the people he hunted. Then the risen Lord stopped him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). To strike at those in Christ was to strike at Christ. Now the hunter is in Christ too, and calls the hunted his kinsmen and fellow prisoners.

What if my service goes unnoticed? Then you are in the company of Mary, and of most of the faithful who have ever lived. God keeps a record of every weary hour spent in his service, and does not need your work to be seen in order to reward it. Your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:4), and God is not unjust so as to overlook the love you have shown for his name in serving the saints (Hebrews 6:10). Serve for his eye, not for applause. And do what Paul did here: notice the hidden labourers in your church and thank them by name.

Where Christians differ: was Junia an apostle? Some say Junia was a female apostle, and so women may hold any office. Others insist the name must be male, or the phrase must mean only “known to the apostles.” This commentary’s view: The ESV reading, well known to the apostles, is grammatically defensible, though many scholars prefer outstanding among the apostles. But even then, the New Testament uses apostle in two senses: the unique apostles of Christ (the Twelve and Paul), who had seen the risen Lord and laid the church’s foundation; and messengers or missionaries sent by churches (2 Corinthians 8:23; Philippians 2:25). Andronicus and Junia could only be apostles in the second sense, as travelling missionaries, as Barnabas is called an apostle in Acts 14:14. This neither overturns the New Testament’s teaching on eldership (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7) nor reopens the apostolic office, whose foundational work ended with the apostles of Christ (Ephesians 2:20). What it does show is a woman who shared Paul’s chains for Christ and was honoured by name for it.

Uncertain wording. “Well known to the apostles” (ESV) or “outstanding among the apostles” (as many other translations have it): the Greek (episēmoi en tois apostolois) can mean either. The adjective is clear: notable, conspicuous. What is uncertain is whether “among the apostles” counts the two as apostles or says that the apostles held them in high regard, and scholars still debate how the phrase was used in Greek of the time.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the name may be read Junias (a man’s name). Andronicus and Junia had become believers before Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets three men with ordinary names, probably slaves or freedmen, calling two of them his beloved and one his fellow worker.

Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Several of these names were common among slaves and freedmen in Rome, and Ampliatus is found in inscriptions of the imperial household. Such a man had no standing in the Roman world, and Paul calls him beloved in a letter read aloud in every century since. That is the grace of God: he passes by the great houses and calls their slaves his beloved. A tomb in one of Rome’s oldest Christian catacombs bears this name in unusually careful lettering; whether it is this man cannot be shown.

Urbanus and Stachys. Urbanus is a common Roman slave name (from urbs, city), and he is “our fellow worker”. Stachys means ear of grain. Three names in two verses, two of them called beloved.

The Lord’s freedman. Paul says it all “in the Lord” or “in Christ”, and that changes their status at the root. A slave called in the Lord is a freedman of the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:22). Ampliatus might still answer to a human master on Monday, but sin and death no longer owned him, and no master on earth could stand between him and his Lord (6:18, 22). Rome counted him as property; Christ counts him as his own, bought with a price and set free. And the Lord who did it first took the form of a slave himself (Philippians 2:7) and died by crucifixion, the death Rome reserved for slaves and rebels. So the apostle can call a slave beloved without condescension: they stand on the same ground, owned and loved by the same Master.

The kind of church the doctrine produces. An apostle lists a slave among the people he loves, by name, for the record (see the note on vv. 1–2). It also searches the heart. If my worth rests on whom I know and who knows me, a church like this feels like a loss of status; if it rests on being known and loved by Christ, it feels like home.

How can a church make people of low status truly belong? By treating them as Paul treats Ampliatus: by name, with affection, as co-workers. That means more than being polite on Sunday. Ask the cleaner, the refugee or the man with no job to serve alongside the professionals, not only to be served. Eat in each other’s homes. Choose leaders for godliness, not wealth or polish (James 2:1–5). Visit those who can never repay the visit. A church where everyone in leadership looks the same, earns the same and lives in the same streets should ask whether the gospel has finished its work there.
verseByVerse.note: Several of these names were common among slaves and freedmen in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus. Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets a believer whose faith has been tested and proved genuine, a fellow Jew linked by name to the Herods, and the Christians in two great households.

Apelles, who is approved in Christ. “Approved” (dokimos) means tested and proved genuine, like metal that has come through the fire. Paul gives him only one phrase, perhaps the best a Christian can receive.

The family of Aristobulus. The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus probably included the slaves and freedmen of important men. Aristobulus may have been the grandson of Herod the Great, a prince who lived in Rome as a private citizen; when such a man died, his slaves often passed to the emperor while keeping their old master’s name.

My kinsman Herodion. A fellow Jew, whose name suggests a link with the Herod family. If so, a member of the household that killed John the Baptist and mocked Christ is greeted as a kinsman and brother, a few lines from a slave and a woman who works too hard.

The family of Narcissus. Narcissus may be the powerful freedman of the emperor Claudius, forced to commit suicide in AD 54. “Those in the Lord”: only some in that household were believers. The faith often spread not by converting a great house but by taking root among its servants, a few at a time; a few years later Paul would send greetings from those of Caesar’s household (Philippians 4:22).

Approved in Christ. Not approved by the church, but in Christ. The only life ever tested at every point and found true is Christ’s, tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). A believer’s faith survives the fire because it is joined to him (1 Peter 1:7). Apelles went through something that could have broken his faith, and it did not break, because Christ held on to him (John 10:28).

What if I am the only Christian in my home or workplace? Then you stand where these believers stood. Live as one approved in Christ: faithful, honest, hard-working and kind, adorning the doctrine of God our Saviour in everything (Titus 2:10). Do not hide your faith, but let your life speak before your words do (1 Peter 3:1–2). Pray daily for the people around you by name. Find fellowship in a church where you are known and fed; you cannot be the only light in a dark house without being refuelled. God has often begun his work in a household or an office through one believer who simply stayed faithful.
verseByVerse.note: The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus probably included their slaves and freedmen.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul honours three women for their hard work in the Lord, and greets Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who had been a mother to Paul as well.

Tryphaena, Tryphosa and Persis. The first two were possibly sisters. Their names mean dainty and delicate, yet they were hard workers (kopiaō) in the Lord; Paul may be smiling as he writes it. Persis means Persian woman, perhaps a former slave. Paul says she “has worked hard”, in the past tense, which may mean her years of strength are behind her; Paul has not forgotten them.

Rufus. He may be the son of Simon of Cyrene: Mark, probably writing for the church in Rome, names Simon’s sons, Alexander and Rufus, as people his readers knew (Mark 15:21). If so, the man who carried Jesus’ cross had a son in the Roman church, and the woman who mothered Paul may have been Simon’s wife. Simon’s burden, the cross carried behind Jesus (Luke 23:26), is the picture of discipleship (Luke 9:23), and the cross he was forced to carry became the cross that saved his family.

His mother, who has been a mother to me as well. She had cared for Paul like a mother, perhaps in Antioch, where men from Cyrene were among the church’s leaders (Acts 11:20; 13:1). It is one of the warmest things Paul ever wrote, over in a moment. Consider the man writing it: no wife, no household, flogged five times, beaten with rods three times, stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:19), shipwrecked, hungry, cold and short of clothing (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). Somewhere in all that, a woman took him in and treated him as her own: fed him, presumably made him rest, possibly told him off. She is not even named. To anyone who has quietly done that for a Christian worker and assumed it counted for little: the apostle put it in Scripture.

A mother for a homeless apostle. The God who chose Rufus before the world began sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6), and he gave a homeless, beaten apostle a mother in the faith. His Son promised not to leave his people as orphans (John 14:18), and here is the promise being kept, in a house in Rome.

In everyday life. If you are older and your days of hard labour are past, like Persis, your prayers, your counsel and your example are still labour in the Lord.

What does “chosen in the Lord” mean, if every believer is chosen? Whichever sense of the word Paul intends (see below), it rests on what he has taught in this letter: God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything in them, but in love (8:29–30; 9:11; Ephesians 1:4–5). Here it is a term of affection: to be chosen in the Lord is to be loved by God from eternity, and every believer may say it of himself with wonder. Christians have long differed over what election rests on, some seeing it as God’s foreknowledge of faith; this commentary follows the reading of Romans 9 that it rests on God’s free love alone, while honouring brothers who read it otherwise.

Can I be a spiritual mother or father if I have no children? Yes, and the church badly needs you to be. Rufus’s mother mothered a man who was not her son. Paul called Timothy his true child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2), and Jesus promised those who leave family for his sake mothers and brothers and children a hundredfold in this age (Mark 10:29–30). Single and childless believers can be the steadiest spiritual parents a young Christian ever has. Have someone younger to your table regularly, pray for their battles, ask how they really are and listen, teach them what you have learned of Christ, and let them see your faith in hard days.

Uncertain wording. “Chosen” (eklektos) usually means elect, chosen by God. Since that is true of every believer, Paul may simply be saying it of Rufus warmly. Or he may use the word in its other sense, choice or outstanding, as we speak of choice fruit. Both senses are well attested, and either fits.
verseByVerse.note: Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene, whom Mark mentions as if known to his readers.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets two more groups of believers, probably house churches, naming people of whom we know nothing else and, with them, all the unnamed saints who met with them.

Asyncritus and Philologus, and those with them. Probably two house churches, or believers who lived or worked together; Philologus and Julia may have been husband and wife. Here the names arrive with nothing attached: no “my beloved”, no “who has worked hard”, no “approved in Christ”, and we know nothing else about a single one of them. Behind both clusters stand the ones not named at all, “the brothers who are with them”, “all the saints who are with them”: rooms full of people reduced to a phrase.

The names. Paul names twenty-six people and greets twenty-four directly (Aristobulus and Narcissus are named only for their households). Seven of the twenty-four are women, and two more women are greeted without their names. He knew so many in a city he had never visited because believers travelled, and many had met him elsewhere.

All the saints. They are saints not because they had done anything remarkable, but because they were sanctified in Christ Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:2), and brothers because the Son is the firstborn among many brothers (8:29). Nobody here has a title or a story, but every one has the two names that matter, saint and brother, both given by Christ.

The real proportion of the church. A handful of people are remembered for something, more only for having been present; most are not written down anywhere, though every one of them got up on ordinary mornings and believed and was faithful and died. Patrobas and Olympas are unknown to history and known to God, as most of the saints who have ever lived are, and the record that matters is kept in heaven, with room for every name.

In everyday life. Pray by name for five people in your church you rarely speak to. And if you feel like one of the unnamed, take heart: the church has always mostly been made of people like you, and God has not lost track of you.

Among so many believers, does God really know me personally? Yes. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3), numbers the hairs on your head (Matthew 10:30) and has engraved his people on the palms of his hands (Isaiah 49:16). God does not love his church in bulk. He chose each one, Christ died for each one, and the Spirit dwells in each one. On the last day you will not be lost in the crowd; you will be known, and welcomed by name (Luke 10:20).

Hasn’t Christianity always been bad for women? Many assume so, and Christian men who used Scripture to belittle or silence women have given them reasons, to the shame of Christ’s name. But look at the world this list was written into. A papyrus letter survives from Egypt, written in 1 BC by a man called Hilarion to his wife. If the child she is carrying is a boy, he tells her, she is to keep it; if a girl, she is to throw it out. The rest of the letter is affectionate. The sociologist Rodney Stark argued in The Rise of Christianity that the early church grew especially fast among women, partly because it gave them security and standing the surrounding culture did not: it refused to abandon baby girls, required husbands as well as wives to be faithful, and cared for widows instead of discarding them. Then read Paul’s greetings: women named one by one, praised in the word he uses of his own work (v. 6), a patron trusted with his letter, a mother who mothered him. The gospel did not invent the dignity of women. It saw the image of God that was always there, and paid for it with the blood of a Son born of woman (Galatians 4:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul tells the Roman believers to greet one another as family, with a holy kiss, and sends them the love of all the churches of Christ.

A holy kiss. A kiss on the cheek was a common greeting between family and friends; a holy one is pure, expressing the love of brothers and sisters in Christ (1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:26). “One another” carries the weight. In a congregation that has argued about food and days, with a member of Herod’s circle, several slaves and a wealthy patroness, it is the gesture of family, extended across every barrier the ancient world had built. By the second century Christians gave it just before they shared the bread and cup.

All the churches of Christ greet you. Congregations in Corinth and Philippi and Ephesus, many of whose members had never met anyone on this list, send their love to a church Paul has never visited. This exact phrase, “the churches of Christ”, appears nowhere else in the New Testament.

One family out of strangers. The churches are not Paul’s, nor their members’, but Christ’s, who loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). That is why strangers in Corinth can greet strangers in Rome as family, and why the kiss is holy. A slave and a city treasurer, a Jew and a Gentile, an apostle and a woman who mothered him: every Sunday, in every time zone, the churches of Christ greet one another across oceans. That is no human achievement, but the work of the Son who is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

Must Christians greet each other with a kiss today? The command is repeated (1 Corinthians 16:20; 1 Peter 5:14), but what it commands is the warmth, not the form. Where a kiss carries that meaning it may still be used; where it does not, a handshake or an embrace obeys the command. What is not optional is greeting one another as family, and always in a way that is holy: pure, appropriate, and safe for everyone, especially children and the vulnerable.

What if I find greeting people at church hard? Many believers do, from shyness, anxiety or past hurt, and Paul is not commanding you to become the loudest person in the room. Start small. Learn three names and use them. Greet the person sitting nearest you. Look for the newcomer standing alone, who is probably more nervous than you. If conversation is hard, a warm handshake and a simple “it is good to see you” obeys this verse. Ask God to help you, and remember that the people you greet are your family in Christ, not an audience judging you.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — Final Warning and the Doxology of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What the gospel has built must be guarded, and everything ends in the glory of God. Paul warns against those who cause divisions contrary to the doctrine the Romans were taught (vv. 17–18). This does not undo two chapters of bearing with one another over disputed matters: these people serve their own appetites and deceive by flattery. The safeguard is to know the good well, and the God of peace will soon crush Satan under his people’s feet (vv. 19–20). Paul’s companions in Corinth send greetings, Tertius the scribe among them (vv. 21–24). Then the doxology gathers up the letter: the gospel, the mystery now made known to all nations, the obedience of faith that opened the letter (1:5), and glory to the only wise God through Jesus Christ (vv. 25–27).
verseByVerse.theology:
The mystery revealed: one gospel in both Testaments

Romans 16:25–27 returns to 1:1–4: the gospel was promised beforehand through the prophets. The Old Testament is the gospel in promise, the New the gospel fulfilled (on the mystery the Old Testament was carrying all along, see the note on vv. 25–26). Calvin’s principle applies: the two Testaments are one Bible and one gospel of grace, given in different ways but pointing to the same Saviour.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The warning against divisive teachers stands at the end of Paul’s fullest statement of the gospel. Teaching as deep as this, on election, freedom and grace, can be twisted into a weapon, so the warning belongs here. Now: Every generation has its smooth-talking teachers who use the language of theology to build a following. Paul’s instruction still stands: watch them, avoid them, and trust the God of peace (v. 20).

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. — Romans 16:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch out for those who split the church by teaching against the gospel, and turn away from them, for they serve their own appetites, not Christ, and win the unsuspecting with flattery. The warmth of the greetings turns suddenly sharp, because the church the greetings have displayed must be guarded.

Watch out for those who cause divisions. “Watch out” (skopeō) means keep an eye on, mark. Divisions (dichostasiai, standing apart) means splitting the church into parties. Such a teacher is not to be debated endlessly or accommodated in the hope that he will improve, but identified and avoided, not with contempt but with the clear sight of people who know what they have been taught.

Contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught. “Obstacles” (skandala) are things that trip people into sin. The problem is not differences over food (chapter 14), but false teaching that undermines the gospel, “the standard of teaching” to which they had become obedient from the heart (6:17). The test is not whether a teaching is new or old, or popular, but the apostolic teaching Paul has spent fifteen chapters expounding: the church that has this letter has the measuring rod.

Avoid them. “Avoid” (ekklinō) means turn away from: do not give them a platform or follow them (Titus 3:10).

Who were they? Paul does not say. They may have been like the teachers he fought in Galatia and Philippi, who demanded the law of Gentile believers, or the opposite kind, who turned grace into licence (3:8; 6:1); serving their own appetites fits either (Philippians 3:2, 18–19). That he names no one suggests they had not yet gained a hold in Rome: the warning is prevention rather than cure.

Their own appetites. Literally, their own belly, the organ of appetite (Philippians 3:19). The mark is personal as much as doctrinal: whatever is being said at the front, something is being fed at the back, money, a following, or the pleasure of seeing what others have missed.

By smooth talk and flattery. “Smooth talk” (chrēstologia, fine words) and “flattery” (eulogia, nice speech): the method is not argument. The divisive man does not begin by attacking the church; he begins by being remarkably nice to you, telling you that you are more discerning than the others. Flattery is the tool because it recruits: you cannot build a faction out of people you have insulted. “Naive” (akakoi) means unsuspecting, without guile: not fools, but good-hearted people who assume others mean what they say, which is why Paul goes on to ask them to be wise as to what is good (v. 19).

Not our Lord Christ. The contrast is exact. The Lord they claim to serve is the one who did not please himself (15:3), who emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7). Teachers who serve themselves come and go, and their factions crumble; the church built on the apostles’ doctrine still stands after two thousand years, because the Lord Christ is its master and it serves him.

What it does not mean. Not avoiding every Christian you disagree with; the verse is easily abused. Chapters 14 and 15 told these same people whom to welcome despite disagreement (14:1–15:7); this verse tells them whom not to follow. Disputed matters call for patience; false teaching against the gospel calls for watchfulness.

In everyday life. Take the voice that has most shaped your thinking this year, a preacher, a book, a podcast, and ask whether it works by making you feel more discerning than your church. Flattery, from anyone, is one of the surest signs that somebody wants something from you.

How do I tell a false teacher from a Christian who simply disagrees with me? Look for Paul’s three marks together. First, the teaching denies or distorts the apostolic gospel itself: who Christ is, his atoning death and resurrection, justification by faith, the authority of Scripture, or the call to holiness. Second, the man is serving himself: his teaching keeps leading back to his money, his following or his importance. Third, he works by flattery and private recruiting rather than open argument. Someone who differs on a disputed matter and says so plainly is the person chapter 14 told you to welcome; someone quietly assembling a party around himself is the person to walk away from. The difference is not how strongly he disagrees, but what he is building.

Who am I to call anyone a false teacher? It would be arrogance if the standard were our own opinion. But Paul measures teachers by the doctrine you have been taught, the gospel God gave through his apostles. Every serious community draws a line somewhere: a pharmacist who handed over whatever was asked for rather than offend the customer would not be humble but negligent. The truly arrogant thing is to treat the gospel as ours to revise. And the same standard judges the one who uses it. Paul has just forbidden judging or despising a brother over disputed matters (14:10), so whoever enjoys calling others heretics should search his own heart first: the pleasure of being right can become an idol too.

What does avoiding them involve? Do I cut them off? It means refusing them influence: do not sit under their teaching, follow their channels, invite them to speak, or let them recruit you or others. If such a person is in your church, the elders must deal with it, warning him and, if he will not repent, removing him from fellowship (Titus 3:10–11; Matthew 18:15–17); do not run your own private campaign. But avoiding is not hating: do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:15). Pray for him, speak the truth to him when it is right, and keep the door to his return open.

verseByVerse.quote: For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul rejoices in the Romans’ well-known obedience but wants them wise in what is good and untouched by evil, sure that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under their feet. Their faith was famous (1:8); he warns because he loves what he sees and wants it kept.

Wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. Know the good and do it well; have no part in evil and no taste for it (akeraios, innocent, means unmixed, pure). Jesus said to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16). You do not need to taste evil to understand it.

The God of peace will soon crush Satan. The promise echoes God’s word to the serpent in Eden: the offspring of the woman would crush its head (Genesis 3:15), often called the first gospel promise, here in the last chapter of Romans. The verb is violent, to break in pieces, and Paul attaches it to the God of peace (15:33). Peace is not made by leaving the hostility in place; a God of peace who could not crush anything would have no peace to offer. The false teachers, Satan’s agents (2 Corinthians 11:13–15), will share his defeat.

Under your feet. Christ himself crushed the serpent’s head at the cross. Yet Paul does not say under Christ’s feet: he tells a mixed, quarrelling congregation of slaves, patrons and former idolaters that the last act will happen under their shoes, because they are united to the Victor. The God of peace, who made peace by blood, will grind the enemy under the feet of the very people the enemy once held captive.

Soon. This does not set a date (on the word, see below). Some of it may come quickly: every time false teachers are exposed and a church is preserved, Satan tastes defeat in advance. The final crushing comes at Christ’s return, nearer now than when we first believed (13:11). Two thousand years must be faced honestly, but Paul did not miscalculate: the outcome is fixed, and Christ’s return is the next great event in God’s plan, however long the wait, though Scripture names things that come before it (2 Thessalonians 2:3). With the Lord one day is as a thousand years (2 Peter 3:8), and the wait will seem short in the light of eternity (8:18; 2 Corinthians 4:17).

A word for the tired. For the reader tired of waiting, groaning with the whole creation (8:22–23): the groaning is real. But Paul does not write “may God crush”; he writes “will”. The outcome is settled; only the waiting is left.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. A benediction: the letter began with grace (1:7) and returns to it.

In everyday life. Leaning on the Spirit at work in you, choose one way to grow wise in the good, such as a book of the Bible or a mature Christian to learn from, and one thing to be innocent of: an app, a channel or a kind of entertainment you do not need to know so well.

How can I be innocent about evil without being naive? Know the good thoroughly, and do not go looking at evil to understand it. Those trained to spot forged banknotes learn the genuine note so well that a fake stands out at once; the believer who knows Scripture, the gospel and the character of Christ deeply will sense what is false without immersing himself in it. So be careful what you watch, read and scroll through, not out of fear but because you do not need to be expert in sin. And be wise in the good: honest about how temptation and manipulation work, alert to flattery, and willing to ask a mature believer when something feels wrong.

Why has Satan not been crushed yet? He is decisively defeated, but not yet destroyed. At the cross Christ disarmed the powers and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15); Satan is a beaten enemy who still prowls (1 Peter 5:8), but on a chain, unable to stop the gospel going to the nations (Revelation 20:1–3). Every time someone is converted, his house is plundered (Mark 3:27). God delays the final blow in patience, not wishing that any should perish, while the full number of his people is gathered (2 Peter 3:9). When the last of them is in, Christ will return, and the serpent will be thrown into the lake of fire for ever (Revelation 20:10). This commentary reads the binding of Revelation 20 as describing the present age (the amillennial view, which takes the thousand years as the time between Christ’s two comings); many faithful Christians expect a future thousand-year reign, and all share the hope of his final victory.

Uncertain wording. “Soon” translates en tachei, which can mean either soon, before long, or quickly, swiftly when it comes. Jesus uses it of God’s answer to his people’s cries: “he will give justice to them speedily” (Luke 18:8). Either way it promises a certain end, not a date.
verseByVerse.note: The promise echoes God’s word to the serpent in Eden.

parallels.desc: he shall bruise your head

verseByVerse.quote: Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s companions in Corinth add their greetings: Timothy, three Jewish co-workers, and Tertius, the scribe who wrote the letter down.

Timothy, my fellow worker. Timothy was Paul’s closest companion and spiritual son (Acts 16:1–3). Others seek their own interests, Paul says elsewhere, not those of Jesus Christ, but Timothy had proved his worth (Philippians 2:21–22).

Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. Fellow Jews. Lucius may be Lucius of Cyrene (Acts 13:1), Jason the man who hosted Paul in Thessalonica (Acts 17:5–9), and Sosipater the Sopater of Berea who set out with the collection (Acts 20:4). Three Jewish co-workers in a largely Gentile mission: the unity Paul has been describing, standing beside him as he writes. The first list showed the church in Rome; this one shows the church around Paul in Corinth, the same kind of family at both ends of the road Phoebe is about to travel.

I Tertius, who wrote this letter. Paul dictated his letters; Tertius was the scribe who wrote this one down. It is the only moment of its kind in the New Testament: for hours, likely across several sittings, a man has been taking down Romans as Paul spoke it, and at the end he adds a greeting of his own. Paul often signed in his own hand at the end (Galatians 6:11), and using a scribe does not lessen the letter’s authority: the words are Paul’s, inspired by the Spirit.

Three and Four. Tertius means Third, and a verse later Quartus means Fourth: ordinary Roman names taken from numbers, common among slaves and freedmen. God chose a man named Third to set down in ink the gospel of justification by faith, and then let him sign his name in the margin of Scripture. The word of the Lord endures for ever, and some of it is in Tertius’s handwriting.

Greet you in the Lord. A scribe in Corinth and strangers in Rome are joined in the same Christ. For hours his pen has carried the gospel concerning God’s Son (1:3–4), the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ (3:22), the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (8:39). Every line Tertius wrote was leading to Christ, and so is his greeting.

In everyday life. Thank one of the hidden servants who have brought God’s word to you: a translator, the person at the sound desk, the Sunday school helper. And if your own work for Christ is mostly holding the pen for someone else, do it with joy. Tertius never preached Romans, but the church has been reading what he wrote down ever since.

If humans wrote the Bible down, how is it God’s word? Because God was at work in the whole process. Scripture is breathed out by God (2 Timothy 3:16): men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21). God did not bypass their minds or personalities; Paul’s logic, his warmth, his grief for Israel and his list of friends are truly his. But God so superintended what they wrote that the result is exactly what he intended to say, without error: the scribe’s pen, the apostle’s voice and the Spirit’s breath worked together. That is why we can read Romans as Paul’s letter to Rome and, at the same time, as God’s word to us (Westminster 1.2, 1.4; 1689 1.2, 1.4).
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters; Tertius was the scribe who wrote this one down.

verseByVerse.quote: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gaius the host, Erastus the city official and Quartus the brother greet the Romans together: men of very different rank, on the same footing in Christ.

Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church. Probably the Gaius whom Paul baptised in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14), whose hospitality stretched to Paul and, it seems, to the whole church there.

Erastus, the city treasurer. “City treasurer” (oikonomos tēs poleōs): a public official of Corinth. An inscription at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a public square at his own expense in return for his office as aedile. He may be the same man.

The whole argument in one room. Set the three men in this verse side by side and the argument of the letter is standing in one room. The city treasurer, the host of the whole church and the man named after a number send a joint greeting, and the only title Quartus needs is brother. Outside that house Roman society gave such men almost nothing in common. When Paul said God shows no partiality (2:11) and there is no distinction (10:12), he did not mean it as a sentiment; he meant that a room would exist in which it was simply true, and he is writing from one. The footing is Christ: there is neither slave nor free, for you are all one in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3:28). Rank still existed in Corinth, but every man in that room owed everything to the same Saviour and had nothing he did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7). The Saviour took the lowest place so that the high and the low could stand on level ground at the foot of his cross.

How should a wealthy or powerful Christian relate to poorer believers? As Gaius and Erastus did: as a brother, and as a steward. Paul tells Timothy to charge the rich not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on uncertain riches, but on God, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–19). James tells the rich brother to boast in his humiliation, because he too will fade like a flower (James 1:9–11). In practice: open your home, use your influence for the vulnerable, give quietly and generously, and never expect deference in church, where your position counts for nothing and your service for much. And the poorer brother is to honour you without envy, as a fellow servant of the same Lord.
verseByVerse.note: An inscription found at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a street at his own expense, perhaps the same man.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This blessing, found in some manuscripts but not in the ESV text, prays that the grace of Christ rest on every believer in Rome.

Grace with you all. Grace (charis), the free favour of God in Christ, runs through the whole letter: the grace of apostleship (1:5), of justification (3:24), in which we stand (5:2), that abounds all the more where sin increased (5:20), of election (11:5) and of gifts (12:6). It is the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, because it is never handed out apart from him (5:15). With you all: strong and weak, Jew and Gentile, slave and free.

Can I trust that my Bible says what was originally written? Yes, with great confidence. The New Testament is by far the best-attested book of the ancient world: thousands of Greek manuscripts, some from within a few generations of the apostles, besides early translations and quotations. With so many copies, a scribe’s slip can be seen and corrected by comparing them, as here. Modern Bibles are open about the few places where manuscripts differ, a sign of honesty, not weakness, and no doctrine of the faith rests on a disputed reading. God has kept his word pure in all ages by his singular care and providence (Westminster 1.8; 1689 1.8).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, insert verse 24, with this benediction. The earliest and best manuscripts do not have it, so the ESV leaves it out of the text, and it is shown here from the margin. If your Bible skips from verse 23 to verse 25, that is why. It appears to be a copyist’s repetition of the benediction already given in verse 20, and the instinct was sound: grace is how this letter starts (1:7), and grace is how it should stop.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 24: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul gives glory to the God who is able to make believers stand firm through the gospel, the long-hidden mystery now revealed in Christ and made known to every nation, to bring them to the obedience of faith. One long sentence of praise (vv. 25–27) gathers up the great themes of Romans and mirrors its opening (1:1–5).

Him who is able to strengthen you. “Strengthen” (stērizō) means establish, make firm, and it closes a loop. Paul longed to come and strengthen them (1:11), but he could not yet, and when he finally arrived it would be in chains. So the letter ends by handing the task to God.

According to my gospel. The gospel entrusted to Paul (2:16), not a different one. It is not merely information about Christ; it is the power by which God strengthens his people (1:16).

The mystery that was kept secret for long ages. A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God (11:25; Ephesians 3:4–6): here the gospel of Christ, especially that Jews and Gentiles together would be saved through faith in him. Through Abraham, the exodus, the law, the kings and the exile, God was holding back something he fully intended to say; the nations were in his plan before Israel was a nation (Ephesians 1:4).

Now disclosed, through the prophetic writings. Revealed in the coming of Christ, and explained by the prophetic writings, the Old Testament (1:2; 3:21). There is a deliberate paradox here: a mystery kept secret for long ages, yet made known through writings that had existed the whole time. Chapters 9 to 11 show it: Hosea and Isaiah and Moses and the Psalms were saying that the nations would come in, on the page in every synagogue. What was missing was not the words but the event that makes them plain, and once Christ had come, Paul could go back through the same scrolls and show that they had been saying it all along. A mystery in Paul’s sense is not a puzzle nobody could solve. It is something that could not be seen until God did the thing it was about.

The command of the eternal God. The mission to the Gentiles is not Paul’s idea or the church’s strategy (Matthew 28:19), but the decree of the God who has no beginning and no end, carried out in time.

Not the apostle, not you, but him. Every page of the Old Testament was written by someone who did not know how the story would end, carried along by Someone who did. And he is able to strengthen you: not the apostle, who could not reach Rome when he wished; not you, who cannot keep yourself standing; but him, who has never once let one of his own fall out of his hand.

Does “the obedience of faith” make obedience part of what saves us? No. The phrase repeats 1:5, framing the whole letter, and Paul means the obedience that faith is and the obedience faith produces: to believe the gospel is to obey God’s summons, and those who believe go on to obey. The whole letter between 1:5 and this verse has argued that we are justified by faith apart from works (3:28). Obedience is the fruit of faith, never its price.

How does God actually strengthen me? Through the gospel, as this verse says, and the ordinary means he has appointed for it: the gospel preached and heard with faith, Scripture read and pondered, prayer, the Lord’s Supper setting Christ’s death before you, and fellow believers speaking the truth in love. His Spirit works through these, often quietly, so that you may not notice the strengthening until you find yourself still standing in a trial that once would have flattened you. When you feel weak, do not look for something new. Go back to the old gospel, and to the means God uses to apply it.

Textual note. Many later manuscripts put this doxology after 14:23, one early papyrus puts it after 15:33, and a few have it twice or not at all. The oldest and best manuscripts put it here, at the end of the letter; some scholars doubt it was part of Paul’s original, but its words fit Romans closely, echoing 1:1–5. Nothing in the text of Romans is in doubt because of this; the question is only where the closing praise stood.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All glory belongs to the only wise God, and it reaches him through Jesus Christ, for ever. The letter ends not with a summary but with worship.

To the only wise God. Only God is truly wise, and Romans has displayed his wisdom in a plan of salvation no one could have imagined (11:33): the cross, by which God is just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (3:26), and the Gentiles brought in through Israel’s stumbling.

The sentence that breaks. Read verses 25–27 as one sentence and it does not quite resolve. It begins “Now to him who is able to strengthen you”, adds clause after clause, and never completes the thought in the expected way, arriving instead at glory. Paul set out to say something about God, could not get to the end of the subject, and the sentence gives way under the weight and turns into worship. He did the same at the end of chapter 11: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (11:33). The reasoning goes as far as reasoning can, and then the only thing left is to give God glory. That is not the failure of the theology. It is what the theology is for.

Amen. So be it, truly. The letter began with a slave of Christ set apart for a gospel promised beforehand, to bring about the obedience of faith among all the nations (1:1–5). Sixteen chapters later, through wrath and justification and no condemnation and the olive tree and the weak brother and the greetings from Three and Four, it ends on the same three things: the gospel, the nations, and the obedience of faith. The letter has added nothing to its first paragraph; it has unfolded what it held.

Glory through Jesus Christ. Giving God glory adds nothing to him; it gladly confesses that all the credit for salvation is his. Christ crucified is himself the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24–25), and the letter that began with the gospel of God concerning his Son (1:1–3) ends with glory to God through his Son. There is no one else to give the glory to: not the reader, who contributed nothing; not the apostle; not the church, which exists only because of what God has done. One God, who found a way to be just and to justify the ungodly, is gathering a people from every nation into one family through his Son. From him and through him and to him are all things, and the letter’s last word is not an argument. It is Amen.

What does it mean to give God glory through Jesus Christ? All our praise reaches the Father by way of the Son. Our worship, even at its best, is mixed with sin, but Christ is our great high priest, who lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25), and through him we offer up a sacrifice of praise (Hebrews 13:15). So when you pray or sing, you come in his name, trusting him to present your praise to the Father, cleansed and accepted. And God is most glorified in what he has done in Christ: the cross and resurrection are the brightest display of his glory there will ever be.

I have read Romans. What now? Do what Paul does at the end: worship. Then live it. Rest your whole confidence on Christ’s righteousness, not your own (3:21–26). Fight sin as one who is dead to it and alive to God (6:11). Walk by the Spirit, assured that nothing can separate you from God’s love (8:38–39). Present your body as a living sacrifice (12:1). Welcome the brother who differs from you (15:7). Support the spread of the gospel to the nations (15:20–24). And come back to it. Romans is not a book to be finished but a book to be lived in, and the church has found for two thousand years that it never runs dry.

16.text: <sup>1</sup>I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae,<sup>2</sup>that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well.<sup>3</sup>Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus,<sup>4</sup>who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.<sup>5</sup>Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.<sup>6</sup>Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you.<sup>7</sup>Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.<sup>8</sup>Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.<sup>9</sup>Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.<sup>10</sup>Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus.<sup>11</sup>Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.<sup>12</sup>Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord.<sup>13</sup>Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord; also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.<sup>14</sup>Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them.<sup>15</sup>Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.<sup>16</sup>Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.<sup>17</sup>I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them.<sup>18</sup>For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive.<sup>19</sup>For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil.<sup>20</sup>The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.<sup>21</sup>Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen.<sup>22</sup>I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.<sup>23</sup>Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.<sup>25</sup>Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages<sup>26</sup>but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith—<sup>27</sup>to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.

keyVerse.quote: to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
keyVerse.note: The letter ends where all its argument was heading. After the gospel set out, the mystery revealed and the family of names greeted, nothing is left but to give God the glory, and Paul gives it through Jesus Christ, the only way any sinner’s praise reaches the Father. Every name in this chapter, and every reader of the letter, has been brought in for this.

16.reflection:
Paul greets more than two dozen people by name, slaves and patrons, Jews and Gentiles, men and women, and calls many of them beloved (vv. 3–15). What does this list show about the church the gospel creates? Who in your church would you not naturally greet as family?

Several people here are honoured for hidden service: Mary’s hard work, a mother who mothered Paul, Tertius holding the pen (vv. 6, 13, 22). How does it help to know that God notices what no one else sees? Whose hidden service could you thank this week?

Paul warns against those who divide the church by self-serving teaching and flattery (vv. 17–18), yet two chapters earlier he told the Romans to welcome those who differ over disputed matters. How can we tell the difference, and how do we guard our own hearts against flattery?

Romans ends not with a summary but with worship (vv. 25–27). What has this letter shown you about God that moves you to give him glory, and how will you keep coming back to it?
